locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Intro · ¶1
text: California’s driving under the influence (DUI) laws apply to both alcohol and drugs. It is illegal to drive while under the influence of alcohol or any drug that affects your ability to drive safely. As you age, your tolerance to alcohol decreases, which increases the risk of alcohol-related driving problems. The law does not see a difference between illegal drugs and medications you get from a doctor or pharmacy. They can all affect your ability to drive safely and react to what you see and hear.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Intro · ¶2
text: No matter what age you are, it is illegal to drive after:

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Intro · item 1
text: Drinking excessive amounts of alcohol in any form. This includes medications like cough syrup.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Intro · item 2
text: Taking any drug that affects your ability to drive. This includes prescriptions or over-the-counter medications.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Intro · item 3
text: Using any combination of alcohol or drugs that decreases your ability to drive safely.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Intro · ¶3
text: Make sure you read medication labels and know the effects of any drug you use. If a law enforcement officer thinks you are driving while under the influence of drugs or alcohol, they have the right to ask you to take a blood or urine test. If you refuse to take one, DMV will suspend or revoke your driving privilege for one year.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Intro · ¶4
text: Important If you are 13 to 20 years old and convicted of operating a bicycle while under the influence of alcohol or drugs, your driving privilege may be suspended or delayed for one year once you are eligible to drive.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Use or Possession of Alcohol or Cannabis Products in a Vehicle · ¶1
text: The law is very strict about carrying alcohol or cannabis products in your vehicle with you. It is illegal to drink any alcohol, to smoke or eat a cannabis product while you are driving or riding as a passenger in a vehicle. If you are carrying any alcohol or cannabis in your vehicle, the container must be sealed and unopened. If it is open, you must keep the container in the trunk or place where passengers do not sit. It is also illegal to keep an open container of alcohol in your glove box. This law does not apply if you are a passenger in a bus, taxi, camper, or motorhome.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶1
text: When you consume alcohol, traces of it enter your bloodstream. Your BAC measures how much alcohol is present in your bloodstream.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶2
text: It is illegal for you to drive if you have a BAC of:

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 1
text: 0.08% or higher if you are over 21 years old.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 2
text: 0.01% or higher if you are under 21 years old.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 3
text: 0.01% or higher at any age if you are on DUI probation.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 4
text: 0.04% or higher if you drive a vehicle that requires a commercial driver’s license.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · item 5
text: 0.04% or higher if you are driving a passenger for hire.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶3
text: If you drive with an illegal BAC, a law enforcement officer can charge you with DUI. Even if your BAC is below legal limits, that does not mean it is safe for you to drive. Almost everyone feels negative effects of alcohol, even at levels lower than the legal limit. Depending on how badly you are impaired, you may be arrested and convicted of a DUI even without a BAC measurement.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶4
text: The table below shows BAC estimates based on how many drinks are consumed, gender, and body weight. Remember, even one drink can affect your ability to drive safely.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · image
heading: Alt text: “Table displaying Blood Alcohol Concentration estimates based on how many drinks are consumed, gender, and body weight.”
text: Table displaying Blood Alcohol Concentration estimates based on how many drinks are consumed, gender, and body weight.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) Limits · ¶5
text: Note It is illegal to drink alcohol or take drugs when you are operating a boat, jet ski, water skis, aquaplane, or similar vessels. Learn more in the California Harbors and Navigation Code .

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Arrests · ¶1
text: When you drive in California, you consent to a breath, blood, or urine test if a law enforcement officer suspects you of DUI. If you agreed to take a preliminary alcohol screening (PAS) or breath test, you may still be required to take a blood or urine test to detect the presence of drugs. If you refuse, DMV will suspend or revoke your driving privilege. If you are arrested for DUI:

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Arrests · item 1
text: California’s Administrative Per Se law requires DMV to suspend your driving privilege.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Arrests · item 2
text: The law enforcement officer may take your driver’s license and give you a temporary driver’s license for 30 days.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Arrests · item 3
text: You may request a DMV administrative hearing within 10 days from the date of your arrest.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · ¶1
text: If you are convicted of a DUI, DMV will suspend or revoke your driving privilege and you:

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 1
text: Must complete a DUI program.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 2
text: Must file a California Insurance Proof Certificate (SR 22/SR 1P).

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 3
text: Must pay any applicable license reissue or restriction fees.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 4
text: May be required to install an ignition interlock device (IID) on your vehicle.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · ¶2
text: Here are some additional penalties if you are convicted of DUI:

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 5
text: You may be sentenced to up to six months in jail.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 6
text: You may have to pay a fine.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 7
text: Law enforcement may impound your vehicle and you may have to pay a storage fee.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · item 8
text: If you cause serious injury or death while driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol, you may face civil lawsuits.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › DUI Convictions · ¶3
text: All DUI convictions remain on your driver’s record for 10 years. If you get any other DUIs during that time, the court or DMV may give you an additional penalty.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Drivers Under 21 · ¶1
text: If you are under 21 years old, there are additional laws for possessing and consuming alcohol.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Drivers Under 21 › Possessing alcohol: · item 1
text: You may not carry any alcohol beverage inside a vehicle unless an individual who is 21 years old or older is with you. The container must be full, sealed, and unopened. If opened, the alcohol must be kept in the trunk or place where passengers do not sit. Exception : If you are working for someone with an off-site liquor sales license, you may carry alcoholic beverages in closed containers.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Drivers Under 21 › Possessing alcohol: · item 2
text: If you are caught with alcohol in your vehicle, law enforcement can impound your vehicle for up to 30 days. The court may fine you and suspend your driver’s license for one year. If you do not already have a driver’s license, the court may ask DMV to delay giving you your first driver’s license for up to one year.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 1
text: If a law enforcement officer suspects you of consuming alcohol, they can require you to take a hand-held breath test, PAS, or another chemical test.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 2
text: If you are convicted of a DUI with a BAC of 0.01% or higher, DMV may revoke your driving privilege for one year. You must also complete a licensed DUI program.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 3
text: If your PAS shows a BAC of 0.05% or higher, the officer may require you to take a breath or blood test.

locator: Section 9: Alcohol and Drugs › Drivers Under 21 › Consuming alcohol: · item 4
text: If a later test shows you have a BAC of 0.05% or higher, you may be arrested for a DUI and your driving privilege may be suspended.

locator: Section 4: Changing, Replacing, and Renewing Your Driver’s License › Changes to Your License · ¶1
text: If you legally change your name or need an update to your driver’s license, such as your physical description or gender identity, visit dmv.ca.gov/dlservices .

locator: Section 4: Changing, Replacing, and Renewing Your Driver’s License › Change Your Address · ¶1
text: If you move, you must notify DMV of your new address within ten days. Submit a change of address online at dmv.ca.gov/addresschange or by mail. It is your responsibility to ensure DMV has your correct mailing address on record.

locator: Section 4: Changing, Replacing, and Renewing Your Driver’s License › Change Your Address · ¶2
text: You do not automatically get a new driver’s license when you change your address. You may request a replacement for a fee.

locator: Section 4: Changing, Replacing, and Renewing Your Driver’s License › Replace or Renew Your Driver’s License · ¶1
text: It is against the law to drive with an expired driver’s license. To renew or replace a lost, stolen, or damaged driver’s license, visit dmv.ca.gov/dlservices . If ineligible to renew online, visit a DMV office.

locator: Section 4: Changing, Replacing, and Renewing Your Driver’s License › Replace or Renew Your Driver’s License · ¶2
text: Before DMV can issue you a driver’s license, you may need to provide additional proof of your identity. Your driver’s license and identity document may expire on the same date. If so, you will be required to provide a valid identity document. If you are a minor, your parent or guardian must sign the application. Once you receive your replacement card, your old card is no longer valid. If you find the old card, destroy it.

locator: Section 4: Changing, Replacing, and Renewing Your Driver’s License › Extend Your Driver’s License · ¶1
text: If you are out-of-state and cannot renew, you may request a one year extension of your driver’s license. Before your driver’s license expires, submit a request with your name, driver’s license number, birth date, California residence address, and out-of-state address to dl-extensions@dmv.ca.gov .

locator: Section 4: Changing, Replacing, and Renewing Your Driver’s License › Extend Your Driver’s License · ¶2
text: note Limited-term driver’s licenses are not eligible for this extension.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Intro · ¶1
text: Eventually, every driver will need to evaluate and assess their driving skills and abilities. If you are concerned about your driving, ask a trusted driver with a valid driver’s license to sit in the passenger seat and observe your driving. Your observer should note any dangerous driving behaviors and give suggestions for improvement. Listen carefully and apply what you have learned. Consider professional driving lessons or driving classes as an alternative.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · ¶1
text: The Vehicle Code allows DMV to investigate and reexamine every driver’s ability to operate a motor vehicle safely. A physical or mental condition or poor driver’s record can be the basis for a reexamination, not a driver’s age. Drivers with a physical or mental condition can be referred to DMV by a physician, law enforcement, or family member by submitting a completed Request for Driver Reexamination (DS 699) form.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · ¶2
text: Cognitive disorders, such as dementia, seizure disorder, brain tumor, Parkinson’s disease, stroke, or vertigo, present a significant challenge to safe driving. Individuals suffering from these conditions may lose their ability to drive safely.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · ¶3
text: Note When a referral or diagnosis for a driver with a mild cognitive impairment is received by DMV, the Driver Safety team will schedule a reexamination. For more information regarding the reexamination process, visit dmv.ca.gov/reexamination .

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · ¶4
text: DMV may do the following:

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · item 1
text: Request medical information from you or your physician.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · item 2
text: Conduct an in-person or over the telephone reexamination.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · item 3
text: Require you to take a knowledge, vision, or driving test(s).

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · item 4
text: Issue you a limited term driver’s license.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · item 5
text: Immediately suspend or revoke your driving privilege if your physical or mental condition presents an immediate threat to public safety.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Reexamination · item 6
text: Take no action against your driving privilege.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Priority Reexamination · ¶1
text: If you come in contact with law enforcement and receive a Notice of Priority Reexamination of Driver with a check mark in the top box, carefully read the form. You have five working days to contact DMV to initiate the process or your driving privilege will be automatically suspended.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Priority Reexamination · image
heading: Alt text: “example of a Notice of Priority Reexamination of Driver”
text: example of a Notice of Priority Reexamination of Driver

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Driver’s License Restrictions · ¶1
text: DMV places restrictions on a driver’s license to ensure a driver is operating a vehicle within their ability. Restrictions may be imposed by DMV or required by law. Restrictions placed on your driving privilege will be reasonable and necessary for your safety and the safety of others. Restrictions and conditions may include:

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Driver’s License Restrictions · item 1
text: Requiring a driver to place special mechanical devices on their vehicle, such as hand controls.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Driver’s License Restrictions · item 2
text: Limiting when and where a person may drive, such as no night or freeway driving.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Driver’s License Restrictions · item 3
text: Requiring eyeglasses or corrective contact lenses.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Driver’s License Restrictions · item 4
text: Requiring additional devices, such as outside mirrors.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Driver’s License Restrictions · ¶2
text: Note There are no specific restrictions for seniors. All restrictions are based on conditions, not age.

locator: Section 12: Driver Safety › Driver’s License Restrictions · ¶3
text: Any restriction placed on your driver’s license is based on the examiner’s findings and recommendations.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Intro · ¶1
text: You must have your proof of financial responsibility (insurance) when you drive and for a drive test. If you get into a collision, you must show proof to the other drivers involved in the collision.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Insurance Requirements · ¶1
text: Your insurance must cover at least:

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Insurance Requirements · item 1
text: $30,000 for a single death or injury.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Insurance Requirements · item 2
text: $60,000 for death or injury to more than one person.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Insurance Requirements · item 3
text: $15,000 for property damage.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Insurance Requirements · ¶2
text: Parents or guardians take on financial responsibility for drivers younger than 18 years old and pay for damages if the driver is involved in a collision. Drivers who are 18 years old and older take on their own financial responsibility.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Insurance Requirements · ¶3
text: Before you buy insurance, make sure that the agent, broker, or insurance provider is licensed by the California Department of Insurance. For more information, visit insurance.ca.gov/license-status/ .

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Driving Without Insurance · ¶1
text: Your driving privilege will be suspended for up to four years if you are in a collision and do not have proper insurance coverage. It does not matter who was at fault.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Driving Without Insurance · ¶2
text: You can get your driver’s license back during the last three years of the suspension if you provide a California Insurance Proof Certificate (SR 22/SR 1P) and maintain it during the three-year period.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Low-cost Insurance · ¶1
text: If you cannot afford liability insurance, you may be eligible for the California Low Cost Automobile Insurance Program. For more information, visit mylowcostauto.com or call 1-866-602-8861.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions · ¶1
text: Understand factors that lead to collisions so you can try to avoid them.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶1
text: The most common causes of collisions are:

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 1
text: Driver distractions.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 2
text: Unsafe speed.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 3
text: Improper turns.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 4
text: Not following the right-of-way rules.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 5
text: Not following stop signals and signs.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 6
text: Driving on the wrong side of the road.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · item 7
text: A vehicle traveling faster or slower than the flow of traffic.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶2
text: If you see a vehicle’s emergency flashers ahead, slow down. There may be a collision or other road emergency. Pass carefully.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶3
text: Avoid driving near collisions, if possible. If anyone is injured, they will get help faster if other vehicles are not blocking the road.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 1
text: If you are in a collision:

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 2
text: You must stop. Someone could be injured and need your help. Failing to stop or leaving the scene of an accident is called a hit-and-run. The punishment is severe if you are convicted of a hit-and-run.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 3
text: Call 911 right away if anyone is hurt.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 4
text: Move your vehicle out of traffic if no one is hurt. Then call 911.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 5
text: Show your driver’s license, vehicle registration card, insurance information, and current address to the other driver, law enforcement officer, and anyone else involved in the collision.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 6
text: You must make a report to law enforcement within 24 hours of the collision if anyone is injured or killed. Your insurance agent, broker, or legal representative can also file the report.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 7
text: Try to find the owner if your vehicle hits or rolls into a parked car or other property. If you cannot find the owner, leave a note with your name, phone number, and address. Securely attach the note to the vehicle or property. Report the collision to law enforcement.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › What to Do if You Are in a Collision · item 8
text: If you kill or injure an animal, call the nearest humane society or law enforcement. Do not try to move an injured animal.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Reporting a Collision · ¶1
text: If you are in a collision, you must report it to DMV within 10 days if:

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Reporting a Collision · item 1
text: The collision caused more than $1,000 in damage to property.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Reporting a Collision · item 2
text: Anyone was injured or killed. This applies even if the injuries were minor.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Reporting a Collision · ¶2
text: Each driver must file a Report of Traffic Accident Occurring in California (SR 1) with DMV at dmv.ca.gov/accidentreport . You (or your representative) must file a report whether or not you caused the collision. This applies even if the collision happened on private property.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Reporting a Collision · ¶3
text: Your driving privilege will be suspended if you fail to file a report. Law enforcement will not make a report for you.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions on Your Driver’s Record · ¶1
text: If you are involved in a collision resulting in $1,000 in damage, or where anyone is injured or dies, it is your responsibility to report the collision to DMV. DMV will add it to your driver’s record. It does not matter who caused the collision.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Intro · ¶1
text: If you do not have a driver’s license from California or another state, you must apply for an instruction permit before taking the behind-the-wheel drive test to get your driver’s license.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › What You Need · ¶1
text: To apply for an instruction permit or driver’s license, you must provide:

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › What You Need · item 1
text: Proof of identity: Proving who you are.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › What You Need · item 2
text: Two proofs of residency: Proving you live in California. Exceptions may apply.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › What You Need · item 3
text: Legal full name document: Proving your current name if the name on your identity document and application do not match.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › What You Need · item 4
text: Social security number: Exceptions may apply.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › What You Need · ¶2
text: For REAL ID requirements, current acceptable documents, and eligibility, visit dmv.ca.gov/realid .

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Register To Vote · ¶1
text: For information on registering to vote, visit California Secretary of State at sos.ca.gov .

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit · ¶1
text: To apply for a Class C instruction permit:

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit · item 1
text: Complete a Driver’s License & ID Card Application.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit · item 2
text: Provide your documents.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit · item 3
text: Pay a non-refundable application fee.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit · item 4
text: Pass your knowledge test(s).

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit · item 5
text: Pass a vision test.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit · ¶2
text: For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/instructionpermit for a complete list of application steps and requirements.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 1
text: Be at least 15½ years old.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 2
text: Complete a driver education program.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 3
text: Have a parent or guardian sign to approve the application and accept financial responsibility (see Section 10). If your parents or guardians share joint custody of you, both must sign.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For An Instruction Permit › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 4
text: Wait to use your instruction permit until you start behind-the-wheel driver training with an instructor who will validate the permit.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Driving Schools · ¶1
text: Driver education and driver training are offered at DMV-licensed driving schools and some high schools. Instructors must carry an instructor’s ID card. Ask to see it.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Driving Schools · ¶2
text: See the Driver Training Schools page at dmv.ca.gov/driver-ed for more information about selecting a driving school.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For A Driver’s License › To get your driver’s license after you have your instruction permit, you need to: · item 1
text: Practice driving with a California-licensed driver who is at least 18 years old (25 for minors). This person must sit close enough to take control of the vehicle if needed.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For A Driver’s License › To get your driver’s license after you have your instruction permit, you need to: · item 2
text: Pass a behind-the-wheel drive test.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For A Driver’s License › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 1
text: Be at least 16 years old.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For A Driver’s License › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 2
text: Have an instruction permit from California or another state for at least 6 months (or turn 18 years old) before scheduling your behind-the-wheel drive test.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For A Driver’s License › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 3
text: Prove that you completed both driver education and driver training.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For A Driver’s License › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · item 4
text: Practice driving for at least 50 hours with a California-licensed driver who is at least 25 years old. Ten hours must be at night.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Applying For A Driver’s License › If you are under 18 years old, you will also need to: · ¶1
text: See the Driver’s Licenses page at dmv.ca.gov/teendriver for the complete list of application steps, requirements, the Parent Teen Driving Contract, and Driving Performance Evaluation (DPE) Score Sheet.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · ¶1
text: When you are under 18 years old, your driver’s license will have the word provisional. As a provisional driver, you cannot drive:

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · item 1
text: Between 11 p.m. and 5 a.m. during the first 12 months you have your license.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · item 2
text: With passengers under 20 years old, unless your parent or guardian or other California-licensed driver (at least 25 years old) rides with you.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · item 3
text: For pay or operate vehicles that require a commercial Class A, B, or C license.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · ¶2
text: There are exceptions to these restrictions if you:

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · item 4
text: Have a medical need and cannot reasonably find another way to travel. You must carry a note signed by your physician. The note must have your medical condition and date you are expected to recover.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · item 5
text: Drive for schooling or a school activity. You must carry a note signed by your school principal, dean, or designee.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · item 6
text: Must drive for work reasons. You must carry a note signed by your employer. The note must confirm your employment.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · item 7
text: Must drive an immediate family member. You must carry a note signed by your parent or legal guardian. The note must state the reason you need to drive, the family member, and date when the need will end.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · ¶3
text: Note A parent or guardian may cancel their teen’s license by completing a Request for Cancellation or Surrender of a Driver License or ID Card form.

locator: Section 2: Getting an Instruction Permit and Driver’s License › Minor’s Restrictions and Exceptions · ¶4
Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 1
text: Behind-the-wheel drive test | A drive test where you have control of the vehicle and are accompanied by a DMV examiner who is evaluating your driving skills.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 2
text: Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) | Your BAC is the amount of alcohol in your blood. For example, if your BAC is 0.10%, that means you have 0.10 grams of alcohol in 100 milliliters of blood.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 3
text: Driving performance evaluation (DPE) | DPE is the portion of the behind-the-wheel drive test when you drive your car with a DMV examiner who evaluates your driving skills.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 4
text: Pedestrian | A pedestrian is a person walking and can also be a person with a disability using a tricycle, quadricycle, or wheelchair for transportation.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 5
text: Right-of-way | Helps determine who is allowed to go first in situations where vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists meet on the road.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 6
text: Three-second rule | A driving rule that helps you estimate how closely you should follow other vehicles. When the vehicle in front of you passes a certain point, such as a sign, count three seconds. If you pass the same point before you finish counting, you are following too closely.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 7
text: Traffic citation | Also known as a ticket, a traffic citation is an official summons issued by law enforcement for violating a traffic law.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 8
text: Vulnerable road users (VRU) | VRUs are non-motorized road users, such as cyclists, pedestrians, and persons with disabilities or reduced mobility and orientation using a wheelchair, tricycle, or quadricycle.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 9
text: Yield | Yield means to wait for, slow down, and be ready to stop (if necessary) to allow other vehicles or pedestrians who have right-of-way to proceed.

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶1
text: Dear fellow Californian,

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶2
text: All who use our streets, roads and highways must follow and understand the rules of the road. Whether driving a car, motorcycle, commercial vehicle or riding a bicycle, it is critical we adhere to the rules to share the road safely and responsibly.

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶3
text: The California Driver’s Handbook is available in nine languages and offers valuable information for Californians who are getting their driver’s license for the first time or seasoned drivers who wish to update their knowledge of traffic rules.

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶4
text: A driver’s license offers the opportunity to travel to essential services, a favorite vacation spot, education, loved ones and more—and to do so well into one’s golden years. It also enables truck drivers to transport goods and services to support our economy.

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶5
text: The driver’s license application can be started from the comfort of home by visiting the DMV website at dmv.ca.gov . Due to the department’s expanding online services, most DMV transactions can be completed on this site. Some of these transactions include driver’s license renewal, vehicle registration and others. The DMV has been modernizing interactions with its customers, making Californians’ digital experience easier, faster and more convenient. Try online first, as it can be a timesaver.

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶6
text: Remember that driving or riding is a privilege, and above all, safety must be the priority. Always buckle up, follow traffic laws, pay attention to other drivers, bicyclists and pedestrians, and put down that cell phone when behind the wheel or handlebars. Do not operate a vehicle, motorcycle or bicycle while distracted or impaired—it could mean the difference between life and death.

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶7
text: Wishing you safe journeys,

locator: California Driver’s Handbook › Secretary’s Message · ¶8
text: Sincerely,
