locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Intro · ¶1
text: Your health may affect your driving.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Intro · ¶2
text: Vision – You must be able to notice hazards in different types of lighting, judge distances, adjust to traffic speed, and read road signs.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Intro · ¶3
text: Hearing – You must be able to hear horns, sirens, motorcycles, or screeching tires that may alert you of hazards. It is illegal to wear a headset or earplugs in both ears while driving.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Intro · ¶4
text: Fatigue and Drowsiness – Can affect your vision and increase reaction time to hazards.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Intro · ¶5
text: Physical and Mental – You must be alert to quickly decide the correct course of action in any type of traffic situation, including unexpected ones.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Intro · ¶6
text: Medications – Prescription and over-the-counter medications can make you an unsafe driver. Some medicines can make you sleepy. It is your responsibility to know the effects of the medications you take.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Intro · ¶7
text: Health – Physicians are required to report patients, who are at least 14 years old, to DMV for medical conditions that may affect your ability to drive safely, such as lapse of consciousness.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle · ¶1
text: To control your vehicle, it is critical to keep both hands on the wheel whenever possible.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-to-Hand Steering (Push/Pull) · ¶1
text: To use this steering wheel method:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-to-Hand Steering (Push/Pull) · item 1
text: Start with your hands at 9 and 3 o’clock or 8 and 4 o’clock.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-to-Hand Steering (Push/Pull) · item 2
text: Do not cross your hands over the middle of the steering wheel.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-to-Hand Steering (Push/Pull) · item 3
text: Keep your hands in these positions, even when making turns.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · ¶1
text: Use this steering wheel method when you turn at low speeds, park, or need to recover from a skid. To use this method:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 1
text: Start with your hands at 8 and 4 o’clock.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 2
text: Reach across the steering wheel to grasp the opposite side.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 3
text: Let go of the steering wheel with your other hand.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › Hand-Over-Hand Steering · item 4
text: Reach across the arm still holding the wheel, grip the wheel, and pull up.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › One-Hand Steering · ¶1
text: There are only two situations that may require steering with one hand:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › One-Hand Steering · item 1
text: When you are turning while backing up to see where you are going behind you. Place your hand at the 12 o’clock position on the steering wheel.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Controlling the Vehicle › One-Hand Steering · item 2
text: When you are operating vehicle controls that require you to remove a hand from the steering wheel.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights · ¶1
text: Your signals, horn, and headlights are important for communicating with other drivers, pedestrians, and bicyclists.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶1
text: Always signal when you turn, change lanes, slow down, or stop.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶2
text: You can signal using your vehicle’s signal lights or using hand-and-arm positions. If your signal lights are not functioning, or bright sunlight makes your signal lights hard to see, use the hand-and-arm signals shown in the image below.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · image
Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · image
Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · image
Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶3
text: Bicyclists may signal a turn with their arm held straight out, pointing in the direction they plan to turn.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶4
text: You should signal:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 1
text: At least 100 feet before you turn.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 2
text: Before every lane change.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 3
text: At least five seconds before you change lanes on a freeway.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 4
text: Before pulling next to the curb or away from the curb.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 5
text: Even when you do not see other vehicles around you.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · item 6
text: When you are almost through the intersection if you plan to turn shortly after crossing the intersection.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Signaling · ¶5
text: Remember to turn off your signal when you no longer need it.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Horn · ¶1
text: Use your vehicle’s horn to let other drivers know you are there or warn others of a hazard. Use your horn to:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Horn · item 1
text: Avoid collisions.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Horn · item 2
text: Alert oncoming traffic on narrow mountain roads where you cannot see at least 200 feet ahead.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · ¶1
text: Your vehicle’s headlights help you see what is in front of you. They also make it easier for other drivers to see your vehicle. Dim your high-beam headlights to low beams within 500 feet of a vehicle coming toward you or within 300 feet of a vehicle you are following. It is illegal to drive using only parking lights. Use your headlights:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 1
text: When it is too dark to see from 1,000 feet away.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 2
text: Beginning 30 minutes after sunset.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 3
text: Until 30 minutes before sunrise.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 4
text: In adverse weather. If you need to use your windshield wipers due to fog, rain, or snow, you must turn on your low-beam headlights.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 5
text: When conditions (such as clouds, dust, smoke, or fog) prevent you from seeing other vehicles.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 6
text: On mountain roads and tunnels (even on sunny days).

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 7
text: When a road sign states that headlights must be on.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Headlights · item 8
text: To help other drivers see your vehicle, especially when the sun is low on the horizon.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · ¶1
text: If you can see a collision or hazard ahead, warn drivers behind you using these methods:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 1
text: Turn on your emergency flashers.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 2
text: Lightly tap your brake pedal three or four times.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 3
text: Use a hand signal when slowing and stopping.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · ¶2
text: If you need to stop because of vehicle trouble:

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 4
text: Turn on your emergency flashers. If your vehicle does not have emergency flashers, use your turn signals.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 5
text: If possible, pull off the road away from all traffic.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 6
text: If you cannot get completely off the road, stop where people can see you and your vehicle from behind.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 7
text: Do not stop just over a hill or just around a curve. Other drivers may not see your vehicle in time to avoid a collision.

locator: Section 5: An Introduction to Driving › Signals, Horns, And Headlights › Using Your Emergency Flashers · item 8
text: Call for emergency roadside assistance and stay in your vehicle until help arrives.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road · ¶1
text: Drivers need to share the road with other vehicles, pedestrians, bicyclists, road workers, and large vehicles.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Blind Spots (the No Zone) · ¶1
text: Large vehicle and truck drivers have a better view in front of them and bigger mirrors. But they also have large blind spots, also called No Zones. In these areas, your vehicle can disappear from a large vehicle or truck driver’s view. If you cannot see the truck’s side mirrors, the truck driver cannot see you.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Blind Spots (the No Zone) · image
Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Blind Spots (the No Zone) · ¶2
text: The shaded areas in this image are the truck driver’s blind spots.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Braking · ¶1
text: Large vehicles and commercial trucks take longer to stop than passenger vehicles traveling at the same speed. When traveling, they create extra space in front of their vehicle to use if they need to stop suddenly. The average passenger vehicle traveling at 55 mph can stop within 300 feet. A large vehicle traveling at the same speed can take up to 400 feet to stop. The heavier the vehicle and the faster it is moving, the longer it takes to safely stop, so a loaded truck will take longer to stop than an empty truck. Do not move in front of a large vehicle and suddenly slow down or stop. The large vehicle will not be able to stop fast enough to avoid crashing into you.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Turning · ¶1
text: When a vehicle turns, the rear wheels follow a shorter path than the front wheels. The longer the vehicle, the greater the difference in the length of the turning path. This is why large vehicles and truck drivers must often swing wide to complete a turn. When you follow a large vehicle, look at its turn signals before you start to pass. It may appear to be turning one direction but instead is swinging wide in the opposite direction in order to turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · ¶1
text: Large vehicles and trucks are not as easy to maneuver as passenger vehicles. On a divided highway with four or more traffic lanes in one direction, they may be driven in the two lanes farthest to the right. When driving near large vehicles and trucks, do not:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 1
text: Change lanes directly in front of them to reach an exit or turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 2
text: Drive next to them longer than you need to. Always pass a large vehicle on the left side. After you pass the large vehicle or truck, move ahead of it. Driving alongside a large vehicle makes it hard for the driver to avoid dangers in the road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 3
text: Follow too closely. Tailgating decreases a vehicle’s safety distance.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 4
text: Underestimate their size and speed as they often appear to be traveling slower.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶1
text: Safety zones are spaces set aside for pedestrians waiting for buses, streetcars, and trolleys. Safety zones are marked by raised buttons or markers on a road. Do not drive through a safety zone under any condition.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶2
text: When a bus, streetcar, or trolley is stopped at a safety zone or traffic light, you may pass at no more than 10 mph.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · image
heading: Alt text: “Trolley next to demarked safe zone.”
text: Trolley next to demarked safe zone.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶3
text: Safe Zones are marked by dotted white lines.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶4
text: Do not overtake and pass a light rail vehicle or streetcar on the left side, whether it is moving or standing, unless:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 1
text: When the tracks are so close to the right side that the passenger vehicle cannot pass on the right.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 2
text: You are on a one-way street.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 3
text: A traffic officer directs you to pass on the left.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · ¶1
text: On public roads, light rail vehicles have the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicles. To safely share the road with light rail vehicles:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 1
text: Be aware of where they operate. Buildings, trees, and other items can cause blind spots for the operator.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 2
text: Never turn in front of an approaching light rail vehicle.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 3
text: Maintain a safe distance.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · item 4
text: Check for approaching light rail vehicles before you turn across the tracks. Complete your turn only when the traffic light indicates you may proceed. Be aware they can interrupt traffic lights.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · image
heading: Alt text: “Light rail travelling down street. One car drives parallel to the train, while another car turns directly into the train's path.”
text: Light rail travelling down street. One car drives parallel to the train, while another car turns directly into the train's path.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Light Rail Vehicles · ¶2
text: Do not turn in front of light rail vehicles.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · ¶1
text: Motorcyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicle drivers. To safely share the road with motorcyclists:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 1
text: Check for motorcycles and use your mirrors when you change lanes or enter a road. Motorcycles are smaller in size and harder to see so they easily disappear in vehicle blind spots.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 2
text: Allow a safe three-second following distance. This space will help you avoid hitting a motorcyclist if they brake suddenly or fall.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 3
text: Whenever possible, give a motorcycle the full lane. It is legal to share lanes with motorcycles, this is known as lane splitting.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 4
text: Never try to pass a motorcycle in the same lane as you.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 5
text: Check for motorcyclists before you open your door next to traffic.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 6
text: When possible, move to one side of your lane to give motorcyclists more room to pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · ¶2
text: Road conditions can cause motorcyclists to suddenly change speed or direction.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶1
text: Give the right-of-way to any law enforcement vehicle, fire engine, ambulance, or other emergency vehicle using a siren and red lights. Failure to pull over may result in a ticket. Drive to the right edge of the road and stop until the emergency vehicle(s) have passed.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · image
heading: Alt text: “Car pulling over to let fire truck pass.”
text: Car pulling over to let fire truck pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶2
text: Yield to emergency vehicles.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶3
text: When approaching a stationary emergency vehicle with flashing emergency signal lights (hazard lights), move over and slow down.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶4
text: If you are in an intersection when you see an emergency vehicle, continue through the intersection. Drive to the right as soon as it is safe and stop.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶5
text: Obey any direction, order, or signal given by a law enforcement officer, or firefighter. Follow their orders even if they conflict with existing signs, signals, or laws.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶6
text: It is against the law to follow within 300 feet of any fire engine, law enforcement vehicle, ambulance, or other emergency vehicle when their siren or flashing lights are on.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶7
text: You can be arrested if you drive to the scene of a fire, collision, or other disaster. When you do this, you are getting in the way of firefighters, ambulance crews, or other rescue and emergency personnel.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · ¶1
text: They can take longer to get up to speed when entering traffic. Large trucks, bicycles, and some cars lose speed on long or steep hills. Some slow-moving vehicles have an orange and red triangle on their back, such as road maintenance vehicles, which usually travel at 25 mph or less.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · image
heading: Alt text: “Bulldozer with orange-red "slow vehicle" triangle.”
text: Bulldozer with orange-red "slow vehicle" triangle.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · ¶2
text: An example of a slow-moving vehicle.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · ¶3
text: Other types of slow-moving motorized vehicles that may operate on public roads include:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · item 1
text: Scooters

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · item 2
text: Neighborhood electric vehicles

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · item 3
text: Golf carts

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Slow-moving Vehicles · ¶4
text: Adjust your speed to share the road with these vehicles.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV) · ¶1
text: Watch for slow-moving vehicles when you see these signs or markings:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV) · item 1
text: NEV USE ONLY

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV) · item 2
text: NEV ROUTE

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Neighborhood Electric Vehicles (NEV) and Low-speed Vehicles (LSV) · ¶2
text: NEVs and LSVs reach a maximum speed of 25 mph. They are restricted from roads where the speed limit is greater than 35 mph.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Animal-drawn Vehicles · ¶1
text: Horse-drawn vehicles and people riding horses or other animals are allowed to share the road with motor vehicles. It is against the law to intentionally scare horses or livestock.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Animals · ¶1
text: If you see a sign with a picture of an animal, watch for animals on or near the road. If you see animals or livestock near the road, slow down or stop and proceed when it is safe. Be sure to follow directions from the person in charge of the animals.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles · ¶1
text: Bicyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other drivers.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles · ¶2
text: Bicyclists may:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 1
text: Legally ride on certain sections of freeways where there is no alternate route and bicycling is not forbidden by law.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 2
text: Move left to avoid hazards. These may include parked or moving vehicles, bicycles, animals, or trash.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 3
text: Choose to ride near the left curb or edge of a one-way street.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles · item 4
text: Choose to use crosswalks by stopping and crossing as a pedestrian.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · ¶1
text: As a bicyclist, you must:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 1
text: Obey all traffic signs, signal lights, and basic right-of-way rules.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 2
text: Ride in the same direction as traffic.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 3
text: Always look over your shoulder to make sure the lane is clear before turning or changing lanes.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 4
text: Yield to pedestrians.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 5
text: Wear a helmet (if under 18 years old).

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 6
text: Stay visible (for example, never weave between parked vehicles).

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 7
text: Ride as near to the right curb or edge of the roadway as possible.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 8
text: Not ride on the sidewalk (unless allowed by the city).

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 9
text: Make left and right turns in the same way drivers do, using hand signals and turn lanes.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 10
text: Use a bike lane, whenever possible, or use a through traffic lane.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · item 11
text: Have fully functional brakes.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · image
heading: Alt text: “Intersection showing left and right turn options for a bicyclist. The bicyclist uses the left lane to turn left, and the right shoulder to turn right.”
text: Intersection showing left and right turn options for a bicyclist. The bicyclist uses the left lane to turn left, and the right shoulder to turn right.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · ¶2
text: Examples of turns for bicyclist.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · image
heading: Alt text: “Intersection showing options for bicyclist to turn left or go straight. The bicyclist uses the left lane to turn left. To go straight, the cyclist used the inside line of the right lane to enter the intersection, then shifts to the bike lane as they exit the intersection.”
text: Intersection showing options for bicyclist to turn left or go straight. The bicyclist uses the left lane to turn left. To go straight, the cyclist used the inside line of the right lane to enter the intersection, then shifts to the bike lane as they exit the intersection.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicyclist Responsibilities · ¶3
text: Intersection with special lanes for bicyclists.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · ¶1
text: When it is dark out, bicyclists should avoid wearing dark clothing. Your bicycle must have the following equipment:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 1
text: A front lamp with a white light visible from 300 feet.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 2
text: A built-in rear red reflector, solid red light, or flashing red light. This must be visible from 500 feet.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 3
text: A white or yellow reflector on each pedal, the bicyclist’s shoes, or their ankles. These must be visible from 200 feet.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling at Night · item 4
text: A white or yellow reflector on the front wheel, a white or red reflector on the rear wheel, or reflectorized tires.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · ¶1
text: Bicyclists traveling slower than the flow of traffic must ride as close as possible to the right curb or edge of the road, unless :

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 1
text: Passing a vehicle or another bicycle in the same direction.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 2
text: Preparing to make a left turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 3
text: Avoiding a hazard or road condition.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 4
text: A lane is too narrow for a bicycle and a vehicle to safely travel side-by-side in the lane.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 5
text: Approaching a right turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 6
text: On a one-way road with two or more lanes. In this case, a bicyclist may ride near the left curb or edge of the road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · ¶2
text: Drivers should follow at a safe distance. When it is safe, the bicyclist should move to a position that allows vehicles to pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶1
text: To safely pass a bicyclist that is in the travel lane, you may need to change to another lane. In this case, pass safely, then return to your original lane. Leave space between your vehicle and the bicyclist.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · image
heading: Alt text: “Car passing a cyclist. The car leaves enough space between itself and the bicyclist as it passes.”
text: Car passing a cyclist. The car leaves enough space between itself and the bicyclist as it passes.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶2
text: Right

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · image
heading: Alt text: “Car attempting to pass a cyclist without leaving any room. The car hits the cyclist.”
text: Car attempting to pass a cyclist without leaving any room. The car hits the cyclist.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶3
text: Wrong

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶4
text: When you cannot change lanes to pass a bicyclist, allow at least three feet between your vehicle and the bicyclist. If you cannot give three feet of space, do not pass the cyclist until three feet of clearance can be given. This will help you avoid putting the bicyclist in danger. Remember to:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 1
text: Give bicyclists enough space so they are not forced into parked vehicles or open vehicle doors.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 2
text: Only merge toward the curb or into the bike lane when it is safe.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 3
text: Merge safely behind a bicyclist when preparing to make a turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 4
text: Enter a bike lane no more than 200 feet before starting a turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 5
text: Check for bicyclists when changing lanes or entering traffic. They may be hidden in a vehicle’s blind spots.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 6
text: Be careful when approaching or passing a bicyclist on a two-lane road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · ¶1
text: You will see warning signs and message boards when there are workers, slow-moving equipment, and closed lanes ahead.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · ¶2
text: Go through the work zone carefully by:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 1
text: Slowing down.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 2
text: Allowing extra space between vehicles.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 3
text: Expecting sudden slowing or stopping.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 4
text: Watching for drivers changing lanes.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · item 5
text: Avoiding distractions.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones · ¶3
text: Cones, drums, or other barriers will guide you through the work zone. Prepare to slow down or stop for highway equipment. Merge as soon as it is safe without crossing the cones or drums. Watch for bicycles if lanes are narrow or the shoulder is closed. Obey special signs or instructions from workers such as flaggers.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Fines and Double Fine Zones · ¶1
text: Fines for traffic violations in a work zone can be $1,000 or more. Anyone convicted of assaulting a highway worker faces fines of up to $2,000 and imprisonment for up to one year.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Fines and Double Fine Zones · ¶2
text: Certain roads are chosen as Safety Enhanced-Double Fine Zones. This is due to increased collision-related injuries and fatalities. Fines are doubled in these zones.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Fines and Double Fine Zones · ¶3
text: Fines are also doubled in highway construction or maintenance zones when workers are present.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · ¶1
text: Drivers must move over and slow down for emergency and road work vehicles. These include:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · item 1
text: Stationary emergency vehicles or tow trucks displaying flashing amber warning lights.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · item 2
text: Stopped road work vehicles displaying emergency flashing or amber warning lights.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Vehicles with Hazardous Loads · ¶1
text: A diamond-shaped sign on a truck means that the truck’s load may be dangerous (gas, explosives, etc.). Vehicles with these signs must stop before crossing railroad tracks.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Vehicles with Hazardous Loads · image
heading: Alt text: “Hazard symbols for "Flammable," "Radioactive," "Explosives," and "Poison."”
text: Hazard symbols for "Flammable," "Radioactive," "Explosives," and "Poison."

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Vehicles with Hazardous Loads · ¶2
text: Examples of hazardous load placards.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Heavy Traffic or Bad Weather · ¶1
text: You must drive slower when there is heavy traffic or bad weather. At the same time, you should not block normal and reasonable traffic flow by driving too slowly. If you drive faster or slower than the speed limit, you may be cited. When another driver is close behind you and wishes to drive faster, move to the right. If you choose to drive slower than other traffic, drive in the right lane. Refer to Choosing a Lane in Section 6 for more information.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Towing · ¶1
text: You must drive in the far-right lane or a lane marked for slower vehicles when you:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Towing · item 1
text: Tow a vehicle or trailer.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Towing · item 2
text: Drive a truck with three or more axles.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Towing · ¶2
text: If no lanes are marked and there are four or more lanes in your direction, you may only drive in the two lanes closest to the right edge of the road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · image
heading: Alt text: “School bus with red lights flashing and a crossing guard next to it. Students are near the bus. Cars are stopped around the bus.”
text: School bus with red lights flashing and a crossing guard next to it. Students are near the bus. Cars are stopped around the bus.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · ¶1
text: All vehicles must stop for school buses.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · ¶2
text: The speed limit is 25 mph within 500 feet of a school while children are outside or crossing the street. Some school zones may have speed limits as low as 15 mph. When near schools, look for:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 1
text: Bicyclists and pedestrians.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 2
text: School safety patrols or crossing guards. Be sure to obey their directions at all times.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 3
text: Stopped school buses and children crossing the street.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 4
text: Some school buses flash yellow lights when preparing to stop to let children off the bus. The yellow flashing lights warn you to slow down and prepare to stop.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 5
text: When the bus flashes red lights (located at the top, front, and back of the bus), you must stop from either direction until the children are safely across the street and the lights stop flashing. Remain stopped while the red lights are flashing. If you fail to stop, you may be fined up to $1,000 and your driving privilege could be suspended for one year.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 6
text: If the school bus is on the other side of a divided or multilane highway (two or more lanes in each direction), you do not need to stop.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Blind Intersections · ¶1
text: An intersection is considered blind if it has no stop signs at any corner.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Blind Intersections · ¶2
text: If your view is blocked, move slowly forward until you can see. The speed limit for a blind intersection is 15 mph.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Alleys · ¶1
text: An alley is any road no wider than 25 feet that is used to access the rear or side entrances of buildings or properties. You may drive on or cross a sidewalk to enter or exit a driveway or alley. The speed limit in an alley is 15 mph.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · ¶1
text: The speed limit is 15 mph within 100 feet of a railroad crossing and you cannot see the tracks for 400 feet in both directions. You may drive faster than 15 mph if the crossing is controlled by gates, a warning signal, or a flagman. At railroad or train crossings:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 1
text: Flashing red warning lights indicate you must stop and wait. Do not proceed over the railroad tracks until the red lights stop flashing, even if the gate rises.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 2
text: When the crossing devices or a person warns you a train is coming, stop at least 15 feet from the nearest track.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 3
text: Do not go under lowering gates or around lowered gates. If the gates are lowered and you do not see a train approaching, call the posted railroad emergency toll-free number or 911.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 4
text: Stop, look, and listen. If you see a train coming or hear a horn or bell, do not cross. Many crossings have multiple tracks. Look in both directions and only cross when it is safe.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 5
text: Expect a train on any track, at any time, traveling in either direction.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 6
text: Never stop on the railroad tracks. Wait and do not begin proceeding if you do not have enough room to completely cross the tracks. If you are on the tracks, you risk injury or death.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Near Railroad or Light Rail Tracks · item 7
text: Watch for vehicles that must stop before they cross train tracks. These vehicles include buses, school buses, and vehicles marked with a hazardous materials placard.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Business or Residential Districts · ¶1
text: The speed limit is 25 mph, unless otherwise posted.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · ¶1
text: You must:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 1
text: Not smoke when a minor is in the vehicle. You can be fined.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 2
text: Not dump or abandon animals on a highway. This crime is punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, six months in jail, or both.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 3
text: Not drive a vehicle so overloaded that you cannot control it, see ahead, or see to the sides of your vehicle.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 4
text: Not drive a vehicle with an unsecured load that is a safety hazard.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 5
text: Not carry anything in or on a passenger vehicle which extends beyond the fenders on the left side or more than 6-inches beyond the fenders on the right side.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 6
text: Cargo that extends more than 4 feet from the back-rear bumper of the vehicle must display a 12-inch red or fluorescent orange square flag.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 7
text: At night, this cargo must be marked with two red lights.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 8
text: Not allow a person to ride in the back of a pickup or other truck unless the vehicle has secure seats and seat (safety) belts.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 9
text: Not transport animals in the back of a pickup or other truck unless the animal is properly secured. This prevents the animal from falling, jumping, or being thrown from the vehicle.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 10
text: Not drive a vehicle equipped with a video monitor visible to the driver, unless it only displays vehicle information, navigation system, media player, or radio.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 11
text: Not throw a cigarette, cigar, or other flaming or glowing substance from your vehicle.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 12
text: Not put signs or other objects on the front windshield or side rear windows that block your view. Do not hang objects on the mirror. Objects may only be affixed in these locations:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 13
text: A 7-inch square on the lower corner of the passenger’s side windshield or the lower corner of the rear window.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 14
text: A 5-inch square on the lower corner of the driver’s side window.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 15
text: A 5-inch square located in the center uppermost portion of your windshield for an electronic toll payment device.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 16
text: On the side windows behind the driver.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 17
text: Not interfere with a funeral procession. A funeral procession is led by a traffic officer and has the right-of-way. All vehicles taking part in the procession have windshield markers to identify them and have their headlights on. You can be ticketed if you interrupt a funeral procession.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 18
text: Not operate a vehicle with an illegible license plate.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information · item 19
text: Not alter a license plate in any way.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶1
text: It is a misdemeanor to use a motor vehicle to flee or attempt to evade law enforcement performing their duties. This is punishable by imprisonment in a county jail for one year or less.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶2
text: A person convicted of causing serious bodily injury during a law enforcement pursuit is subject to imprisonment in a state prison for up to seven years, or a county jail for one year or less.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶3
text: A person convicted of manslaughter resulting from evading law enforcement during a pursuit is subject to imprisonment in a state prison for a minimum of 4 to 10 years.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Evading Law Enforcement · ¶4
text: If an unlicensed person is caught driving your vehicle, it may be impounded for 30 days.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Speed Contests and Reckless Driving · ¶1
text: A person convicted of reckless driving or engaging in a speed contest that causes injury to another person is subject to imprisonment, a fine, or both.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · ¶1
text: DMV monitors your driver’s record. If you are stopped by a law enforcement officer and cited (ticketed) for a traffic violation, you sign the ticket as a promise to appear in traffic court. As an adult or minor, if you get a traffic ticket and fail to appear (FTA) in court, DMV may suspend your driving privilege until you appear. If you do not keep your promise to appear in court, the FTA goes on your driver’s record.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · ¶2
text: Each time you are convicted of a moving traffic violation, the court notifies DMV. The conviction is placed on your driver’s record. Convictions reported by other states and juvenile court are also added to your driver’s record. Traffic convictions and collisions stay on your record for 36 months or longer, depending on the type of conviction. As an adult, your license may be suspended if your driver’s record shows one of the following point totals:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · item 1
text: 4 points in 12 months.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · item 2
text: 6 points in 24 months.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Points on Your Driver’s Record · item 3
text: 8 points in 36 months.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Traffic Violator School · ¶1
text: If you are given a one-point traffic violation, the judge may offer you the choice to attend a traffic violator school to have the citation not reported to your insurance company but remain on your driving record. You can do this once in any 18-month period. The school will report your course completion to the court. You will also get a completion receipt.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Traffic Violator School · ¶2
text: If you are a commercial driver cited in a noncommercial vehicle, see the California Commercial Driver’s Handbook .

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Suspension or Revocation · ¶1
text: If you have too many points on your driver’s record, you will be considered a negligent driver. DMV will place you on probation, suspend, or revoke your driving privilege. When this happens, you have the right to a hearing. DMV will notify you in writing of any action taken against your driving privilege and inform you of your legal rights, including your right to a hearing.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Suspension or Revocation · ¶2
text: DMV will revoke your driving privilege if you are convicted of a hit-and-run or reckless driving that resulted in injury. Courts also have the authority to suspend a person’s driving privilege.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Suspension or Revocation · ¶3
text: At the end of your suspension or revocation, you may apply for a replacement driver’s license. You must show proof of financial responsibility (such as SR 22/SR 1P).

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · ¶1
text: If you get into collisions or commit traffic violations within the first 12 months of obtaining your minor’s driver’s license, DMV may restrict or suspend your driving privilege. You cannot drive if your driving privilege is suspended or revoked.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · ¶2
text: As a minor, DMV may take action against your license if you have:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 1
text: One at fault collision or traffic violation conviction: An at fault collision means you were found responsible.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 2
text: Two at fault collisions, two traffic violation convictions, or one of each: You cannot drive for 30 days unless a licensed adult, at least 25 years old, rides with you.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 3
text: Three at fault collisions, three traffic violation convictions, or a combination: Your driving privilege will be suspended for six months. You will be on probation for one year.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 4
text: If you have more at fault collisions or traffic violation convictions while on probation, your license will be suspended again.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · item 5
text: A conviction of using alcohol or a controlled substance, or both and are 15-20 years old: The court will order DMV to suspend your driving privilege for one year or delay your eligibility to apply for a driver’s license.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Maintaining Your Minor’s (Provisional) Driver’s License · ¶3
text: Note Turning 18 years old does not erase or end existing restrictions, suspensions, or probation sentences.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Administrative Hearing · ¶1
text: Administrative hearings are conducted by DMV. If you received notification that a proposed action is being taken against your driving privilege, you must request a hearing within 10 days of being served or 14 days from the date the notice is mailed. If you do not make a timely request, your right to a hearing will be lost.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Administrative Hearing · ¶2
text: This hearing provides you with an opportunity to be heard before an action is taken against your driving privilege. You may also have to appear in court for the same reason. Any action taken by the court is independent of the action taken by DMV.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · ¶1
text: You have the right to:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · item 1
text: Present relevant evidence and witnesses on your behalf.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · item 2
text: Testify on your behalf or be represented by an attorney or other representative at your expense. Representation by an attorney is not required.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · item 3
text: Review the evidence and cross examine the testimony of any witness. DMV bases its case only on written documents. If you wish to question someone who prepared a document or is listed on a document used as evidence, it is your responsibility to acquire a subpoena.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Your Hearing Rights · ¶2
text: For more information regarding Administrative Hearings, visit dmv.ca.gov/driversafety .

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Other Important Roadway Information › Unsafe Driver · ¶1
text: If you know someone who no longer drives safely, you may submit a Request for Driver Reexamination (DS 699) to DMV to review their driving qualifications. To obtain a form, visit dmv.ca.gov/reexamination .

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Record Confidentiality · ¶1
text: Most information in your driver’s record is available to the public, except physical or mental conditions, address, and social security number.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Record Confidentiality · ¶2
text: You can get a copy of your driver’s record online or at a kiosk. For more information on record requests, visit dmv.ca.gov/record-requests .

text: When at or approaching traffic signals or signs, yield to pedestrians, bicyclists, and other nearby vehicles that may have the right-of-way. See Right of Way Rules: Who Goes First , in this section.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? · ¶1
text: Right-of-way rules help you understand who goes first when vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists meet on the road. The vehicle that arrives to the intersection first has the right-of-way. Other vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians must wait for the person who has the right-of-way. Never assume that other drivers will give you the right-of-way. Give up your right-of-way when it will help prevent collisions.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · ¶1
text: An intersection is any place where one road meets another road. Controlled intersections have signs or traffic signal lights. Uncontrolled and blind intersections do not. Before entering an intersection, look left, right, and ahead to check for vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians. Be prepared to slow down and stop if necessary. Pedestrians always have the right-of-way. Here are some right-of-way rules at intersections:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 1
text: Without STOP or YIELD signs: The vehicle that arrives to the intersection first has the right-of-way. However, if a vehicle, pedestrian, or bicyclist gets to the intersection at the same time as you, give the right-of-way to the vehicle, pedestrian, or bicyclist on your right. If you approach a stop sign and there is a stop sign on all four corners, stop first and proceed as above.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 2
text: T intersections without STOP or YIELD signs: Vehicles, bicyclists, and pedestrians on the through road (continuing to go straight) have the right-of-way.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 3
text: Turning left: Check for pedestrians. Give the right-of-way to any pedestrian or approaching vehicle that is close enough to be dangerous.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 4
text: Turning right: Always check for pedestrians crossing the street, and motorcycles and bicycles riding next to you.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 5
text: Green traffic signal light: Proceed with caution. Pedestrians have the right-of-way.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Intersections · item 6
text: Entering traffic: When entering traffic, you must proceed with caution and yield to the traffic already occupying the lanes. It is against the law to stop or block an intersection where there is not enough space to completely cross before the traffic signal light turns red.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · ¶1
text: In a roundabout, traffic travels in one direction around a central island.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · ¶2
text: How to use a roundabout:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 1
text: Slow down as you approach.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 2
text: Yield to all traffic already in the roundabout.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 3
text: Enter heading to the right when there is a big enough gap in traffic to merge safely.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 4
text: Watch for signs and lane markings that guide you.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 5
text: Travel in a counter-clockwise direction. Do not stop or pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 6
text: Signal when you change lanes or exit.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 7
text: If you miss your exit, continue around until you return to your exit.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · ¶3
text: If the roundabout has multiple lanes, choose your entry or exit lane based on your destination. This is shown in the image below. To:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 8
text: Turn right (yellow car): Choose the right lane and exit in the right lane.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 9
text: Go straight (red car): Choose either lane. Exit in the lane you entered.

text: Turn left: Enter and continue driving until you reach the exit in the direction you choose (blue car).

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶2
text: From left to right: Tricycle, Quadricycle, Standard Wheelchair, Electric Wheelchair.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶3
text: Although pedestrians have the right-of-way, they also must follow the rules of the road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶4
text: When there is a pedestrian crossing a roadway with or without a crosswalk, you must use caution, reduce your speed, or stop to allow the pedestrian to safely finish crossing.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶5
text: Other things to keep in mind:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 4
text: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. You may not be able to see a pedestrian crossing the street.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 5
text: If a pedestrian makes eye contact with you, they are ready to cross the street. Yield to the pedestrian.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 6
text: Always allow pedestrians enough time to safely cross a street as some groups such as seniors, people with small children, and people with disabilities may require extra time.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Crosswalks · ¶1
text: A crosswalk is the part of the road set aside for pedestrians to safely cross the road. They are often marked with white lines. School crossings may have yellow crosswalk lines. Not all crosswalks are marked.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Crosswalks · ¶2
text: Pedestrians have the right-of-way in marked or unmarked crosswalks. If there is a limit line before the crosswalk, stop at the limit line and allow pedestrians to cross the street.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Crosswalks · ¶3
text: Some crosswalks have flashing lights. Whether or not the lights are flashing, look for pedestrians and be prepared to stop.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · ¶1
text: Pedestrians using guide dogs or white canes have the right-of-way at all times. These pedestrians are partially or totally blind. Be careful when you are turning or backing up. This is particularly important if you are driving a hybrid or electric vehicle because blind pedestrians rely on sound to know there is a vehicle nearby.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · item 1
text: Do not stop in the middle of a crosswalk. This could force a blind pedestrian to walk into traffic outside of the crosswalk.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · item 2
text: Do not honk your horn at a blind person.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians › Pedestrians who are Blind · item 3
text: When a blind person pulls in their cane and steps away from the intersection, this gesture usually means you may go.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Mountain Roads · ¶1
text: If two vehicles meet on a steep narrow road and neither vehicle can pass, the vehicle facing uphill has the right-of-way. The vehicle facing downhill has more control when backing up the hill. The vehicle facing downhill should back up until the vehicle going uphill can pass.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶1
text: Parallel parking is when you park in line with the road and other parked vehicles. To parallel park:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶2
text: 1. Find a space. Look for a space at least three feet longer than your vehicle. When you find a space, turn on your signal to show that you plan on parking.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶3
text: 2. Pull up alongside the vehicle in front of the space. Leave about two feet between your vehicle and the vehicle next to you. Stop once your rear bumper is aligned with the front of your parking space. Keep your signal on.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · image
heading: Alt text: “Find a parallel parking space”
text: Find a parallel parking space

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶4
text: 3. Check your blind spots. Look in your rearview mirror and over your shoulder for approaching vehicles and pedestrians.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶5
text: 4. Begin backing up. Turn your steering wheel to back into the space at about a 45-degree angle.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · image
heading: Alt text: “Parallel Parking: Checking Blind Spots”
text: Parallel Parking: Checking Blind Spots

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶6
text: 5. Straighten out. Begin turning the steering wheel away from the curb when your rear wheel is within 18 inches of the curb. You may need to pull forward and backward to straighten out. Your vehicle should now be parallel and within 18 inches of the curb.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · image
heading: Alt text: “Parallel Parking”
text: Parallel Parking

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶7
text: Turn off your vehicle and set the parking brake. Before you exit your vehicle, look carefully for passing vehicles, bicycles, and motorcycles. Exit when safe.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Straight Line Backing · ¶1
text: To back up in a straight line:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 1
text: Traffic check. Observe traffic and check appropriate blind spots.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 2
text: Signal . Activate the turn signal before pulling up to the curb. Cancel the turn signal once completed.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 3
text: Check your blind spots. Look in your rearview mirror and over your shoulder for approaching vehicles and pedestrians.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 4
text: Begin backing up. Back in a straight line for three vehicle lengths while remaining within three feet of the curb. Stay aware of what is behind you when backing up.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Straight Line Backing · item 5
text: Control. To maintain control of the vehicle, back at a smooth, safe speed and adjust the steering wheel when needed. Practice until you can keep the vehicle straight. Repeat steps 1 and 2 to pull away from the curb.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking on a Hill · image
Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking on a Hill · ¶1
text: When you park on a hill, your vehicle could roll due to equipment failure. Remember to set the parking brake and leave the vehicle in park, or in gear for manual transmission. To park:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 1
text: On a sloping driveway: Turn the wheels so the vehicle will not roll into the street, leave the vehicle in park and set the parking brake.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 2
text: Headed downhill: Turn your front wheels into the curb or right toward the side of the road.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 3
text: Headed uphill: Turn your front wheels away from the curb (left-towards the center of the road) and let your vehicle roll back a few inches. The wheel should gently touch the curb.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking on a Hill · item 4
text: Headed either uphill or downhill when there is no curb: Turn the wheels to the right so the vehicle will roll away from the center of the road if the brakes fail.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · ¶1
text: Painted colored curbs have special parking rules.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · image
heading: Alt text: “Parking at Colored Curbs”
text: Parking at Colored Curbs

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 1
text: White : Stop only long enough to pick up or drop off passengers.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 2
text: Green : Park for a limited time. The time limit may be posted on signs or painted on the curb.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 3
text: Yellow : Load and unload passengers and freight. Do not stop longer than the time posted. If you drive a noncommercial vehicle, you are usually required to stay with your vehicle.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 4
text: Red : No stopping, standing, or parking. Buses may stop at a red zone marked for buses only.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 5
text: Blue : Parking for a disabled person or someone driving a disabled person with a special placard or special license plate.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parking at Colored Curbs · item 6
text: To learn more about disabled parking placards and license plates, visit dmv.ca.gov/disabled-person-parking .

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · ¶1
text: Never park or leave your vehicle:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 1
text: Where a NO PARKING sign is posted.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 2
text: On a marked or unmarked crosswalk.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 3
text: On a sidewalk, partially blocking a sidewalk, or in front of a driveway.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 4
text: Within three feet of a sidewalk ramp for disabled persons.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 5
text: In front of or on a curb that provides wheelchair access to a sidewalk.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 6
text: In the crosshatched (diagonal lines) area next to a designated disabled parking space.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 7
text: In a space designated for parking or fueling zero-emission vehicles, unless you are driving a zero-emission vehicle.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 8
text: In a tunnel or on a bridge, unless permitted by signs.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 9
text: Within 15 feet of a fire hydrant or fire station driveway.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 10
text: Within 20 feet of an unmarked or marked crosswalk, or within 15 feet of a crosswalk where a curb extension is present.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 11
text: Between a safety zone and curb.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 12
text: Double parked.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 13
text: On the wrong side of the street or on a freeway, except:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 14
text: In an emergency.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 15
text: When a law enforcement officer requires a stop.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · item 16
text: Where a stop is specifically permitted.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Illegal Parking · ¶2
text: If you must stop on a freeway, park completely off the pavement and stay in your vehicle with the doors locked until help arrives. A vehicle that is stopped, parked, or left standing on a freeway for more than four hours may be removed.
