locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Electric Vehicles · ¶1
text: Local authorities can reserve parking spaces on public streets for electric vehicle charging.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Electric Vehicles · image
heading: Alt text: “Electric Vehicles”
text: Electric Vehicles

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Driving Green · ¶1
text: Maximize your fuel efficiency while helping to lower emissions by following these practices:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Driving Green · item 1
text: Speed up and slow down smoothly. Drive at a steady speed.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Driving Green · item 2
text: Regularly inflate your tires, get oil changes, and check filters.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Driving Green · item 3
text: Get rid of extra weight in your vehicle.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Driving Green · ¶2
text: For more information, visit fueleconomy.gov .

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 1
text: Turn on your right turn signal to acknowledge that you see the officer.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 2
text: Move completely onto the right shoulder, even if in the carpool/HOV lane. Stop in a well-lit area when possible.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 3
text: Turn off your radio.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 4
text: Remain inside your vehicle unless directed to get out by the officer.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 5
text: Roll down your window after stopping your vehicle and before the officer makes contact with you.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · item 6
text: The driver and all passengers should place their hands in clear view before the officer makes contact with them.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › During a Law Enforcement Stop · ¶1
text: Law enforcement officers must state the reason for a traffic or pedestrian stop before they begin any questioning related to a criminal investigation or traffic violation. An exception is made if an officer reasonably believes withholding the reason is necessary to protect life or property from imminent threat. The reason for the stop must be documented on the traffic citation also known as a traffic ticket issued or law enforcement report completed.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶1
text: If an officer asks your permission to do something, you have a right to say no. However, if you say no and the officer says they are going to do it anyway, you do not have a right to interfere with their actions. For example, an officer may request to search part or all of your vehicle. You have a right to decline that request, but the officer may have the legal authority to search your vehicle under certain circumstances. If you do not want the officer to search your vehicle, you should clearly say that you do not give your permission, but you do not have a right to resist or obstruct the officer if they search your vehicle.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶2
text: The driver of a stopped vehicle must produce a driver’s license, proof of insurance, and vehicle registration when stopped by law enforcement. If a driver does not produce these documents, officers may conduct a limited search for them. An officer may also request the names or identification of passengers. Passengers can decline that request, but under some circumstances the passengers may be required to identify themselves. If passengers do not want to produce their identification, they should clearly say so. Passengers should not interfere with the officer’s duties in conducting the traffic stop, and if an officer demands identification, passengers should not interfere with the officer’s actions. During a traffic stop, an officer can legally require the driver and all passengers to exit or stay inside the vehicle. If you are told to exit the vehicle or stay inside, you must do so.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶3
text: In California, only federal law enforcement officers can ask you about your immigration status. California law prohibits state and local officers from asking drivers or passengers about their immigration status. If a California law enforcement officer asks you about your immigration status, you can decline to answer.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶4
text: In general, the First Amendment protects the right of drivers and passengers to record interactions with law enforcement in public spaces. If you are recording, you should immediately make that clear. You do not have a right to interfere with the officer’s lawful duties during the enforcement stop, and you should not reach into concealed areas to retrieve your recording device without the officer’s permission. If your recording is not interfering with the officer’s ability to lawfully do their job, an officer cannot confiscate your recording device, delete the recording, or destroy the device just because you are using it to record. In general, you also have the right to deny a request to unlock a cellular phone or provide a password to it, though under some circumstances, such as if you are on parole, you may have to give permission in response to such requests. Finally, no government employee can retaliate against you just because you recorded something in public.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Law Enforcement Stops › Your Rights During the Enforcement Stop · ¶5
text: Even if you believe your rights were violated, you should not engage in physical resistance or violence against the officer. If an officer does something that you believe violates your rights, you can voice your objection, but you should not physically resist. Everyone has the right to be safe during a traffic stop. Your safety and the officer’s safety could be jeopardized if the situation escalates with physical resistance or violence. All members of the public have a right to file a complaint against any law enforcement agency, and it is against the law for any government employee to retaliate against you for doing so. You can file a complaint with the law enforcement agency that employs the officer. You have a right to be free from discrimination based on your actual or perceived race, sex, color, ethnicity, national origin, age, religion, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, mental or physical disability, medical condition, or citizenship status. You also have other rights guaranteed by the United States and California Constitutions, as well as California and federal laws. When you file a complaint, the agency that employs the officer must investigate the complaint. Links to contact information for California law enforcement agencies can be found at post.ca.gov/le-agencies .

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes · ¶1
text: A traffic lane is a section of road for a single line of traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings · ¶1
text: Lane markings on road surfaces help drivers know which part of the road to use and understand traffic rules.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Single Solid Yellow Line · ¶1
text: A single solid yellow line marks the center of a road with two-way traffic. Do not pass a vehicle in front of you if there is only one lane of traffic going your direction and a solid yellow line on your side of the road.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · ¶1
text: Do not pass over double solid yellow lines. Stay to the right of these lines unless you are:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · image
heading: Alt text: “Double Solid Yellow Lines. End Divided Road Sign and U-Turn OK Sign”
text: Double Solid Yellow Lines. End Divided Road Sign and U-Turn OK Sign

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 1
text: In a high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) carpool lane that has a designated entrance on the left.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 2
text: Instructed by construction or other signs to drive on the other side of the road because your side is closed or blocked.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 3
text: Turning left across a single set of double yellow lines to enter or exit a driveway or private road or make a U-turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · ¶2
text: Two sets of solid double yellow lines spaced two or more feet apart are considered a barrier. Do not drive on or over this barrier, make a left turn, or make a U-turn across it, except at designated openings.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Broken Yellow Line · ¶1
text: A broken yellow line indicates you may pass if the broken line is next to your driving lane. Only pass when it is safe.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Single Solid White Line · ¶1
text: A single solid white line marks traffic lanes going in the same direction. This includes one-way streets.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid White Lines · ¶1
text: Double solid white lines indicate a lane barrier between a regular use and a preferential use lane, such as a carpool (HOV) lane. You may also see double solid white lines in or near freeway on and off ramps. Never change lanes over double solid white lines. Wait until you see a single broken white line.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Broken White Lines · ¶1
text: Broken white lines separate traffic lanes on roads with two or more lanes in the same direction.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Broken White Lines · image
heading: Alt text: “End of Lane Markings”
text: End of Lane Markings

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › End of Lane Markings · ¶1
text: Ending freeway and street lanes are usually marked with large broken lines. If you are driving in a lane marked with broken lines, be prepared to exit the freeway or for the lane to end. Look for a sign that tells you to exit or merge.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Yield Line · ¶1
text: A yield line is a line of solid white triangles that shows approaching vehicles where to yield or stop. The triangles point towards approaching vehicles.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Yield Line · image
Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · ¶1
text: Traffic lanes are often referred to by number. The left (or fast) lane is called the Number 1 Lane. The lane to the right of the Number 1 Lane is called the Number 2 Lane. Then the Number 3 Lane, etc.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · image
heading: Alt text: “Example of numbered traffic lanes.”
text: Example of numbered traffic lanes.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · ¶2
text: Example of numbered traffic lanes

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · ¶3
text: Here are some tips for choosing a lane:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · item 1
text: Use the left lane to pass or turn left.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · item 2
text: Use the right lane to enter or exit traffic or when you enter the road from a curb or shoulder.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · ¶1
text: Before you change lanes:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 1
text: Signal.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 2
text: Check your mirrors.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 3
text: Check traffic behind and beside you.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 4
text: Look over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move to make sure the lane is clear.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 5
text: Check your blind spots for other vehicles, motorcyclists, and bicyclists. Do not let the vehicle drift into another lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · item 6
text: Be sure there is enough space for your vehicle in the next lane. It is not necessary to slow down before a lane change.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Changing Lanes · ¶2
text: Stay in one lane as much as possible. Do not weave in and out of traffic. Last minute lane or direction changes may increase the risk of collisions. Once you start moving through an intersection, keep going. If you start to make a turn, follow through. If you miss a turn, keep driving until you can safely and legally turn around.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Passing Lanes · ¶1
text: On a multilane road, the passing lane (far left lane) is the lane closest to the center divider and is used to pass other vehicles.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · ¶1
text: An HOV lane is a special lane reserved for carpools, buses, motorcycles, or low-emission vehicles with decals. To use an HOV lane, one of these must apply:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · image
Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · image
Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · item 1
text: You have a certain number of people in your vehicle. There will be signs at the on-ramp or along the road to tell you the minimum number of people. Road signs also list the hours when the HOV rules apply.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · item 2
text: You are driving a low emission or zero emission vehicle. You must display a special DMV-issued decal.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · item 3
text: You are riding a motorcycle (unless otherwise posted).

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Carpool/High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) Lanes · ¶2
text: The road surface in a HOV lane is marked with a diamond symbol and the words Carpool Lane. Do not cross over double solid lines to enter or exit an HOV lane. Use designated entrances and exits.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · ¶1
text: A center left turn lane is located in the middle of a two-way street. It is marked on both sides by two painted lines. The inner line is broken and the outer line is solid. Use the center left turn lane to prepare for and make a left turn or U-turn. It is not a regular traffic lane or passing lane. You may only drive for 200 feet in the center left turn lane. To turn left from this lane:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 1
text: Look for other vehicles coming toward you in the center left turn lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 2
text: Signal.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 3
text: Look over your shoulder to check your blind spots.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 4
text: Merge completely into the center left turn lane so you do not block traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · item 5
text: Turn when it is safe.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · image
heading: Alt text: “Image of cars navigating thru a Center Left Turn Lane”
text: Image of cars navigating thru a Center Left Turn Lane

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · ¶2
text: Example of Center Left Turn Lane

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · ¶1
text: Some two-lane roads have special turnout areas or lanes. Merge into these areas or lanes to allow cars behind you to pass.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · image
heading: Alt text: “Slower Traffic Use Turnouts”
text: Slower Traffic Use Turnouts

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · ¶2
text: You must use a turnout area or lane to let other vehicles pass when you are driving slowly on a two-lane road, where passing is unsafe, and there are five or more vehicles following you.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶1
text: Bicycle lanes are for bicyclists only and run alongside vehicle traffic. They are typically marked by a single solid white line and signs. They are sometimes painted bright green to make them easier to see.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · image
heading: Alt text: “Bicycle Lane”
text: Bicycle Lane

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶2
text: Example of shared roadway. Three (3) feet of distance must be maintained between the car and cyclist.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶3
text: It is illegal to drive in a bicycle lane unless you are:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 1
text: Parking (where permitted).

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 2
text: Entering or leaving the road.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 3
text: Turning (within 200 feet of an intersection).

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶4
text: There are multiple types of bike lanes and markings:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 4
text: Bike lane: Established along streets adjacent to vehicle traffic. Typically marked by a single solid white line that turns into a dash-line near an intersection.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 5
text: Buffered bike lane: Uses chevrons or diagonal markings to provide greater separation from traffic and on-street parking.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 6
text: Bike route: Uses bike route signs and shared road markings to designate a preferred route for bicyclists on streets shared with vehicle traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 7
text: Bicycle boulevard: Prioritizes bicycle travel on streets shared with vehicle traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 8
text: Separated bikeway: Is physically separated from motor vehicle traffic and for exclusive use of bicyclists. They are also known as a cycle track or protected bike lanes. The separation may include flexible posts, grade separation, inflexible barriers, or on-street parking.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · item 9
text: Shared roadway bicycle markings: Alert drivers that bicyclists can occupy the lane and help bicyclists maintain a safe lane position in traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶5
text: Note Check your blind spots before entering a bike lane. If you drive a motorized bicycle, use caution to avoid other bicyclists. Travel at a reasonable speed and do not endanger the safety of other bicyclists.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Image of a vehicle making a right turn”
text: Image of a vehicle making a right turn

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · ¶1
text: Example of a right turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · ¶2
text: To make a right turn:­

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 1
text: Drive close to the right edge of the road.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 2
text: If a designated right turn lane is available, enter at the opening.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 3
text: You can drive in a bike lane within 200 feet from the turn. Check for bicyclists in your blind spots.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 4
text: Watch for pedestrians, bicyclists, or motorcyclists between your vehicle and the curb.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 5
text: Start signaling about 100 feet before the turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 6
text: Look over your right shoulder and reduce your speed.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 7
text: Stop behind the limit line. A limit line is a wide white line that shows the drivers where to stop before an intersection or crosswalk. If there is no limit line, stop before you enter the crosswalk. If there is no crosswalk, stop before you enter the intersection.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 8
text: Look both ways (left-right-left) and turn when it is safe.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns · item 9
text: Complete your turn in the right lane. Do not turn wide into another lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn Against a Red Light · ¶1
text: You may turn right at a red light after a complete stop unless there is a No Turn on Red sign. Follow the same steps listed above for right turns.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn Against a Red Arrow · ¶1
text: You may not turn right if you are stopped at a red arrow light. Wait until the light changes to green before making your turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn at a Public Transit Bus Lane · ¶1
text: It is illegal to drive, stop, park, or leave a vehicle in an area designated for public transit buses. Signs will be posted to indicate the lanes are for bus only use. However, you may cross a bus lane to make a right turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn onto a Road with a Dedicated Lane · ¶1
text: A dedicated right turn lane does not merge into another lane and allows you to make a right turn without stopping. You may make your turn even if there is a red light for vehicles going straight through the intersection. If there is a traffic light or sign on the right curb of the right turn lane, you must obey that light or sign. Always yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk when turning.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn onto a Road with a Dedicated Lane · image
heading: Alt text: “Right Turn onto a Road with a Dedicated Lane”
text: Right Turn onto a Road with a Dedicated Lane

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Right Turns › Right Turn onto a Road with a Dedicated Lane · ¶2
text: Example of a Right Turn into a Dedicated Lane

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Left Turn”
text: Left Turn

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · ¶1
text: Example of a left turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · ¶2
text: To turn left:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 1
text: Drive close to the center divider or into the left turn lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 2
text: Enter a designated left turn lane at the opening. Do not cross any solid line.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 3
text: Enter a two-way center left turn lane within 200 feet of the turn. Respect the right-of-way of any vehicle, bicyclist, or motorcyclist already in the lane. Always yield to pedestrians.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 4
text: Start signaling 100 feet before the turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 5
text: Look over your left shoulder and reduce your speed.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 6
text: Stop behind the limit line. If there is no limit line, stop before you enter the crosswalk. If there is no crosswalk, stop before you enter the intersection.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 7
text: Look both ways (left-right-left) and begin your turn when it is safe.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 8
text: Proceed into the intersection while turning to complete your turn in the left lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 9
text: Do not turn the steering wheel too soon and enter the lane of oncoming vehicles.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 10
text: Keep your wheels pointed straight ahead until it is safe to start your turn. If your wheels are pointed to the left and a vehicle hits you from behind, you could be pushed into oncoming traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 11
text: Accelerate smoothly during and after the turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns · item 12
text: Allow the steering wheel to straighten in the new lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Left Turns › Left Turn Against a Red Light · ¶1
text: You may turn left against a red light when you are turning from a one-way street onto a one-way street. Make sure there is no sign prohibiting the turn. Yield to other vehicles, pedestrians, or bicyclists who have a green light. Look both ways and turn when it is safe.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · ¶1
text: A U-turn is when you turn your vehicle around to go back in the direction you came. To make a U-turn, signal and use the left turn lane or far-left lane. You may make a U-turn:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 1
text: Across a double yellow line.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 2
text: In a residential district if no vehicles are approaching you within 200 feet.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 3
text: At an intersection on a green traffic light or green arrow, unless a NO U-TURN sign is posted.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 4
text: On a divided highway if a center divider opening is provided.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · ¶2
text: Never make a U-turn:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 5
text: Where a NO U-TURN sign is posted.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 6
text: At or on a railroad crossing.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 7
text: On a divided highway by crossing a dividing section, curb, strip of land, or two sets of double yellow lines.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 8
text: When you cannot see clearly for 200 feet in each direction.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 9
text: On a one-way street.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 10
text: In front of a fire station. Never use a fire station driveway to turn around.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 11
text: In business districts (the part of a city or town where most offices and businesses are).

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › U-TURN · item 12
text: Except at an intersection, or on a divided highway where an opening has been provided.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶1
text: The descriptions below refer to the numbers next to the cars in the images. Watch for pedestrians, motorcycles, and bicycles between your vehicle and the curb. When making turns, there may be signs or arrows that indicate you can turn from or end in more than one lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · item 1
text: Left turn from a two-way street. Start the turn in the left lane closest to the middle of the street. To reduce the risk of collision, end the turn in the left lane closest to the middle of the street going in your vehicle’s direction.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Left turn from a two-way street”
text: Left turn from a two-way street

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶2
text: 2. Right turn. Begin and end the turn in the lane closest to the right edge of the road. Do not swing wide into another lane of traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶3
text: 3. Left turn from a two-way street onto a one-way street. Start the turn from the lane closest to the middle of the street (far-left lane). If there are three or more lanes in your direction of travel, you may end your turn in any lane that is open.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Left turn from a two-way street onto a one-way street”
text: Left turn from a two-way street onto a one-way street

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶4
text: 4. Left turn from a one-way street onto a two-way street. Start the turn from the far-left lane. To reduce the risk of collision, end the turn in the left lane closest to the middle of the street going in your vehicle’s direction.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Left turn from a one-way street onto a two-way street”
text: Left turn from a one-way street onto a two-way street

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶5
text: 5. Left turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street. Start the turn from the far-left lane. Bicyclists can legally use the left turn lane for their left turns. If there are three or more lanes in your direction of travel, you may end your turn in any lane that is open.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Left turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street”
text: Left turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶6
text: 6. Right turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street. Start the turn in the far-right lane. If safe, you may end the turn in any lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Right turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street”
text: Right turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · ¶7
text: 7. Turn at a “T” intersection from a one-way street onto a two-way street. Traffic going straight through the intersection has the right-of-way. You may turn either right or left from the center lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Examples of Turns · image
heading: Alt text: “Turn at a "T" intersection from a one-way street onto a two-way street”
text: Turn at a "T" intersection from a one-way street onto a two-way street

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Braking · item 1
text: Remove your foot from the accelerator and allow the vehicle to slow down. Lightly press the brake until you come to a full stop. Give yourself enough space and time to perform this maneuver.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Turns › Braking · item 2
text: When stopping at a limit line, do not cross over the line. If stopping behind a vehicle, leave enough space to see their rear wheels.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · ¶1
text: Highway traffic has the right-of-way. For more information, see Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First in Section 7. When you enter a highway, you will need to:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 1
text: Be in the proper lane on the on-ramp.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 2
text: Be at or near the speed of traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 3
text: Merge into highway traffic when safe to do so. Do not stop unless absolutely necessary.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 4
text: Merge into a space large enough for your vehicle to safely join the lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 5
text: Use your mirrors and turn signals.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 6
text: Turn your head quickly to look over your shoulder before changing lanes or merging into traffic.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 7
text: Make sure you can stop safely by leaving three seconds of space between you and the vehicle in front of you.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Merging · item 8
text: Make sure you do not cross over any solid lines when merging. If you need to cross several lanes, signal and cross them one at a time. Check your blind spots for vehicles, motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians each time.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Exiting · ¶1
text: To exit a highway safely:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 1
text: Know your exit and be aware of when it is approaching.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 2
text: If you plan to change lanes, do so one at a time. Signal and look over your shoulder to check your blind spots.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 3
text: When in the proper lane, signal five seconds (approximately 400 feet) before you exit.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 4
text: Make sure you are at a safe speed to exit.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Exiting · item 5
text: Do not cross over any solid lines when exiting.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · ¶1
text: When entering traffic from a full stop, signal and leave a large enough space to get up to the speed of traffic. To merge, enter, or exit traffic, you need a space that is:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · item 1
text: Half a block on city streets, which is about 150 feet.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · item 2
text: A full block on the highway, which is about 300 feet.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · ¶2
text: Even if you have a green light, do not start across the intersection if there are pedestrians or vehicles blocking your pathway.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Merging And Exiting › Crossing or Entering Traffic · ¶3
text: When turning left, do not assume that an oncoming vehicle with its right turn signal on is turning before it reaches you. The driver may have their signal on by mistake or plan to turn just beyond you. Wait for the vehicle to start its turn before beginning the left turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · ¶1
text: You must judge whether you have enough space to pass whenever you approach:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 1
text: An oncoming vehicle or bicyclist.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 2
text: A hill, curve, intersection, or road obstruction. To safely pass, the hill or curve should be at least one-third of a mile ahead.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · ¶2
text: Before you pass, look ahead for road conditions that may cause other vehicles to move into your lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · ¶3
text: Do not pass:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 3
text: If you are approaching a hill or curve and cannot see if other traffic is approaching. This is very dangerous on one and two lane roads.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 4
text: Within 100 feet of an intersection, bridge, tunnel, railroad crossing, or other hazardous area.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 5
text: At crossroads and driveways.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 6
text: Unless you have enough space to return to your lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · ¶1
text: When you are going to pass on an open highway:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 1
text: Signal that you plan on passing.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 2
text: Look over your shoulder to check your blind spots.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 3
text: Drive into the passing lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 4
text: Speed up to pass the vehicle.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 5
text: Signal and return to your original lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · ¶2
text: You may pass on the right only when:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 6
text: An open highway has two or more lanes going in your direction.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 7
text: The driver ahead of you is turning left and you can safely pass on the right. Never pass on the left if the driver is signaling a left turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 8
text: You are on a one-way street.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · ¶3
text: Never drive off the paved or main-traveled part of the road to pass.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › Being Passed · ¶1
text: If a vehicle is passing you or signals that they plan on passing, allow the vehicle to pass. Maintain your lane position and your speed.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶1
text: You and your passengers must wear seat belts. You can get a ticket if you do not. If your passenger is under 16 years old, you can also get a ticket if they are not wearing their seat belt.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶2
text: Wearing the lap belt and shoulder harness of a seat belt will increase your chance of survival in most types of collisions. This image shows what can happen in a collision.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶3
text: When you are in a collision, your vehicle stops. But you keep moving at the same speed you were traveling. You only stop when you hit the dashboard or windshield. If you are struck from the side, the impact could push you back and forth across the seat. Seat and shoulder belts keep you in a better position to control the vehicle. They may also minimize serious injuries.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶4
text: It is important to wear the seat belt correctly to avoid injury or death:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 1
text: Wear the shoulder harness across your shoulder and chest. There should be little to no slack. Do not wear the shoulder belt under your arm or behind your back.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 2
text: Adjust the lap belt so that it is snug and lies low across your hips. Otherwise you might slide out of the belt in a crash.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 3
text: If you are pregnant, wear the lap belt as low as possible under your abdomen. Place the shoulder strap between your breasts and to the side of your abdomen’s bulge.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · image
heading: Alt text: “Image showing how your body would be thrown during an traffic collision.”
text: Image showing how your body would be thrown during an traffic collision.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · ¶5
text: IMPACT – If the red arrow were another car hitting your car on the driver’s side:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 1
text: You would first be thrown against the driver’s side door,

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Seat Belts · item 2
text: Then you would “rebound” and be thrown toward the passenger’s side door.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · ¶1
text: You must secure children with a federally-approved child passenger restraint system or safety belt. The requirements depend on the child’s height and age.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 1
text: Children who are under 2 years old, under 40 pounds, and under 3 feet 4 inches tall: Secure in a rear-facing child passenger restraint system.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · ¶2
text: Note A child in a rear-facing child passenger restraint system may not ride in the front seat of an airbag-equipped vehicle.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 2
text: Children who are under 8 years old, or who are less than 4 feet 9 inches tall: Secure in a child passenger restraint system in a rear seat. In some cases, children under 8 years old may ride in the front seat of a vehicle in a federally-approved child passenger restraint system. They may ride in the front seat if:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 3
text: There is no rear seat.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 4
text: The rear seats are side-facing jump seats.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 5
text: The rear seats are rear-facing seats.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 6
text: The child passenger restraint system cannot be installed properly in the rear seat.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 7
text: All rear seats are already occupied by children 7 years old or younger.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 8
text: Medical reasons prevent the child from riding in the back seat.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · item 9
text: Children who are 8 years old or older, or at least 4 feet 9 inches tall: May use a properly secured safety belt that meets federal standards.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Child Restraint System and Safety Seats · ¶3
text: Your local law enforcement agency or fire department can check the installation of your child passenger restraint system. As your child grows, check that the child passenger restraint system is the right size.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Air Bags · ¶1
text: Air bags are a valuable safety feature on many vehicles. They can help keep you safer than a seat belt alone.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Air Bags · ¶2
text: Ride at least 10 inches from the airbag cover, as long as you can maintain full control of your vehicle. Measure from the center of the steering wheel to your breastbone. Contact your vehicle dealer or manufacturer if you cannot safely sit 10 inches away from the air bag. They may have advice about additional ways to move back from your air bag. Passengers should also sit at least 10 inches away from the passenger-side air bag.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Air Bags · ¶3
text: Note Children seated next to a side air bag may be at risk of serious or fatal injury.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Unattended Children and Pets · ¶1
text: It is illegal to leave a child who is six years old or younger unattended in a vehicle. A child may be left under the supervision of a person who is at least 12 years old.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Protect Yourself and Your Passengers › Unattended Children and Pets · ¶2
text: It is dangerous and illegal to leave children or animals in a hot vehicle. The temperature inside a parked vehicle can rise rapidly when it is sitting in the sun. This is true even if a window is left slightly open. Too much exposure to heat can lead to dehydration, heat stroke, and death.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · ¶1
text: In California, you may never drive faster than is safe for the current road conditions. This is known as the Basic Speed Law.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · ¶2
text: Make sure you manage your speed and slow down when conditions call for it. Regardless of the posted speed limit, your speed should depend on:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · item 1
text: The number of vehicles on the road.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · item 2
text: The speed of other vehicles on the road.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · item 3
text: The road surface: smooth, rough, graveled, wet, dry, wide, or narrow.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · item 4
text: Bicyclists or pedestrians on or crossing the road.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · item 5
text: Weather: rain, fog, snow, wind, or dust.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · item 6
text: Traffic congestion: small changes in your driving habits can help reduce congestion. Avoid weaving in and out of freeway lanes.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Manage Your Speed · ¶3
text: There are also situations with specific speed limit laws and conditions where you should reduce your speed. Unless otherwise posted, the ideal maximum speed limit on most California highways is 65 mph. It is 55 mph on a two-lane undivided highway and for vehicles towing trailers.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Choose Between Hazards · ¶1
text: Sometimes dangers will be on both sides of the road at the same time. For example, parked cars to the right and oncoming cars to the left.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Choose Between Hazards · ¶2
text: If one danger is greater than the other, give more space to the most dangerous situation. Suppose you are on a two-lane road with an oncoming vehicle to the left and a bicyclist ahead to your right. Instead of driving between the vehicle and the bicyclist, take one danger at a time. Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass. When the vehicle has passed, move to the left to allow plenty of space (at least three feet) to pass the bicyclist. If there is a steady flow of oncoming vehicles, use as much of the left lane as you safely can to pass the bicyclist.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies · ¶1
text: There are many types of emergencies you may encounter when you drive. Knowing how to handle emergencies can help keep you safe.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · ¶1
text: If you have a tire blowout, do not panic or overreact. Suddenly braking or abruptly removing your foot from the accelerator can result in a loss of control over the vehicle. Instead, you should take the following steps recommended by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 1
text: Hold the steering wheel with both hands.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 2
text: Maintain your vehicle speed if possible and safe.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 3
text: Gradually release the accelerator.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 4
text: Correct the steering as necessary to stabilize your vehicle and regain control.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 5
text: Look and steer in the direction you want your vehicle to go.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Tire Blowout · item 6
text: Once your vehicle has stabilized, continue to slow down and pull off the road where and when it’s safe.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · ¶1
text: If your wheels drift off the pavement:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 1
text: Grip the steering wheel firmly.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 2
text: Remove your foot from the accelerator.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 3
text: Brake gently.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 4
text: Check for traffic behind you.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · item 5
text: Carefully steer back onto the pavement.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Driving Off the Pavement · ¶2
text: Do not pull or turn your steering wheel with too much force. This may cause you to drive into oncoming traffic.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · ¶1
text: In extreme heat, you should:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 1
text: Watch the temperature gauge.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 2
text: Avoid driving at high speeds for long periods.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 3
text: Turn off the air conditioner.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · ¶2
text: In extreme cold, you should:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 4
text: Watch the temperature gauge. The engine may not have the correct level of antifreeze.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · item 5
text: Use the defroster or slightly open your windows to keep them from fogging up.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Overheating Conditions · ¶3
text: Note See the vehicle owner’s manual for more information.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · ¶1
text: If your vehicle stops working on the freeway:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 1
text: Safely pull over to the right shoulder.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 2
text: Exit on the right side so you are away from traffic if you must get out of the vehicle.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 3
text: Dial 511 from your cell phone or locate call box for assistance..

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 4
text: Return to your vehicle as soon as you can. Get back into the vehicle from the right side (away from traffic).

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 5
text: Stay inside your vehicle with your seat belt on until help arrives.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 6
text: Use your emergency flashers at your discretion. They can help other vehicles see you at night and in different weather conditions.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · ¶2
text: There are certain circumstances where it is safer to get out of your vehicle and stay away. These include situations where there is:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 1
text: Not enough space on the shoulder.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 2
text: A guardrail.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway · item 3
text: An area for you to safely stay away from freeway lanes.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶1
text: During commute times, the CHP FSP provides free emergency roadside services in certain areas. If you get stuck on the freeway because your vehicle stops running, FSP will:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 1
text: Provide a gallon of gas if you run out.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 2
text: Jump start your vehicle if the battery is dead.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 3
text: Refill your radiator and tape hoses.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 4
text: Change a flat tire.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 5
text: Report a collision to CHP.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶2
text: If FSP cannot start your vehicle, they will have it towed (free of charge) to a CHP-approved location. CHP will notify an auto club or towing service.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶3
text: FSP will not:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 6
text: Tow your vehicle to a private repair service or residence.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 7
text: Recommend tow service companies or repair and body shops.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 8
text: Tow motorcycles.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · item 9
text: Help vehicles which have been involved in a collision, unless they are directed to by CHP.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › If Your Vehicle Becomes Disabled on the Freeway › California Highway Patrol (CHP) Freeway Service Patrol (FSP) · ¶4
text: Call 511 for FSP information and assistance.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · ¶1
text: If your vehicle stalls or stops while blocking part of a train track with a train approaching and warning lights flashing:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · item 1
text: Immediately exit your vehicle. Run away from the tracks diagonally in the direction the train is coming from. Then call 911.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · ¶2
text: If you do not see a train approaching and warning lights are not flashing:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · item 2
text: Exit your vehicle. Dial the number located on the railroad crossing posts or metal control box near the tracks. Provide the crossing number (if posted). Tell them a vehicle is on the tracks. Then call 911.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Know How to Handle Emergencies › Disabled Vehicles on Railroad Tracks · image
heading: Alt text: “A car is stalled on railroad tracks with an oncoming train. The image includes overlaid text reading “Crash area” marking the hazardous zone in front of the train in the direction it is traveling.”
text: A car is stalled on railroad tracks with an oncoming train. The image includes overlaid text reading “Crash area” marking the hazardous zone in front of the train in the direction it is traveling.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Do Not Drive Distracted · ¶1
text: Avoid distractions while you drive. Some common distractions are:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Do Not Drive Distracted · item 1
text: Looking at a phone, navigation system, children, and pets.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Do Not Drive Distracted · item 2
text: Changing music or volume.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Do Not Drive Distracted · item 3
text: Applying makeup or shaving.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Cell Phones and Texting · ¶1
text: Cell phones are the main source of distracted driving. Driving while using a handheld cell phone is unsafe and illegal.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Cell Phones and Texting · ¶2
text: Adult drivers should only use a cell phone in hands-free mode when necessary.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Cell Phones and Texting · item 1
text: Do not answer your cell phone if it rings. Let the call go to voicemail. If you must return or make a call, pull safely off the road.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Cell Phones and Texting · item 2
text: Do not send or read text messages or emails while driving.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Cell Phones and Texting · item 3
text: Mount your cell phone on the windshield, dashboard, or center console. It cannot block your view of the road.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Cell Phones and Texting · item 4
text: Use the single swipe or touch feature on the mounted cell phone.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Minors And Cell Phones · ¶1
text: It is against the law for a minor to use a cell phone or electronic wireless device to answer calls and send or respond to text messages while driving.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Minors And Cell Phones · ¶2
text: EXCEPTION : Minors may use a cell phone to make a call for emergency assistance.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Familiar with New Technology · ¶1
text: The technology in vehicles is always advancing. We will see more self-driving vehicles and vehicles with advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) on the road. Vehicles with these systems may respond to road situations differently than a human driver would.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · ¶1
text: All gas-powered vehicles produce carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide is a deadly odorless gas released from a vehicle’s exhaust pipe. Never start your vehicle inside the garage with the door closed. Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning include:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 1
text: Tiredness

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 2
text: Yawning

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 3
text: Dizziness

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 4
text: Nausea

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 5
text: Headache

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · item 6
text: Ringing in the ears

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Be Aware of Carbon Monoxide · ¶2
text: If you are experiencing any of these symptoms, have your exhaust system checked.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings · ¶1
text: To drive safely, you need to know what is around you. This helps you make good decisions and react to hazards on the road. This image shows the areas around your vehicle.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 1
text: Green: Ahead of you.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 2
text: Blue: Next to you.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 3
text: Yellow: Blind spots.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings · item 4
text: Red: Behind you.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings · image
heading: Alt text: “Image showing a driver's field of vision.”
text: Image showing a driver's field of vision.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Scan Your Surroundings · ¶1
text: To give yourself time to react, avoid last minute moves and hazards, always keep your eyes moving and scan the road at least 10 seconds ahead of your vehicle.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · ¶1
text: Tailgating makes it harder for you to see the road ahead because the vehicle in front of you blocks your view. You will not have enough time to react if the driver in front of you brakes suddenly. Use the three-second rule to ensure a safe following distance and avoid a collision. Following other vehicles at a safe distance gives you enough time to react if another driver makes a mistake.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · ¶2
text: If a vehicle merges in front of you too closely, take your foot off the accelerator. This creates space between you and the vehicle ahead.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · ¶3
text: Create more space in front of your vehicle when:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · item 1
text: A tailgater is behind you. Maintain your course and speed. Then, when safe to do so, merge right to change into another lane and allow the tailgater to pass.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · item 2
text: Following motorcyclists on metal surfaces (bridge gratings, railroad tracks, etc.), and gravel.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · ¶1
text: Be aware of what is on each side of you. To maintain enough space to maneuver safely and react to other drivers:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 1
text: Do not stay in another driver’s blind spot.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 2
text: Avoid driving directly alongside other vehicles.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 3
text: Make space for vehicles entering freeways, even if you have the right-of-way. Be ready for rapid changes and watch for signals from other drivers.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 4
text: Keep space between your vehicle and parked vehicles.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is At Your Side · item 5
text: Look both ways, even at intersections where traffic has a red light or stop sign.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · ¶1
text: Every vehicle has blind spots. These are areas around the vehicle that a driver cannot see when looking straight ahead or using the mirrors. For most vehicles, the blinds spots are at the sides, slightly behind the driver.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · ¶2
text: To check your blind spots, look over your right and left shoulders out of your side windows. Only turn your head when you look. Do not turn your whole body or steering wheel. Check your blind spots before you:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 1
text: Change lanes.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 2
text: Turn at an intersection.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 3
text: Merge with traffic.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 4
text: Back up.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 5
text: Leave a parking space.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 6
text: Parallel park.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 7
text: Pull out from the curb.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · item 8
text: Open your car door.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · image
heading: Alt text: “Image depicting a driver's blind spots.”
text: Image depicting a driver's blind spots.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Blind Spots · ¶3
text: The shaded areas are your blind spots

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · ¶1
text: Knowing what is behind you can help you avoid rear-end collisions. Check traffic behind you often by using your rearview mirror, side mirrors, and turning your head when you:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 1
text: Change lanes.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 2
text: Check your blind spots.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 3
text: Reduce your speed.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 4
text: Turn into a side road or driveway.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 5
text: Stop to pull into a parking space.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 6
text: Pull up to and away from the curb.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Know What is Behind You · item 7
text: Back up.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · ¶1
text: When driving at night, use your high-beam headlights on open country roads or dark city streets. Make sure you can stop in the distance lit by your headlights. Do not use high-beam headlights in areas where they are illegal. Dim your high-beam headlights to avoid blinding the driver of an oncoming vehicle. If another vehicle’s lights are too bright:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 1
text: Do not look directly into the oncoming headlights.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 2
text: Look toward the right edge of your lane.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 3
text: Watch the oncoming vehicle out of the corner of your eye.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 4
text: Do not react to the other driver by keeping your high-beam headlights on. This only makes it harder for both of you to see.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · ¶2
text: When it is raining, use your low-beam headlights. Do not drive using only your parking lights. When you drive at night, remember:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 5
text: Motorcycles, pedestrians, and bicyclists are much harder to see.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 6
text: Highway construction can take place at night. Reduce your speed in highway construction zones.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 7
text: When you leave a brightly lit place, drive slowly until your eyes adjust to the darkness.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Darkness · item 8
text: When a vehicle with one light drives toward you, drive as far to the right as possible. It could be a bicyclist, motorcyclist, or vehicle with a missing headlight.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · ¶1
text: To help manage sun glare:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 1
text: Keep the inside and outside of your windshield clean.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 2
text: Wear polarized sunglasses.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 3
text: Maintain enough space between your vehicle and the vehicles around you.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 4
text: Make sure your car visor works and is free of anything that would restrict use.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 5
text: Be aware of pedestrians. You may have difficulty seeing them.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Sun Glare · item 6
text: Try to avoid driving during sunrise and sunset.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids · ¶1
text: A skid is when one or more of the tires lose traction with the road and the vehicle starts to slip. You may not be able to control your vehicle. There are a few different types of skids.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · ¶1
text: Ice and packed snow on the road can cause your vehicle to skid. This is even more likely if you are driving too fast or going downhill. Drive slowly and leave space between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead of you. To prevent skidding on slippery surfaces:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 1
text: Slow down as you approach intersections and curves. For sharp curves, slow down as you approach and move through.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 2
text: Avoid fast turns and quick stops.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 3
text: Shift to low gear before going down a steep hill.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 4
text: Avoid areas like ice patches, wet leaves, oil, or standing water.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · ¶2
text: If you start to skid, follow these steps:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 1
text: Slowly remove your foot from the accelerator

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 2
text: Do not use the brakes.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 3
text: Turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Slippery Surface Skids · item 4
text: Try to get a wheel on dry pavement.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶1
text: A locked wheel skid is usually caused by braking too hard when you are going too fast. If this happens, your vehicle will skid no matter which way the steering wheel is turned. To get out of a locked wheel skid if your vehicle is equipped with:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 1
text: Four-wheel antilock braking system (ABS), apply firm pressure on the brake pedal.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 2
text: Rear-wheel ABS (common in light trucks):

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 3
text: Ease up on the brake pedal while maintaining just enough pressure to allow the front wheels to roll again so you can steer.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 4
text: Stop braking and turn the steering wheel into the direction of the skid.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 5
text: Front-wheel ABS, remove your foot from the brake pedal to unlock the wheels. Steer in the direction you want to go and straighten the front wheels as the vehicle begins to straighten out.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶2
text: Note To determine if your vehicle has ABS, refer to the vehicle owner’s manual.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶3
text: If your vehicle is not equipped with ABS and begins to skid, quickly pump your brakes until you are at a safe speed. If you:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 6
