text: Press the brake pedal and it sinks to the floor, quickly pump the brakes by gently applying and releasing pressure on your brake pedal.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · item 7
text: Pump the brakes, down shift your vehicle into a lower or neutral gear to slow down. Then try using your emergency brake to stop.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Skids › Locked Wheel Skids · ¶4
text: If your brakes get wet, you can dry them by lightly pressing the accelerator and brake pedals at the same time. Only do this until the brakes dry.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶1
text: Rain, snow, or mud can make the roads slippery. Drive more slowly than you would on a dry road and allow for more space between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead of you.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶2
text: Adjust your speed for different conditions:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 1
text: Wet road: Reduce your speed by 5 to 10 mph.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 2
text: Packed snow: Reduce your speed by half.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 3
text: Ice: Reduce your speed to no more than 5 mph.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶3
text: Some road surfaces are more slippery than others when wet. These usually have warning signs posted. Here are situations where the road may be more slippery:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 4
text: Shade from trees or buildings can hide icy spots on cold, wet days. These areas freeze first and dry out last.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 5
text: Bridges and overpasses tend to freeze before the rest of the road. They can have icy spots.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · item 6
text: When it starts to rain, the pavement can be very slippery.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶4
text: Slow down at the first sign of rain, drizzle, or snow on the road. This is especially true if it has been dry and hot for some time, because oil and dust on the road’s surface have not been washed away.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Slippery Roads · ¶5
text: Turn on your windshield wipers, low-beam headlights, and defroster. In a heavy rainstorm or snowstorm, you may not be able to see more than 100 feet in front of your vehicle. If you cannot see farther than 100 feet, it is not safe to drive faster than 30 mph. You may have to stop from time to time to wipe mud or snow off your windshield, headlights, and taillights. If you drive in snowy areas, carry snow chains for your tires. Snow chains give your tires more traction. Carry the correct number and type of chains for your vehicle.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · ¶1
text: Hydroplaning occurs when driving in wet or rainy conditions. Hydroplaning is a vehicle riding on water because the tires lose all contact with the road. A slight change of direction, applying the brakes, or a gust of wind could throw the vehicle into a skid. To avoid hydroplaning:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 1
text: Drive slowly.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 2
text: Steer around standing water, if possible.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 3
text: Slow down if you hear sloshing sounds from the tires.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 4
text: Slow down when changing lanes or direction.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · ¶2
text: If your vehicle starts to hydroplane:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 5
text: Slow down gradually.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Hydroplaning · item 6
text: Do not use the brakes. Sudden braking may cause you to lose control of your vehicle.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · ¶1
text: If stuck in the snow or mud, follow these steps:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 1
text: Shift into a low gear and keep the front wheels straight.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 2
text: Gently step on the accelerator. Avoid spinning the wheels.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 3
text: Drive slowly forward as far as possible.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 4
text: Shift into reverse and slowly back up as far as possible. Do not spin the wheels.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 5
text: Shift into a low gear again and drive forward.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 6
text: Repeat a forward-backward motion until the vehicle rolls free.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Stuck in Snow or Mud · item 7
text: In deep mud or snow, put boards, tree branches, etc., under the tires. Only take this action when the vehicle is stopped.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · ¶1
text: Excessive water on a road may cause flooding. This can happen gradually or suddenly. It is important to understand the dangers of water on the road, including:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 1
text: Being swept off the road.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 2
text: Floating debris and unseen hazards.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 3
text: The road collapsing.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 4
text: Vehicle malfunction.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · item 5
text: Electrocution if there are fallen power lines.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Flooded Roads · ¶2
text: It may not be possible to determine the depth of the flood by looking. If the water is deep, the road may be too dangerous to cross. It is best to find another route. If you have no other option but to drive through a flooded road, drive slowly. After you make it through the water, test your brakes to make sure they work correctly.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · ¶1
text: High winds can be a hazard while driving. This is especially true for larger vehicles such as trucks, campers, and vehicles with trailers. When driving in high winds:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 1
text: Reduce your speed. This gives you better control over your vehicle. You will have more time to react if your vehicle gets hit by a strong gust of wind.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 2
text: Maintain a firm hand position on the steering wheel. Strong wind gusts are unpredictable. If you are not holding the wheel properly and a gust hits, you can lose control of the vehicle.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 3
text: Be alert. Look ahead and watch for any debris on the road. Give yourself enough time to react to road hazards.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 4
text: Do not use cruise control. Maintain maximum control of the accelerator if a gust occurs.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 5
text: Be proactive. It may be safer to pull over and wait for the storm to pass.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · ¶1
text: It is best to avoid driving in heavy fog or smoke. Consider postponing your trip until the fog clears. If you must drive in heavy fog or smoke:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 1
text: Drive slowly.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 2
text: Use your low-beam headlights. High-beam headlights will reflect back and cause glare.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 3
text: Never drive using only your parking or fog lights.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 4
text: Make sure you can stop within the space you can see ahead.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 5
text: Increase your following distance.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 6
text: Use your windshield wipers and defroster as necessary.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 7
text: Avoid crossing lanes or passing traffic unless absolutely necessary.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 8
text: Listen for traffic you cannot see.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · ¶2
text: If the fog becomes too thick to drive safely, consider pulling off the road. Activate your emergency flashers and wait for conditions to improve.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · ¶1
text: During a traffic break, the officer turns on their emergency lights and slowly weaves across lanes. Law enforcement uses traffic breaks to:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 1
text: Slow or stop traffic to remove hazards from the road.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 2
text: Slow or stop traffic during heavy fog or unusual traffic conditions.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 3
text: Prevent collisions during unusual conditions.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · ¶2
text: You should:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 4
text: Turn on your emergency flashers to warn other drivers.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 5
text: Slowly decrease your speed to the same speed as the officer. Do not brake suddenly unless necessary to avoid a collision. Keep a safe distance from the patrol vehicle ahead of you.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 6
text: Not drive past the patrol vehicle. Do not speed up until the officer turns off their emergency lights and traffic conditions allow you to return to your normal speed.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · ¶1
text: Senior drivers often have unique needs and concerns about driving. Driving requires certain physical, visual, and mental abilities. We all want to continue driving as long as we can. However, the time may come when we must limit or stop driving temporarily or permanently. Here are some warning signs of an unsafe driver:

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 1
text: Getting lost in familiar places.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 2
text: Dents and scrapes on the car, fences, mailbox, garage doors, etc.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 3
text: Frequent close calls or collisions.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · ¶2
text: Senior drivers may consider:

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 4
text: Limiting or not driving at night.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 5
text: If night driving is necessary, choose a well-lit route.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 6
text: Driving during the time of day when traffic is light.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 7
text: Avoiding difficult intersections.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 8
text: Driving for short distances or limiting driving to essential places.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 9
text: No freeway driving.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · item 10
text: Installing an additional right-side mirror.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Intro · ¶3
text: To get the Driver Skills Self-Assessment Questionnaire, visit dmv.ca.gov/driver-skills .

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Driver’s License Renewal · ¶1
text: If you are 70 years old or older at the time your driver’s license expires, you are required to renew your driver’s license in person and pass a vision test. In some cases, other exams may be required. If a knowledge test is required, you may be eligible to select “eLearning” when completing your application online. DMV sends a renewal notice to your address of record about 90 days before your driver’s license expires. If you do not receive a renewal notice, complete a Driver License or Identification Card Application at dmv.ca.gov/dlservices or at a DMV office. Visit dmv.ca.gov/driver-ed for more information and sample tests.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › DMV’s Community Liaison and Outreach · ¶1
text: The Community Liaison’s primary function is to represent public safety interests for all Californians, with a focus in addressing the concerns of senior drivers and teens. The liaison can assist as a go-between to ensure drivers are treated fairly, consistently with laws and regulations, and with dignity and respect. While the Community Liaison cannot represent you in a DMV hearing or reexamination, they can provide you with useful tools and information.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › DMV’s Community Liaison and Outreach · ¶2
text: For information about outreach services in your area or to speak to a liaison, contact Community Liaison and Outreach at (833) 493-0675.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Cognitive Impairment · ¶1
text: Seniors suffering from dementia present a significant challenge to safe driving. Individuals with progressive dementia ultimately lose their ability to drive safely. It is often up to caregivers, physicians, and law enforcement, to stop these seniors from driving and arrange alternative transportation. For more information about the reexamination process, visit dmv.ca.gov/reexamination .

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Mature Driver Program · ¶1
text: The Mature Driver Improvement Program is an eight-hour course for drivers 55 years old and older. It covers a range of topics that are of special interest to mature drivers.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Mature Driver Program · ¶2
text: Your insurance company may offer discounts if you complete the program. Contact your insurance provider with a copy of your completion certificate. Your certificate is valid for three years. You can renew it by completing another four-hour course.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Mature Driver Program · ¶3
text: You can take the course through DMV-approved providers. Visit dmv.ca.gov/seniors for more information, including locations near you.

locator: Section 13: Seniors and Driving › Senior ID Cards · ¶1
text: If you are 62 years old or older, you are eligible for a no-fee Senior ID card. Drivers of any age who are unable to continue driving safely due to a physical or mental condition may be eligible to exchange their driver’s license for a no-fee ID card. The ID card serves as identification only. Details may be found at dmv.ca.gov/id-cards .

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Intro · ¶1
text: A California driver’s license allows you to drive on public roads.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Intro · ¶2
text: Before you can get a driver’s license in California, you are required to pass the knowledge and behind-the-wheel drive tests based on information in this handbook.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Intro · ¶3
text: You must have the correct license to drive your vehicle type. Most people need a noncommercial Class C driver’s license. To operate commercial vehicles, motorcycles, and other types of vehicles, you must have a different class of license.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Intro · ¶4
text: For information on vehicles covered by a Class C, visit dmv.ca.gov/dl .

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › REAL ID Driver’s License · ¶1
text: Beginning May 2025, your driver’s license or identification (ID) card must be REAL ID compliant if you use it to:

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › REAL ID Driver’s License · item 1
text: Board an airplane for domestic flights.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › REAL ID Driver’s License · item 2
text: Enter military bases.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › REAL ID Driver’s License · item 3
text: Enter most federal facilities.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › REAL ID Driver’s License · ¶2
text: Visit dmv.ca.gov/realid to learn more about applying for a REAL ID.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › Driver’s Licenses for Undocumented Residents · ¶1
text: California offers driver’s licenses for all residents regardless of immigration status. For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/dl .

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › Organ and Tissue Donor · ¶1
text: For information, visit donateLIFEcalifornia.org .

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › Veterans · ¶1
text: Visit dmv.ca.gov/veterans to learn more about the requirements and benefits of a Veteran designation.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › ID Cards · ¶1
text: ID cards are issued for identification purposes to eligible persons of any age. They do not permit you to drive. To get an ID, you must provide your identity document, residency documents, and social security number.

locator: Section 1: The California Driver’s License › Card Designations › ID Cards · ¶2
text: Visit dmv.ca.gov/id-cards to complete an ID card application and get information on current acceptable documents and reduced-fee, no-fee, or senior ID cards.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests · ¶1
text: Here is an overview of the driver’s license tests:

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests · item 1
text: Vision Test DMV tests all applicants to ensure they can see well enough to drive safely. If you take your vision test with corrective or contact lenses, your driver’s license will have a corrective lenses restriction. If you do not pass your vision test, you will be asked to have your eye doctor complete a Report of Vision Examination (DL 62) form. For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/vision-standards .

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests · item 2
text: Knowledge Test When you apply for an original driver’s license, you must pass a knowledge test with multiple choice questions. You are allowed three attempts to pass before you must reapply. Minors must wait seven days to retake a failed knowledge test, not including the day of the failure. When renewing your driver’s license, eLearning may be an alternative testing option. This is a no-fail, self-paced interactive modulated course with quizzes after each module. The course can be taken on a computer, laptop, tablet, or mobile device. Testing options will be available once you complete your application at dmv.ca.gov/dl . Important You are not allowed to use any testing aids during knowledge tests, such as a California Driver’s Handbook or cell phone.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests · item 3
text: Behind-the-Wheel Drive Test When you apply for an original driver’s license, you will be tested on your ability to safely drive a vehicle. Upon renewal, drivers with a vision or medical condition may be required to take a behind-the-wheel test. The examiner may give two or more instructions at one time to determine whether you can understand and properly follow both directions. For example, “At the next street, make a left turn, and then at the first intersection make another left turn.” Visit dmv.ca.gov/make-an-appointment to schedule a behind-the-wheel drive test appointment.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › On the day of your behind-the-wheel test, you must bring: · item 1
text: Your instruction permit or driver’s license (if you have one).

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › On the day of your behind-the-wheel test, you must bring: · item 2
text: Another California-licensed driver who is at least 18 years old (25 for minors), unless you are already licensed to drive.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › On the day of your behind-the-wheel test, you must bring: · item 3
text: A vehicle that is safe to drive for your test.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › On the day of your behind-the-wheel test, you must bring: · item 4
text: Valid proof of insurance and vehicle registration.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › On the day of your behind-the-wheel test, you must bring: · item 5
text: If you plan to use a rental vehicle for your drive test, your name must be listed on the rental contract. The contract must not exclude behind-the-wheel drive tests.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › On the day of your behind-the-wheel test, you must bring: · ¶1
text: Note Minors must wait 14 days to retake a failed behind-the-wheel drive test, not including the day of the failure.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › Before you begin, the DMV examiner will ask you to locate and demonstrate the following: · item 1
text: Driver window – The window on the driver side must open.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › Before you begin, the DMV examiner will ask you to locate and demonstrate the following: · item 2
text: Windshield – The windshield must allow a full, clear, unblocked view for you and the DMV examiner. Windshield cracks may postpone your test.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › Before you begin, the DMV examiner will ask you to locate and demonstrate the following: · item 3
text: Rear-view mirrors – At least two rearview mirrors. One of them must be on the left side of your vehicle.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › Before you begin, the DMV examiner will ask you to locate and demonstrate the following: · item 4
text: Brake lights – The right and left brake lights must be operational.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › Before you begin, the DMV examiner will ask you to locate and demonstrate the following: · item 5
text: Tires – The tires must have at least 1/32-inch of uniformed tread depth. The use of a donut tire is not allowed during a drive test.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › Before you begin, the DMV examiner will ask you to locate and demonstrate the following: · item 6
text: Foot brake – There must be at least one inch of clearance between the bottom of the brake pedal and the floorboard when depressed.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Driver’s License Tests › Before you begin, the DMV examiner will ask you to locate and demonstrate the following: · ¶4
text: The use of a recording device, including a video/audio recorder, is prohibited during a behind-the-wheel drive test. If the recording device cannot be powered off or disabled, the applicant must block it so there is no visual or audio recording during the drive test.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Other Things to Know for Your Behind-the-Wheel Test · ¶1
text: The drive test is intended to determine your skill in operating a motor vehicle in most road situations and evaluate your abilities, not the vehicle’s technology. Therefore, advanced driver assistance systems technologies, such as automated parallel parking, lane departure, and adaptive cruise control, are not permitted during the drive test. Vehicle safety technology, such as backup cameras and blind spot monitors, may be used on the drive test, but are not a replacement for an actual visual check of your mirrors and blind spots.

locator: Section 3: The Testing Process › Other Things to Know for Your Behind-the-Wheel Test · ¶2
text: To view a sample of the Driving Performance Evaluation (DPE) Score Sheet, visit dmv.ca.gov/teendrivers . For a sample of the Supplemental/Area DPE Score Sheet, visit dmv.ca.gov/seniors .

locator: Section 11: Vehicle Registration Requirements › Intro · ¶1
text: You need to register your vehicle in California to use it in the state. For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/vrservices .

locator: Section 11: Vehicle Registration Requirements › Buying or Selling a Vehicle · ¶1
text: When you buy a vehicle, you have 10 days to transfer ownership to your name.

locator: Section 11: Vehicle Registration Requirements › Buying or Selling a Vehicle · ¶2
text: When you sell a vehicle, you must notify DMV within five days by completing a Notice of Transfer and Release of Liability at dmv.ca.gov/nrl .

locator: Section 11: Vehicle Registration Requirements › Out-of-State Vehicles · ¶1
text: You have 20 days to register your vehicle after you become a resident or get a job in California. For more information, visit dmv.ca.gov/outofstatevr .

locator: Section 11: Vehicle Registration Requirements › Out-of-State Vehicles · ¶2
text: All vehicles registered in California are required to meet California requirements including vehicle emission controls in support of California’s clean air standards. DMV cannot register a vehicle if it does not qualify.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Single Solid Yellow Line · ¶1
text: A single solid yellow line marks the center of a road with two-way traffic. Do not pass a vehicle in front of you if there is only one lane of traffic going your direction and a solid yellow line on your side of the road.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Passing Lanes · ¶1
text: On a multilane road, the passing lane (far left lane) is the lane closest to the center divider and is used to pass other vehicles.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · ¶2
text: You should:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · item 6
text: Not drive past the patrol vehicle. Do not speed up until the officer turns off their emergency lights and traffic conditions allow you to return to your normal speed.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Choose Between Hazards · ¶1
text: Sometimes dangers will be on both sides of the road at the same time. For example, parked cars to the right and oncoming cars to the left.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving (Continued) › Choose Between Hazards · ¶2
text: If one danger is greater than the other, give more space to the most dangerous situation. Suppose you are on a two-lane road with an oncoming vehicle to the left and a bicyclist ahead to your right. Instead of driving between the vehicle and the bicyclist, take one danger at a time. Slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass. When the vehicle has passed, move to the left to allow plenty of space (at least three feet) to pass the bicyclist. If there is a steady flow of oncoming vehicles, use as much of the left lane as you safely can to pass the bicyclist.

locator: Section 10: Financial Responsibility, Insurance Requirements, and Collisions › Collisions › Causes of Collisions · ¶2
text: If you see a vehicle’s emergency flashers ahead, slow down. There may be a collision or other road emergency. Pass carefully.

locator: Section 14: Glossary › Intro · row 6
text: Three-second rule | A driving rule that helps you estimate how closely you should follow other vehicles. When the vehicle in front of you passes a certain point, such as a sign, count three seconds. If you pass the same point before you finish counting, you are following too closely.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Center Left Turn Lanes · ¶1
text: A center left turn lane is located in the middle of a two-way street. It is marked on both sides by two painted lines. The inner line is broken and the outer line is solid. Use the center left turn lane to prepare for and make a left turn or U-turn. It is not a regular traffic lane or passing lane. You may only drive for 200 feet in the center left turn lane. To turn left from this lane:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · ¶1
text: Some two-lane roads have special turnout areas or lanes. Merge into these areas or lanes to allow cars behind you to pass.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · image
text: Slower Traffic Use Turnouts

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Turnout Areas or Lanes · ¶2
text: You must use a turnout area or lane to let other vehicles pass when you are driving slowly on a two-lane road, where passing is unsafe, and there are five or more vehicles following you.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · image
text: Bicycle Lane

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Types of Lanes › Bicycle Lanes · ¶2
text: Example of shared roadway. Three (3) feet of distance must be maintained between the car and cyclist.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · ¶1
text: You must judge whether you have enough space to pass whenever you approach:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 1
text: An oncoming vehicle or bicyclist.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 2
text: A hill, curve, intersection, or road obstruction. To safely pass, the hill or curve should be at least one-third of a mile ahead.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · ¶1
text: Do not pass over double solid yellow lines. Stay to the right of these lines unless you are:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · ¶2
text: Before you pass, look ahead for road conditions that may cause other vehicles to move into your lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · ¶3
text: Do not pass:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 3
text: If you are approaching a hill or curve and cannot see if other traffic is approaching. This is very dangerous on one and two lane roads.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 4
text: Within 100 feet of an intersection, bridge, tunnel, railroad crossing, or other hazardous area.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 5
text: At crossroads and driveways.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing · item 6
text: Unless you have enough space to return to your lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · ¶1
text: When you are going to pass on an open highway:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 1
text: Signal that you plan on passing.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 2
text: Look over your shoulder to check your blind spots.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 3
text: Drive into the passing lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 1
text: In a high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) carpool lane that has a designated entrance on the left.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 4
text: Speed up to pass the vehicle.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 5
text: Signal and return to your original lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · ¶2
text: You may pass on the right only when:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 6
text: An open highway has two or more lanes going in your direction.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 7
text: The driver ahead of you is turning left and you can safely pass on the right. Never pass on the left if the driver is signaling a left turn.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · item 8
text: You are on a one-way street.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › How to Pass · ¶3
text: Never drive off the paved or main-traveled part of the road to pass.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Passing › Being Passed · ¶1
text: If a vehicle is passing you or signals that they plan on passing, allow the vehicle to pass. Maintain your lane position and your speed.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads (Continued) › Parking › Parallel Parking · ¶7
text: Turn off your vehicle and set the parking brake. Before you exit your vehicle, look carefully for passing vehicles, bicycles, and motorcycles. Exit when safe.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Traffic Control › Signs › Red YIELD Sign · ¶1
text: Slow down and be ready to stop to let any vehicle, bicyclist, or pedestrian pass before you proceed.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 2
text: Instructed by construction or other signs to drive on the other side of the road because your side is closed or blocked.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Traffic Control › Signs › Yellow and Black Circular Sign or X-shaped Sign · ¶1
text: You are approaching a railroad crossing. Look, listen, slow down, and prepare to stop. Let any trains pass before you proceed.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Traffic Control › Signs › White Rectangular Sign · ¶1
text: Communicates many important rules you must obey.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Traffic Control › Signs › Warning Signs · image
text: Examples of Red and White Regulatory Signs, White Regulatory Signs, Highway Construction and Maintenance Signs, Guide Signs, Hazardous Loads Placards, and Slow Moving Vehicle Placard

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · ¶2
text: How to use a roundabout:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Roundabouts · item 5
text: Travel in a counter-clockwise direction. Do not stop or pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · ¶5
text: Other things to keep in mind:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Pedestrians · item 4
text: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. You may not be able to see a pedestrian crossing the street.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road › Right-of-Way Rules: Who Goes First? › Mountain Roads · ¶1
text: If two vehicles meet on a steep narrow road and neither vehicle can pass, the vehicle facing uphill has the right-of-way. The vehicle facing downhill has more control when backing up the hill. The vehicle facing downhill should back up until the vehicle going uphill can pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Turning · ¶1
text: When a vehicle turns, the rear wheels follow a shorter path than the front wheels. The longer the vehicle, the greater the difference in the length of the turning path. This is why large vehicles and truck drivers must often swing wide to complete a turn. When you follow a large vehicle, look at its turn signals before you start to pass. It may appear to be turning one direction but instead is swinging wide in the opposite direction in order to turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · ¶1
text: Large vehicles and trucks are not as easy to maneuver as passenger vehicles. On a divided highway with four or more traffic lanes in one direction, they may be driven in the two lanes farthest to the right. When driving near large vehicles and trucks, do not:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid Yellow Lines · item 3
text: Turning left across a single set of double yellow lines to enter or exit a driveway or private road or make a U-turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Maneuvering · item 2
text: Drive next to them longer than you need to. Always pass a large vehicle on the left side. After you pass the large vehicle or truck, move ahead of it. Driving alongside a large vehicle makes it hard for the driver to avoid dangers in the road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶1
text: Safety zones are spaces set aside for pedestrians waiting for buses, streetcars, and trolleys. Safety zones are marked by raised buttons or markers on a road. Do not drive through a safety zone under any condition.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶2
text: When a bus, streetcar, or trolley is stopped at a safety zone or traffic light, you may pass at no more than 10 mph.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · image
text: Trolley next to demarked safe zone.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶3
text: Safe Zones are marked by dotted white lines.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · ¶4
text: Do not overtake and pass a light rail vehicle or streetcar on the left side, whether it is moving or standing, unless:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 1
text: When the tracks are so close to the right side that the passenger vehicle cannot pass on the right.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 2
text: You are on a one-way street.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Buses, Streetcars, Trolleys · item 3
text: A traffic officer directs you to pass on the left.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · ¶1
text: Motorcyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other vehicle drivers. To safely share the road with motorcyclists:

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Broken Yellow Line · ¶1
text: A broken yellow line indicates you may pass if the broken line is next to your driving lane. Only pass when it is safe.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 3
text: Whenever possible, give a motorcycle the full lane. It is legal to share lanes with motorcycles, this is known as lane splitting.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 4
text: Never try to pass a motorcycle in the same lane as you.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Motorcycles · item 6
text: When possible, move to one side of your lane to give motorcyclists more room to pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶1
text: Give the right-of-way to any law enforcement vehicle, fire engine, ambulance, or other emergency vehicle using a siren and red lights. Failure to pull over may result in a ticket. Drive to the right edge of the road and stop until the emergency vehicle(s) have passed.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Emergency Vehicles · ¶3
text: When approaching a stationary emergency vehicle with flashing emergency signal lights (hazard lights), move over and slow down.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · ¶1
text: Bicyclists traveling slower than the flow of traffic must ride as close as possible to the right curb or edge of the road, unless :

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 1
text: Passing a vehicle or another bicycle in the same direction.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 2
text: Preparing to make a left turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 3
text: Avoiding a hazard or road condition.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 4
text: A lane is too narrow for a bicycle and a vehicle to safely travel side-by-side in the lane.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Lane Markings › Double Solid White Lines · ¶1
text: Double solid white lines indicate a lane barrier between a regular use and a preferential use lane, such as a carpool (HOV) lane. You may also see double solid white lines in or near freeway on and off ramps. Never change lanes over double solid white lines. Wait until you see a single broken white line.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 5
text: Approaching a right turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · item 6
text: On a one-way road with two or more lanes. In this case, a bicyclist may ride near the left curb or edge of the road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Bicycling in Travel Lanes · ¶2
text: Drivers should follow at a safe distance. When it is safe, the bicyclist should move to a position that allows vehicles to pass.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶1
text: To safely pass a bicyclist that is in the travel lane, you may need to change to another lane. In this case, pass safely, then return to your original lane. Leave space between your vehicle and the bicyclist.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · image
text: Car passing a cyclist. The car leaves enough space between itself and the bicyclist as it passes.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶2
text: Right

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · image
text: Car attempting to pass a cyclist without leaving any room. The car hits the cyclist.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶3
text: Wrong

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · ¶4
text: When you cannot change lanes to pass a bicyclist, allow at least three feet between your vehicle and the bicyclist. If you cannot give three feet of space, do not pass the cyclist until three feet of clearance can be given. This will help you avoid putting the bicyclist in danger. Remember to:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 1
text: Give bicyclists enough space so they are not forced into parked vehicles or open vehicle doors.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · ¶3
text: Here are some tips for choosing a lane:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 2
text: Only merge toward the curb or into the bike lane when it is safe.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 3
text: Merge safely behind a bicyclist when preparing to make a turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 4
text: Enter a bike lane no more than 200 feet before starting a turn.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 5
text: Check for bicyclists when changing lanes or entering traffic. They may be hidden in a vehicle’s blind spots.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Bicycles › Passing a Bicyclist · item 6
text: Be careful when approaching or passing a bicyclist on a two-lane road.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · ¶1
text: Drivers must move over and slow down for emergency and road work vehicles. These include:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · item 1
text: Stationary emergency vehicles or tow trucks displaying flashing amber warning lights.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Road Workers and Work Zones › Move Over and Slow Down · item 2
text: Stopped road work vehicles displaying emergency flashing or amber warning lights.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Heavy Traffic or Bad Weather · ¶1
text: You must drive slower when there is heavy traffic or bad weather. At the same time, you should not block normal and reasonable traffic flow by driving too slowly. If you drive faster or slower than the speed limit, you may be cited. When another driver is close behind you and wishes to drive faster, move to the right. If you choose to drive slower than other traffic, drive in the right lane. Refer to Choosing a Lane in Section 6 for more information.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · image
text: School bus with red lights flashing and a crossing guard next to it. Students are near the bus. Cars are stopped around the bus.

locator: Section 6: Navigating the Roads › Traffic Lanes › Choosing a Lane · item 1
text: Use the left lane to pass or turn left.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · ¶1
text: All vehicles must stop for school buses.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · ¶2
text: The speed limit is 25 mph within 500 feet of a school while children are outside or crossing the street. Some school zones may have speed limits as low as 15 mph. When near schools, look for:

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 5
text: When the bus flashes red lights (located at the top, front, and back of the bus), you must stop from either direction until the children are safely across the street and the lights stop flashing. Remain stopped while the red lights are flashing. If you fail to stop, you may be fined up to $1,000 and your driving privilege could be suspended for one year.

locator: Section 7: Laws and Rules of the Road (Continued) › Sharing the Road › Around Children · item 6
text: If the school bus is on the other side of a divided or multilane highway (two or more lanes in each direction), you do not need to stop.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · ¶3
text: Create more space in front of your vehicle when:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Be Aware of Your Surroundings › Tailgating (Following Too Closely) · item 1
text: A tailgater is behind you. Maintain your course and speed. Then, when safe to do so, merge right to change into another lane and allow the tailgater to pass.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › High Winds · item 5
text: Be proactive. It may be safer to pull over and wait for the storm to pass.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · ¶1
text: It is best to avoid driving in heavy fog or smoke. Consider postponing your trip until the fog clears. If you must drive in heavy fog or smoke:

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Fog or Heavy Smoke · item 7
text: Avoid crossing lanes or passing traffic unless absolutely necessary.

locator: Section 8: Safe Driving › Understand the Road Conditions › Law Enforcement Traffic Breaks · ¶1
text: During a traffic break, the officer turns on their emergency lights and slowly weaves across lanes. Law enforcement uses traffic breaks to:

locator: Changing directions › Intro · ¶1
text: Before you turn a corner, back up, change lanes or turn around, you need to know what is beside and behind you. Always check your mirrors and over your shoulder to make sure the way is clear and you have enough space to complete the move safely.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶1
text: To turn a corner, signal well before the turn. When the way is clear, move into the proper lane, either the far right lane for a right turn or the far left lane in your direction for a left turn. Signal your turn and look from side to side and check your blind spots to make sure the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶2
text: Slow down before you enter the turn; the sharper the turn, the slower you should go. To keep full control of the vehicle, finish braking before you turn the steering wheel.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶3
text: For a sharp turn, turn the steering wheel with one hand and cross the other hand over it. Grip the wheel on the other side and continue turning. This is called “hand over hand steering.” When you have completed the turn, relax your grip on the steering wheel and let it slip or gently feed it through your hands to return to the straight-ahead position. Do not turn the steering wheel with one finger or the flat palm of your hand. Gradually increase speed as you complete the turn.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶4
text: Remember, drivers often lose control of vehicles and skid because they try to do more than one thing at a time. Try not to brake and steer at the same time.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · image
heading: Diagram 2-30 | Alt text: “a right turn at a red light”
text: a right turn at a red light

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶1
text: Unless signs or pavement markings tell you not to, always begin and end a right turn close to the right side of the road.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶2
text: To make a right turn, signal well before the turn and move into the right-hand lane when the way is clear. If the right-hand lane is not marked, keep as far to the right of the road as possible. Look ahead, left, right and left again before starting to turn. If you have not seen any smaller vehicles or pedestrians, check your right rear blind spot. Let cyclists, limited-speed motorcycles, or moped riders go through the intersection before you turn. When it is safe, complete your turn into the right-hand lane of the road you are entering.

locator: Changing directions › Right turn on a red light · ¶1
text: Unless a sign tells you not to, you may make a right turn facing a red light as long as you first come to a complete stop and wait until the way is clear. Remember to signal your turn and yield to pedestrians and others using the road.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶1
text: Unless signs or pavement markings tell you not to, always begin and end a left turn in the far left lane in your direction.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶2
text: To make a left turn, signal well before the turn and move into the far left lane when the way is clear. Look ahead, behind, left, right and left again and check your blind spots. Make your turn when the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶3
text: When you are stopped at an intersection waiting for approaching traffic to clear, don't turn your steering wheel to the left until you can complete the turn. With your wheels turned to the left, your vehicle could be pushed into the path of oncoming traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶4
text: When two vehicles coming from opposite directions meet in an intersection waiting to turn left, each should turn to the left of the other after yielding the right-of-way to pedestrians and oncoming traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶5
text: Motorcycles, bicycles, limited-speed motorcycles and mopeds turn left at intersections in the same way as larger vehicles. If you are making a left turn behind one of these vehicles, do not pull up beside it to make your turn at the same time. Stay behind and turn when the way is clear. Wait for the smaller vehicle to move right before you pass.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶6
text: The following diagrams show you the correct way to turn left on different types of roads:

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · image
heading: Diagram 2-31: Two-way road to a two-way road. | Alt text: “a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road”
text: a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶7
text: Turn from the lane closest to the centre line to the lane right of the centre line, following a smooth arc. Then, when you can, move into the right curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · image
heading: Diagram 2-32: Two-way road to a one-way road. | Alt text: “a left turn from a two-way road to a one-way road”
text: a left turn from a two-way road to a one-way road

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶8
text: Turn from the lane closest to the centre line to the left curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · image
heading: Diagram 2-33: One-way road to a two-way road. | Alt text: “a left turn from a one-way road to a two-way road”
text: a left turn from a one-way road to a two-way road

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶9
text: Turn from the left curb lane to the lane just right of the centre line. Then, when you can, move into the right curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · image
heading: Diagram 2-34: One-way road to a one-way road. | Alt text: “a left turn from a one-way road to a one-way road”
text: a left turn from a one-way road to a one-way road

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶10
text: Turn from the left curb lane to the left curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · image
heading: Diagram 2-35 | Alt text: “an intersection with marked left-turn lanes”
text: an intersection with marked left-turn lanes

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶1
text: Some roads have special lanes for vehicles turning left (Diagram 2-35). At an intersection where left-turn lanes are marked on the pavement, make your turn from the marked lane. Keep this lane position as you turn onto the other road.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · image
heading: Diagram 2-36 | Alt text: “a roadway with a centre lane marked as a two-way left-turn lane”
text: a roadway with a centre lane marked as a two-way left-turn lane

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶2
text: The centre lane of some roads is used as a two-way left-turn lane (Diagram 2-36). This lets left-turning vehicles from both directions wait for a chance to turn without holding up traffic. To use a two-way, left-turn lane, follow these steps:

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · item 1
text: Signal and move into the centre lane shortly before your turn. Slow down.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · item 2
text: Carefully move forward to a spot opposite the road or driveway where you want to turn.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · item 3
text: Make your turn when the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶3
text: Remember that vehicles from the opposite direction also use this lane to turn left. As they wait in front of you, it may be hard for you to see oncoming traffic. Only go when you are sure the way is clear. These left-turn lanes are not to be used for passing.

locator: Changing directions › Left turn on a red light · ¶1
text: You may turn left from a one-way road to a one-way road on a red light after coming to a complete stop and making sure the way is clear. Yield to pedestrians and traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts · image
heading: Diagram 2-37 | Alt text: “a two-laned roundabout”
text: a two-laned roundabout

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · image
heading: Diagram 2-38 | Alt text: “a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road”
text: a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: As you approach the roundabout, look for signage to choose your exit. Choose which lane to use as you would for any other intersection (See Diagram 2-37). Use the left lane to turn left or to go straight. Use the right lane to turn right or to go straight. (See Diagram 2-38). Do not enter a roundabout from the right lane if you want to turn left. Cyclists generally keep to the centre of the appropriate lane, or dismount and use the roundabout as a pedestrian would. (See Diagram 2-39.)

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 2
text: Slow down and watch for pedestrians on the approach to the yield line at the entrance of the roundabout. Stay in your lane.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · image
heading: Diagram 2-39 | Alt text: “a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road”
text: a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 1
text: Visual checks : Do visual checks of all vehicles already in the roundabout and those waiting to enter (including cyclists).

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 2
text: Look left : Traffic in the roundabout has the right-of-way. When preparing to enter the roundabout, pay special attention to the vehicles to your left. Adjust your speed or stop at the yield sign if necessary.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 3
text: Adequate gap : Watch for a safe opportunity to enter the roundabout. Enter when there is an adequate gap in the circulating traffic flow. Don't enter directly beside another already in the roundabout, as that may be exiting at the next exit.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 4
text: Travel counter-clockwise : Once in the roundabout, always keep to the right of the central island and travel in a counter-clockwise direction.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 5
text: Keep moving : Once you are in the roundabout, do not stop except to avoid a collision; you have the right-of-way over entering traffic. Do not change lanes while in the roundabout. If in the inside lane and you miss your exit, you must continue around until you meet your exit again.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · image
heading: Diagram 2-40 | Alt text: “a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road”
text: a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 1
text: Signal: Be sure to signal your exit and watch for pedestrians.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 2
text: Maintain your lane: Stay to the left if you entered from the left lane, or stay to the right if you entered from the right lane.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 3
text: Maintain your position: Maintain your position relative to other vehicles.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 4
text: Signal intent to exit: Once you have passed the exit before the one you want, use your right-turn signal.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 5
text: Left lane exit: If exiting from the left lane, watch out for vehicles on the right that continue to circulate around the roundabout.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Consider large vehicles · image
heading: Diagram 2-41 | Alt text: “a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road”
text: a left turn from a two-way road to a two-way road

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Consider large vehicles · ¶1
text: Allow extra room alongside large vehicles (trucks and buses). Large vehicles may have to swing wide on the approach or within the roundabout. Give them plenty of room. See (Diagram 2-41)

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Pull over for emergency vehicles · ¶1
text: If you are in a roundabout when an emergency vehicle approaches, exit at your intended exit and proceed beyond the traffic island before pulling over. If you have not entered the roundabout yet, pull over to the right if possible and wait until the emergency vehicle has passed.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶1
text: A driver negotiating a roundabout in a large vehicle (such as a truck or bus) may need to use the full width of the roadway, including the apron (a mountable portion of the centre island adjacent to the roadway) if provided. Prior to entering the roundabout, the vehicle may need to occupy both lanes. Give large vehicles plenty of room to manoeuvre.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶2
text: Note: In some areas of Ontario, older “traffic circles” exist. They are larger than roundabouts, allowing higher speeds, and force traffic to merge and weave. Modern roundabouts have a smaller inscribed circle diameter and use splitter islands (to deflect traffic) at the entry points to slow traffic speeds, or to provide pedestrian refuge. The entry is also controlled by the “yield to the left” principle; for example, cars circulating within the roundabout have the right-of-way over entering vehicles.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶1
text: Take extra care and move slowly when backing up (reversing) your vehicle. Before you begin, check that the way is clear behind you. Be especially careful to look for children and cyclists.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶2
text: While firmly holding the steering wheel, put the gear selector in reverse and turn sideways in your seat to look over your shoulder in the direction you are moving. If you are reversing straight back or to the right, turn your body and head to the right and look back over your right shoulder (Diagram 2-42).

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · image
heading: Diagram 2-42 | Alt text: “the proper body positioning when reversing a vehicle straight back or to the right”
text: the proper body positioning when reversing a vehicle straight back or to the right

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶3
text: If you are reversing to the left, turn your body and head to the left and look over your left shoulder (Diagram 2-43). Always check the opposite shoulder as well. If you are turning as you reverse, check that the front end of your vehicle does not hit anything.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶4
text: You don't have to wear a seatbelt while backing up. If you need to remove your seatbelt to turn your body to see properly when reversing, do so. But don't forget to buckle up again before moving forward.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · image
heading: Diagram 2-43 | Alt text: “the proper body positioning when reversing a vehicle to the left”
text: the proper body positioning when reversing a vehicle to the left

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶5
text: It is illegal to drive in reverse on a divided road that has a speed limit of more than 80 km/h . This applies to the travelled section of the road and the shoulder. The only exception to this rule is if you are trying to help someone in trouble.

locator: Changing directions › Turning around · ¶1
text: You may need to turn around when driving if you miss a turn or go too far along a road. There are several ways to do this safely.

locator: Changing directions › Turning around · ¶2
text: The simplest and safest way is to drive around the block, but there may be times when this is not possible. In such cases, a U-turn or a three-point turn may be necessary.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶1
text: Before you make a U-turn, check to make sure there is no sign saying not to.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶2
text: To make a U-turn safely, you must be able to see well in both directions. It is illegal to make a U-turn on a curve in the road, on or near a railway crossing or hilltop, or near a bridge or tunnel that blocks your view. Never make a U-turn unless you can see at least 150 metres in both directions.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶3
text: To make a U-turn, signal for a right turn, check your mirror and over your shoulder and pull over to the right side of the road. Stop. Signal a left turn and when traffic is clear in both directions, move forward and turn quickly and sharply into the opposite lane. Check for traffic as you turn.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶1
text: On narrow roads you need to make a three-point turn to change directions. As shown in Diagram 2-44, a three-point turn starts from the far right side of the road. Make sure you do not make a three-point turn on a curve in the road, on or near a railway crossing or hilltop, or near a bridge or tunnel that blocks your view.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: Signal for a left turn. When the way is clear in both directions, move forward, turning the steering wheel sharply left towards the curb on the far side of the road. When you have reached the left side of the road, stop. Shift the vehicle into reverse. Signal a right turn. After checking that the way is still clear, turn the steering wheel sharply to the right, while backing up slowly to the other side of the road. Stop. Shift to forward gear and check traffic. When the way is clear, drive forward.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · image
heading: Diagram 2-44 | Alt text: “how to make a three-point turn”
text: how to make a three-point turn

locator: Changing positions › Intro · ¶1
text: Changing your position on the road involves changing lanes or overtaking and passing another vehicle. Before beginning, be sure you have enough space and time to complete the move safely.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶1
text: Changing lanes is a movement from one lane to another on roads with two or more lanes in the same direction. You may have to change lanes to overtake another vehicle, to avoid a parked vehicle or when the vehicle ahead slows to turn at an intersection.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶2
text: Never change lanes without giving the proper signal and looking to make sure the move can be made safely.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶3
text: Here are the steps for making a lane change:

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 1
text: Check your mirrors for a space in traffic where you can enter safely.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 2
text: Check your blind spot by looking over your shoulder in the direction of the lane change. Be especially careful to check for bicycles and other small vehicles. Signal that you want to move left or right.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 3
text: Check again to make sure the way is clear and that no one is coming too fast from behind or from two lanes over on a multi-lane road.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 4
text: Steer gradually into the new lane. Do not slow down, maintain the same speed or gently increase it.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶4
text: Never make sudden lane changes by cutting in front of another vehicle, including bicycles. Other drivers expect you to stay in the lane you are already in. Even if you signal, they expect you to yield the right-of-way.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶5
text: Avoid unnecessary lane changes or weaving from lane to lane. You are more likely to cause a collision, especially in heavy traffic or bad weather. Don't change lanes in or near an intersection. Remember that spending a few seconds behind another vehicle is often safer than going around it.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · image
heading: Diagram 2-45 | Alt text: “how to make a lane change”
text: how to make a lane change

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶1
text: Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle. While all public roads have speed limits, not all vehicles travel at the same speed. For example, cyclists, road service vehicles and drivers ahead that are preparing to turn are usually slower than the through traffic. You may want to pass some slow-moving vehicles when you are following them.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶2
text: Never overtake and pass another vehicle unless you are sure you can do so without danger to yourself or others. Don't pass moving snow plows under any conditions. If in doubt, do not pass.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶3
text: Here are the steps for passing a vehicle:

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 1
text: Use your left-turn signal to show that you want to pass and check that the way is clear ahead and behind before moving into the passing lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 2
text: Watch for bicycles and small vehicles that may be hidden from view in front of the vehicle you are about to pass. Also watch for vehicles that may be turning left in front of you and vehicles or pedestrians entering the road from another road or driveway.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 3
text: Change lanes only after signalling. After overtaking, signal that you want to move back into the lane you started from, and when you can see the entire front of the vehicle you are passing in your inside mirror, make the lane change. Be careful not to cut off a vehicle by suddenly moving in front of it.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 4
text: If the vehicle you are passing speeds up, do not race. Go back to your original lane. And do not speed up when another driver is trying to pass you. It is unlawful and dangerous.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · image
heading: Diagram 2-46 | Alt text: “how to pass another vehicle”
text: how to pass another vehicle

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶4
text: Passing within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover is not permitted. Passing left of a centreline is not permitted 30 metres from a bridge, viaduct or tunnel. Don't attempt to pass when approaching the crest of a hill or on a curve where your vision of oncoming traffic is obstructed and there is not enough clear distance ahead to pass in safety.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶5
text: When passing parked vehicles, watch carefully for people suddenly opening doors or for doors opened to load and unload.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶6
text: Motorcycles, bicycles, limited-speed motorcycles and mopeds often need to pull to the left or right side of their lane to avoid dangerous road conditions or to be seen by other drivers. Do not take this as an invitation to pass in the same lane. If you do want to pass these vehicles, do so by changing lanes.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶7
text: When faster traffic wants to pass you, move to the right and let it pass in safety. When being passed on an undivided road where the passing driver has pulled into the opposite lane, pay attention to oncoming traffic and move closer to the right side of the lane. Be prepared to slow down to let the passing driver get in front of you more quickly to prevent a collision.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶8
text: On many high-speed roads with three or more lanes in each direction, trucks are not allowed to drive in the far left-hand lane. This means that the lane next to it is the truck passing lane. If you are in this lane and a truck wants to pass, move into the right-hand lane as soon as you can.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · image
heading: Diagram 2-47 | Alt text: “how to pass another vehicle”
text: how to pass another vehicle

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · ¶1
text: Be very careful when you pass other vehicles at night. If you have to pass and the way is clear, follow these steps:

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 1
text: Switch your headlights to low beams as you approach a vehicle from behind.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 2
text: Signal, check your mirrors and blind spot, and pull out to pass. As you move alongside the vehicle you are passing, switch on your high beams. This will let you see more of the road ahead.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 3
text: When you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror, you are far enough ahead to pull back into the right lane. Remember to signal.

locator: Changing positions › Passing and climbing lanes · image
heading: Diagram 2-48 | Alt text: “a passing or climbing lane”
text: a passing or climbing lane

locator: Changing positions › Passing and climbing lanes · ¶1
text: Some roads have special passing or climbing lanes. These lanes let slower vehicles move into the right-hand lane so that faster ones can pass safely in the left lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing and climbing lanes · ¶2
text: An advance sign tells drivers they will soon have a chance to pass. Another sign warns when the lane is ending so drivers in the right-hand lane can begin to merge safely with traffic in the left-hand lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the shoulder · ¶1
text: You may drive on the right shoulder only to pass a vehicle turning left and only if the shoulder is paved. You may not pass on the left shoulder, paved or not.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the right · ¶1
text: Most passing is done on the left. You may pass on the right on multi-lane or one-way roads and when overtaking a streetcar or a left-turning vehicle.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the right · ¶2
text: Passing on the right can be more dangerous than passing on the left. If you are driving in the left most lane with a slower vehicle in front of you, wait for the vehicle to move to the right. Do not suddenly change lanes and pass on the right; the driver in front may realize you want to pass and move to the right at the same time you do.

locator: Changing positions › Passing streetcars · image
heading: Diagram 2-49 | Alt text: “a vehicle stopped the required two metres behind the rear doors of a stopped streetcar”
text: a vehicle stopped the required two metres behind the rear doors of a stopped streetcar

locator: Changing positions › Passing streetcars · ¶1
text: You must pass streetcars on the right unless you are driving on a one-way road.

locator: Changing positions › Passing streetcars · ¶2
text: At streetcar stops, stay at least two metres behind the rear doors where passengers are getting off or on. This rule does not apply at stops where an area has been set aside for streetcar passengers. Always pass these areas at a reasonable speed and be prepared for pedestrians to make sudden or unexpected moves.

text: By the end of this section, you should know:
