locator: Dealing with emergencies › Intro · ¶1
text: If you drive often or travel alone, you need to be ready to deal with emergencies. Here are some suggestions for coping with some common road emergencies.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your brakes fail · ¶1
text: Try pumping the brake pedal to temporarily restore hydraulic brake pressure. If this does not work, apply the parking brake gently but firmly while holding the release button. It is a good idea for new drivers to practice a parking-brake emergency stop under controlled conditions with a qualified driving instructor. Total brake failure is very rare on modern vehicles. If your brakes do fail and you manage to stop, do not drive away. Call for help.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your gas pedal sticks · ¶1
text: First try to lift the pedal by slipping your foot under it. Do not reach down with your hands while the vehicle is moving. If this does not work, turn on your hazard lights, shift to neutral and stop as soon as you safely can, preferably off the road. Turn off the ignition and do not drive away. Call for help.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your headlights go out · ¶1
text: Check the switch immediately. If the lights stay out, turn on your hazard lights and bring your vehicle to a safe stop off the road. Call for help. It is dangerous and illegal to drive at night without lights.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶1
text: At the first sign of trouble, begin to pull over. Do not wait for your vehicle to stall on the freeway. Check your mirrors, put on your hazard lights, take your foot off the gas pedal and pull over to the nearest shoulder as quickly as possible. Never stop in the driving lanes.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶2
text: Be careful getting out of your vehicle. If possible, leave through the door away from traffic. Do not raise the hood.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶3
text: While you wait for help, stay in your vehicle with the doors locked. If someone stops to help, ask them to call the police or automobile club for you. If you have a cellular phone, call for help yourself.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶4
text: The Queen Elizabeth Way, the 400-series freeways and many other high-speed roads are patrolled by the Ontario Provincial Police. Stay with your vehicle, and help will arrive shortly.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your wheels go off the pavement · ¶1
text: Don't panic. Grip the steering wheel firmly. Take your foot off the gas pedal to slow down. Avoid heavy braking. When the vehicle is under control, steer toward the pavement. Be prepared to correct your steering and increase speed when your wheels are fully back on the pavement.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If a tire blows out · ¶1
text: Blowouts can cause tremendous steering and wheel vibration, but don't be alarmed. Take your foot off the gas pedal to slow down and steer the vehicle firmly in the direction you want to go. Bring the vehicle to a stop off the road.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶1
text: St. John Ambulance recommends that all drivers carry a well-stocked first-aid kit and know how to use it. Consider reading a book about first aid or sign up for a first-aid course. It could mean the difference between life and death in a collision.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶2
text: Every driver involved in a collision must stay at the scene or return to it immediately and give all possible assistance. If you are not personally involved in a collision, you should stop to offer help if police or other officials have not arrived.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶3
text: In a collision with injuries, possible fuel leaks or serious vehicle damage, stay calm and follow these steps:

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 1
text: Call for help or have someone else call. By law, you must report any collision to the police when there are injuries or damage to vehicles or other property exceeding $5,000.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 2
text: Turn off all engines and turn on emergency flashers. Set up warning signals or flares, or have someone warn approaching drivers.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 3
text: Do not let anyone smoke, light a match or put flares near any vehicle, in case of a fuel leak. If a vehicle is on fire, get the people out and make sure everyone is well out of the way. If there is no danger of fire or explosion, leave injured people where they are until trained medical help arrives.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 4
text: If you are trained in first aid, treat injuries in the order of urgency, within the level of your training. For example, clear the person's airway to restore breathing, give rescue breathing or stop bleeding by applying pressure with a clean cloth.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 5
text: If you are not trained in first aid, use common sense. For example, people in collisions often go into shock. Cover the person with a jacket or blanket to reduce the effects of shock.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 6
text: Stay with injured people until help arrives.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 7
text: Disabled vehicles on the road may be a danger to you and other drivers. Do what you can to make sure everyone involved in a collision is kept safe.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · ¶1
text: Follow these steps in a collision where there are no injuries:

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 1
text: If the vehicles are drivable, move them as far off the road as possible as this should not affect the police officer's investigation. This is especially important on busy or high-speed roads where it may be dangerous to leave vehicles in the driving lanes. So in a minor collision with no injuries, if you can “Steer it, Clear it”. If you cannot move the vehicles off the road, set up warning signals or flares far enough away to give other traffic time to slow down or stop.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 2
text: Call police (provincial or local, depending on where the collision takes place). By law, you must report any collision to the police when there are injuries or damage to vehicles or property exceeding $5,000.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 3
text: Give all possible help to police or anyone whose vehicle has been damaged. This includes giving police your name and address, the name and address of the registered owner of the vehicle, the vehicle plate and permit number and the liability insurance card.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 4
text: Get the names, addresses and phone numbers of all witnesses.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 5
text: If damage is less than $5,000, you are still required by law to exchange information with anyone whose vehicle has been damaged. However, the collision does not have to be reported to the police.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 6
text: If you have a camera or cell phone with a camera and it is safe to do so, take photos of the collision scene.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 7
text: If your vehicle must be towed, get the name and licence number of the tow truck operator and/or company. Make sure you understand where your vehicle is being towed.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 8
text: Contact your insurance company as soon as possible if you intend to make a claim.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Summary · item 1
text: What to do in emergency situations such as vehicle component failure, driving off the pavement or vehicle trouble on a freeway

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Summary · item 2
text: The steps to take if you are involved in a collision with or without injuries

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶1
text: Aggressive-driving behaviours, such as tailgating, speeding, failing to yield the right-of-way and cutting in front of someone too closely, may cause other drivers to become frustrated and angry and lead to a road-rage conflict between drivers. An angry driver may attempt dangerous retaliatory action. Avoid becoming angry on the road by following these tips:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 1
text: Know the warning signs of stress and combat them by getting fresh air, breathing deeply and slowly, and listening to relaxing music.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 2
text: Make a conscious decision not to take your problems with you when driving.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 3
text: If you are on a long trip, take a break from driving every few hours.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 4
text: Don't compete with another driver, or retaliate for what you believe to be inconsiderate behaviour.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 5
text: If someone else's driving annoys you, don't try to “educate” the person. Leave traffic enforcement to the police.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 6
text: Don't take other drivers' mistakes or behaviours personally.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 7
text: Avoid honking your horn at other drivers, unless absolutely necessary. A light tap on the horn is usually sufficient.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶2
text: Remember that if you drive responsibly and courteously, you are less likely to spark a road rage situation.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 8
text: Plan your route in advance. Some of the most erratic and inconsiderate driving occurs when a driver is lost.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 9
text: Drive in a courteous and consid­erate manner.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 10
text: Yield the right-of-way when it is courteous to do so.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 11
text: Be polite and let other drivers in front of you when they are signalling that they would like to do so.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 12
text: If you make a mistake while driving, indicate that you are sorry. An apology can greatly reduce the risk of conflict.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 13
text: Don't return aggression. Avoid eye contact and do not gesture back. Keep away from erratic drivers.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶3
text: If you are in a situation in which you feel threatened by another driver, do the following:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 14
text: Stay in your vehicle and lock the doors.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 15
text: If you have a cell phone, call police.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 16
text: Use your horn and signals to attract attention.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 17
text: If you believe you are being followed, do not drive home. Drive to a police station or a busy public place.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Street racing · ¶1
text: Street racing is one of the most serious and reckless forms of aggressive driving. It shows a callous disregard for other drivers and road users, and it puts everyone on the road at serious risk of injury or death. Street racers run the risk of being charged under the Criminal Code of Canada.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶1
text: Drowsiness has been identified as a causal factor in a growing number of collisions resulting in injury and fatality. Tired drivers can be as impaired as drunk drivers. They have a slower reaction time and are less alert.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶2
text: Studies have shown that collisions involving drowsiness tend to occur during late night/early morning hours (between 2 a.m. and 6 a.m.) or late afternoon (between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.). Studies also indicate that shift workers, people with undiagnosed or untreated sleep disorders, and commercial-vehicle operators, are at greater risk for such collisions.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶3
text: Always avoid driving when you are feeling drowsy. Scientific research confirms that you can fall asleep without actually being aware of it. Here are eight important warning signs that your drowsiness is serious enough to place you at risk:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 1
text: You have difficulty keeping your eyes open.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 2
text: Your head keeps tilting forward despite your efforts to keep your eyes on the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 3
text: Your mind keeps wandering and you can't seem to concentrate.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 4
text: You yawn frequently.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 5
text: You can't remember details about the last few kilometres you have travelled.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 6
text: You are missing traffic lights and signals.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 7
text: Your vehicle drifts into the next lane and you have to jerk it back into your lane.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 8
text: You have drifted off the road and narrowly avoided a crash.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶4
text: If you have one of these symptoms, you may be in danger of falling asleep. Pull off the road and park your vehicle in a safe, secure place. Use well-lit rest stops or truck stops on busy roads. Lock your doors, roll up your windows and take a nap.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶5
text: Stimulants are never a substitute for sleep. Drinks containing caffeine can help you feel more alert but, if you are sleep deprived, the effects wear off quickly. The same is true of turning up the volume of your radio or CD player and opening the window. You cannot trick your body into staying awake; you need to sleep. Remember, the only safe driver is a well-rested, alert driver.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶1
text: Be extra careful when driving through construction zones and areas where people are working on or near the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶2
text: When approaching a construction zone, proceed with caution and obey all warning signs, people and/or devices that are directing traffic through the area. Often, lower speed limits are posted to increase worker safety and reflect increased road hazards, such as construction vehicles in the area, uneven or gravel surfaces, narrowed lanes and so on. In the construction zone, drive carefully and adjust your driving to suit the conditions, do not change lanes, be ready for sudden stops and watch for workers and related construction vehicles and equipment on the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶3
text: Other types of workers and vehicles may also be present on the road and pose a hazard, such as roadside assistance and disable vehicles, surveyors, road maintenance or utility workers. Always slow down and pass with caution to prevent a collision. If safe to do so, move over a lane to increase the space between your vehicle and the hazard.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶4
text: Traffic-control workers direct vehicle traffic in work zones and prevent conflicts between construction activity and traffic. Whether you are driving during the day or at night, watch for traffic-control people and follow their instructions.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶5
text: Treat people working on roads with respect, and be patient if traffic is delayed. Sometimes traffic in one direction must wait while vehi­cles from the other direction pass through a detour. If your lane is blocked and no one is directing traffic, yield to the driver coming from the opposite direction. When the way is clear, move slowly and carefully around the obstacle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶6
text: Recent changes to the Highway Traffic Act have resulted in doubled fines for speeding in a construction zone when workers are present. It is also an offence to disobey STOP or SLOW signs displayed by a traffic-control person or firefighter.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶1
text: Crashes involving animals (mainly moose and deer) are a growing problem. Motor vehicle/wild animal collisions increased from 8,964 in 1999 to 12,791 collisions in 2008. This represents an increase of 43 per cent over a 10-year period. Many of these collisions go unreported.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶2
text: You may encounter domestic, farm or wild animals on the road anywhere in Ontario. Scan the road ahead from shoulder to shoulder. If you see an animal on or near the road, slow down and pass carefully as they may suddenly bolt onto the road. Many areas of the province have animal crossing signs which warn drivers of the danger of large animals (such as moose, deer or cattle) crossing the road. Be cautious when you see these signs, especially during dusk-to-dawn hours when wild animals are most active.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶3
text: To reduce your chances of hitting an animal:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 1
text: Reduce speed in darkness, rain and fog. These conditions can reduce your ability to see an animal on or near the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 2
text: Travel at a safe speed and stay alert. Driver inattention and speed are common factors in animal-vehicle crashes.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 3
text: Watch for shining eyes at the roadside. If you do see shining eyes, slow down and be ready to stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 4
text: Keep your windshield clean and headlights properly adjusted.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 5
text: Use high beams whenever possible and safe to do so, and scan both sides of the road ahead.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶4
text: If you see an animal:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 6
text: Slow down and sound your horn.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 7
text: Be alert for other animals that may be with the one you've seen.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 8
text: Don't try to drive around the animal. Animal movements are unpredictable.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 9
text: If you wish to watch an animal, find a safe place to pull completely off the road and park first. Do not park on the shoulder of the road, as other drivers may be distracted by the animal and hit your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 10
text: Stay in your vehicle; getting out increases your chance of being hit by another vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 11
text: If you hit a deer or moose, report it to the local police service or the Ministry of Natural Resources. Do not try to move an injured animal.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶1
text: Driving is a job that requires your full attention every time you get behind the wheel, even if your vehicle has driver-assistance features. Any secondary activity will detract from your ability to drive properly and safely. You must reduce distractions and focus on your driving.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶2
text: Ontario’s distracted driving laws apply to the use of hand-held communication/entertainment devices and certain display screens.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶3
text: While you are driving, including when you are stopped in traffic or at a red light, it is illegal to :

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 1
text: use a phone or other hand-held wireless communication device to text or dial, except to call 911 in an emergency

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 2
text: use a hand-held electronic entertainment device, such as a tablet or portable gaming console

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 3
text: view display screens unrelated to driving, such as watching a video

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 4
text: program a GPS device, except by voice commands

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶4
text: You are allowed to use hands-free wireless communications devices with an earpiece, lapel button or Bluetooth. You can view GPS display screens as long as they are built into your vehicle’s dashboard or securely mounted.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶5
text: Other actions such as eating, drinking, grooming, smoking, reading and reaching for objects are not part of Ontario’s distracted driving law. However, you can still be charged with careless or dangerous driving.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶6
text: Learn more about distracted driving .

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Careless driving · ¶1
text: You could face charges for careless driving if you endanger other people because of any kind of distraction. This includes distraction caused by both hand-held (e.g., phone) or hands-free (e.g., Bluetooth) devices.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Careless driving · ¶2
text: You could even be charged with dangerous driving – a criminal offence that carries heavier penalties, including long jail terms.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · ¶1
text: Use any of these tips to avoid distracted driving and its penalties:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 1
text: turn off your phone or switch it to silent mode before you get in the car

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 2
text: put it in the glove compartment (lock it, if you have to) or in a bag on the back seat

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 3
text: before you leave the house, record an outgoing message that tells callers you’re driving and you’ll get back to them when you’re off the road

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 4
text: some apps can block incoming calls and texts, or send automatic replies to people trying to call or text you

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 5
text: ask a passenger to take a call or respond to a text for you

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 6
text: if you must respond, or have to make a call or send a text, carefully pull over to a safe area

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 7
text: silence notifications that tempt you to check your phone

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · ¶1
text: About 100 people are killed and 16,000 are injured by distracted drivers every year in Ontario. About one in four of those deaths are vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · ¶2
text: Research shows that young people 16-25 are more likely to drive distracted than any age group and are the most likely to be killed or injured in a distracted driving collision.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · item 1
text: Texting or browsing on your phone takes your eyes off the road and increases your risk of crashing by 10 times. In fact, a recent study found that drivers who were texting or changing music on their phones traveled 28 metres further (nearly half a hockey rink) before responding to a hazard than drivers who were paying attention. It can be a matter of life and death for a child who runs out on the street unexpectedly, or a family crossing at a crosswalk. For every 10-year increase in the driver’s age, drivers were 44% less likely to text, 38% less likely to use a handheld phone, and 28% less likely to use a hands-free phone.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Emergency vehicles · ¶1
text: Emergency vehicles – police, fire, ambulance and special public-utility vehicles – are easily identified through their use of flashing red or blue lights, a siren or bell, or alternating flashes of white light from their headlamp high beams. Also, be aware that police, fire and ambulance services use many different types of vehicles, such as bicycles, snowmobiles, all-terrain vehicles, motorcycles, buses and trucks.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: When an emergency vehicle is approaching your vehicle from any direction with its flashing red or red and blue lights, or siren or bell sounding, you are required to bring your vehicle to an immediate stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶2
text: When bringing your vehicle to a stop, you are required to bring your vehicle as near as is practical to the right-hand curb or edge of the roadway. When on a one-way road or divided highway having more than two lanes of traffic, move to the closest curb or edge of the roadway. Your vehicle should be parallel to the roadway and clear of any intersections, including highway on/off ramps. Do not move onto or stop on the shoulder of the roadway, as emergency vehicles may be travelling along it.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶3
text: Use extreme caution when stopping your vehicle because other drivers may not yet be aware of or are already reacting to the approaching emergency vehicle. Look to the front, both sides and toward the rear of your vehicle, signal your intention to pull over well in advance and begin to adjust your vehicle's speed to merge with any traffic to the side you are pulling to. Once you have moved your vehicle to the side, brake gradually as required and bring your vehicle to a safe stop. Avoid any sudden changes in direction or excessive braking and be aware of any vehicles approaching fast to the rear of your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶4
text: If you are in an intersection and preparing to make a turn when an emergency vehicle is approaching, you should abandon the turn and clear the intersection by proceeding straight when safe to do so, then pull to the right and stop. This will clear the intersection and minimize the possibility of a collision with the emergency vehicle should it be passing you on the side you intended to turn towards.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶5
text: When the emergency vehicle has passed, check to make sure the way is clear and signal before merging back into traffic. Remain vigilant for additional emergency vehicles, and remember it is illegal to follow within 150 metres of a fire vehicle responding to an alarm.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶6
text: Note: Some firefighters and volunteer medical responders may display a flashing green light when using their own vehicles to respond to a fire or medical emergency. Please yield the right-of-way to help them respond to an emergency call quickly and safely.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶7
text: Police or other enforcement officers may require you to pull over and bring your vehicle to an immediate stop. Typically, the officer may signal this requirement by driving their vehicle with its emergency lights flashing and/or siren on behind your vehicle or by using hand gestures from the side of the road. When stopping your vehicle, follow the previous procedures, except that you should bring your vehicle to a stop outside of traffic lanes and onto the shoulder of the roadway where possible, or turn and stop on a side street with less traffic if in the immediate vicinity. If the officer gives direction as to where to stop, follow the officer's directions.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶8
text: Stay alert

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶9
text: When you see an approaching emergency vehicle with its lights or siren on, prepare to clear the way.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 1
text: React quickly but calmly. Don't slam on the brakes or pull over suddenly. Use your signals to alert other drivers you intend to pull over.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 2
text: Check your rearview mirrors. Look in front and on both sides of your vehicle. Allow other vehicles to also pull over. Pull to the right and gradually come to a stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 3
text: Wait for the emergency vehicle to pass and watch for other emergency vehicles that may be responding to the same call. Check to make sure the way is clear and signal before merging back into traffic.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 4
text: Don't drive on or block the shoulder on freeways. Emergency vehicles will use the shoulder of the road if all lanes are blocked.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · image
heading: Diagram 2-56 | Alt text: “vehicles pulling over to the right to allow emergency vehicle to pass”
text: vehicles pulling over to the right to allow emergency vehicle to pass

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · image
heading: Diagram 2-57 | Alt text: “approaching an emergency vehicle”
text: approaching an emergency vehicle

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶1
text: When approaching any emergency vehicle that is stopped with its red, or red and blue, lights flashing or a tow truck with its amber lights flashing in the same direction of your travel, you are required to reduce the speed of your vehicle and proceed with caution. When reducing your speed, you are required to assess the speed of the surrounding traffic and the condition of the roadway (such as fog, rain, snow). To ensure safety, brake early and gradually to allow surrounding traffic to better adjust to a reduced speed and to ensure you have full control of your vehicle when braking.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶2
text: If your vehicle has a manual transmission, it is recommended that you use your brakes, versus shifting down to a lower gear, in order to activate your rear brake lights and indicate to other drivers that you are slowing down.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: When the roadway has two or more lanes of traffic in the same direction of your travel, you are required to move into a lane away from the emergency vehicle or tow truck, if safe to do so, in addition to reducing the speed of your vehicle and proceeding with caution. Similar to the procedures noted above, when slowing down and moving over, look in front and on both sides of your vehicle, and check your rearview mirrors, to determine the speed of the traffic around you and condition of the roadway. Proceed to decrease your speed similar to surrounding traffic speed, use your turn signal prior to making the lane change, and double check your rearview mirrors and shoulder check your blind spots to ensure no other vehicles are moving into or approaching that lane too fast. When safe to do so, change lanes well in advance of an emergency vehicle or a stopped tow truck with its flashing amber lights. Once in the lane, brake gradually and continue to reduce the speed of your vehicle when safe to do so. Be aware of any vehicles approaching fast to the rear of your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶4
text: Tips to remember

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 1
text: Stay alert. Avoid distractions. Keep the noise level down in your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 2
text: Remain calm, and do not make sudden lane changes or brake excessively.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 3
text: Before changing direction or speed, consider road conditions, check surrounding traffic, use your mirrors, look to blind spots, and signal and brake early.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 4
text: Keep roadway shoulders, intersections and highway ramps clear for emergency-vehicle use.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 5
text: If your vehicle is being pulled over, in this instance, bring it to a safe stop on the shoulder of the roadway, away from traffic, following any directions from the officer.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: Take emergency flashing lights and sirens seriously. Proceed with caution, clear the way and bring your vehicle to a stop, where required. It's the law. If you don’t stop, you can be fined and get three demerit points for a first offence. For additional offences, fines increase and you could also go to jail for up to six months.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶2
text: Please note the above law, fines and penalties are also applicable to a tow truck with its lamp producing intermittent flashes of amber light that is stopped on a highway.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 1
text: How to manoeuvre your vehicle through construction zones

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 2
text: What to do if you encounter animals on the road

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 3
text: Things that may distract you when driving and how to minimize those distractions

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 4
text: What to do when you encounter an emergency vehicle

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶1
text: Always be aware of traffic around you as you drive. Develop a routine for looking ahead, behind and from side to side. Check your mirrors every five seconds or so, and check your blind spots by turning your head to look over your shoulder. Keep other drivers out of your blind spot by changing your speed and don't drive in other vehicles' blind spots. This is especially true when driving around large commercial vehicles, as they typically have large blind spots to the sides and back. Be extra careful at dusk and dawn when everyone has difficulty adjusting to the changing light.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶2
text: Keep a cushion of space around your vehicle and be prepared for the unexpected. Anticipate other drivers movements and make allowances for every possible error. Look well ahead and watch for people in parked vehicles, they may be about to pull out in front of you or to open a door. Watch for smaller vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians.

locator: Driving along › Steer smoothly · ¶1
text: All steering should be smooth and precise. You should do most steering and lane changes without taking either hand off the wheel. You must be able to steer in a straight line while shifting gears, adjusting controls or checking your blind spot.

locator: Driving along › Steer smoothly · ¶2
text: Picture the steering wheel as a clock and place your hands at nine o'clock and three o'clock.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · image

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶1
text: Signals tell other drivers what you want to do, alerting them to your intention to turn or stop.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶2
text: Use your turn signals and brake lights to signal before stopping, slowing down, turning, changing lanes, leaving the road or moving out from a parked position. Give the correct signal well before taking the action and make sure other drivers can see it. Check that the way is clear before you act, just signalling is not enough. Follow the rules for turns, whether left or right, on lane changes and on yields to other vehicles and pedestrians.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶3
text: If your turn signals and brake lights are not working, use hand and arm signals. The pictures on the previous page show how to make hand and arm signals. When watching for signals made by others, remember that cyclists may signal right turns by holding their right arms straight out.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶4
text: After signalling, move only when it is safe to do so.

locator: Driving along › Keep right · ¶1
text: Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads unless you want to turn left or pass another vehicle. This is especially important if you are driving more slowly than other vehicles.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶1
text: Obey the maximum speed limit posted on signs along the road, but always drive at a speed that will let you stop safely. This means driving below the maximum speed in bad weather, in heavy traffic or in construction zones. School zones and construction zones often have lower speed limits to protect children and those who work on or near the road.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶2
text: Where there are no posted speed limits, the maximum speed is 50 km / h in cities, towns and villages, and 80 km / h elsewhere.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶3
text: Cruise control is a driver aid that can improve fuel economy and prevent you from inadvertently exceeding the speed limit. However, there are some circumstances in which cruise control should not be used, such as adverse driving conditions (wet, icy or slippery roads), in heavy traffic or when you are feeling fatigued.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶4
text: Speed measuring warning devices are illegal. If you get caught driving with such a device, you will be fined and accumulate demerit points.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶1
text: When police officers are directing traffic, you must follow their directions, even if the directions are different from traffic lights or signs.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶2
text: When a police officer signals you to pull your vehicle over, you must pull over as far to the right as you safely can and come to a complete stop. Stay in your vehicle and wait for the police officer. You must immediately, upon the police officer’s request, surrender your driver’s licence, vehicle permit (or copy) and insurance. Contrary to popular belief, you do not have 24 hours to present these documents. If you do not obey a police officer’s direction to pull over, you risk being fined, having your licence suspended or even serving time in prison.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶1
text: As a general rule, drive at the same speed as traffic around you without going over the speed limit. Leave a cushion of space around your vehicle to let other drivers see you and to avoid a collision.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶2
text: Whenever you follow another vehicle, you need enough space to stop safely if the other vehicle brakes suddenly. A safe following distance is at least two seconds behind the vehicle in front of you. This lets you see around the vehicle ahead and gives you enough distance to stop suddenly.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶3
text: Do not block the normal and reasonable movement of traffic.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · image
heading: Diagram 2-9 | Alt text: “the 2 to 3 second rule for following distance”
text: the 2 to 3 second rule for following distance

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶4
text: To give yourself a two-second space, follow these steps:

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · item 1
text: Pick a marker on the road ahead, such as a road sign or telephone pole.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · item 2
text: When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes the marker, count "one thousand and one, one thousand and two".

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · item 3
text: When the front of your vehicle reaches the marker, stop counting. If you reach the marker before you count "one thousand and two," you are following too closely.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶5
text: Remember that the two-second rule gives a minimum following distance. It applies only to ideal driving conditions. You will need extra space in certain situations, such as bad weather, when following motorcycles or large trucks, or when carrying a heavy load.

locator: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶1
text: Vehicles powered by gasoline and diesel give off air pollutants and gases such as oxides of carbon, nitrogen and sulphur, hydrocarbons and soot. These pollutants affect the quality of the air we breathe, our health, crop yields and even the global climate.

locator: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶2
text: Hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen react in sunlight to form ground-level ozone, better known as smog. Smog is a major health hazard responsible for respiratory ailments and other illnesses. Oxides of sulphur and nitrogen combine with water vapour to form acid rain, which damages our lakes, forests and crops.

locator: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶3
text: Global warming is the result of too much carbon dioxide and other gases trapping heat in our atmosphere. Global warming could cause average temperatures to rise, causing droughts, crop failures, lower water levels and more frequent and severe storms.

locator: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶4
text: A car gives off less carbon dioxide than a larger vehicle, such as an airplane, truck, bus or train, does. However, because so many people own cars and drive them so often, cars are responsible for nearly half the carbon dioxide produced by all forms of transportation. Vehicles that carry large numbers of passengers, such as buses, produce less carbon dioxide per passenger than cars.

locator: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶5
text: As a driver, you can help to protect the environment from the harmful effects of driving by following these suggestions. Many of them can also save you money. For further information visit the Fleetsmart website.

locator: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 1
text: Plan ahead. Combine several errands into one trip.

locator: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 2
text: Avoid driving during rush hours. Driving in off-peak times takes less time, uses less fuel and releases fewer emissions.

locator: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 3
text: Pay attention to smog alerts. It is especially important to follow these suggestions on days when smog is bad.

locator: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 4
text: For short trips, consider walking or cycling.

locator: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 5
text: For longer trips, public transit is an environmentally friendly alternative to driving alone.

locator: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 6
text: Carpool whenever possible. If you want to meet at a central location, there are free carpool lots in many parts of the province.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 1
text: Avoid starting your vehicle unnecessarily. A large burst of pollutants is emitted when a cold engine is started.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 2
text: Turn off your vehicle if parked more than 10 seconds. Even in cold weather, vehicle engines warm up within 30 seconds.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 3
text: Obey the speed limits. Driving at high speed uses more fuel and increases your chances of a serious collision.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 4
text: On the freeway, use your vehicle’s overdrive gear and cruise control for better fuel efficiency.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 5
text: Remove unnecessary weight from your vehicle, such as heavy baggage, wet snow and winter sand or salt.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 6
text: Maintain your vehicle’s aerodynamics. Remove roof racks and compartments when not in use. At high speeds, use your vents instead of opening the windows.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 7
text: Use your vehicle’s air conditioning wisely. Use your windows and vents in city and stop-and-go traffic. At high speeds, using your air conditioning is usually more fuel efficient than opening your windows and reducing the vehicle’s aerodynamics.

locator: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 8
text: Don't “top-off” the tank when refueling. Spilled fuel releases harmful vapours.

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 1
text: Regular maintenance will keep your vehicle running at maximum efficien­cy, reducing the fuel you need to buy and the pollutants your vehicle emits.

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 2
text: Keep your vehicle’s engine well tuned. Worn spark plugs, dragging brakes, low transmission fluid or a transmission not going into high gear can increase fuel consumption substantially.

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 3
text: Follow the recommended maintenance schedule in your vehicle owner’s manual to maximize fuel efficiency.

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 4
text: Have any fluid leaks checked by a specialist to avoid engine damage and harming the environment.

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 5
text: Keep your tires properly inflated to reduce your fuel bill, emissions and tire wear.

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 6
text: Have your vehicle’s alignment checked regularly to reduce uneven tire wear and fuel consumption.

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · ¶1
text: (For more information on driving efficiently, see the section on maintaining your vehicle ).

locator: Driving efficiently › At the garage · ¶2
text: Drivers are reminded that many collisions occur when the driving environment is less than optimal. Whether driving at night, during times of reduced visibility or when road conditions are wet and slippery, drivers are encouraged to use the appropriate safe-driving tips provided in this handbook.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 1
text: Don't drink and drive. Don't drive when you're taking medication that will affect your driving.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 2
text: Always wear your seatbelt and make sure passengers are using the appropriate child car seat,booster seat or seatbelt.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 3
text: Obey the speed limits. Slow down when road and weather conditions are poor.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 4
text: Don't take risks: don't cut people off in traffic, make sudden lane changes or run yellow lights.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 5
text: Don't drive when you're tired, upset or sick.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 6
text: If you're in doubt, let the other driver go first - yield the right-of-way.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 7
text: Keep at least a two-second space between your vehicle and the one ahead. To check your distance: start counting when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed object, stop counting when your vehicle reaches the same spot.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 8
text: Cut the distractions: don't overcrowd the vehicle or play loud music.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 9
text: Always check your blind spot: look in your mirror and over your shoulder before you change lanes.

locator: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 10
text: Check traffic in all directions, including any sidewalks and paths/trails, before entering an intersection.

text: By the end of this section, you should know:

text: Ways to reduce the amount you drive

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Intro · ¶1
text: At night and in weather conditions such as rain, snow or fog, you cannot see as far ahead, even with headlights. Slow down when driving at night, especially on unlit roads and whenever weather conditions reduce your visibility.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Overdriving your headlights · ¶1
text: You are overdriving your headlights when you go so fast that your stopping distance is farther than you can see with your headlights. This is a dangerous thing to do, because you may not give yourself enough room to make a safe stop. Reflective road signs can mislead you as well, making you believe you can see farther than you really can. This may cause you to over-drive your headlights if you are not careful (Diagram 2-58).

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Overdriving your headlights · image
heading: Diagram 2-58 | Alt text: “(1) a vehicle driving within the range of its low beam headlights (2) a vehicle overdriving the range of its low beam headlights”
text: (1) a vehicle driving within the range of its low beam headlights (2) a vehicle overdriving the range of its low beam headlights

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Glare · ¶1
text: Glare is dazzling light that makes it hard for you to see and be aware what others around you are doing. It can be a problem on both sunny and overcast days, depending on the angle of the sun’s rays and your surroundings. Glare can also be a problem at night when you face bright headlights or see them reflected in your rear view mirror.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Glare · ¶2
text: When meeting oncoming vehicles with bright headlights at night, look up and beyond and slightly to the right of the oncoming lights. In daytime glare, use your sun visor or keep a pair of good quality sunglasses in your vehicle. When you enter a tunnel on a bright day, slow down to let your eyes adjust to the reduced light. Remove your sunglasses and turn on your headlights.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Glare · ¶3
text: Cut down glare at night by following the rules of the road for vehicle lights. Use your low-beam headlights within 150 metres of an oncoming vehicle or when following a vehicle within 60 metres. On country roads, switch to low beams when you come to a curve or hilltop so you can see oncoming headlights and won't blind oncoming drivers. If you can't see any headlights, switch back to high beams.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog · ¶1
text: Fog is a thin layer of cloud resting on the ground. Fog can reduce visibility for drivers, resulting in difficult driving conditions.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog · ¶2
text: The best thing to do is to avoid driving in fog. Check weather forecasts and if there is a fog warning, delay your trip until it clears. If that is not possible or you get caught driving in fog, there are a number of safe driving tips you should follow. If visibility is decreasing rapidly, move off the road and into a safe parking area to wait for the fog to lift.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog · ¶1
text: Before you drive - and during your trip - check weather forecasts. If there is a fog warning, delay your trip until it clears. If you are caught driving in fog, follow these safe-driving tips:

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 1
text: Slow down gradually and drive at a speed that suits the conditions.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 2
text: Make sure the full lighting system of your vehicle is turned on.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 3
text: Use your low-beam headlights. High beams reflect off the moisture droplets in the fog, making it harder to see.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 4
text: If you have fog lights on your vehicle, use them, in addition to your low beams.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 5
text: Be patient. Avoid passing, changing lanes and crossing traffic.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 6
text: Use pavement markings to help guide you. Use the right edge of the road as a guide, rather than the centre line.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 7
text: Increase your following distance. You will need extra distance to brake safely.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 8
text: Look and listen for any hazards that may be ahead.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 9
text: Reduce the distractions in your vehicle. For example, turn off the cell phone. Your full attention is required.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 10
text: Watch for any electronically operated warning signs.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 11
text: Keep looking as far ahead as possible.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 12
text: Keep your windows and mirrors clean. Use your defroster and wipers to maximize your vision.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › DO: · item 13
text: If the fog is too dense to continue, pull completely off the road and try to position your vehicle in a safe parking area. Turn on your emergency flashers, in addition to keeping on your low-beam headlights.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › Don’t: · item 1
text: Don't stop on the travelled portion of the road. You could become the first link in a chain-reaction collision.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › Don’t: · item 2
text: Don't speed up suddenly, even if the fog seems to be clearing. You could find yourself suddenly back in fog.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › Don’t: · item 3
text: Don't speed up to pass a vehicle moving slowly or to get away from a vehicle that is following too closely.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › REMEMBER: · item 1
text: Watch your speed. You may be going faster than you think. If so, reduce speed gradually.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › REMEMBER: · item 2
text: Leave a safe braking distance between you and the vehicle ahead.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › REMEMBER: · item 3
text: Remain calm and patient. Don't pass other vehicles or speed up suddenly.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › REMEMBER: · item 4
text: Don't stop on the road. If visibility is decreasing rapidly, pull off the road into a safe parking area and wait for the fog to lift.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Fog › Tips for driving safely in fog › REMEMBER: · item 5
text: Use your low-beam lights.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Rain · ¶1
text: Rain makes road surfaces slippery, especially as the first drops fall. With more rain, tires make less contact with the road. If there is too much water or if you are going too fast, your tires may ride on top of the water, like water skis. This is called hydroplaning. When this happens, control becomes very difficult. Make sure you have good tires with deep tread, and slow down when the road is wet.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Rain · ¶2
text: Rain also reduces visibility. Drive slowly enough to be able to stop within the distance you can see. Make sure your windshield wipers are in good condition. If your wiper blades do not clean the windshield without streaking, replace them.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Rain · ¶3
text: In rain, try to drive on clear sections of road. Look ahead and plan your movements. Smooth steering, braking and accelerating will reduce the chance of skids Leave more space between you and the vehicle ahead in case you have to stop. This will also help you to avoid spray from the vehicle ahead that can make it even harder to see.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Rain · ¶4
text: Avoid driving in puddles. A puddle can hide a large pothole that could damage your vehicle or its suspension, or flatten a tire. The spray of water could obstruct the vision of adjacent motorists and result in a collision, cause harm to nearby pedestrians or drown your engine, causing it to stall. Water can also make your brakes less effective.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Rain · image
heading: Diagram 2-59 | Alt text: “glare on a wet roadway at night”
text: glare on a wet roadway at night

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Flooded roads · ¶1
text: Avoid driving on flooded roads, water may prevent your brakes from working. If you must drive through a flooded stretch of road, test your brakes afterward to dry them out. Test your brakes when it is safe to do so by stopping quickly and firmly at 50 km/h. Make sure the vehicle stops in a straight line, without pulling to one side. The brake pedal should feel firm and secure, not spongy, that’s a sign of trouble. If you still feel a pulling to one side or a spongy brake pedal even after the brakes are dry, you should take the vehicle in for repair immediately.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids · ¶1
text: A skid may happen when one or more tires lose their grip with the road’s surface. Skids most often happen on a slippery surface, such as a road that is wet, icy or covered with snow, gravel or some other loose material. Most skids result from driving too fast for road conditions. Hard braking and overly aggressive turning or accelerating can cause your vehicle to skid and possibly go out of control.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids · ¶2
text: To avoid a skid on a slippery road, drive at a reduced speed and operate the vehicle’s controls in a smooth and constrained manner. Increasing tire forces, such as by braking or accelerating while steering may push tires even closer to a skid condition. It’s essential that the vehicle’s speed be maintained at a safe level and that turns be made gently.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids · ¶3
text: If your vehicle begins to skid, try not to panic - it is possible to maintain control of your vehicle, even in a skid. Ease off on the accelerator or brake and on a very slippery surface slip the transmission into neutral if you can. Continue to steer in the direction you wish to go. Be careful not to oversteer. Once you regain control, you can brake as needed, but very gently and smoothly.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids › Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) · ¶1
text: If your vehicle is equipped with anti-lock brakes, practise emergency braking to understand how your vehicle will react. It is a good idea to practise doing this under controlled conditions with a qualified driving instructor.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids › Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) · ¶2
text: ABS is designed to sense the speed of the wheels on a vehicle during braking. An abnormal drop in wheel speed, which indicates potential wheel lock, causes the brake force to be reduced to that wheel. This is how ABS prevents tire skid and the accompanying loss of steering control. This improves vehicle safety during heavy brake use or when braking with poor traction.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids › Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) · ¶3
text: Although anti-lock braking systems help to prevent wheel lock, you should not expect the stopping distance for your vehicle to be shortened.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids › Anti-lock braking systems (ABS) · ¶4
text: Drivers unfamiliar with anti-lock braking may be surprised by the pulsations that they may feel in the brake pedal when they brake hard. Make sure you know what to expect so you will not be distracted by the pulsation or tempted to release the pedal during emergency braking manoeuvres.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids › Threshold braking · ¶1
text: Threshold braking should bring you to a reasonably quick controlled stop in your own lane, even in slippery conditions. This technique is generally practised in a vehicle that is not equipped with ABS . Brake as hard as you can until a wheel begins to lock up, then release pressure on the pedal slightly to release the wheel. Press down on the brake pedal, applying as much braking force as possible without inducing a skid. If you feel any of the wheels begin to lock up, release the brake pressure slightly and re-apply. Don't pump the brakes. Continue braking this way until you have slowed the vehicle to the desired speed.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Skids › Threshold braking · ¶2
text: Vehicles equipped with ABS should provide controlled braking on slippery surfaces automatically. Press the brake pedal hard and allow the system to control wheel lock-up.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Snow · ¶1
text: Snow may be hard-packed and slippery as ice; rutted, full of hard tracks and gullies; or smooth and soft. Look ahead and anticipate what you must do based on the conditions. Slow down on rutted, snowy roads. Avoid sudden steering, braking or accelerating that could cause a skid. Do not use cruise control during times of snow and other inclement weather.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts · ¶1
text: Blowing snow may create whiteouts where snow completely blocks your view of the road. When blowing snow is forecast, drive only if necessary and with extreme caution.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions · ¶1
text: Before you drive - and during your trip - check weather forecasts and road reports. If there is a weather warning, or reports of poor visibility and driving conditions, delay your trip until conditions improve, if possible. If you get caught driving in blowing snow or a whiteout, follow these safe driving tips:

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 1
text: Slow down gradually and drive at a speed that suits the conditions.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 2
text: Make sure the full lighting system of your vehicle is turned on.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 3
text: Use your low-beam headlights. High beams reflect off the ice particles in the snow, making it harder to see. If you have fog lights on your vehicle, use them, in addition to your low beams.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 4
text: Be patient. Avoid passing, changing lanes and crossing traffic.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 5
text: Increase your following distance. You will need extra space to brake safely.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 6
text: Stay alert. Keep looking as far ahead as possible.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 7
text: Reduce the distractions in your vehi­cle. Your full attention is required.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 8
text: Keep your windows and mirrors clean. Use defroster and wipers to maximize your vision.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DO: · item 9
text: Try to get off the road when visibility is near zero. Pull into a safe parking area if possible.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DON'T: · item 1
text: Don't stop on the travelled portion of the road. You could become the first link in a chain-reaction collision.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › DON'T: · item 2
text: Don't attempt to pass a vehicle moving slowly or speed up to get away from a vehicle that is following too closely.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › REMEMBER: · item 1
text: Watch your speed. You may be going faster than you think. If so, reduce speed gradually.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › REMEMBER: · item 2
text: Leave a safe braking distance between you and the vehicle ahead.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › REMEMBER: · item 3
text: Stay alert, remain calm and be patient.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › REMEMBER: · item 4
text: If visibility is decreasing rapidly, do not stop on the road. Look for an opportunity to pull off the road into a safe parking area and wait for conditions to improve.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › REMEMBER: · item 5
text: If you become stuck or stranded in severe weather, stay with your vehicle for warmth and safety until help arrives. Open a window slightly for ventilation. Run your motor sparingly. Use your emergency flashers.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › REMEMBER: · item 6
text: Be prepared and carry a winter driving survival kit that includes items such as warm clothing, non-perishable energy foods, flashlight, shovel and blanket.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Whiteouts › Tips for driving in blowing snow and whiteout conditions › REMEMBER: · item 7
text: It is important to look ahead and watch for clues that indicate you need to slow down and anticipate slippery road conditions.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Ice · ¶1
text: As temperatures drop below freezing, wet roads become icy. Sections of road in shaded areas or on bridges and overpasses freeze first. It is important to look ahead, slow down and anticipate ice. If the road ahead looks like black and shiny asphalt, be suspicious. It may be covered by a thin layer of ice known as black ice. Generally, asphalt in the winter should look gray-white in colour. If you think there may be black ice ahead, slow down and be careful.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Snow plows · ¶1
text: Snow-removal vehicles on public roadways are equipped with flashing blue lights that can be seen from 150 metres.

locator: Driving at night and in bad weather › Snow plows · ¶2
text: Flashing blue lights warn you of wide and slow-moving vehicles: some snow plows have a wing that extends as far as three metres to the right of the vehicle. On freeways, several snow plows may be staggered across the road, clearing all lanes at the same time by passing a ridge of snow from plow to plow. Do not try to pass between them. This is extremely dangerous because there is not enough room to pass safely, and the ridge of wet snow can throw your vehicle out of control.

locator: Driving through intersections › Intro · ¶1
text: Be alert as you come to intersections and look carefully for pedestrians, cyclists, other motor vehicles, yield signs, stop signs and traffic lights. Be sure to scan any sidewalks and paths/trails as well as the roadways. Bear in mind that children are often unaware of traffic laws and also that cycling on the sidewalk may be permitted by local bylaw.

locator: Driving through intersections › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 2-18 | Alt text: “an uncontrolled intersection”
text: an uncontrolled intersection

locator: Driving through intersections › Intro · ¶2
text: There are two main types of intersections: controlled and uncontrolled.

locator: Driving through intersections › Controlled intersections · image
heading: Diagram 2-19 | Alt text: “an controlled intersection”
text: an controlled intersection

locator: Driving through intersections › Controlled intersections · ¶1
text: Controlled intersections have traffic lights, yield signs or stop signs to control traffic (Diagram 2-19).

locator: Driving through intersections › Controlled intersections · ¶2
text: At a controlled intersection where you face a green light, drive carefully through the intersection at a steady speed. If the light has been green for a while, be prepared to stop when it turns yellow. However, if you are already so close that you cannot stop safely, drive through the intersection with caution. Where you face a red light, come to a complete stop and wait until the light turns green.

locator: Driving through intersections › Controlled intersections · ¶3
text: When you approach an intersection on a main road, and the intersection is blocked with traffic, stop before entering the intersection and wait until the traffic ahead moves on. This does not apply if you are turning left or right.

locator: Driving through intersections › Controlled intersections · ¶4
text: At a controlled intersection where you face a yield sign, slow down or stop if necessary and wait until the way is clear before driving through the intersection.

locator: Driving through intersections › Controlled intersections · ¶5
text: At a controlled intersection where you face a stop sign, come to a complete stop. Drive through the intersection only when the way is clear (Diagram 2-19).

locator: Driving through intersections › Uncontrolled intersections · ¶1
text: Uncontrolled intersections have no signs or traffic lights. They are usually found in areas where there is not much traffic. Be extra careful around these intersections. If two vehicles come to an uncontrolled intersection from different roads at the same time, the driver on the left must let the driver on the right go first. This is called yielding the right-of-way.

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · ¶1
text: There are times when you must yield the right-of-way. This means you must let another driver go first. Here are some rules about when you must yield the right-of-way.

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · image
heading: Diagram 2-18 | Alt text: “an uncontrolled intersection”
text: an uncontrolled intersection

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · ¶2
text: At an intersection without signs or lights, you must yield the right-of-way to a vehicle approaching the intersection before you, and if you arrive at the same time, the vehicle approaching from the right has the right-of-way (Diagram 2-18).

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · image
heading: Diagram 2-19 | Alt text: “an controlled intersection”
text: an controlled intersection

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · ¶3
text: At an intersection with stop signs at all corners, you must yield the right-of-way to the first vehicle to come to a complete stop. If two vehicles stop at the same time, the vehicle on the left must yield to the vehicle on the right (Diagram 2-19).

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · image
heading: Diagram 2-20 | Alt text: “a vehicle yielding the right-of-way to approaching vehicle turning right and a pedestrian crossing intersection”
text: a vehicle yielding the right-of-way to approaching vehicle turning right and a pedestrian crossing intersection

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · ¶4
text: At any intersection where you want to turn left or right, you must yield the right-of-way. If you are turning left, you must wait for approaching traffic to pass or turn and for pedestrians in or approaching your path to cross. If you are turning right, you must wait for pedestrians to cross if they are in or approaching your path (Diagram 2-20). You should also check your blind spot for cyclists approaching from behind, particularly in a bike lane to your right, on a sidewalk or a trail. A yield sign means you must slow down or stop if necessary and yield the right-of-way to traffic in the intersection or on the intersecting road.

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · image
heading: Diagram 2-21 | Alt text: “a vehicle yielding the right-of-way to vehicles on the road and pedestrians crossing on the sidewalk when entering road from a private driveway or road”
text: a vehicle yielding the right-of-way to vehicles on the road and pedestrians crossing on the sidewalk when entering road from a private driveway or road

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · ¶5
text: When entering a road from a private road or driveway, you must yield to vehicles on the road and pedestrians on the sidewalk (Diagram 2-21).

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · image
heading: Diagram 2-22 | Alt text: “vehicles yielding the right-of-way at a pedestrian crossover”
text: vehicles yielding the right-of-way at a pedestrian crossover

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · ¶6
text: You must yield the right-of-way and wait for pedestrians to completely cross the road at pedestrian crossovers (Diagram 2-22) and school crossings with crossing guards.

locator: Driving through intersections › Yielding the right-of-way · ¶7
text: Remember, signalling does not give you the right-of-way. You must make sure the way is clear.

text: By the end of this section you should know:

text: The difference between controlled and uncontrolled intersections and how to safely navigate them
