locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle · ¶1
text: Off-road vehicles (sometimes called ORVs) are any two- or three-wheeled motorized vehicles, as well as specific vehicles with four or more wheels as prescribed by regulation, intended for recreational use. Examples of off-road vehicles include all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), two-up ATV s, side-by-side ATV s, utility terrain vehicles (UTVs), amphibious ATV s, off-road motorcycles and dune buggies.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle · ¶2
text: Note: Electric and motorized scooters (commonly known as go-peds) and pocket bikes (which are miniature motorcycles about two feet in height and with a speed of 70-80 km/h ) are not off-road vehicles and, as such, cannot be registered as off-road vehicles. These vehicles also do not comply with motorcycle standards and cannot be registered as motorcycles.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › What you need to drive an off-road vehicle in Ontario · ¶1
text: You must be 12 years of age or older to drive an off-road vehicle, except on land occupied by the vehicle owner or under the close supervision of an adult. Direct and close supervision by an adult is recommended.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › What you need to drive an off-road vehicle in Ontario · ¶2
text: While off-road vehicles are generally not allowed on public roads, there are some exceptions. (See the section " Where you can and cannot drive. ")

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶1
text: Off-road vehicles must be registered with the Ministry of Transportation at a ServiceOntario centre. This applies to both new and used vehicles. You must be 16 years or older to register an off-road vehicle, and you must be able to prove you own the vehicle.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶2
text: If you buy a new off-road vehicle, you must get a certificate of sale from the dealer.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶3
text: If you buy or transfer ownership of a used off-road vehicle, you must present the signed vehicle portion of the vehicle permit from the previous owner.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶4
text: You must pay a fee to register your off-road vehicle. After regi­stering, you will be given a vehicle permit and licence plate. You should carry the vehicle permit at all times unless you are operating the vehicle on land occupied by the owner of the vehicle.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶5
text: If you have a two- or three-wheeled vehicle, attach the licence plate to the front of the vehicle in plain view. If you have a vehicle with four or more wheels, attach the licence plate to the rear of the vehicle.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶6
text: You must register your vehicle within six days of becoming the owner. If you change your address, you must notify the Ministry of Transportation within six days of the change. You may do this in person at a ServiceOntario centre, by mail to the Ministry of Transportation, P.O. Box 9200, Kingston, ON K7L 5K4, or on the ServiceOntario website .

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶7
text: If you are driving your off-road vehicle anywhere other than on the vehicle owner’s property, you must also have vehicle liability insurance. You must carry the insurance card with you and show it if requested by a police officer. If someone else uses your off-road vehicle with your consent, you are both responsible for any penalties, damages or injuries that may occur.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Registering and insuring your off-road vehicle · ¶8
text: The following vehicles do not need to be registered as off-road vehicles: road-building machines, farm vehicles, golf carts and motorized wheelchairs. In addition, off-road vehicles participating in a rally or competition sponsored by a motorcycle association with more than 25 members do not need to be registered for the event.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Wear a helmet · ¶1
text: You must wear a motorcycle helmet, as required by the Highway Traffic Act , whenever you drive or ride on an off-road vehicle or on any vehicle towed by an off-road vehicle. The only exception is when you operate the vehicle on the property of the vehicle owner. The helmet must meet the standards approved for motorcycle helmets, or motor-assisted vehicle helmets, and must be fastened properly under the chin.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Protect your face and body · ¶1
text: Always wear a face shield or goggles. A face shield can help prevent windburn, sunblindness and watering eyes from the wind. It can also protect your eyes from branches and twigs when driving through wooded areas. Wear pants that cover your legs, a long-sleeved shirt or jacket to protect your arms and gloves. Boots should be high enough to cover your ankles. To make yourself more visible to others while driving, wear brightly coloured clothing.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · ¶1
text: Before every trip, check your vehicle to make sure it is in good working order. Your life may depend upon it. Check the vehicle thoroughly before you start to drive, including the following:

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · item 1
text: Check the brake control to make sure it moves freely. Adjust if necessary.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · item 2
text: Check that the throttle opens and closes smoothly in all steering positions.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · item 3
text: Check the condition of the tires and tire pressure.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · item 4
text: Check the fuel lines andconnections to make sure there are no leaks.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · item 5
text: Check that you have enough fuel and oil.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · item 6
text: Check that the engine is running smoothly. Make sure the is in neutral before starting the engine.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · item 7
text: Check that your lights are in good working condition.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · ¶2
text: Before you drive anywhere, read the owner’s manual.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Make sure your vehicle is in good condition · image
heading: Alt text: “a fully-protected left turn light with green arrow”

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › I. Getting ready to drive an off-road vehicle › Be well prepared for every trip · ¶1
text: Carefully preparing for every trip is an important safety measure. Check local weather forecasts and make sure you tell someone where you will be travelling and when you expect to be back. Use the buddy system; drive with others, not alone. Take along a first-aid kit, a vehicle repair kit, an extra ignition key, a drive belt, spark plugs and a rope. On long trips, include a map and a compass (or a GPS unit and know how to use it), flashlight, hunting knife, hatchet, extra fuel and matches in a waterproof box.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · ¶1
text: You may not drive an off-road vehicle on most public roads in Ontario. This includes the area between the boundary or property lines, including medians, shoulders and ditches.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · ¶2
text: There are some exceptions:

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · item 1
text: You may drive an off-road vehicle directly across some public roads.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · item 2
text: You may drive certain off-road vehicles with three or more wheels along some public roads when using the vehicle for farming, for licensed hunting or for the trapping of fur-bearing animals, provided that the vehicle weighs 450 kilograms or less and does not have an overall width greater than 1.35 metres (excluding mirrors).

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · item 3
text: You may drive an off-road vehicle within a provincial or public park if it is permitted by the park authority.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · item 4
text: Emergency personnel, such as police officers and firefighters, who are performing necessary duties in the course of their work or who are responding to an emergency, may drive off-road vehicles on public roads.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · ¶3
text: There are also exceptions for the category of off-road vehicles known as all-terrain vehicles (ATVs).

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · ¶4
text: If you do drive an off-road vehicle on or across a public road, you must be at least 16 years of age and have a valid Ontario driver’s licence (Class G2, M2 or higher).

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · ¶5
text: You may not operate an ATV in such a way as to disrupt or destroy the natural environment, including fish habitats, property and plants or trees.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Where you can and cannot drive · ¶6
text: For more specific information on where you may operate off-road vehicles, and what rules you must follow when doing so, you should refer to the Highway Traffic Act and the Off-road Vehicles Act .

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · ¶1
text: All-terrain vehicles are off-road vehicles with the following characteristics: four wheels, all of which are in contact with the ground; steering handlebars; and a seat designed to be straddled by the driver.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · ¶2
text: There are sections of provincial highways in Ontario where you may drive an ATV on the shoulder, provided the ATV weighs 450 kilograms or less, does not have an overall width greater than 1.35 metres (excluding mirrors), meets the requirements of the federal Motor Vehicle Safety Act and the American National Standards Institute Standard, and is designed to carry only a driver and no passengers. You must travel in the same direction as the traffic using that side of the road. If there is no shoulder, if the shoulder is obstructed or if you are crossing a level railway crossing, you may drive your vehicle on the paved part of the highway. Keep as close as safely possible to the right of the shoulder or edge of the highway as you can.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · ¶3
text: Where a road or highway falls under the authority of a municipality, the municipality must enact a bylaw for ATV s to be allowed access to the road. If there is no bylaw in place, you cannot drive an ATV on that road. The municipality may also pass bylaws to decide where andwhen ATV s may be used on these local roads.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · ¶4
text: For those roads and highways where you are permitted to drive an ATV , you must obey all licensing and operational requirements, and your vehicle must conform to all equipment requirements, as listed in the Highway Traffic Act and the Off-road Vehicles Act . Remember the following rules:

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · item 1
text: You must have a valid Ontario driver’s licence (G2, M2 or higher).

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · item 2
text: You must wear a motorcycle helmet with a chin strap that is securely fastened.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · item 3
text: You cannot carry passengers on your vehicle.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · item 4
text: You must drive at speed limits lower than those posted: where the posted speed is 50 km/h or less, you must drive 20 km/h or less; where the posted speed is over 50 km/h , you must drive 50 km/h or less.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · ¶5
text: In general, ATV s are not permitted on controlled-access highways, such as the 400 series highways and most parts of the Trans-Canada Highway, but are allowed access to highways 500 to 899, the 7000 series highways and highways with low traffic volumes.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · ¶6
text: For more details about which highways ATV s may drive on, please refer to the Highway Traffic Act , Ontario Regulation 316/03.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › All-terrain vehicles (ATVs) · image
heading: Alt text: “a fully-protected left turn light with green arrow”
text: a fully-protected left turn light with green arrow

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Obey the rules · ¶1
text: You must stop if a police officer signals you to do so. You can also be stopped by a landowner when you are driving on private property. If signalled to stop by an authorized person, you must stop and, if asked, properly identify yourself.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Obey the rules · ¶2
text: Everyone who drives an off-road vehicle without care and attention or without reasonable consideration for other people and property may be charged with careless driving. Other offences, such as dangerous driving and alcohol related offences, apply to drivers of off-road vehicles. When you drive an off-road vehicle on a public road, the Highway Traffic Act offences also apply.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Report collisions to the police · ¶1
text: You must report to the police immediately any collision on a public highway that results in injury to any person or damage to property apparently exceeding $5,000.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶1
text: It is against the law to drive an off-road vehicle when you are impaired by alcohol or drugs.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶2
text: Drinking and driving is a deadly combination.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶3
text: Consuming any amount of alcohol before you ride affects your ability to make good decisions. Even one drink can reduce your ability to concentrate and react to things that happen suddenly when you are driving. With more alcohol in your blood, you could have trouble judging distances and your vision may become blurred. Factors like tiredness, your mood, and how long ago you ate and how much, can make a difference in how alcohol affects your driving ability.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶4
text: The police can stop any driver to determine if alcohol or drug testing is required. They may also do roadside spot checks. When stopped by the police, you may be told to blow into a machine that tests your breath for alcohol, a roadside screening device, or perform physical co-ordination tests. If you fail or refuse to provide a breath sample or to perform the physical co-ordination tests, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶5
text: If the reading on the machine shows you have been drinking, you may be taken to a police station for a breathalyzer test. The breathalyzer uses your breath to measure the amount of alcohol in your bloodstream.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶6
text: If you cannot give a breath sample or it is impractical to obtain a sample of breath, the police officer can require you to provide a blood sample instead.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶7
text: If the police believe that a driver is impaired because of the consumption of a drug or a combination of alcohol and a drug, they can also require a driver to submit to an evaluation and then require a driver to provide blood, oral fluid or urine samples. If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶8
text: Driving impaired or with more than 80 milligrams of alcohol in 100 millilitres of blood (.08) is an offence under the Criminal Code. Even if your blood-alcohol concentration (BAC) is less than .08, you can still be charged with impaired driving under the Criminal Code.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶9
text: You will receive an immediate 90-day administrative driver’s licence suspension if BAC is more than .08 or if you fail or refuse to provide a breath or bodily fluid sample, perform a physical co-ordination test or submit to an evaluation.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶10
text: If you register in the “warn range” of .05 to .08 on a roadside screening device, you will receive an immediate driver’s licence suspension. For a first occurrence, you will be suspended for three days. For a second occurrence in a five-year period, you will be immediately suspended for seven days and you must undergo a remedial alcohol-education program. For a third or subsequent time in a five-year period, you will be immediately suspended for 30 days, and you must undergo a remedial alcohol-treatment program and have an ignition interlock condition placed on your licence for six months. If you choose not to install an ignition interlock device, you must not drive until the condition is removed from your licence.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶11
text: If you are 21 years old and under and hold a full-class driver’s licence, you must not drive if you have been drinking alcohol. Your blood-alcohol level must be zero. If you are caught driving with alcohol in your blood, you will receive an immediate driver’s licence suspension at the roadside for 24 hours and, if convicted, you will face a fine and a 30-day licence suspension.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶12
text: Drivers of all ages in either Level One or Level Two of Ontario’s graduated licensing system must also have a blood-alcohol level of zero when driving. New drivers caught drinking and driving will receive an immediate driver’s licence suspension at the roadside for 24 hours and, if convicted, will face a fine and will receive a suspension period as per the Novice Driver Escalating Sanctions scheme. For the first occurrence, you will be suspended for 30 days. For the second occurrence, in a five-year period, you be suspended for 90 days. For the third occurrence in a five-year period, the novice portion of your driver’s licence will be cancelled, and you must reapply for a G1 licence.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not drink and drive · ¶13
text: Novice drivers will also be charged under the Criminal Code if their BAC exceeds .08 and will be issued a “warn range” suspension if they register a BAC from .05 to .08.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Drugs · ¶1
text: Any drug that changes your mood or the way you see and feel about the world around you will affect the way you drive. Criminal Code and HTA sanctions apply to drivers impaired by alcohol or a drug.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Drugs · ¶2
text: In circumstances involving possible impairment by a drug or a combination of alcohol and a drug, police can require a driver to perform physical co-ordination tests and to submit to an evaluation and then require a driver to provide blood, oral fluid or urine samples. If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code. You will also receive an immediate 90-day administrative driver’s licence suspension.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Drugs · ¶3
text: Illegal drugs such as marijuana and cocaine are not the only problem. Some drugs that your doctor may prescribe for you and some over-the-counter drugs can also impair your driving. Here are some points you should remember:

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Drugs · item 1
text: If you use prescription medicines or get allergy shots, ask your doctor about side effects such as dizziness, blurred vision, nausea or drowsiness that could affect your driving.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Drugs · item 2
text: Read the information on the package of any over-the-counter medicine you take. Any stimulant, diet pill, tranquillizer or sedative may affect your driving. Even allergy and cold remedies may have ingredients that could affect your driving.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Drugs · item 3
text: Drugs and any amount of alcohol together can have dangerous effects, even several days after you have taken the drug. Do not take a chance; ask your doctor or pharmacist.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Do not carry passengers · ¶1
text: Do not carry passengers on an off-road vehicle designed for one person. Carrying passengers changes the weight distribution of the vehicle and limits your ability to shift position on the vehicle for control and stability.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Practice safe driving skills · ¶1
text: Driving an off-road vehicle is different than driving any other type of vehicle, and takes more skill than you might think. Be sure to read your owner’s manual before you begin to drive.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Practice safe driving skills · ¶2
text: If you are a beginner, practise driving your vehicle in an open area that is free of obstacles, until you become skilled at handling it. Choose ground that is uniform, either dirt, sand or snow. Avoid paved surfaces when driving an off-road vehicle. ATV s are designed for off-road use and are more difficult to manoeuvre on paved surfaces. When driving, keep both feet on the footrests at all times. Do not try to stabilize a tipping vehicle by putting your foot down. You could run over your foot or leg.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Practice safe driving skills · ¶3
text: Be extremely careful driving through water. Driving fast across unknown water is dangerous. Hidden rocks or holes could throw you off the vehicle and cause serious injury or drowning. First, check that the water is not too deep. Drive slowly and carefully so you can steer around rocks and other obstacles.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Practice safe driving skills · ¶4
text: Always use a flag mast when driving in dunes and hills. Remember that you need a running start to climb most hills. Be extra cautious when driving among pedestrians, horseback riders, sunbathers or bicyclists.

locator: Off-road Vehicles & Snowmobiles › Driving an Off-road vehicle › II. Safe and responsible off-road vehicle driving › Practice safe driving skills · ¶5
text: Read the Snowmobiler’s Code of Ethics , and follow it when driving your off-road vehicle.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Intro · ¶1
text: To promote safe driving for Ontarians, the province has some of the strictest driving laws regarding driving while impaired by alcohol or drugs, careless driving, “stunt” driving, fleeing police or a collision scene, and so on. In addition to lengthy suspensions for driving offences, court sanctions can quickly escalate and include fines in the tens of thousands of dollars, reinstatement fees, licence restrictions, lifetime bans and even jail time.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · ¶1
text: Your licence may also be suspended for the following reasons:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 1
text: Escalating sanctions

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 2
text: Zero Blood-Alcohol Concentration ( BAC ) for novice and young drivers

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 3
text: Medical suspension

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 4
text: Discretionary HTA suspensions

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 5
text: Mandatory HTA suspensions

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 6
text: Administrative driver’s licence suspension ( ADLS )

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 7
text: "Warn-range" suspension

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 8
text: Novice-driver violations

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · ¶1
text: Escalating sanctions for novice drivers would apply if any of the following occurrences have taken place within a five-year period:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · item 1
text: Any repeat violations of novice restrictions

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · item 2
text: Any HTA convictions for four or more demerit points

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · item 3
text: Court-ordered licence suspensions.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶1
text: The risk of a fatality or serious injury is almost five times greater for vehicles crashing at 50 km/h or more above the posted highway limit. The increase in risk is even greater on roads with lower posted limits. For example, on roads with a posted limit of 60 km/h or less, the risk of a fatality or serious injury is almost eight times greater for vehicles colliding at 50 km/h or more above the posted limit.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶2
text: Other types of aggressive driving include:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 1
text: driving 40 km/h or more above the posted speed limit on roads with a speed limit less than 80km/h

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 2
text: driving 50 km/h or more above the posted speed limit

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 3
text: driving a motor vehicle to prevent another vehicle from passing

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 4
text: intentionally cutting off another vehicle

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 5
text: street racing

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 6
text: driving stunts

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶3
text: The use of a connected nitrous-oxide system while driving on a highway is prohibited.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶4
text: For information on the regulation, you can visit the ontario.ca/laws .

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – careless driving · ¶1
text: Careless driving is defined as: driving without due care, attention or without reasonable consideration for other persons using the highway; and, anyone, who chooses to put themselves and other road users at risk by driving aggressively or carelessly. If convicted of careless driving a driver can face tough sanctions.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Zero Blood-Alcohol Concentration (BAC) for novice and young drivers · ¶1
text: All drivers who are 21 and under, regardless of licence class, must have a BAC level of zero when operating a motor vehicle. You will receive a 24-hour roadside driver-licence suspension. If convicted, you could face a fine and at least a 30-day licence suspension.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Medical suspension · ¶1
text: All doctors must report the names and addresses of everyone 16 years or older who has a condition that may affect their ability to drive safely (for example, a stroke, heart condition or dizziness, among others). Doctors report this information to the Ministry of Transportation, and it is not given to anyone else. Your driver’s licence may be suspended until new medical evidence shows that the condition does not pose a safety risk.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Mandatory HTA suspensions · ¶1
text: Your licence will be suspended:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Mandatory HTA suspensions · item 1
text: If you fail to stop for a police officer (a minimum of five years)

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Mandatory HTA suspensions · item 2
text: If you don't pay a traffic fine when ordered by the court

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · ¶1
text: Your licence will be suspended immediately for 90 days:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · item 1
text: If your BAC is more than 80 milligrams in 100 millilitres of blood (.08)

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · item 2
text: If you fail or refuse to give a breath, blood, oral fluid or urine sample when asked by police

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · item 3
text: If you fail or refuse to perform physical co-ordination tests or submit to a drug evaluation when required by police

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · ¶2
text: This suspension takes effect at the roadside or police station. It is separate from any criminal charges or prosecution that may also take place.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · ¶1
text: Drivers who register a blood-alcohol concentration in the “warn range” of .05 to .08 pose an immediate danger to themselves and other road users. If caught driving in the warn range, you will receive an immediate driver’s-licence suspension at the roadside:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · item 1
text: For three days for a first occurrence

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · item 2
text: For seven days for a second occurrence, and you must undergo a remedial alcohol-education program

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · item 3
text: Substantially increased penalties and sanctions for each subsequent occurrence

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Novice-driver violations · ¶1
text: Drivers holding novice licences must follow the specific rules for their class of licence. If you violate any of the graduated-licensing conditions, your licence will be suspended for 30 days. This suspension takes effect from the time you surrender your licence. You can lose your licence for up to two years if you fail to hand it over.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 1
text: If you fail a driver’s re-examination

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 2
text: If you don't pay your reinstatement fee or administrative monetary penalty following a suspension

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 3
text: If your cheque for licence fees are not honoured by your bank

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 4
text: If you voluntarily surrender your driver’s licence to the Ministry of Transportation, or it is surrendered or returned by another jurisdiction

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · ¶1
text: You will receive a one-year licence suspension the first time you are convicted of a Criminal Code offence. Subsequent offences increase substantially to a lifetime ban from driving. Convictions will remain on your driver’s record for a minimum of 10 years.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · ¶2
text: Your licence will be suspended if you are convicted of any of the following Criminal Code offences:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 1
text: Driving or having care and control of a vehicle, including boats, when your BAC is more than 80 milligrams per 100 millilitres of blood (.08)

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 2
text: Refusing to submit to a breath test for alcohol

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 3
text: Failing or refusing to provide a breath sample for roadside testing

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 4
text: Failing to remain at the scene of a collision

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 5
text: Dangerous driving

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 6
text: Causing death or bodily harm by criminal negligence

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 7
text: Failing to stop for police

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Remedial measures · ¶1
text: There are several types of remedial measures. The mandatory Back on Track program is for all drivers convicted of impaired, driving-related Criminal Code offences. Drivers with more than one “Warn Range” conviction will be required to take an alcohol-education and/or alcohol-treatment program. If your driver’s licence has been suspended because of a Criminal Code conviction, your licence will remain suspended until you have completed the remedial requirements.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Driving under suspension · ¶1
text: You may not drive, under any circumstances, when your licence is suspended. If you are convicted of driving while your licence is suspended for an HTA offence, you will face fines in the thousands of dollars. The court may order you to spend up to six months in jail. Six months will be added to your current suspension as well. If you are found guilty of driving while your licence is suspended for a Criminal Code offence, you can face fines of tens of thousands of dollars and spend time in jail.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Driving while prohibited · ¶1
text: This is a prohibition order under the Criminal Code conviction. When convicted of violation of the order, you will get a suspension of one year for a first offence or two years for a subsequent offence.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · ¶1
text: To counter the dangerous behaviours of impaired and suspended driving, Ontario law includes seven-day vehicle impoundments for:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · item 1
text: Drivers operating a vehicle while under a Highway Traffic Act licence suspension

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · item 2
text: Drivers caught without a required ignition interlock

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · item 3
text: All drivers caught with a BAC over .08, or who fail/refuse to comply with a demand made by a police officer under the Criminal Code of Canada

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · ¶2
text: If you are caught driving while your licence is suspended for a Criminal Code offence, the vehicle you are driving will be impounded for a minimum of 45 days. These vehicle impoundments apply regardless of whether the vehicle is borrowed from a friend or family member, business, employer or is rented. The owner of the vehicle must pay the towing and storage costs before the vehicle will be released.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · ¶3
text: The Vehicle-Impoundment Program makes vehicle owners responsible for ensuring that anyone driving their vehicles is not suspended. People loaning or renting their vehicles can verify that a driver’s licence is valid by phone or online. You can also get a driver’s abstract at any Service Ontario centre. There is a nominal fee for each licence checked.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶1
text: Driving when your ability is impaired by alcohol or a drug is a crime in Canada. Your vehicle does not have to be moving; you can be charged if you are impaired behind the wheel, even if you have not started to drive.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶2
text: In circumstances involving possible impairment by a drug or a combination of alcohol and a drug, police can require a driver to:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 1
text: provide breath samples

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 2
text: perform standardized field sobriety tests

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 3
text: conduct a drug recognition evaluation

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 4
text: provide oral fluid, urine or blood samples for screening

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶3
text: If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶4
text: If you are 21 years of age and under, you must not drive if you have been drinking alcohol. Your blood- alcohol level must be zero.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶5
text: For more information on impaired driving measures in Ontario, please visit the Ministry of Transportation website at: www.mto.gov.on.ca/english/safety/impaired-driving.shtml

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Alcohol · ¶1
text: The police can stop any driver to determine if alcohol or drug testing is required. They may also do roadside spot checks. When stopped by the police, you may be told to blow into a machine that tests your breath for alcohol, a roadside screening device, or perform physical co-ordination tests.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Alcohol · ¶2
text: If you cannot give a breath sample or it is impractical to obtain a sample of breath, the police officer can require you to provide a blood sample instead. The police may also require a driver to provide, blood, oral or urine samples. If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · ¶1
text: Criminal Code and HTA sanctions apply to drivers impaired by alcohol or a drug. In circumstances involving possible impairment by drugs or a combination of alcohol and a drug, police can require a driver to perform physical co-ordination tests and submit to a drug evaluation, and then require a driver to provide blood, oral fluid or urine samples. If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · ¶2
text: Some drugs that your doctor may prescribe for you and some over-the-counter drugs can also impair your driving. Here are some points you should remember:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 1
text: If you use prescription medicines or get allergy shots, ask your doctor about side effects such as dizziness, blurred vision, nausea or drowsiness that could affect your driving.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 2
text: Read the information on the package of any over-the-counter medicine, including cold, allergy, sedative or diet pills.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 3
text: Drugs and any amount of alcohol together can have dangerous effects, even several days after you have taken the drug.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 4
text: Do not take a chance; ask your doctor or pharmacist.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶1
text: Ontario leads the way in combating drinking and driving through some of the toughest laws and programs in North America, including licence suspensions, heavy fines, vehicle impoundment, mandatory alcohol-education and -treatment programs, and the ignition interlock program. Depending on your number of prior convictions, you may be fined up to $50,000, serve time in jail or lose your licence permanently.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶2
text: For impaired driving that causes injury or death, the penalties are even more severe. If you are convicted of impaired driving causing bodily harm, you may be sentenced to up to 14 years in prison. Impaired driving causing death can carry a sentence of imprisonment for life.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶3
text: If you drink and drive and are involved in a collision, you may suffer serious injury or cause serious injury to someone else. Your insurance company might not pay for your medical or rehabilitation costs, or for the damage to your or the other person’s vehicle. Your insurance costs may rise significantly. You may have to pay substantial legal costs as well.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶4
text: If you are required to drive on the job, a licence suspension could mean losing your employment.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Driver-improvement interview · ¶1
text: The other remedial-measures program is for drivers convicted of non-drinking-and-driving-related Criminal Code offences who have no previous alcohol-related convictions. You must undergo a Ministry of Transportation driver-improvement interview.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Driver-improvement interview · ¶2
text: If you have not completed the driver-improvement interview by the time your Criminal Code suspension expires, your licence will be further suspended until you have completed the remedial requirements.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Driver-improvement interview · ¶3
text: This program also applies to Ontario residents convicted of driving-related Criminal Code offences in any other province of Canada, or equivalent offences in the states of Michigan and New York, as well as to out-of-province drivers who are convicted in Ontario.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Summary · item 1
text: Your responsibility to maintain a valid driver’s licence with the most correct and up-to-date information

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Summary · item 2
text: How the demerit-point system works for new and fully licensed drivers

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Summary · item 3
text: The driving offences that result in a loss of points upon conviction.

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Summary · item 4
text: Common circumstances where your licence can be cancelled or suspended

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Summary · item 5
text: How alcohol and drugs affect your ability to drive

locator: Other ways to lose your licence › Summary · item 6
text: The consequences that can result from a suspended licence including reinstatement fees, remedial measures, ignition interlock, vehicle impoundment and jail time

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · ¶1
text: Since parking rules change from road to road and place to place, always watch for and obey signs that say you may not stop or limit stopping, standing or parking. Be aware that not all parking by-laws are posted on signs.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · ¶2
text: Here are some basic parking rules:

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 1
text: Never park on the travelled part of a road. Drive off the road onto the shoulder if you must stop for some reason.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 2
text: Never park on a curve, hill or anywhere you do not have a clear view for at least 125 metres in both directions.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 3
text: Do not park where you will block a vehicle already parked or where you will block a sidewalk, crosswalk, pedestrian crossing or road entrance.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 4
text: Do not park within three metres of a fire hydrant, on or within 100 metres of a bridge or within six metres of a public entrance to a hotel, theatre or public hall when it is open to the public.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 5
text: Do not park within nine metres of an intersection or within 15 metres if it is controlled by traffic lights.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 6
text: Do not park within 15 metres of the nearest rail of a level railway crossing.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 7
text: Do not park where you will get in the way of traffic or snow clearing.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · item 8
text: Never open the door of your parked vehicle without first making sure that you will not endanger any other person or vehicle or interfere with traffic. Generally, a good practice is to use the Dutch reach method, meaning you open the driver’s door with your right hand as this will force a shoulder check at the same time.. Take extra precautions to avoid opening a door in the path of cyclists, who often ride close to parked cars (Diagram 2-50). When you must open a door next to traffic, keep it open only long enough to load or unload passengers.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 2-50 | Alt text: “a warning to drivers to look before opening a door next to traffic”
text: a warning to drivers to look before opening a door next to traffic

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · ¶3
text: After parking your vehicle, always turn off the ignition and the lights, remove the key and lock the door to deter theft. Do not leave children or animals in the vehicle.

locator: Parking along roadways › Intro · ¶4
text: Before moving from a parked position, always signal and check for traffic, pulling out only when it is safe to do so.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · image
heading: Diagram 2-51 | Alt text: “an Accessible Parking Permit”
text: an Accessible Parking Permit

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · ¶1
text: The Accessible Parking Permit, formerly known as the Disabled Person Parking Permit, is a laminated card that may be displayed on the dashboard or turned-down sun visor of any vehicle in which a person with a disability is travelling. The permit entitles the vehicle in which the person named on the permit is travelling to park in designated disabled parking, standing and stopping areas. The permit is issued to the permit holder, not a specific vehicle.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · ¶2
text: People who have the old version of the permit, the Disabled Person Parking Permit, may continue to use this permit until it expires. Upon its expiry, any new permit issued will be the Accessible Parking Permit.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · ¶3
text: The Accessible Parking Permit is issued free of charge to qualified individuals. To qualify for an Accessible Parking Permit, a licensed physician, chiropractor, nurse practitioner (extended class) physiotherapist or occupational therapist must certify that the applicant has one or more of the conditions detailed on the Accessible Parking Permit application form.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · ¶4
text: There are four types of Accessible Parking Permits.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · item 1
text: A regular permit (blue) is issued to people with permanent disabilities and is valid for five years. Until 2011, all individuals will need to be re-certified before renewing their permit. After that date, only individuals whose condition is deemed “subject to change” will need to be re-certified before renewing their permit.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · item 2
text: A temporary permit (red) is issued when the disability is expected to last more than two months, but is not a permanent disability. The temporary permit is not renewable.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · item 3
text: A traveller permit (purple) is valid for up to one year and is issued upon request to individuals who hold a valid Accessible Parking Permit and plan to fly from any Ontario airport. The permit holder places the traveller permit on the dashboard or sun visor of their vehicle when leaving it parked at the airport. The person’s regular permit travels with them.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · item 4
text: A company permit (green) is valid for up to five years and is issued to companies and non-profit organizations that own or lease vehicles used to transport people with physical disabilities.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · ¶5
text: Misuse or abuse of an Accessible Parking Permit should be reported to the police. Misuse of an Accessible Parking Permit will result in fines and revoked privileges. Accessible Parking Permit applications are available at any Service Ontario Centre or by sending a request to the ministry at the following address:

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · ¶6
text: Service Ontario Licence Renewals Unit P.O. Box 9800 Kingston, ON K7L 5N8

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking for people with disabilities · ¶7
text: Never park in a space designated for people with disabilities unless you display an Accessible Parking Permit in the windshield of your vehicle. The permit must belong to you or one of your passengers. This also applies to standing or stopping at curb areas reserved for picking up and dropping off passengers with disabilities.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · ¶1
text: Parallel parking means parking a vehicle with its wheels parallel and next to the curb or side of the road. Park parallel to the curb on roads where parking is allowed, unless there are signs saying that vehicles should be parked at an angle. Park on the right side of the road in the direction of traffic. Unless there are signs saying otherwise, you can parallel park on both sides of a one-way road.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · image
heading: Diagram 2-52 | Alt text: “how to parallel park a vehicle”
text: how to parallel park a vehicle

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · ¶2
text: To parallel park on the right-hand side of the road, find a space that is about one and one-half times longer than your vehicle. Check the traffic beside and behind and signal your wish to pull over and stop. Drive alongside, or parallel to, the vehicle ahead of the empty space, leaving about a metre between the vehicles. Stop when your rear bumper is in line with the other vehicle. Follow these steps:

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · item 1
text: Slowly and carefully reverse into the space, turning the steering wheel fully toward the curb.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · item 2
text: When you can see the outside rear corner of the vehicle in front of your space, straighten your wheels as you continue to reverse.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · item 3
text: Turn the steering wheel fully toward the road to bring your vehicle in line with the curb.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · item 4
text: If your vehicle is not parallel to the curb, drive forward to straighten.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · item 5
text: When you are properly parked, set the parking brake and move the gear selector into park, or shift into first or reverse gear if your vehicle has a manual transmission.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parallel parking · item 6
text: Turn off the engine. Remember to remove the key from the ignition. Check traffic before opening your door. Lock your vehicle.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking on a hill · ¶1
text: When parking facing downhill, turn your front wheels towards the curb or right shoulder. This will keep the vehicle from rolling into traffic if the brakes become disengaged (Diagram 2-53 A).

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking on a hill · ¶2
text: Turn the steering wheel to the left so the wheels are turned towards the road if you are facing uphill with a curb. The tires will catch the curb if it rolls backward (Diagram 2-53 B).

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking on a hill · ¶3
text: When facing uphill without a curb, turn the wheels sharply to the right. If the vehicle rolls, it will go off the road rather than into traffic (Diagram 2-53 C).

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking on a hill · ¶4
text: When parking on a hill, always set the parking brake and move the gear selector into park, or shift into first or reverse gear if your vehicle has a manual transmission. Turn off the engine and remove the key. Check for traffic before opening the door and remember to lock your vehicle.

locator: Parking along roadways › Parking on a hill · image
heading: Diagram 2-53 | Alt text: “how to park a vehicle when facing downhill”
text: how to park a vehicle when facing downhill

locator: Parking along roadways › Roadside stop · ¶1
text: When you need to stop by the side of the road for a short time to check something outside your vehicle, or to look for directions on a map, for example, follow these directions:

locator: Parking along roadways › Roadside stop · item 1
text: Before slowing down, check your mirrors and blind spot to see when the way is clear.

locator: Parking along roadways › Roadside stop · item 2
text: Turn on your signal before slowing down unless there are vehicles waiting to enter the road from side roads or driveways between you and the point where you intend to stop. Wait until you have passed these entrances so that drivers will not think you are turning before the stopping point.

locator: Parking along roadways › Roadside stop · item 3
text: Steer to the side of the road, steadily reducing speed, and stop parallel to the curb or edge of the road. You should not be more than about 30 centimetres away from it. Do not stop where you will block an entrance or other traffic.

locator: Parking along roadways › Roadside stop · item 4
text: Turn off your signal and turn on your hazard lights.

locator: Parking along roadways › Roadside stop · ¶2
text: If your vehicle has an automatic transmission, put the gear selector in park and set the parking brake. If your vehicle has a manual transmission, set the parking brake and shift into neutral if not turning off the engine, or shift into low or reverse if turning off the engine. When parking on a hill, set your wheels against the curb, in the appropriate direction to keep your vehicle from rolling.

locator: Parking along roadways › Pulling out from a roadside stop · ¶1
text: When pulling out from a roadside stop, do the following:

locator: Parking along roadways › Pulling out from a roadside stop · item 1
text: Release the parking brake and move the gear selector to drive or shift into first gear.

locator: Parking along roadways › Pulling out from a roadside stop · item 2
text: Turn off your flashers and turn on your left-turn signal.

locator: Parking along roadways › Pulling out from a roadside stop · item 3
text: Just before pulling away from the stop, check your mirrors and blind spot to make sure the way is clear of vehicles and cyclists.

locator: Parking along roadways › Pulling out from a roadside stop · item 4
text: Return to normal traffic speed by accelerating smoothly to blend with the traffic around you. In light traffic, accelerate moderately. In heavier traffic, you may have to accelerate more quickly. In a vehicle with manual trans­mission, shift gears as you increase speed.

locator: Parking along roadways › Pulling out from a roadside stop · item 5
text: Turn off your left-turn signal as soon as you are back on the road.

text: By the end of this section, you should know:

text: Basic parking rules that may not appear on posted street signs

locator: Parking along roadways › Summary · item 2
text: What an Accessible Parking Permit is, and who is eligible to park in spaces designated for people with disabilities

locator: Parking along roadways › Summary · item 3
text: What parallel parking is and what steps to follow to complete it successfully

locator: Parking along roadways › Summary · item 4
text: How to safely pull over your vehicle for a roadside stop and re-enter traffic

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶1
text: Pavement markings combine with road signs and traffic lights to give you important information about the direction of traffic and where you may and may not travel. Pavement markings divide traffic lanes, show turning lanes, mark pedestrian crossings, indicate obstacles and tell you when it is not safe to pass.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶2
text: Yellow lines separate traffic travelling in opposite directions. White lines separate traffic travelling in the same direction.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 3-1 | Alt text: “a four-lane highway with double solid yellow lines for opposing traffic and white broken lines for same-way traffic”
text: a four-lane highway with double solid yellow lines for opposing traffic and white broken lines for same-way traffic

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶3
text: A solid line at the left of your lane means it is unsafe to pass. ('A' should not pass.)

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 3-2 | Alt text: “vehicles travelling beside a solid yellow line”
text: vehicles travelling beside a solid yellow line

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶4
text: A broken line at the left of your lane means you may pass if the way is clear. ('A' may pass if there are enough broken lines ahead to complete the pass safely.)

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 3-3 | Alt text: “vehicles travelling beside broken yellow lines”
text: vehicles travelling beside broken yellow lines

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶5
text: Broken lines that are wider and closer together than regular broken lines are called continuity lines. When you see continuity lines on your left side, it generally means the lane you are in is ending or exiting and that you must change lanes if you want to continue in your current direction. Continuity lines on your right mean your lane will continue unaffected.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 3-4 | Alt text: “three examples of continuity lines on on-ramps and off-ramps”
text: three examples of continuity lines on on-ramps and off-ramps

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶6
text: A stop line is a single white line painted across the road at an intersection. It shows where you must stop. If there is no stop line marked on the road, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not. If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk. If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 3-5 | Alt text: “a stop line at an intersection”
text: a stop line at an intersection

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶7
text: A crosswalk is marked by two parallel white lines painted across the road. However, crosswalks at intersections are not always marked. If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk. If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk. If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 3-6 | Alt text: “a crosswalk at an intersection”
text: a crosswalk at an intersection

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶8
text: A white arrow painted on a lane means you may move only in the direction of the arrow.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 3-7 | Alt text: “white directional arrows at an intersection”

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶9

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶1
text: Pedestrian signals help pedestrians cross at intersections with traffic lights. The signal for pedestrians to walk is a white walking symbol. A flashing or steady orange hand symbol means pedestrians must not begin to cross.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · image

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶2
text: A pedestrian facing a walk signal may cross the road in the direction of the signal. While crossing, pedestrians have the right-of-way over all vehicles.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶3
text: A pedestrian facing a flashing or steady hand symbol should not begin to cross the road. Pedestrians who have already begun to cross when the hand signal appears, should go as quickly as possible to a safe area. While they are crossing, pedestrians still have the right-of-way over vehicles.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶4
text: At intersections with traffic lights where there are no pedestrian signals, pedestrians facing a green light may cross. Pedestrians may not cross on a flashing green light or a left-turn green arrow.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶1
text: Where there are pedestrian push-buttons, a pedestrian must use the button to bring on the walk signal. Pedestrian signals give people more time to cross than regular traffic lights. On a busy main road, an intersection pedestrian signal helps people to cross the road safely by signalling traffic to stop. The intersection pedestrian signal has one or more crosswalks; pedestrian walk and don't walk signals; push buttons for pedestrians; and, traffic signal lights on the main road only. Stop signs control traffic on the smaller, less busy crossroad.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶2
text: You must observe, obey the traffic rules and use safe driving skills to drive through these intersections. See also the section on driving through intersections .

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶1
text: Being a safe and responsible driver takes a combination of knowledge, skill and attitude.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶2
text: To begin, you must know the traffic laws and driving practices that help traffic move safely. Breaking these “rules of the road” is the major cause of collisions.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶3
text: Traffic laws are made by federal, provincial and municipal governments, and police from each level can enforce them. If you break a traffic law, you may be fined, sent to jail or lose your driver’s licence. If you get caught driving while your licence is suspended, your vehicle may be impounded.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶4
text: But you need to do more than just obey the rules. You must care about the safety of others on the road. Everyone is responsible for avoiding collisions. Even if someone else does something wrong, you may be found responsible for a collision if you could have done something to avoid it.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶5
text: Because drivers have to co-operate to keep traffic moving safely, you must also be predictable, doing what other people using the road expect you to do. And you must be courteous. Courteous driving means giving other drivers space to change lanes, not cutting them off and signalling your turns and lane changes properly.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶6
text: You must be able to see dangerous situations before they happen and to respond quickly and effectively to prevent them. This is called defensive or strategic driving. There are collision avoidance courses available where you can practice these techniques.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶7
text: Defensive driving is based on three ideas: visibility, space and communication.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶8
text: Visibility is about seeing and being seen. You should always be aware of traffic in front, behind and beside you. Keep your eyes constantly moving, scanning the road ahead and to the side and checking your mirrors every five seconds or so. The farther ahead you look, the less likely you will be surprised, and you will have time to avoid any hazards. Make sure other drivers can see you by using your signal lights as required.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶9
text: Managing the space around your vehicle lets you see and be seen and gives you time and space to avoid a collision. Leave a cushion of space ahead, behind and to both sides. Because the greatest risk of a collision is in front of you, stay well back.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶10
text: Communicate with other road users to make sure they see you and know what you are doing. Make eye contact with pedestrians, cyclists and drivers at intersections and signal whenever you want to slow down, stop, turn or change lanes. If you need to get another person’s attention, use your horn.
