locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Intro · ¶1
text: Ontario’s roads accommodate many road users, including pedestrians, motorcycles, bicycles, large trucks, buses and farm machinery. Be aware of other road users, the speed at which they travel and the space they occupy on the road.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶1
text: Road safety is a responsibility that is shared between pedestrians and drivers. Pedestrians must ensure that drivers have seen them and that drivers are stopped, or are about to stop, before entering the roadway. Drivers need to exercise due diligence in the care and operation of their vehicles, to properly respond to the presence of pedestrians. In most cases, that means yielding to the pedestrian.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶2
text: Reminder: Eye contact between the pedestrian and driver is one of the keys to pedestrian safety.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶3
text: Watch for children – Drive slowly and cautiously through school zones, residential areas and any other location where children may be walking or playing. A driver should not rely on a child's knowledge of traffic laws, so expect the unexpected. A child might dart out from between parked cars or try to cross a street without checking for traffic. Be extra cautious at twilight when children may still be playing outside, but are difficult to see.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶4
text: Watch for all crosswalks – A crosswalk can be the portion of a roadway that:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · item 1
text: connects sidewalks on opposite sides of the roadway into a continuous path

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · item 2
text: has signs, lines or other markings on the roadway for pedestrian crossing Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. A stopped vehicle may be a clue that a pedestrian is crossing.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶5
text: Reminder: Not all crosswalks are marked, but nearly all intersections have crosswalks.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶6
text: Watch for school crossings and guards – Drivers, including cyclists, must stop and yield the whole roadway at pedestrian crossovers, school crossings and other locations where there is a crossing guard.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶7
text: Only when pedestrians and school crossing guards have crossed and are safely on the sidewalk can drivers and cyclists proceed.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶8
text: Watch for community safety zones – Signs indicate areas where the community has identified that there is a special risk to pedestrians.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶9
text: Watch for slow pedestrians – Many modern urban roads often do not allow sufficient time to cross for slow pedestrians during the normal traffic cycle. So be patient and allow all pedestrians time to cross.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶10
text: Seniors or pedestrians with disabilities need extra caution and courtesy from drivers, as they may be slow in crossing the road.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶11
text: Pedestrians who are blind or with a visual disability may use a white cane or guide dog to help them travel safely along sidewalks and across intersections.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶12
text: Watch when driving quiet vehicles – Drivers of hybrid or electric vehicles should be aware that vision-impaired people often rely on the sound of an engine before entering an intersection. When you are slowing or stopping, your vehicle makes little or no discernible noise, so extra caution is required.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶13
text: Watch for wheelchairs and medical scooters – People operating motorized wheelchair and medical scooters are pedestrians too.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶14
text: Watch for streetcars – Some streetcar stops have a special safety island or zone for passengers getting on and off. Pass these safety islands and zones at a reasonable speed. Always be ready, in case pedestrians make sudden or unexpected moves.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶15
text: Watch for texters – A no-texting rule isn’t only for drivers. Pedestrians are often distracted while using devices, including cell phones, ear buds, hand-held device, GPS, and music players. People using ear buds/headphones often can't hear car horn or other traffic noise.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶16
text: Watch for dark clothing – Pedestrians in dark clothing, especially at night, are difficult to see. Extra care is needed when driving in low-light conditions. Twilight and dark clothing often initiate a collision.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶17
text: Watch for new transport – With the introduction of new technology, more vehicles such as e-bikes and e-scooters are appearing on roadways. These vehicles may require increased awareness for all road users.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶18
text: Watch during turns – Safer, signaled crosswalks aren’t immune to vehicle-pedestrian collisions. Many more people get hit by cars turning left than by cars turning right, because both parties are looking elsewhere: The drivers are busy negotiating the intersection while street-crossers are looking straight ahead.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶1
text: Bicycles and mopeds travelling at a lower speed than other traffic are expected to ride about one metre from the curb or parked cars, or as close as practical to the right-hand edge of the road when there is no curb. However, they can use any part of the lane if necessary for safety, such as to:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 1
text: Avoid obstacles such as puddles, ice, sand, debris, rutted or grooved pavement, potholes and sewer grates

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 2
text: Cross railway or streetcar tracks at a 90° angle

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 3
text: Discourage passing where the lane is too narrow to be shared safely

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 4
text: A bike lane may exist adjacent to parking bays (See Diagram 2-10)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · image
heading: Diagram 2-10 | Alt text: “bike lane adjacent to parking bays”
text: bike lane adjacent to parking bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶2
text: Cyclists are not required to ride close to the right edge of the road when they are travelling at or faster than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place, or when they are turning left, or getting in position to turn left. (Cyclists are permitted to make a left turn from a left-turn lane, where one is available.)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · image
heading: Diagram 2-11 | Alt text: “bike lane adjacent to parking bays”
text: bike lane adjacent to parking bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶3
text: When passing a cyclist, drivers of motor vehicles must maintain a minimum distance of one metre, where practical between their vehicle and the cyclist. (See Diagram 2-11.) Failure to do so may result in a fine and an additional two demerit points on the driver’s record. Whenever possible, you should change lanes to pass.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶4
text: Do not follow too closely behind cyclists. They do not have brake lights to warn you when they are slowing or stopping.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶5
text: Intersections – To avoid collisions with bicyclists at intersections, remember the following:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 5
text: When turning right, signal and check your mirrors and the blind spot to your right to make sure you do not cut off a cyclist.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 6
text: When turning left, you must stop and wait for oncoming bicycles to pass before turning.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 7
text: When driving through an intersection, be careful to scan for cyclists waiting to turn left.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶6
text: Do not sound your horn unnecessarily when you are overtaking a cyclist. It may frighten them and cause them to lose control. If you feel that you must use your horn, tap it quickly and lightly while you are still some distance away from the cyclist.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · image
heading: Diagram 2-12 | Alt text: “bike lane adjacent to parking bays”
text: bike lane adjacent to parking bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶7
text: Bike lanes are reserved for cyclists. They are typically marked by a solid white line. Sometimes you will need to enter or cross a bike lane to turn right at a corner or driveway. (See Diagram 2-12) Take extra care when you do this. Enter the bike lane only after ensuring that you can do so safely, and then make the turn.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶8
text: Watch for cyclists' hand signals. A cyclist may indicate a right-hand turn by extending their right arm.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶9
text: Try to make eye contact when possible with cyclists.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · image
heading: Diagram 2-13 | Alt text: “bike lane adjacent to parking bays”
text: bike lane adjacent to parking bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶10
text: Bike boxes help prevent collisions between motorists and bicycles at intersections. It is typically a painted box on the road with a white bicycle symbol inside. Bicycle lanes approaching and leaving the box may also be painted. As a driver, you must stop for a traffic signal behind the bike box. Do not stop in the box. See (Diagram 2-13)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · image
heading: Diagram 2-14 | Alt text: “bike lane adjacent to parking bays”
text: bike lane adjacent to parking bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶11
text: Sharrows A bicycle sharrow, two chevrons painted above a bicycle symbol on the road, indicates the lane is shared. Vehicle or bicycle traffic may be in the lane. Although you should always keep on the lookout for bicyclists, this serves as an additional warning to watch for them in the lane. See (Diagram 2-14)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶12
text: Children riding bicycles on the street may lack the necessary training and skills for safe cycling. They may not be aware of all the dangers or the rules of the road. Watch for children on oversized bicycles, as they may not have the ability to control it. When parked on the side of the roadway, look behind you and check your mirrors and blind spots for a passing cyclist before opening a door.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶1
text: Motorcycles, limited-speed motor­cycles, mopeds and bicycles are harder to see because of their size. Drivers of these vehicles may make sudden moves because of uneven road surfaces or poor weather conditions. Because they are less protected, they are more likely to be injured in a collision.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶2
text: Motorcycles use a full lane; treat them like other vehicles when driving. Since many motorcycle turn signals do not automatically shut off, be careful when turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle with its turn signal on. Make sure the motorcyclist is actually turning; he or she may have just forgotten to switch off the turn signal.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶1
text: It is extremely important to know how to drive safely when sharing the road with large commercial vehicles such as tractor-trailers and buses. Recent data show that the majority of fatalities resulting from collisions involving large commercial trucks are not the result of the truck driver’s actions, but of the other driver’s actions. Therefore, sharing the road with large commercial vehicles means you must always be aware of a large vehicle’s capabilities and limitations, such as of the following:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶2
text: 1. Blind Spots - Large commercial vehicles have big blind spots on both sides. Avoid tailgating a large vehicle. The driver cannot see you if you are directly behind. If the vehicle stops suddenly, you have no place to go. Remember that if you can't see the driver’s face in the large vehicle’s side-view mirror, the driver cannot see you.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · image
heading: Diagram 2-15 | Alt text: “the blind spots for a tractor-trailer”
text: the blind spots for a tractor-trailer

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶3
text: 2. Stopping Distance - Large commercial vehicles require a much longer distance to stop than smaller vehicles. When passing a large vehicle, do not cut in front closely. Not only is this discourteous, it is dangerous; it reduces the space cushion large vehicles require in order to stop safely. Allow more room when passing a large vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · image
heading: Diagram 2-16 | Alt text: “the stopping distance of a tractor-trailer compared to that of much smaller vehicle going the same speed”
text: the stopping distance of a tractor-trailer compared to that of much smaller vehicle going the same speed

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶4
text: 3. Wide Turns - When making a right turn, a large vehicle may need to first swing wide to the left and around, in order to avoid hitting the right curb. If a large vehicle in front of you is making a right turn, do not move up into the space that opens up in the right lane; you are putting yourself into a very dangerous position. Once the front of the vehicle has cleared the corner, the rest will move partially back into the right lane. If you are in that lane, your vehicle will be squeezed between the trailer and the curb. Stay well back until the truck has completely cleared the lane.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶5
text: This situation can occur on expressway off-ramps that have two left turning lanes. Do not drive up into the left lane when a large vehicle is making a left turn in front of you. Stay well back until the truck has cleared the left turn, or else you may get squeezed between the truck and the curb.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶6
text: 4. Rolling Back - Leave plenty of room if you are stopped behind a large vehicle. When the driver of a large vehicle releases the brakes after being stopped, the vehicle may roll back.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶7
text: 5. Spray - In bad weather, large vehicles are capable of spraying up large amounts of mud, snow and debris, which could land on your windshield and temporarily block your vision.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶8
text: 6. Turbulence - Due to various factors such as air pressure and airflow, a large vehicle can create heavy air turbulence. This may affect your ability to control your vehicle when passing a large one.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · ¶1
text: Many municipal roadways have special indented stopping areas for municipal buses, called bus bays, where passengers can get on and off. There are three types of bus bays:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 1
text: Mid-block indented bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 2
text: Indentations immediately before and after intersections

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 3
text: Bus-stop areas between two designated parking areas

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · ¶2
text: When a bus in a bus bay begins flashing its left-turn signals, indicating that it is ready to leave the bus bay, and you are approaching in the lane adjacent to the bus bay, you must allow the bus to re-enter traffic.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · image
heading: Diagram 2-17 | Alt text: “the blind spots for a tractor-trailer”
text: the blind spots for a tractor-trailer

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 4
text: A: Mid-block indented bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 5
text: B: An indentation before an intersection

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 6
text: C: An indentation after an intersection

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 7
text: D: Bus stops between legally parked cars

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶1
text: Farm machinery moves quite slowly compared to other road users. Most tractors and combines have a maximum speed of 40 km/h , but travel at less than 40 km/h when towing implements or wagons. Farm machinery is often oversized, wide or long or both, making it difficult for the driver to see vehicles coming up from behind. Farmers often turn directly into fields rather than roads or lanes, or move from lane to lane. Remember that it is common for farmers to be on the roads after dark during peak planting and harvesting seasons.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶2
text: Farm machinery on the road must display an orange and red slow-moving sign on the rear of the vehicle. The sign warns other drivers that the vehicle is travelling at 40 km/h or less. If you see one of these signs, slow down and be cautious. Stay well back and do not pass until it is safe to do so.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶1
text: Horse-drawn vehicles are one of the slowest moving of all road users. These vehicles range from two-person carts to open or closed buggies carrying up to eight people, and large, wide farm wagons used to carry crops, equipment and other goods. These vehicles will travel primarily on the shoulder of roadways, but may straddle or enter the paved lane where shoulders are narrow or no shoulder exists – such as bridge crossings. Remember that it is common to see horse-drawn vehicles throughout southwestern Ontario and increasingly in eastern and northern Ontario.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: Horse-drawn vehicles on the road must display an orange and red slow-moving sign on the rear of the buggy. In addition, many buggies have highly reflective tape affixed to the side and rear of the vehicle. The sign warns other drivers that this vehicle is travelling at 40 km/h or less, and the reflective tape illuminates as headlights hit the buggy. If you see a horse-drawn vehicle, slow down and be very cautious. Maintain a safe following distance and only pass when it is safe to do so. When approaching a horse-drawn vehicle travelling in the opposite direction, move to the far right of your lane. When passing, give as much distance between you and them as possible. Passing too closely could scare or startle the horse, causing it to change direction suddenly on the roadway.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶1
text: When you see a school bus with its overhead amber lights flashing:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 1
text: These signals indicate that the bus is coming to a stop to pick up or drop off passengers

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 2
text: Slow down and prepare to stop whether you are behind or approaching the bus

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 3
text: If you are on a road with a median strip, only vehicles approach from the rear of the bus should prepare to stop

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶2
text: Diagram 2-18

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶3
text: When you see a school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 4
text: You must stop whether you are behind or approaching the bus

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 5
text: If you are on a roadway with a median strip, only vehicles approaching from the rear of the bus must stop

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 6
text: If you are approaching from the rear of the vehicle, stop at least 20 meters away

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 7
text: Do not proceed on your route until the bus moves, the overhead red lights have stopped flashing and its stop arm is no longer activated

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 8
text: It is dangerous and illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶4
text: Diagram 2-19

text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶1
text: Traffic signs give you important information about the law, warn you about dangerous conditions and help you find your way. Signs use different symbols, colours and shapes for easy identification.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶2
text: Here are some of the many signs you will see on Ontario roads:

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: A stop sign is eight-sided and has a red background with white letters. It means you must come to a complete stop. Stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement. If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk. If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk. If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection. Wait until the way is clear before entering the intersection.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶1
text: Knowing how to stop safely and properly is an important driving skill. Safe and responsible drivers see stops ahead, check their mirrors, begin braking early and stop smoothly. Braking is easier when you sit properly. Use your right foot for both brake and gas pedals so you won't step on both pedals at the same time or activate your brake lights unnecessarily. Press the brake pedal firmly and evenly.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶2
text: In a vehicle with manual transmission, try shifting into a lower gear going down long, steep hills. This will help control your speed and you won't have to brake as sharply. Downshift before starting downhill since it may not be possible once you are going downhill. As a guide, you should be in the same gear going downhill as uphill.

locator: Stopping › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 2-23 | Alt text: “a vehicle stopped at the marked stop line behind a stop sign”
text: a vehicle stopped at the marked stop line behind a stop sign

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶3
text: You must come to a complete stop for all stop signs and red traffic lights. Stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement (Diagram 2-23).

locator: Stopping › Intro · image
heading: Diagram 2-24 | Alt text: “a vehicle stopped at the edge of the intersection where there is no marked stop line”
text: a vehicle stopped at the edge of the intersection where there is no marked stop line

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶4
text: If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not. If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk. If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection (Diagram 2-24). Wait until the way is clear before entering the intersection.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: All railway crossings on public roads in Ontario are marked with large red and white “X” signs. Watch for these signs and be prepared to stop. You may also see yellow advance warning signs and large “X” pavement markings ahead of railway crossings. Some railway crossings have flashing signal lights and some use gates or barriers to keep drivers from crossing the tracks when a train is coming. Some less-travelled crossings have stop signs posted. Remember it can take up to two kilometres for a train to stop under full emergency braking. On private roads, railway crossings may not be marked, so watch carefully.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · image
heading: Diagram 2-25 | Alt text: “the white 'X' pavement marking at a railway crossing”
text: the white 'X' pavement marking at a railway crossing

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶2
text: When you come to a railway crossing, remember:

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 1
text: Slow down, listen and look both ways to make sure the way is clear before crossing the tracks.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 2
text: If a train is coming, stop at least five metres from the nearest rail or gate. Do not cross the track until you are sure the train or trains have passed.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 3
text: Never race a train to a crossing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 4
text: If there are signal lights, wait until they stop flashing and, if the crossing has a gate or barrier, wait until it rises before you cross the tracks.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 5
text: Never drive around, under or through a railway gate or barrier while it is down, being lowered or being raised. It is illegal and dangerous.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 6
text: Avoid stopping in the middle of railway tracks; for example, in heavy traffic, make sure you have enough room to cross the tracks completely before you begin.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 7
text: Avoid shifting gears while crossing tracks.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 8
text: If you get trapped on a crossing, immediately get everyone out and away from the vehicle. Move to a safe place and then contact authorities.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 9
text: Most buses and other public vehicles are required to stop at railway crossings that are not protected by gates, signal lights or a stop sign. School buses must stop at railway crossings whether or not they are protected by gates or signal lights. Watch for these buses and be prepared to stop behind them.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 10
text: If you are approaching a railway crossing with a stop sign , you must stop unless otherwise directed by a flagman.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at school crossings · image
heading: Diagram 2-26 | Alt text: “A school-crossing guard displays a red and white stop sign”
text: A school-crossing guard displays a red and white stop sign

locator: Stopping › Stopping at school crossings · ¶1
text: Where a school-crossing guard displays a red and white stop sign, you must stop before reaching the crossing and remain stopped until all people, including the school crossing guard, have cleared the entire roadway and it is safe to proceed. If you have any doubts about when it is safe to drive forward, wait until all the children and the guard have cleared the crossing. Drivers who don't follow the stopping requirements may receive a substantial fine and get three demerit points.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶1
text: School buses in Ontario come in a range of sizes. All are chrome yellow and display the words “School Bus.”

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶2
text: You must stop whenever you approach a stopped school bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing, regardless of whether you are behind the bus or approaching it from the front. When approaching the bus from the front, stop at a safe distance for children to get off the bus and cross the road in front of you. If you are coming from behind the bus, stop at least 20 metres away. Do not go until the bus moves or the lights have stopped flashing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · image
heading: Diagram 2-27 | Alt text: “the required stopping distance on a two-way road for vehicles coming up behind a school bus with lights flashing”
text: the required stopping distance on a two-way road for vehicles coming up behind a school bus with lights flashing

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · image
heading: Diagram 2-28 | Alt text: “the required stopping distance on a roadway with a median strip for vehicles coming up behind a school bus with lights flashing”
text: the required stopping distance on a roadway with a median strip for vehicles coming up behind a school bus with lights flashing

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶3
text: If you are on a road with a median strip, only vehicles coming from behind the bus must stop. (A median is a physical barrier such as a raised, lowered, earth or paved strip constructed to separate traffic travelling in different directions. Vehicles cannot cross over a median strip.)

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶4
text: You must obey the school bus law on any road, no matter how many lanes or what the speed limit. Be prepared to stop for a school bus at any time, not just within school hours.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶5
text: As well as the upper alternating red flashing lights, school buses use a stop sign arm on the driver’s side of the bus. This arm, a standard stop sign with alternating flashing red lights at top and bottom, swings out after the upper alternating red lights begin to flash. Remain stopped until the arm folds away and all lights stop flashing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶6
text: Note: It is illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its red lights flashing. If you don't stop, you can be fined heavily and get six demerit points for a first offence. In Ontario, school bus drivers and other witnesses can report vehicles that have illegally passed a school bus. If you are the vehicle’s registered owner, these fines, but not demerit points or jail time, may be applied to you.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶7
text: Watch for school buses near railway crossings. All school buses must stop at all railway crossings. The upper alternating red lights are not used for these stops, so be alert.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · image
heading: Diagram 2-29 | Alt text: “vehicles stopped at a pedestrian crossover”
text: vehicles stopped at a pedestrian crossover

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶1
text: Pedestrian crossovers (Diagram 2-29) are designated areas that allow pedestrians to safely cross roads where there are no traffic lights. Always watch for pedestrians and people using wheelchairs at these crossings.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶2
text: Pedestrians may push a button to make the overhead yellow lights flash to warn drivers that they will be crossing. Pedestrians should point or make an indication to drivers that they want to cross before entering the roadway (try making eye contact when possible). Drivers including cyclists must yield the right-of-way to pedestrians in the crossover. Only when pedestrians and school crossing guards have crossed and are safely on the sidewalk can drivers and cyclists proceed. You must not pass any vehicle within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶3
text: For more information on pedestrian crossovers visit Driving near pedestrian crossovers and school crossings .

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶1
text: This chapter tells you what you need to know to tow a trailer behind a car, van or small truck in Ontario. This includes licence and registration requirements, trailer size and characteristics, as well as safety tips to follow when towing a trailer.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶2
text: Before you attempt to tow a trailer, consider the size, power and condition of your vehicle. Make sure it is capable of towing both the trailer and the load you intend to carry, and that your trailer and hitch meet all the requirements described in this chapter.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶3
text: Towing a trailer brings unique challenges to drivers. Almost half of the reported collisions while towing a recreational vehicle are single-vehicle collisions. Another 20 per cent involve rear-end collisions. In collisions where the driver was determined to be at fault, about 30 per cent of the drivers had “lost control” of their vehicle.

locator: Towing › Licence and permit · ¶1
text: You must have a valid driver's licence (Class G1, G2 or G) or higher class of licence to tow a trailer with a gross vehicle weight of up to 4,600 kilograms. If your trailer and load exceeds the size and weight specified in the Highway Traffic Act , you may need a higher class of licence or an oversize vehicle permit to tow it. For questions about the Oversize/Overweight Program, please contact the Ministry of Transportation’s permit office: by telephone 416-246-7166 or Toll-free: 1-800-387-7736 or visit the Oversize/Overweight Permit Office website .

locator: Towing › Licence and permit · ¶2
text: It is against the law to tow more than one trailer behind non-commercial vehicles.

locator: Towing › Registering your trailer · ¶1
text: A trailer is considered a separate vehicle. Before you can tow one on any public road, you must register it and pay a one-time registration fee at a ServiceOntario centre. When you register your trailer you will receive a licence plate and vehicle permit. Attach the licence plate to the back of your trailer where it is clearly visible. Always carry your permit, or a copy of it, to show to a police officer when asked.

locator: Towing › Make sure your trailer is in good condition · ¶1
text: Your trailer must be in safe operating condition. If it is not, a police officer may remove your trailer from the road until it is made safe to operate.

locator: Towing › Brakes · ¶1
text: If your trailer has a gross trailer weight, vehicle and load of 1,360 kilograms or more, it must have brakes strong enough to stop and hold the trailer.

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶1
text: Your trailer must have:

locator: Towing › Lights · item 1
text: a white licence plate light

locator: Towing › Lights · item 2
text: a red tail light

locator: Towing › Lights · item 3
text: two red reflectors at the rear of the trailer, as far apart as possible

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶2
text: If your trailer is wider than 2.05 metres, it must also have:

locator: Towing › Lights · item 4
text: two yellow clearance lights, one on each side at the front of the trailer, as far apart as possible, to let drivers coming toward you know the width of your trailer

locator: Towing › Lights · item 5
text: two red clearance lights, or reflectors, one on each side at the rear of the trailer, as far apart as possible, to let drivers behind you know the width of your trailer

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶3
text: Your trailer must have mud guards, fenders and flaps or be designed in such a way that it does not spray or splash traffic travelling behind you.

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶4
text: If the load in your trailer blocks your vision to the rear, you must have additional mirrors that provide a clear view of the road to the rear. Load your trailer carefully so that nothing comes loose or falls off while you are moving.

locator: Towing › Attaching your trailer · ¶1
text: Your trailer must have two separate ways of attaching to your vehicle so that if one fails or comes loose, the trailer will stay attached.

locator: Towing › Attaching your trailer · ¶2
text: If safety chains are used, they must be crossed under the tongue to prevent the tongue from drop­ping to the road if the primary hitch accidentally disconnects. The chain hooks must have latches or devices that will not accidentally become detached.

locator: Towing › No passengers · ¶1
text: You may not carry any person in any trailer, including a house or boat trailer, when it is being towed.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶1
text: Use a good-quality trailer hitch. The class of trailer hitch you use depends upon the gross weight of your trailer - the gross weight being the total weight of the trailer and its load. Make sure you use the right trailer hitch for the weight of your trailer. It should be securely attached to your vehicle following the manufacturer's recommendations.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶2
text: The hitch-ball should be installed so that when the trailer is attached and tightened, it is level with no tilting. If the hitch pulls down the rear of your vehicle, you may need to use a load-equalizing trailer hitch. You may also be able to shift some of the load in the trailer to the rear to reduce the load on the rear of your vehicle.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶3
text: In addition to a ball and hitch, be sure to use safety chains or cables strong enough to hold the trailer and load, in case the ball and hitch accidentally come apart.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · image
heading: Diagram 5-4-1 | Alt text: “a vehicle towing a trailer”
text: a vehicle towing a trailer

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶1
text: When loading your trailer, strap everything down inside, as well as outside. It is an offence to have a load that may become dislodged or fall off. Do not overload your trailer. Too much weight in the trailer can put a strain on your vehicle and damage your tires, wheel bearings and axle. When carrying a boat on a trailer, do not carry cargo in the boat unless your trailer is designed and equipped for the extra weight.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶2
text: The distribution of the weight in your trailer is also very important. Generally, more of the trailer load should be in front of the trailer axle than behind it for proper hitch weight. About five to 10 per cent of the trailer's total weight should be supported on the hitch, within the weight limit marked on the hitch. Poor load balance can cause your trailer to sway or fishtail. The ball and hitch may also become separated, especially if there is too much weight in the rear of the trailer.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶3
text: Heavy and improperly placed loads can pull down the rear of your vehicle, lifting the front end and affecting your steering, especially in wet and slippery conditions. It may also affect the aim of your headlights so that your low beams blind approaching drivers. The alignment of your mirrors may also be affected.

locator: Towing › Starting out · ¶1
text: Before each trip, check the trailer hitch, wheels, tires, lights, load distribution and load security to make sure they are safe. Check your tire pressure with the trailer loaded while the tires are still cold. When you start to drive, accelerate carefully. Drive slowly and carefully.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶1
text: Stay close to the middle of your lane when taking a curve. When making a right turn, check traffic. Look in your right mirror. Signal and slow down. If the turn is sharp, move ahead until your vehicle's front wheels are well ahead of the curb before turning to the right.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶2
text: When making a left turn, check traffic. Signal. Proceed slowly. When you make your turn, swing wide by driving well into the intersection before turning.

locator: Towing › Slowing down and stopping · ¶1
text: A sudden stop can cause your trailer to jackknife or slide sideways or the load to shift. To avoid sudden stops, increase the following distance between you and the vehicle ahead. Keep out of the fast lanes and maintain a speed that will allow you to slow down and stop smoothly in any situation.

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: You cannot accelerate as quickly when you are towing a trailer. You also need more space because the length of your vehicle is much longer with a trailer attached. Before you pass, make sure you have enough time and room to complete the pass. Once you have passed, allow more room before you move back to your lane. Do not cut back into the lane too soon. This can cause your trailer to sway and make it difficult to control.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: If you are holding up a line of traffic, signal, pull over and let the other vehicles pass. Fast-moving trucks and buses create a strong air disturbance behind them. If a large bus or truck passes you, the wall of wind behind it may whip your trailer to the side, pushing it out of control. When you experience this, do not brake. Carefully steer your vehicle and trailer back into position. A slight increase in speed may help.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶1
text: Back up very slowly and have someone outside the vehicle direct you. Use a series of small turns to steer. It is a good idea to practise this skill off the road in an empty parking lot until you are comfortable with your ability.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶2
text: To back up to the right, steer to the left. The front end of the trailer will go left, but the rear end will go right. To back up to the left, steer to the right. The front end of the trailer will go right, but the rear end will go left.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶1
text: If your vehicle breaks down, you should get help from a tow truck designed to tow vehicles. If you must use another vehicle to tow, use warning signals or emergency flashers and make sure you attach the vehicles securely. Someone must sit in the disabled vehicle and use the brakes to keep the tow cable tight. If the engine cannot run, don't tow vehicles that have power braking and steering. Without the engine, braking and steering is difficult and towing may lead to a collision.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶2
text: Trying to start a disabled vehicle by towing is dangerous and could damage both vehicles.

locator: Traffic lights › Intro · ¶1
text: Traffic lights tell drivers and pedestrians what they must do at intersections and along roads. They tell road users when to stop and go, when and how to turn and when to drive with extra caution.

locator: Traffic lights › Green light · ¶1
text: A green light means you may turn left, go straight or turn right after yielding to vehicles and pedestrians already in the intersection. When turning left or right you must yield the right-of-way to pedestrians crossing the intersection.

locator: Traffic lights › Yellow light · ¶1

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶1
text: A red light means you must stop. Bring your vehicle to a complete stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement. If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not. If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk. If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶2
text: Wait until the light changes to green and the intersection is clear before moving through it.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶3
text: Unless a sign tells you not to, you may turn right on a red light only after coming to a complete stop and waiting until the way is clear. You may also turn left on a red light if you are moving from a one-way road onto a one-way road, but you must come to a complete stop first and wait until the way is clear.

locator: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · ¶1
text: When you face a flashing green light or a left-pointing green arrow and a green light, you may turn left, go straight ahead or turn right from the proper lane. This is called an advanced green light because oncoming traffic still faces a red light.

locator: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · ¶2
text: Pedestrians must not cross on a flashing green light unless a pedestrian signal tells them to.

locator: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · image

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶1

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶2
text: After the left-turn green arrow, a yellow arrow may appear. This means the green light is about to appear for traffic in one or both directions. Do not start your left turn. Stop if you can do so safely; otherwise, complete your turn with caution.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶3
text: You can still turn left when the light is green, but only when the way is clear of traffic and pedestrians. If the light turns red when you are in the intersection, complete your turn when it is safe.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶4
text: Pedestrians must not cross on a left-turn green arrow unless a pedestrian signal tells them to.

locator: Traffic lights › Transit priority signals · ¶1
text: Traffic and pedestrians must yield to public transit vehicles at a transit priority signal. The round signal is on top of a regular traffic signal and shows a white vertical bar on a dark background. This allows transit vehicles to go through, turn right or left, while all conflicting traffic faces a red light.

text: Some intersections have separate traffic lights for left-turning traffic and for traffic going through the intersection or turning right.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶2
text: When a left-turn green arrow appears for traffic in the left-turn lane, traffic going straight ahead or turning right will usually see a red light. You may turn left from the left-turn lane when you face a green arrow. Vehicles from the opposite direction may also be turning left.

text: In these intersections, you may not begin turning left after the green light appears for traffic going straight ahead or turning right. If the light turns yellow while you are in the intersection, complete your turn with caution.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Auto insurance – it’s the law! · ¶1
text: Ontario has compulsory automobile insurance. This means every vehicle registered in the province must be insured.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Auto insurance – it’s the law! · ¶2
text: You must show proof that you have insurance coverage before you can register a vehicle or renew your registration. The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario ( FSRA ), regulates insurance in Ontario. Visit FSRA 's website for more information on auto insurance.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶1
text: Vehicle registration includes licence plates and a vehicle permit.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶2
text: Licence plates in Ontario are based on a plate-to-owner system. This means that vehicle licence plates move with the vehicle owner, not the vehicle. When you sell or change vehicles, you must remove your plates.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶3
text: If you do not intend to use them on another vehicle, you may return your plates to a ServiceOntario centre.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶4
text: Learn more about buying, selling and registering a vehicle.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › New residents · ¶1
text: New Ontario residents have 30 days to register their vehicles. To get a permit and Ontario licence plates, go to a ServiceOntario centre. You must bring along:

text: A safety standards certificate

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › New residents · item 2
text: Proof of insurance

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › New residents · item 3

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud · ¶1
text: By being vigilant, Ontario drivers can help put a stop to fraudsters who abuse the automobile insurance system. Keep this in mind to protect yourself from auto insurance fraud.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › When Buying Auto Insurance: · item 1
text: Use a licensed insurance company, agent or broker. The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA), an agency of the Ministry of Finance, regulates insurance in Ontario. Visit FSRA’s website, to check whether an insurance company or agent is licensed. The Registered Insurance Brokers of Ontario (RIBO) is the self-regulatory body for insurance brokers in Ontario. Visit RIBO’s website, to check whether an insurance broker is licensed.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 1
text: Collect as much information as possible. Take photos of the collision scene. Get the names, addresses, phone numbers, licence plate and driver’s licence numbers, and insurance information from all those involved in the collision, including passengers in the other vehicle(s).

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 2
text: Be suspicious of referrals. Be wary if you are pressured or offered money by a tow truck operator to go to a particular body shop, lawyer, paralegal or health-care provider. Contact your insurance company for information on towing and where to take your vehicle to be repaired.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 3
text: Refuse to sign blank forms in advance of receiving any services or health-care treatment related to your collision.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 4
text: Demand detailed repair and medical bills for any goods and services related to your collision, and review them carefully.

locator: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · ¶1
text: Visit the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) website for information on how to avoid, detect and report auto insur­ance fraud.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶2
text: If you are coming from behind the bus, stop at least 20 metres away.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶2
text: Do not go until the bus moves or the lights have stopped flashing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶3
text: If you are on a road with a median strip, only vehicles coming from behind the bus must stop.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶6
text: If you don't stop, you can be fined heavily and get six demerit points for a first offence.

text: If you are making a left turn behind one of these vehicles, do not pull up beside it to make your turn at the same time.

text: Changing your position on the road involves changing lanes or overtaking and passing another vehicle.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Watch for bicycles and small vehicles that may be hidden from view in front of the vehicle you are about to pass. Also watch for vehicles that may be turning left in front of you and vehicles or pedestrians entering the road from another road or driveway.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Change lanes only after signalling. After overtaking, signal that you want to move back into the lane you started from, and when you can see the entire front of the vehicle you are passing in your inside mirror, make the lane change.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Be careful not to cut off a vehicle by suddenly moving in front of it.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: If the vehicle you are passing speeds up, do not race. Go back to your original lane.

text: Passing within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover is not permitted.

text: You must not pass any vehicle within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Passing left of a centreline is not permitted 30 metres from a bridge, viaduct or tunnel.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Don't attempt to pass when approaching the crest of a hill or on a curve where your vision of oncoming traffic is obstructed and there is not enough clear distance ahead to pass in safety.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶3
text: These left-turn lanes are not to be used for passing.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing and climbing lanes
text: Some roads have special passing or climbing lanes. These lanes let slower vehicles move into the right-hand lane so that faster ones can pass safely in the left lane.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing and climbing lanes
text: An advance sign tells drivers they will soon have a chance to pass. Another sign warns when the lane is ending so drivers in the right-hand lane can begin to merge safely with traffic in the left-hand lane.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: While all public roads have speed limits, not all vehicles travel at the same speed. For example, cyclists, road service vehicles and drivers ahead that are preparing to turn are usually slower than the through traffic. You may want to pass some slow-moving vehicles when you are following them.

text: Keep to the right lane except when passing on two-lane sections where climbing or passing lanes are provided.

locator: Freeway driving › Driving along a freeway · ¶1
text: Traffic should keep to the right, using the left lanes for passing.

locator: Freeway driving › Driving along a freeway · ¶5
text: Use the far left lane of a multi-lane freeway to pass traffic moving slower than the speed limit, but don't stay there. Drive in the right-hand lane when possible.

locator: Freeway driving › Driving along a freeway · ¶5
text: Get into the habit of driving in the right lane, leaving the other lanes clear for passing.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing on the right
text: Most passing is done on the left. You may pass on the right on multi-lane or one-way roads and when overtaking a streetcar or a left-turning vehicle.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing on the right
text: Passing on the right can be more dangerous than passing on the left.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing on the right
text: If you are driving in the left most lane with a slower vehicle in front of you, wait for the vehicle to move to the right. Do not suddenly change lanes and pass on the right; the driver in front may realize you want to pass and move to the right at the same time you do.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing on the shoulder
text: You may drive on the right shoulder only to pass a vehicle turning left and only if the shoulder is paved. You may not pass on the left shoulder, paved or not.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing at night
text: Be very careful when you pass other vehicles at night.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2
text: Before beginning, be sure you have enough space and time to complete the move safely.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing at night
text: If you have to pass and the way is clear, follow these steps:

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing at night
text: Switch your headlights to low beams as you approach a vehicle from behind.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing at night
text: Signal, check your mirrors and blind spot, and pull out to pass. As you move alongside the vehicle you are passing, switch on your high beams. This will let you see more of the road ahead.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing at night
text: When you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror, you are far enough ahead to pull back into the right lane. Remember to signal.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶1
text: Use your low beams when you are less than 60 metres behind another vehicle unless you are passing it.

locator: Night and bad weather › Fog › DO · item 5
text: Be patient. Avoid passing, changing lanes and crossing traffic.

locator: Night and bad weather › Fog › Don’t · item 3
text: Don't speed up to pass a vehicle moving slowly or to get away from a vehicle that is following too closely.

locator: Night and bad weather › Fog › REMEMBER · item 3
text: Remain calm and patient. Don't pass other vehicles or speed up suddenly.

locator: Night and bad weather › Whiteouts › DO · item 4
text: Be patient. Avoid passing, changing lanes and crossing traffic.

locator: Night and bad weather › Whiteouts › DON'T · item 2
text: Don't attempt to pass a vehicle moving slowly or speed up to get away from a vehicle that is following too closely.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Never overtake and pass another vehicle unless you are sure you can do so without danger to yourself or others.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: When passing parked vehicles, watch carefully for people suddenly opening doors or for doors opened to load and unload.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Motorcycles, bicycles, limited-speed motorcycles and mopeds often need to pull to the left or right side of their lane to avoid dangerous road conditions or to be seen by other drivers. locator: Sharing the road › Cyclists · ¶3
text: When passing a cyclist, drivers of motor vehicles must maintain a minimum distance of one metre, where practical between their vehicle and the cyclist.

locator: Sharing the road › Cyclists · ¶3

text: Do not sound your horn unnecessarily when you are overtaking a cyclist. It may frighten them and cause them to lose control. If you feel that you must use your horn, tap it quickly and lightly while you are still some distance away from the cyclist.

text: a vehicle stopped the required two metres behind the rear doors of a stopped streetcar

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing streetcars
text: You must pass streetcars on the right unless you are driving on a one-way road.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing streetcars
text: At streetcar stops, stay at least two metres behind the rear doors where passengers are getting off or on. This rule does not apply at stops where an area has been set aside for streetcar passengers.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing streetcars
text: Always pass these areas at a reasonable speed and be prepared for pedestrians to make sudden or unexpected moves.

locator: Sharing the road › Large commercial vehicles · ¶3
text: When passing a large vehicle, do not cut in front closely. Not only is this discourteous, it is dangerous; it reduces the space cushion large vehicles require in order to stop safely. Allow more room when passing a large vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road › Large commercial vehicles · ¶8
text: 6. Turbulence - Due to various factors such as air pressure and airflow, a large vehicle can create heavy air turbulence. This may affect your ability to control your vehicle when passing a large one.

text: Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads unless you want to turn left or pass another vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road › Horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: Maintain a safe following distance and only pass when it is safe to do so.

locator: Sharing the road › Horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: When passing, give as much distance between you and them as possible. Passing too closely could scare or startle the horse, causing it to change direction suddenly on the roadway.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Don't pass moving snow plows under any conditions.

locator: Night and bad weather › Snow plows · ¶2
text: On freeways, several snow plows may be staggered across the road, clearing all lanes at the same time by passing a ridge of snow from plow to plow. Do not try to pass between them. This is extremely dangerous because there is not enough room to pass safely, and the ridge of wet snow can throw your vehicle out of control.

locator: Signs › Temporary condition signs · image
text: a temporary condition sign

locator: Signs › Temporary condition signs · ¶12
text: Do not pass the pilot vehicle or pace vehicle bearing this sign.

locator: Sharing the road › Pedestrians · item 2
text: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. A stopped vehicle may be a clue that a pedestrian is crossing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶6
text: In Ontario, school bus drivers and other witnesses can report vehicles that have illegally passed a school bus.

locator: Particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶1
text: When approaching any emergency vehicle that is stopped with its red, or red and blue, lights flashing or a tow truck with its amber lights flashing in the same direction of your travel, you are required to reduce the speed of your vehicle and proceed with caution.

locator: Particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: When the roadway has two or more lanes of traffic in the same direction of your travel, you are required to move into a lane away from the emergency vehicle or tow truck, if safe to do so, in addition to reducing the speed of your vehicle and proceeding with caution.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Here are the steps for passing a vehicle:

locator: Keeping your licence › Table of offences › Three points · item 17
text: Failing to slow and carefully pass a stopped emergency vehicle

locator: Keeping your licence › Table of offences › Three points · item 18
text: Failing to move, where possible, into another lane when passing a stopped emergency vehicle

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: You cannot accelerate as quickly when you are towing a trailer. You also need more space because the length of your vehicle is much longer with a trailer attached. Before you pass, make sure you have enough time and room to complete the pass. Once you have passed, allow more room before you move back to your lane. Do not cut back into the lane too soon. This can cause your trailer to sway and make it difficult to control.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: If you are holding up a line of traffic, signal, pull over and let the other vehicles pass. Fast-moving trucks and buses create a strong air disturbance behind them. If a large bus or truck passes you, the wall of wind behind it may whip your trailer to the side, pushing it out of control. When you experience this, do not brake. Carefully steer your vehicle and trailer back into position. A slight increase in speed may help.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: When faster traffic wants to pass you, move to the right and let it pass in safety.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: And do not speed up when another driver is trying to pass you. It is unlawful and dangerous.

locator: Losing your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 3
text: driving a motor vehicle to prevent another vehicle from passing

locator: Sample test questions › Intro · ¶6
text: 5. When the driver of another vehicle is about to overtake and pass your vehicle, you must:

locator: Sample test questions › Intro · item 4
text: Move to the right and allow such vehicle to pass.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: When being passed on an undivided road where the passing driver has pulled into the opposite lane, pay attention to oncoming traffic and move closer to the right side of the lane. Be prepared to slow down to let the passing driver get in front of you more quickly to prevent a collision.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: Use your left-turn signal to show that you want to pass and check that the way is clear ahead and behind before moving into the passing lane.

locator: Changing positions page · Chapter 2 › Passing
text: On many high-speed roads with three or more lanes in each direction, trucks are not allowed to drive in the far left-hand lane. This means that the lane next to it is the truck passing lane. If you are in this lane and a truck wants to pass, move into the right-hand lane as soon as you can.

locator: Freeway driving › Driving along a freeway · ¶5
text: On many freeways with three or more lanes in each direction, large trucks cannot travel in the far left lane and must use the lane to the right for passing.

locator: Particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶3
text: Always slow down and pass with caution to prevent a collision.

locator: Particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶2
text: If you see an animal on or near the road, slow down and pass carefully as they may suddenly bolt onto the road.

locator: Signs › Warning signs · ¶20
text: The downward lines show the side on which you may safely pass.

locator: Particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 3
text: Wait for the emergency vehicle to pass and watch for other emergency vehicles that may be responding to the same call.

locator: Sharing the road › Cyclists · ¶12
text: When parked on the side of the roadway, look behind you and check your mirrors and blind spots for a passing cyclist before opening a door.

locator: Changing directions › Intro · ¶1
text: Before you turn a corner, back up, change lanes or turn around, you need to know what is beside and behind you.

locator: Changing directions › Intro · ¶1
text: Always check your mirrors and over your shoulder to make sure the way is clear and you have enough space to complete the move safely.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶1
text: To turn a corner, signal well before the turn.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶1
text: When the way is clear, move into the proper lane, either the far right lane for a right turn or the far left lane in your direction for a left turn.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶1
text: Signal your turn and look from side to side and check your blind spots to make sure the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶2
text: Slow down before you enter the turn; the sharper the turn, the slower you should go.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶2
text: To keep full control of the vehicle, finish braking before you turn the steering wheel.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶3
text: For a sharp turn, turn the steering wheel with one hand and cross the other hand over it.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶3
text: Grip the wheel on the other side and continue turning.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶3
text: This is called “hand over hand steering.”

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶3
text: When you have completed the turn, relax your grip on the steering wheel and let it slip or gently feed it through your hands to return to the straight-ahead position.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶3
text: Do not turn the steering wheel with one finger or the flat palm of your hand.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶3
text: Gradually increase speed as you complete the turn.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶4
text: Remember, drivers often lose control of vehicles and skid because they try to do more than one thing at a time.

locator: Changing directions › Turning a corner · ¶4
text: Try not to brake and steer at the same time.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶1
text: Unless signs or pavement markings tell you not to, always begin and end a right turn close to the right side of the road.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶2
text: To make a right turn, signal well before the turn and move into the right-hand lane when the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶2
text: If the right-hand lane is not marked, keep as far to the right of the road as possible.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶2
text: Look ahead, left, right and left again before starting to turn.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶2
text: If you have not seen any smaller vehicles or pedestrians, check your right rear blind spot.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶2
text: Let cyclists, limited-speed motorcycles, or moped riders go through the intersection before you turn.

locator: Changing directions › Right turns · ¶2
text: When it is safe, complete your turn into the right-hand lane of the road you are entering.

locator: Changing directions › Right turn on a red light · ¶1
text: Unless a sign tells you not to, you may make a right turn facing a red light as long as you first come to a complete stop and wait until the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Right turn on a red light · ¶1
text: Remember to signal your turn and yield to pedestrians and others using the road.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶1
text: Unless signs or pavement markings tell you not to, always begin and end a left turn in the far left lane in your direction.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶2
text: To make a left turn, signal well before the turn and move into the far left lane when the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶2
text: Look ahead, behind, left, right and left again and check your blind spots.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶2
text: Make your turn when the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶3
text: When you are stopped at an intersection waiting for approaching traffic to clear, don't turn your steering wheel to the left until you can complete the turn.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶3
text: With your wheels turned to the left, your vehicle could be pushed into the path of oncoming traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶4
text: When two vehicles coming from opposite directions meet in an intersection waiting to turn left, each should turn to the left of the other after yielding the right-of-way to pedestrians and oncoming traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶5
text: Motorcycles, bicycles, limited-speed motorcycles and mopeds turn left at intersections in the same way as larger vehicles.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶5
text: If you are making a left turn behind one of these vehicles, do not pull up beside it to make your turn at the same time.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶5
text: Stay behind and turn when the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶5
text: Wait for the smaller vehicle to move right before you pass.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶6
text: The following diagrams show you the correct way to turn left on different types of roads:

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶7
text: Turn from the lane closest to the centre line to the lane right of the centre line, following a smooth arc.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶7
text: Then, when you can, move into the right curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶8
text: Turn from the lane closest to the centre line to the left curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶9
text: Turn from the left curb lane to the lane just right of the centre line.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶9
text: Then, when you can, move into the right curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left turns · ¶10
text: Turn from the left curb lane to the left curb lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶1
text: Some roads have special lanes for vehicles turning left (Diagram 2-35).

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶1
text: At an intersection where left-turn lanes are marked on the pavement, make your turn from the marked lane.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶1
text: Keep this lane position as you turn onto the other road.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶2
text: The centre lane of some roads is used as a two-way left-turn lane (Diagram 2-36).

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶2
text: This lets left-turning vehicles from both directions wait for a chance to turn without holding up traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶2
text: To use a two-way, left-turn lane, follow these steps:

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · item 1
text: Signal and move into the centre lane shortly before your turn.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · item 1
text: Slow down.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · item 2
text: Carefully move forward to a spot opposite the road or driveway where you want to turn.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · item 3
text: Make your turn when the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶3
text: Remember that vehicles from the opposite direction also use this lane to turn left.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶3
text: As they wait in front of you, it may be hard for you to see oncoming traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶3
text: Only go when you are sure the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left-turn lanes · ¶3
text: These left-turn lanes are not to be used for passing.

locator: Changing directions › Left turn on a red light · ¶1
text: You may turn left from a one-way road to a one-way road on a red light after coming to a complete stop and making sure the way is clear.

locator: Changing directions › Left turn on a red light · ¶1
text: Yield to pedestrians and traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: As you approach the roundabout, look for signage to choose your exit.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: Choose which lane to use as you would for any other intersection (See Diagram 2-37).

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: Use the left lane to turn left or to go straight.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: Use the right lane to turn right or to go straight.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: (See Diagram 2-38).

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: Do not enter a roundabout from the right lane if you want to turn left.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: Cyclists generally keep to the centre of the appropriate lane, or dismount and use the roundabout as a pedestrian would.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 1
text: (See Diagram 2-39.)

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 2
text: Slow down and watch for pedestrians on the approach to the yield line at the entrance of the roundabout.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Approaching: · item 2
text: Stay in your lane.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 1
text: Visual checks : Do visual checks of all vehicles already in the roundabout and those waiting to enter (including cyclists).

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 2
text: Look left : Traffic in the roundabout has the right-of-way.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 2
text: When preparing to enter the roundabout, pay special attention to the vehicles to your left.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 2
text: Adjust your speed or stop at the yield sign if necessary.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 3
text: Adequate gap : Watch for a safe opportunity to enter the roundabout.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 3
text: Enter when there is an adequate gap in the circulating traffic flow.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 3
text: Don't enter directly beside another already in the roundabout, as that may be exiting at the next exit.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 4
