text: Travel counter-clockwise : Once in the roundabout, always keep to the right of the central island and travel in a counter-clockwise direction.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 5
text: Keep moving : Once you are in the roundabout, do not stop except to avoid a collision; you have the right-of-way over entering traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 5
text: Do not change lanes while in the roundabout.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Entering: · item 5
text: If in the inside lane and you miss your exit, you must continue around until you meet your exit again.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 1
text: Signal: Be sure to signal your exit and watch for pedestrians.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 2
text: Maintain your lane: Stay to the left if you entered from the left lane, or stay to the right if you entered from the right lane.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 3
text: Maintain your position: Maintain your position relative to other vehicles.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 4
text: Signal intent to exit: Once you have passed the exit before the one you want, use your right-turn signal.

locator: Changing directions › Driving through roundabouts › Exiting: · item 5
text: Left lane exit: If exiting from the left lane, watch out for vehicles on the right that continue to circulate around the roundabout.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Consider large vehicles · ¶1
text: Allow extra room alongside large vehicles (trucks and buses).

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Consider large vehicles · ¶1
text: Large vehicles may have to swing wide on the approach or within the roundabout.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Consider large vehicles · ¶1
text: Give them plenty of room.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Consider large vehicles · ¶1
text: See (Diagram 2-41)

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Pull over for emergency vehicles · ¶1
text: If you are in a roundabout when an emergency vehicle approaches, exit at your intended exit and proceed beyond the traffic island before pulling over.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Pull over for emergency vehicles · ¶1
text: If you have not entered the roundabout yet, pull over to the right if possible and wait until the emergency vehicle has passed.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶1
text: A driver negotiating a roundabout in a large vehicle (such as a truck or bus) may need to use the full width of the roadway, including the apron (a mountable portion of the centre island adjacent to the roadway) if provided.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶1
text: Prior to entering the roundabout, the vehicle may need to occupy both lanes.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶1
text: Give large vehicles plenty of room to manoeuvre.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶2
text: Note: In some areas of Ontario, older “traffic circles” exist.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶2
text: They are larger than roundabouts, allowing higher speeds, and force traffic to merge and weave.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶2
text: Modern roundabouts have a smaller inscribed circle diameter and use splitter islands (to deflect traffic) at the entry points to slow traffic speeds, or to provide pedestrian refuge.

locator: Changing directions › Dealing with particular situations at a roundabout › Driving a large vehicle in a roundabout · ¶2
text: The entry is also controlled by the “yield to the left” principle; for example, cars circulating within the roundabout have the right-of-way over entering vehicles.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶1
text: Take extra care and move slowly when backing up (reversing) your vehicle.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶1
text: Before you begin, check that the way is clear behind you.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶1
text: Be especially careful to look for children and cyclists.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶2
text: While firmly holding the steering wheel, put the gear selector in reverse and turn sideways in your seat to look over your shoulder in the direction you are moving.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶2
text: If you are reversing straight back or to the right, turn your body and head to the right and look back over your right shoulder (Diagram 2-42).

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶3
text: If you are reversing to the left, turn your body and head to the left and look over your left shoulder (Diagram 2-43).

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶3
text: Always check the opposite shoulder as well.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶3
text: If you are turning as you reverse, check that the front end of your vehicle does not hit anything.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶4
text: You don't have to wear a seatbelt while backing up.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶4
text: If you need to remove your seatbelt to turn your body to see properly when reversing, do so.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶4
text: But don't forget to buckle up again before moving forward.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶5
text: It is illegal to drive in reverse on a divided road that has a speed limit of more than 80 km/h .

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶5
text: This applies to the travelled section of the road and the shoulder.

locator: Changing directions › Backing up · ¶5
text: The only exception to this rule is if you are trying to help someone in trouble.

locator: Changing directions › Turning around · ¶1
text: You may need to turn around when driving if you miss a turn or go too far along a road.

locator: Changing directions › Turning around · ¶1
text: There are several ways to do this safely.

locator: Changing directions › Turning around · ¶2
text: The simplest and safest way is to drive around the block, but there may be times when this is not possible.

locator: Changing directions › Turning around · ¶2
text: In such cases, a U-turn or a three-point turn may be necessary.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶1
text: Before you make a U-turn, check to make sure there is no sign saying not to.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶2
text: To make a U-turn safely, you must be able to see well in both directions.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶2
text: It is illegal to make a U-turn on a curve in the road, on or near a railway crossing or hilltop, or near a bridge or tunnel that blocks your view.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶2
text: Never make a U-turn unless you can see at least 150 metres in both directions.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶3
text: To make a U-turn, signal for a right turn, check your mirror and over your shoulder and pull over to the right side of the road.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶3
text: Stop.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶3
text: Signal a left turn and when traffic is clear in both directions, move forward and turn quickly and sharply into the opposite lane.

locator: Changing directions › U-turn · ¶3
text: Check for traffic as you turn.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶1
text: On narrow roads you need to make a three-point turn to change directions.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶1
text: As shown in Diagram 2-44, a three-point turn starts from the far right side of the road.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶1
text: Make sure you do not make a three-point turn on a curve in the road, on or near a railway crossing or hilltop, or near a bridge or tunnel that blocks your view.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: Signal for a left turn.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: When the way is clear in both directions, move forward, turning the steering wheel sharply left towards the curb on the far side of the road.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: When you have reached the left side of the road, stop.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: Shift the vehicle into reverse.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: Signal a right turn.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: After checking that the way is still clear, turn the steering wheel sharply to the right, while backing up slowly to the other side of the road.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: Stop.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: Shift to forward gear and check traffic.

locator: Changing directions › Three-point turn · ¶2
text: When the way is clear, drive forward.

locator: Changing directions › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Changing directions › Summary · item 1
text: How to properly turn left or right at intersections

locator: Changing directions › Summary · item 2
text: The rules surrounding turns onto and from one way streets

locator: Changing directions › Summary · item 3
text: How to navigate a roundabout

locator: Changing directions › Summary · item 4
text: Where to look and how to manoeuvre your vehicle when backing up

locator: Changing directions › Summary · item 5
text: Methods of turning your vehicle around to travel back in the opposite direction (U-turns, three-point turns)

locator: Changing positions › Intro · ¶1
text: Changing your position on the road involves changing lanes or overtaking and passing another vehicle.

locator: Changing positions › Intro · ¶1
text: Before beginning, be sure you have enough space and time to complete the move safely.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶1
text: Changing lanes is a movement from one lane to another on roads with two or more lanes in the same direction.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶1
text: You may have to change lanes to overtake another vehicle, to avoid a parked vehicle or when the vehicle ahead slows to turn at an intersection.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶2
text: Never change lanes without giving the proper signal and looking to make sure the move can be made safely.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶3
text: Here are the steps for making a lane change:

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 1
text: Check your mirrors for a space in traffic where you can enter safely.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 2
text: Check your blind spot by looking over your shoulder in the direction of the lane change.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 2
text: Be especially careful to check for bicycles and other small vehicles.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 2
text: Signal that you want to move left or right.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 3
text: Check again to make sure the way is clear and that no one is coming too fast from behind or from two lanes over on a multi-lane road.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 4
text: Steer gradually into the new lane.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · item 4
text: Do not slow down, maintain the same speed or gently increase it.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶4
text: Never make sudden lane changes by cutting in front of another vehicle, including bicycles.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶4
text: Other drivers expect you to stay in the lane you are already in.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶4
text: Even if you signal, they expect you to yield the right-of-way.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶5
text: Avoid unnecessary lane changes or weaving from lane to lane.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶5
text: You are more likely to cause a collision, especially in heavy traffic or bad weather.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶5
text: Don't change lanes in or near an intersection.

locator: Changing positions › Changing lanes · ¶5
text: Remember that spending a few seconds behind another vehicle is often safer than going around it.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶1
text: Passing is changing lanes to move past a slower vehicle.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶1
text: While all public roads have speed limits, not all vehicles travel at the same speed.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶1
text: For example, cyclists, road service vehicles and drivers ahead that are preparing to turn are usually slower than the through traffic.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶1
text: You may want to pass some slow-moving vehicles when you are following them.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶2
text: Never overtake and pass another vehicle unless you are sure you can do so without danger to yourself or others.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶2
text: Don't pass moving snow plows under any conditions.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶2
text: If in doubt, do not pass.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶3
text: Here are the steps for passing a vehicle:

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 1
text: Use your left-turn signal to show that you want to pass and check that the way is clear ahead and behind before moving into the passing lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 2
text: Watch for bicycles and small vehicles that may be hidden from view in front of the vehicle you are about to pass.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 2
text: Also watch for vehicles that may be turning left in front of you and vehicles or pedestrians entering the road from another road or driveway.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 3
text: Change lanes only after signalling.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 3
text: After overtaking, signal that you want to move back into the lane you started from, and when you can see the entire front of the vehicle you are passing in your inside mirror, make the lane change.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 3
text: Be careful not to cut off a vehicle by suddenly moving in front of it.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 4
text: If the vehicle you are passing speeds up, do not race.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 4
text: Go back to your original lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 4
text: And do not speed up when another driver is trying to pass you.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · item 4
text: It is unlawful and dangerous.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶4
text: Passing within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover is not permitted.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶4
text: Passing left of a centreline is not permitted 30 metres from a bridge, viaduct or tunnel.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶4
text: Don't attempt to pass when approaching the crest of a hill or on a curve where your vision of oncoming traffic is obstructed and there is not enough clear distance ahead to pass in safety.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶5
text: When passing parked vehicles, watch carefully for people suddenly opening doors or for doors opened to load and unload.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶6
text: Motorcycles, bicycles, limited-speed motorcycles and mopeds often need to pull to the left or right side of their lane to avoid dangerous road conditions or to be seen by other drivers.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶6
text: Do not take this as an invitation to pass in the same lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶6
text: If you do want to pass these vehicles, do so by changing lanes.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶7
text: When faster traffic wants to pass you, move to the right and let it pass in safety.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶7
text: When being passed on an undivided road where the passing driver has pulled into the opposite lane, pay attention to oncoming traffic and move closer to the right side of the lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶7
text: Be prepared to slow down to let the passing driver get in front of you more quickly to prevent a collision.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶8
text: On many high-speed roads with three or more lanes in each direction, trucks are not allowed to drive in the far left-hand lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶8
text: This means that the lane next to it is the truck passing lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing · ¶8
text: If you are in this lane and a truck wants to pass, move into the right-hand lane as soon as you can.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · ¶1
text: Be very careful when you pass other vehicles at night.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · ¶1
text: If you have to pass and the way is clear, follow these steps:

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 1
text: Switch your headlights to low beams as you approach a vehicle from behind.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 2
text: Signal, check your mirrors and blind spot, and pull out to pass.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 2
text: As you move alongside the vehicle you are passing, switch on your high beams.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 2
text: This will let you see more of the road ahead.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 3
text: When you can see all of the front of the vehicle you are passing in your rear view mirror, you are far enough ahead to pull back into the right lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing at night · item 3
text: Remember to signal.

locator: Changing positions › Passing and climbing lanes · ¶1
text: Some roads have special passing or climbing lanes.

locator: Changing positions › Passing and climbing lanes · ¶1
text: These lanes let slower vehicles move into the right-hand lane so that faster ones can pass safely in the left lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing and climbing lanes · ¶2
text: An advance sign tells drivers they will soon have a chance to pass.

locator: Changing positions › Passing and climbing lanes · ¶2
text: Another sign warns when the lane is ending so drivers in the right-hand lane can begin to merge safely with traffic in the left-hand lane.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the shoulder · ¶1
text: You may drive on the right shoulder only to pass a vehicle turning left and only if the shoulder is paved.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the shoulder · ¶1
text: You may not pass on the left shoulder, paved or not.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the right · ¶1
text: Most passing is done on the left.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the right · ¶1
text: You may pass on the right on multi-lane or one-way roads and when overtaking a streetcar or a left-turning vehicle.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the right · ¶2
text: Passing on the right can be more dangerous than passing on the left.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the right · ¶2
text: If you are driving in the left most lane with a slower vehicle in front of you, wait for the vehicle to move to the right.

locator: Changing positions › Passing on the right · ¶2
text: Do not suddenly change lanes and pass on the right; the driver in front may realize you want to pass and move to the right at the same time you do.

locator: Changing positions › Passing streetcars · ¶1
text: You must pass streetcars on the right unless you are driving on a one-way road.

locator: Changing positions › Passing streetcars · ¶2
text: At streetcar stops, stay at least two metres behind the rear doors where passengers are getting off or on.

locator: Changing positions › Passing streetcars · ¶2
text: This rule does not apply at stops where an area has been set aside for streetcar passengers.

locator: Changing positions › Passing streetcars · ¶2
text: Always pass these areas at a reasonable speed and be prepared for pedestrians to make sudden or unexpected moves.

locator: Changing positions › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Changing positions › Summary · item 1
text: The safety considerations and the sequence of steps to follow when changing lanes or passing

locator: Changing positions › Summary · item 2
text: How to deal with specific situations when passing (for example, at night, streetcars)

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Intro · ¶1
text: If you drive often or travel alone, you need to be ready to deal with emergencies.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Intro · ¶1
text: Here are some suggestions for coping with some common road emergencies.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your brakes fail · ¶1
text: Try pumping the brake pedal to temporarily restore hydraulic brake pressure.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your brakes fail · ¶1
text: If this does not work, apply the parking brake gently but firmly while holding the release button.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your brakes fail · ¶1
text: It is a good idea for new drivers to practice a parking-brake emergency stop under controlled conditions with a qualified driving instructor.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your brakes fail · ¶1
text: Total brake failure is very rare on modern vehicles.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your brakes fail · ¶1
text: If your brakes do fail and you manage to stop, do not drive away.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your brakes fail · ¶1
text: Call for help.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your gas pedal sticks · ¶1
text: First try to lift the pedal by slipping your foot under it.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your gas pedal sticks · ¶1
text: Do not reach down with your hands while the vehicle is moving.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your gas pedal sticks · ¶1
text: If this does not work, turn on your hazard lights, shift to neutral and stop as soon as you safely can, preferably off the road.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your gas pedal sticks · ¶1
text: Turn off the ignition and do not drive away.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your gas pedal sticks · ¶1
text: Call for help.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your headlights go out · ¶1
text: Check the switch immediately.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your headlights go out · ¶1
text: If the lights stay out, turn on your hazard lights and bring your vehicle to a safe stop off the road.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your headlights go out · ¶1
text: Call for help.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your headlights go out · ¶1
text: It is dangerous and illegal to drive at night without lights.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶1
text: At the first sign of trouble, begin to pull over.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶1
text: Do not wait for your vehicle to stall on the freeway.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶1
text: Check your mirrors, put on your hazard lights, take your foot off the gas pedal and pull over to the nearest shoulder as quickly as possible.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶1
text: Never stop in the driving lanes.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶2
text: Be careful getting out of your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶2
text: If possible, leave through the door away from traffic.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶2
text: Do not raise the hood.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶3
text: While you wait for help, stay in your vehicle with the doors locked.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶3
text: If someone stops to help, ask them to call the police or automobile club for you.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶3
text: If you have a cellular phone, call for help yourself.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶4
text: The Queen Elizabeth Way, the 400-series freeways and many other high-speed roads are patrolled by the Ontario Provincial Police.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If you have trouble on a freeway · ¶4
text: Stay with your vehicle, and help will arrive shortly.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your wheels go off the pavement · ¶1
text: Don't panic.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your wheels go off the pavement · ¶1
text: Grip the steering wheel firmly.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your wheels go off the pavement · ¶1
text: Take your foot off the gas pedal to slow down.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your wheels go off the pavement · ¶1
text: Avoid heavy braking.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your wheels go off the pavement · ¶1
text: When the vehicle is under control, steer toward the pavement.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If your wheels go off the pavement · ¶1
text: Be prepared to correct your steering and increase speed when your wheels are fully back on the pavement.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If a tire blows out · ¶1
text: Blowouts can cause tremendous steering and wheel vibration, but don't be alarmed.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If a tire blows out · ¶1
text: Take your foot off the gas pedal to slow down and steer the vehicle firmly in the direction you want to go.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › If a tire blows out · ¶1
text: Bring the vehicle to a stop off the road.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶1
text: St. John Ambulance recommends that all drivers carry a well-stocked first-aid kit and know how to use it.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶1
text: Consider reading a book about first aid or sign up for a first-aid course.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶1
text: It could mean the difference between life and death in a collision.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶2
text: Every driver involved in a collision must stay at the scene or return to it immediately and give all possible assistance.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶2
text: If you are not personally involved in a collision, you should stop to offer help if police or other officials have not arrived.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · ¶3
text: In a collision with injuries, possible fuel leaks or serious vehicle damage, stay calm and follow these steps:

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 1
text: Call for help or have someone else call.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 1
text: By law, you must report any collision to the police when there are injuries or damage to vehicles or other property exceeding $5,000.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 2
text: Turn off all engines and turn on emergency flashers.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 2
text: Set up warning signals or flares, or have someone warn approaching drivers.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 3
text: Do not let anyone smoke, light a match or put flares near any vehicle, in case of a fuel leak.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 3
text: If a vehicle is on fire, get the people out and make sure everyone is well out of the way.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 3
text: If there is no danger of fire or explosion, leave injured people where they are until trained medical help arrives.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 4
text: If you are trained in first aid, treat injuries in the order of urgency, within the level of your training.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 4
text: For example, clear the person's airway to restore breathing, give rescue breathing or stop bleeding by applying pressure with a clean cloth.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 5
text: If you are not trained in first aid, use common sense.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 5
text: For example, people in collisions often go into shock.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 5
text: Cover the person with a jacket or blanket to reduce the effects of shock.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 6
text: Stay with injured people until help arrives.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 7
text: Disabled vehicles on the road may be a danger to you and other drivers.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where someone is injured · item 7
text: Do what you can to make sure everyone involved in a collision is kept safe.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · ¶1
text: Follow these steps in a collision where there are no injuries:

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 1
text: If the vehicles are drivable, move them as far off the road as possible as this should not affect the police officer's investigation.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 1
text: This is especially important on busy or high-speed roads where it may be dangerous to leave vehicles in the driving lanes.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 1
text: So in a minor collision with no injuries, if you can “Steer it, Clear it”.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 1
text: If you cannot move the vehicles off the road, set up warning signals or flares far enough away to give other traffic time to slow down or stop.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 2
text: Call police (provincial or local, depending on where the collision takes place).

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 2
text: By law, you must report any collision to the police when there are injuries or damage to vehicles or property exceeding $5,000.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 3
text: Give all possible help to police or anyone whose vehicle has been damaged.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 3
text: This includes giving police your name and address, the name and address of the registered owner of the vehicle, the vehicle plate and permit number and the liability insurance card.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 4
text: Get the names, addresses and phone numbers of all witnesses.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 5
text: If damage is less than $5,000, you are still required by law to exchange information with anyone whose vehicle has been damaged.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 5
text: However, the collision does not have to be reported to the police.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 6
text: If you have a camera or cell phone with a camera and it is safe to do so, take photos of the collision scene.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 7
text: If your vehicle must be towed, get the name and licence number of the tow truck operator and/or company.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 7
text: Make sure you understand where your vehicle is being towed.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › In a collision where no one is injured · item 8
text: Contact your insurance company as soon as possible if you intend to make a claim.

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Summary · item 1
text: What to do in emergency situations such as vehicle component failure, driving off the pavement or vehicle trouble on a freeway

locator: Dealing with emergencies › Summary · item 2
text: The steps to take if you are involved in a collision with or without injuries

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶1
text: Aggressive-driving behaviours, such as tailgating, speeding, failing to yield the right-of-way and cutting in front of someone too closely, may cause other drivers to become frustrated and angry and lead to a road-rage conflict between drivers.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶1
text: An angry driver may attempt dangerous retaliatory action.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶1
text: Avoid becoming angry on the road by following these tips:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 1
text: Know the warning signs of stress and combat them by getting fresh air, breathing deeply and slowly, and listening to relaxing music.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 2
text: Make a conscious decision not to take your problems with you when driving.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 3
text: If you are on a long trip, take a break from driving every few hours.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 4
text: Don't compete with another driver, or retaliate for what you believe to be inconsiderate behaviour.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 5
text: If someone else's driving annoys you, don't try to “educate” the person.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 5
text: Leave traffic enforcement to the police.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 6
text: Don't take other drivers' mistakes or behaviours personally.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 7
text: Avoid honking your horn at other drivers, unless absolutely necessary.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 7
text: A light tap on the horn is usually sufficient.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶2
text: Remember that if you drive responsibly and courteously, you are less likely to spark a road rage situation.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 8
text: Plan your route in advance.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 8
text: Some of the most erratic and inconsiderate driving occurs when a driver is lost.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 9
text: Drive in a courteous and consid­erate manner.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 10
text: Yield the right-of-way when it is courteous to do so.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 11
text: Be polite and let other drivers in front of you when they are signalling that they would like to do so.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 12
text: If you make a mistake while driving, indicate that you are sorry.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 12
text: An apology can greatly reduce the risk of conflict.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 13
text: Don't return aggression.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 13
text: Avoid eye contact and do not gesture back.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 13
text: Keep away from erratic drivers.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · ¶3
text: If you are in a situation in which you feel threatened by another driver, do the following:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 14
text: Stay in your vehicle and lock the doors.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 15
text: If you have a cell phone, call police.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 16
text: Use your horn and signals to attract attention.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 17
text: If you believe you are being followed, do not drive home.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Aggressive driving and road rage · item 17
text: Drive to a police station or a busy public place.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Street racing · ¶1
text: Street racing is one of the most serious and reckless forms of aggressive driving.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Street racing · ¶1
text: It shows a callous disregard for other drivers and road users, and it puts everyone on the road at serious risk of injury or death.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Street racing · ¶1
text: Street racers run the risk of being charged under the Criminal Code of Canada.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶1
text: Drowsiness has been identified as a causal factor in a growing number of collisions resulting in injury and fatality.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶1
text: Tired drivers can be as impaired as drunk drivers.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶1
text: They have a slower reaction time and are less alert.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶2
text: Studies have shown that collisions involving drowsiness tend to occur during late night/early morning hours (between 2 a.m. and 6 a.m.) or late afternoon (between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.).

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶2
text: Studies also indicate that shift workers, people with undiagnosed or untreated sleep disorders, and commercial-vehicle operators, are at greater risk for such collisions.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶3
text: Always avoid driving when you are feeling drowsy.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶3
text: Scientific research confirms that you can fall asleep without actually being aware of it.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶3
text: Here are eight important warning signs that your drowsiness is serious enough to place you at risk:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 1
text: You have difficulty keeping your eyes open.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 2
text: Your head keeps tilting forward despite your efforts to keep your eyes on the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 3
text: Your mind keeps wandering and you can't seem to concentrate.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 4
text: You yawn frequently.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 5
text: You can't remember details about the last few kilometres you have travelled.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 6
text: You are missing traffic lights and signals.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 7
text: Your vehicle drifts into the next lane and you have to jerk it back into your lane.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · item 8
text: You have drifted off the road and narrowly avoided a crash.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶4
text: If you have one of these symptoms, you may be in danger of falling asleep.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶4
text: Pull off the road and park your vehicle in a safe, secure place.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶4
text: Use well-lit rest stops or truck stops on busy roads.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶4
text: Lock your doors, roll up your windows and take a nap.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶5
text: Stimulants are never a substitute for sleep.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶5
text: Drinks containing caffeine can help you feel more alert but, if you are sleep deprived, the effects wear off quickly.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶5
text: The same is true of turning up the volume of your radio or CD player and opening the window.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶5
text: You cannot trick your body into staying awake; you need to sleep.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Drowsy driving · ¶5
text: Remember, the only safe driver is a well-rested, alert driver.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶1
text: Be extra careful when driving through construction zones and areas where people are working on or near the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶2
text: When approaching a construction zone, proceed with caution and obey all warning signs, people and/or devices that are directing traffic through the area.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶2
text: Often, lower speed limits are posted to increase worker safety and reflect increased road hazards, such as construction vehicles in the area, uneven or gravel surfaces, narrowed lanes and so on.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶2
text: In the construction zone, drive carefully and adjust your driving to suit the conditions, do not change lanes, be ready for sudden stops and watch for workers and related construction vehicles and equipment on the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶3
text: Other types of workers and vehicles may also be present on the road and pose a hazard, such as roadside assistance and disable vehicles, surveyors, road maintenance or utility workers.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶3
text: Always slow down and pass with caution to prevent a collision.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶3
text: If safe to do so, move over a lane to increase the space between your vehicle and the hazard.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶4
text: Traffic-control workers direct vehicle traffic in work zones and prevent conflicts between construction activity and traffic.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶4
text: Whether you are driving during the day or at night, watch for traffic-control people and follow their instructions.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶5
text: Treat people working on roads with respect, and be patient if traffic is delayed.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶5
text: Sometimes traffic in one direction must wait while vehi­cles from the other direction pass through a detour.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶5
text: If your lane is blocked and no one is directing traffic, yield to the driver coming from the opposite direction.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶5
text: When the way is clear, move slowly and carefully around the obstacle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶6
text: Recent changes to the Highway Traffic Act have resulted in doubled fines for speeding in a construction zone when workers are present.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Workers on the road · ¶6
text: It is also an offence to disobey STOP or SLOW signs displayed by a traffic-control person or firefighter.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶1
text: Crashes involving animals (mainly moose and deer) are a growing problem.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶1
text: Motor vehicle/wild animal collisions increased from 8,964 in 1999 to 12,791 collisions in 2008.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶1
text: This represents an increase of 43 per cent over a 10-year period.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶1
text: Many of these collisions go unreported.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶2
text: You may encounter domestic, farm or wild animals on the road anywhere in Ontario.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶2
text: Scan the road ahead from shoulder to shoulder.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶2
text: If you see an animal on or near the road, slow down and pass carefully as they may suddenly bolt onto the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶2
text: Many areas of the province have animal crossing signs which warn drivers of the danger of large animals (such as moose, deer or cattle) crossing the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶2
text: Be cautious when you see these signs, especially during dusk-to-dawn hours when wild animals are most active.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶3
text: To reduce your chances of hitting an animal:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 1
text: Reduce speed in darkness, rain and fog.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 1
text: These conditions can reduce your ability to see an animal on or near the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 2
text: Travel at a safe speed and stay alert.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 2
text: Driver inattention and speed are common factors in animal-vehicle crashes.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 3
text: Watch for shining eyes at the roadside.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 3
text: If you do see shining eyes, slow down and be ready to stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 4
text: Keep your windshield clean and headlights properly adjusted.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 5
text: Use high beams whenever possible and safe to do so, and scan both sides of the road ahead.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · ¶4
text: If you see an animal:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 6
text: Slow down and sound your horn.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 7
text: Be alert for other animals that may be with the one you've seen.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 8
text: Don't try to drive around the animal.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 8
text: Animal movements are unpredictable.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 9
text: If you wish to watch an animal, find a safe place to pull completely off the road and park first.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 9
text: Do not park on the shoulder of the road, as other drivers may be distracted by the animal and hit your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 10
text: Stay in your vehicle; getting out increases your chance of being hit by another vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 11
text: If you hit a deer or moose, report it to the local police service or the Ministry of Natural Resources.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Animals on the road · item 11
text: Do not try to move an injured animal.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶1
text: Driving is a job that requires your full attention every time you get behind the wheel, even if your vehicle has driver-assistance features.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶1
text: Any secondary activity will detract from your ability to drive properly and safely.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶1
text: You must reduce distractions and focus on your driving.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶2
text: Ontario’s distracted driving laws apply to the use of hand-held communication/entertainment devices and certain display screens.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶3
text: While you are driving, including when you are stopped in traffic or at a red light, it is illegal to :

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 1
text: use a phone or other hand-held wireless communication device to text or dial, except to call 911 in an emergency

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 2
text: use a hand-held electronic entertainment device, such as a tablet or portable gaming console

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 3
text: view display screens unrelated to driving, such as watching a video

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · item 4
text: program a GPS device, except by voice commands

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶4
text: You are allowed to use hands-free wireless communications devices with an earpiece, lapel button or Bluetooth.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶4
text: You can view GPS display screens as long as they are built into your vehicle’s dashboard or securely mounted.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶5
text: Other actions such as eating, drinking, grooming, smoking, reading and reaching for objects are not part of Ontario’s distracted driving law.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶5
text: However, you can still be charged with careless or dangerous driving.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Distracted driving · ¶6
text: Learn more about distracted driving .

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Careless driving · ¶1
text: You could face charges for careless driving if you endanger other people because of any kind of distraction.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Careless driving · ¶1
text: This includes distraction caused by both hand-held (e.g., phone) or hands-free (e.g., Bluetooth) devices.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Careless driving · ¶2
text: You could even be charged with dangerous driving – a criminal offence that carries heavier penalties, including long jail terms.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · ¶1
text: Use any of these tips to avoid distracted driving and its penalties:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 1
text: turn off your phone or switch it to silent mode before you get in the car

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 2
text: put it in the glove compartment (lock it, if you have to) or in a bag on the back seat

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 3
text: before you leave the house, record an outgoing message that tells callers you’re driving and you’ll get back to them when you’re off the road

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 4
text: some apps can block incoming calls and texts, or send automatic replies to people trying to call or text you

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 5
text: ask a passenger to take a call or respond to a text for you

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 6
text: if you must respond, or have to make a call or send a text, carefully pull over to a safe area

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Tips to avoid distracted driving · item 7
text: silence notifications that tempt you to check your phone

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · ¶1
text: About 100 people are killed and 16,000 are injured by distracted drivers every year in Ontario.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · ¶1
text: About one in four of those deaths are vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · ¶2
text: Research shows that young people 16-25 are more likely to drive distracted than any age group and are the most likely to be killed or injured in a distracted driving collision.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · item 1
text: Texting or browsing on your phone takes your eyes off the road and increases your risk of crashing by 10 times.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · item 1
text: In fact, a recent study found that drivers who were texting or changing music on their phones traveled 28 metres further (nearly half a hockey rink) before responding to a hazard than drivers who were paying attention.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · item 1
text: It can be a matter of life and death for a child who runs out on the street unexpectedly, or a family crossing at a crosswalk.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › How dangerous is distracted driving? · item 1
text: For every 10-year increase in the driver’s age, drivers were 44% less likely to text, 38% less likely to use a handheld phone, and 28% less likely to use a hands-free phone.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Emergency vehicles · ¶1
text: Emergency vehicles – police, fire, ambulance and special public-utility vehicles – are easily identified through their use of flashing red or blue lights, a siren or bell, or alternating flashes of white light from their headlamp high beams.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Emergency vehicles · ¶1
text: Also, be aware that police, fire and ambulance services use many different types of vehicles, such as bicycles, snowmobiles, all-terrain vehicles, motorcycles, buses and trucks.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: When an emergency vehicle is approaching your vehicle from any direction with its flashing red or red and blue lights, or siren or bell sounding, you are required to bring your vehicle to an immediate stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶2
text: When bringing your vehicle to a stop, you are required to bring your vehicle as near as is practical to the right-hand curb or edge of the roadway.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶2
text: When on a one-way road or divided highway having more than two lanes of traffic, move to the closest curb or edge of the roadway.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶2
text: Your vehicle should be parallel to the roadway and clear of any intersections, including highway on/off ramps.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶2
text: Do not move onto or stop on the shoulder of the roadway, as emergency vehicles may be travelling along it.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶3
text: Use extreme caution when stopping your vehicle because other drivers may not yet be aware of or are already reacting to the approaching emergency vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶3
text: Look to the front, both sides and toward the rear of your vehicle, signal your intention to pull over well in advance and begin to adjust your vehicle's speed to merge with any traffic to the side you are pulling to.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶3
text: Once you have moved your vehicle to the side, brake gradually as required and bring your vehicle to a safe stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶3
text: Avoid any sudden changes in direction or excessive braking and be aware of any vehicles approaching fast to the rear of your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶4
text: If you are in an intersection and preparing to make a turn when an emergency vehicle is approaching, you should abandon the turn and clear the intersection by proceeding straight when safe to do so, then pull to the right and stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶4
text: This will clear the intersection and minimize the possibility of a collision with the emergency vehicle should it be passing you on the side you intended to turn towards.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶5
text: When the emergency vehicle has passed, check to make sure the way is clear and signal before merging back into traffic.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶5
text: Remain vigilant for additional emergency vehicles, and remember it is illegal to follow within 150 metres of a fire vehicle responding to an alarm.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶6
text: Note: Some firefighters and volunteer medical responders may display a flashing green light when using their own vehicles to respond to a fire or medical emergency.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶6
text: Please yield the right-of-way to help them respond to an emergency call quickly and safely.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶7
text: Police or other enforcement officers may require you to pull over and bring your vehicle to an immediate stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶7
text: Typically, the officer may signal this requirement by driving their vehicle with its emergency lights flashing and/or siren on behind your vehicle or by using hand gestures from the side of the road.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶7
text: When stopping your vehicle, follow the previous procedures, except that you should bring your vehicle to a stop outside of traffic lanes and onto the shoulder of the roadway where possible, or turn and stop on a side street with less traffic if in the immediate vicinity.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶7
text: If the officer gives direction as to where to stop, follow the officer's directions.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶8
text: Stay alert

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · ¶9
text: When you see an approaching emergency vehicle with its lights or siren on, prepare to clear the way.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 1
text: React quickly but calmly.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 1
text: Don't slam on the brakes or pull over suddenly.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 1
text: Use your signals to alert other drivers you intend to pull over.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 2
text: Check your rearview mirrors.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 2
text: Look in front and on both sides of your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 2
text: Allow other vehicles to also pull over.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 2
text: Pull to the right and gradually come to a stop.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 3
text: Wait for the emergency vehicle to pass and watch for other emergency vehicles that may be responding to the same call.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 3
text: Check to make sure the way is clear and signal before merging back into traffic.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 4
text: Don't drive on or block the shoulder on freeways.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to an approaching emergency vehicle · item 4
text: Emergency vehicles will use the shoulder of the road if all lanes are blocked.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶1
text: When approaching any emergency vehicle that is stopped with its red, or red and blue, lights flashing or a tow truck with its amber lights flashing in the same direction of your travel, you are required to reduce the speed of your vehicle and proceed with caution.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶1
text: When reducing your speed, you are required to assess the speed of the surrounding traffic and the condition of the roadway (such as fog, rain, snow).

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶1
text: To ensure safety, brake early and gradually to allow surrounding traffic to better adjust to a reduced speed and to ensure you have full control of your vehicle when braking.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶2
text: If your vehicle has a manual transmission, it is recommended that you use your brakes, versus shifting down to a lower gear, in order to activate your rear brake lights and indicate to other drivers that you are slowing down.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: When the roadway has two or more lanes of traffic in the same direction of your travel, you are required to move into a lane away from the emergency vehicle or tow truck, if safe to do so, in addition to reducing the speed of your vehicle and proceeding with caution.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: Similar to the procedures noted above, when slowing down and moving over, look in front and on both sides of your vehicle, and check your rearview mirrors, to determine the speed of the traffic around you and condition of the roadway.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: Proceed to decrease your speed similar to surrounding traffic speed, use your turn signal prior to making the lane change, and double check your rearview mirrors and shoulder check your blind spots to ensure no other vehicles are moving into or approaching that lane too fast.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: When safe to do so, change lanes well in advance of an emergency vehicle or a stopped tow truck with its flashing amber lights.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: Once in the lane, brake gradually and continue to reduce the speed of your vehicle when safe to do so.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶3
text: Be aware of any vehicles approaching fast to the rear of your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · ¶4
text: Tips to remember

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 1
text: Stay alert.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 1
text: Avoid distractions.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 1
text: Keep the noise level down in your vehicle.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 2
text: Remain calm, and do not make sudden lane changes or brake excessively.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 3
text: Before changing direction or speed, consider road conditions, check surrounding traffic, use your mirrors, look to blind spots, and signal and brake early.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 4
text: Keep roadway shoulders, intersections and highway ramps clear for emergency-vehicle use.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck · item 5
text: If your vehicle is being pulled over, in this instance, bring it to a safe stop on the shoulder of the roadway, away from traffic, following any directions from the officer.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: Take emergency flashing lights and sirens seriously.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: Proceed with caution, clear the way and bring your vehicle to a stop, where required.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: It's the law.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: If you don’t stop, you can be fined and get three demerit points for a first offence.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶1
text: For additional offences, fines increase and you could also go to jail for up to six months.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Reacting to a stopped emergency vehicle or tow truck › Failing to respond to an emergency vehicle · ¶2
text: Please note the above law, fines and penalties are also applicable to a tow truck with its lamp producing intermittent flashes of amber light that is stopped on a highway.

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 1
text: How to manoeuvre your vehicle through construction zones

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 2
text: What to do if you encounter animals on the road

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 3
text: Things that may distract you when driving and how to minimize those distractions

locator: Dealing with particular situations › Summary · item 4
text: What to do when you encounter an emergency vehicle

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶1
text: Always be aware of traffic around you as you drive.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶1
text: Develop a routine for looking ahead, behind and from side to side.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶1
text: Check your mirrors every five seconds or so, and check your blind spots by turning your head to look over your shoulder.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶1
text: Keep other drivers out of your blind spot by changing your speed and don't drive in other vehicles' blind spots.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶1
text: This is especially true when driving around large commercial vehicles, as they typically have large blind spots to the sides and back.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶1
text: Be extra careful at dusk and dawn when everyone has difficulty adjusting to the changing light.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶2
text: Keep a cushion of space around your vehicle and be prepared for the unexpected.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶2
text: Anticipate other drivers movements and make allowances for every possible error.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶2
text: Look well ahead and watch for people in parked vehicles, they may be about to pull out in front of you or to open a door.

locator: Driving along › Intro · ¶2
text: Watch for smaller vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians.

locator: Driving along › Steer smoothly · ¶1
text: All steering should be smooth and precise.

locator: Driving along › Steer smoothly · ¶1
text: You should do most steering and lane changes without taking either hand off the wheel.

locator: Driving along › Steer smoothly · ¶1
text: You must be able to steer in a straight line while shifting gears, adjusting controls or checking your blind spot.

locator: Driving along › Steer smoothly · ¶2
text: Picture the steering wheel as a clock and place your hands at nine o'clock and three o'clock.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶1
text: Signals tell other drivers what you want to do, alerting them to your intention to turn or stop.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶2
text: Use your turn signals and brake lights to signal before stopping, slowing down, turning, changing lanes, leaving the road or moving out from a parked position.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶2
text: Give the correct signal well before taking the action and make sure other drivers can see it.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶2
text: Check that the way is clear before you act, just signalling is not enough.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶2
text: Follow the rules for turns, whether left or right, on lane changes and on yields to other vehicles and pedestrians.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶3
text: If your turn signals and brake lights are not working, use hand and arm signals.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶3
text: The pictures on the previous page show how to make hand and arm signals.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶3
text: When watching for signals made by others, remember that cyclists may signal right turns by holding their right arms straight out.

locator: Driving along › Use of turn signals and brake lights · ¶4
text: After signalling, move only when it is safe to do so.

locator: Driving along › Keep right · ¶1
text: Keep to the right of the road or in the right-hand lane on multi-lane roads unless you want to turn left or pass another vehicle.

locator: Driving along › Keep right · ¶1
text: This is especially important if you are driving more slowly than other vehicles.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶1
text: Obey the maximum speed limit posted on signs along the road, but always drive at a speed that will let you stop safely.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶1
text: This means driving below the maximum speed in bad weather, in heavy traffic or in construction zones.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶1
text: School zones and construction zones often have lower speed limits to protect children and those who work on or near the road.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶2
text: Where there are no posted speed limits, the maximum speed is 50 km / h in cities, towns and villages, and 80 km / h elsewhere.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶3
text: Cruise control is a driver aid that can improve fuel economy and prevent you from inadvertently exceeding the speed limit.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶3
text: However, there are some circumstances in which cruise control should not be used, such as adverse driving conditions (wet, icy or slippery roads), in heavy traffic or when you are feeling fatigued.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶4
text: Speed measuring warning devices are illegal.

locator: Driving along › Obey speed limits · ¶4
text: If you get caught driving with such a device, you will be fined and accumulate demerit points.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶1
text: When police officers are directing traffic, you must follow their directions, even if the directions are different from traffic lights or signs.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶2
text: When a police officer signals you to pull your vehicle over, you must pull over as far to the right as you safely can and come to a complete stop.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶2
text: Stay in your vehicle and wait for the police officer.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶2
text: You must immediately, upon the police officer’s request, surrender your driver’s licence, vehicle permit (or copy) and insurance.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶2
text: Contrary to popular belief, you do not have 24 hours to present these documents.

locator: Driving along › Obey police · ¶2
text: If you do not obey a police officer’s direction to pull over, you risk being fined, having your licence suspended or even serving time in prison.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶1
text: As a general rule, drive at the same speed as traffic around you without going over the speed limit.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶1
text: Leave a cushion of space around your vehicle to let other drivers see you and to avoid a collision.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶2
text: Whenever you follow another vehicle, you need enough space to stop safely if the other vehicle brakes suddenly.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶2
text: A safe following distance is at least two seconds behind the vehicle in front of you.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶2
text: This lets you see around the vehicle ahead and gives you enough distance to stop suddenly.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶3
text: Do not block the normal and reasonable movement of traffic.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶4
text: To give yourself a two-second space, follow these steps:

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · item 1
text: Pick a marker on the road ahead, such as a road sign or telephone pole.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · item 2
text: When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes the marker, count "one thousand and one, one thousand and two".

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · item 3
text: When the front of your vehicle reaches the marker, stop counting.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · item 3
text: If you reach the marker before you count "one thousand and two," you are following too closely.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶5
text: Remember that the two-second rule gives a minimum following distance.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶5
text: It applies only to ideal driving conditions.

locator: Driving along › Maintaining space · ¶5
text: You will need extra space in certain situations, such as bad weather, when following motorcycles or large trucks, or when carrying a heavy load.
