locator: Getting ready to drive › Intro · ¶1
text: Before you drive, make sure you are comfortable with your physical, mental and emotional state, your vehicle and the conditions in which you will be driving.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Intro · ¶1
text: If you have doubts about any of them, don't drive.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Intro · ¶2
text: Your ability to drive can change from one day to the next.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Intro · ¶2
text: Illness, fatigue, prescription and over-the-counter drugs, stress and your mental or emotional state can greatly diminish your ability to operate a motor vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Intro · ¶2
text: You should consider these factors before you begin driving, and you should not operate a motor vehicle when you are not fit to do so.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶1
text: You must be in good physical and mental condition to drive.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶1
text: Don't drive when you are sick or injured or when you have been drinking alcohol or taking any drug or medication that may reduce your ability to drive.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶2
text: Don't drive when you are tired.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶2
text: You might fall asleep at the wheel, risking the lives of others on the road.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶2
text: Even if you don't fall asleep, fatigue affects your driving ability.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶2
text: Your thinking slows down and you miss seeing things.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶2
text: In an emergency, you may make the wrong decision or you may not make the right decision fast enough.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶3
text: Don't drive when you are upset or angry.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Be physically and mentally alert · ¶3
text: Strong emotions can reduce your ability to think and react quickly.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶1
text: Diagram 2-1

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶2
text: Get to know your vehicle before you drive it.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶2
text: There are many types of vehicles available today with many different characteristics, including fuel ignition systems, anti-lock brakes, four-wheel drive, and systems for traction control and stability control.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶2
text: Many newer vehicles offer technologies that assist drivers with steering, braking and/or accelerating to help you stay within your lane, avoid, or reduce collisions, and maintain safe following distances.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶2
text: Check the vehicle owner’s manual and other information available from the automaker to learn how these systems work, how to properly operate them, and to understand their limitations.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶3
text: No matter what technologies are available in your vehicle, you must always pay attention to how they operate, be ready to take over control of the vehicle in the event of an unusual or unforeseen situation, and recognize that you remain responsible for all driving tasks.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶4
text: For driving in difficult situations and conditions, see the section on dealing with particular situations .

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶5
text: Make sure you know where all the controls and instruments are and what they do.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶5
text: Check that all warning lights and gauges work.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶5
text: Watch for a warning light that stays on after you drive away; it could mean a serious problem with your vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶6
text: Get to know the controls well enough to turn on wipers and washers, headlights, high beams, heater and defroster without having to look.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Know your vehicle · ¶6
text: Learning to use these essential controls without taking your eyes off the road is an important part of driving.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶1
text: Diagram 2-2

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶2
text: Make sure you sit properly behind the wheel.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶2
text: You should sit high enough in the driver’s seat to see over the steering wheel and hood.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶2
text: You should be able to see the ground four metres in front of the vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶2
text: Use a firm cushion if needed.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶3
text: Be sure that you are sitting straight upright in the seat with your elbows slightly bent.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶3
text: Adjust the seat so your feet reach the pedals easily.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶3
text: To check your position, try placing your feet flat on the floor under the brake pedal.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶3
text: If you can do this without stretching, you are seated properly.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶3
text: This keeps you in the proper, upright sitting position and gives you more stability when manoeuvring your vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶4
text: If your vehicle has an adjustable headrest, you should make sure it is at the right height.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶4
text: The back of your head should be directly in front of the middle of the headrest to protect you in a collision.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶5
text: Check that you have enough room in the front seat to drive properly and safely.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Get into position · ¶5
text: Do not overcrowd your driving space with passengers or property.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Keep a clear view · ¶1
text: Keep a clear view when driving.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Keep a clear view · ¶1
text: Do not put anything in your windows that will block your view.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Keep a clear view · ¶1
text: The windows of your vehicle must not be coated with any material that keeps you from seeing out in any direction.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Keep a clear view · ¶1
text: Neither should the windshield or front door windows be coated to keep someone from seeing inside the vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶1
text: Diagram 2-3

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶2
text: Check and adjust your mirrors and find your blind spots, the area on each side of your vehicle where you cannot see.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶2
text: You may not see people or cyclists when they are in these spots.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶2
text: On some vehicles the blind spot is so large that a vehicle could be there and you would not see it.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: Adjust your mirrors so that there are as few blind spots as possible.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: Blind spots in most vehicles are to the back left and back right of the vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: To reduce the blind spots even more, position the interior mirror so that the centre of the mirror shows the centre of the rear window.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: You should be able to see directly behind the car when the interior mirror is properly adjusted.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: Position the left outside mirror by leaning towards the window and moving the mirror so that you can just see the rear of your car.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: Position the right outside mirror by leaning to the centre of the vehicle and moving the mirror so that you can again just see the rear of your car.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: Avoid overlap in what you can see in your mirrors.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶3
text: Because your side mirrors show only narrow angles of view, turning your head to do shoulder checks is the only way to make sure there is nothing in your blind spots.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶4
text: You should know the blind spots on your own vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Find your blind spots · ¶4
text: You can learn where and how large they are by having someone walk around your car and watching the person in the mirrors.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶1
text: Diagram 2-4

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶2
text: The proper use of a seatbelt can save your life.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶2
text: Even a small increase in the number of people who wear their seatbelts can save many lives.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶3
text: You must use your seatbelt every time you travel in any vehicle equipped with seatbelts.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶3
text: All passengers must be buckled up in their own seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶4
text: Drivers who do not buckle up can be fined and will be given two demerit points.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶4
text: Drivers may also be fined and receive demerit points if they fail to ensure that all passengers under 16 years of age are properly buckled in a seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶4
text: Level One (G1) drivers are only allowed to have his or her accompanying driver as a front-seat passenger, and must have a seatbelt for him or her.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶4
text: Novice drivers must have a seatbelt for every passenger.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶4
text: Drivers who do not ensure there is a working seatbelt for every passenger can lose their licence for at least 30 days.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶5
text: Seatbelts should be worn snugly enough to keep you in your seat during a collision.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶5
text: Never put more than one person into a seatbelt; this can cause serious injury or even death in a collision.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶5
text: Wear the shoulder strap over your shoulder, never under your arm or behind your back.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶5
text: The lap belt should be worn low over the hips, not against the stomach.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶6
text: Use your seatbelt always, even when you are sitting in a position with an active airbag.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶6
text: Airbags do not replace seatbelts.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶6
text: In a collision, your seatbelt will keep you in position so that the airbag can protect you.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶7
text: Note: The safest place a passenger can travel is inside a vehicle, properly buckled in.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶7
text: It is not safe to travel outside a vehicle, such as in the back of a pickup truck, or in a trailer that is being towed.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶7
text: It is important for passengers to be secured within a vehicle to avoid being thrown from the vehicle during a collision.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Fasten your seatbelt · ¶8
text: For more information on seatbelts, visit the Ministry of Transportation website.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶1
text: Diagram 2-5

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶2
text: To be safely protected in a vehicle, children must be properly secured in a child car seat, booster seat or seatbelt, depending on their height, weight and/or age.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶2
text: Research shows that a correctly used child car seat can reduce the likelihood of injury or death by 75 per cent.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶3
text: As a driver, you are responsible for ensuring that all passengers under 16 years of age are properly buckled into a seatbelt, child car seat or booster seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶3
text: In Ontario, all drivers must use proper child car seats and booster seats when transporting young children.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶4
text: Child car seats must meet Canadian Motor Vehicle Safety Standards.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶4
text: Buckles and straps must be fastened according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶4
text: Newer vehicles that come equipped with a lower universal anchorage system (UAS) for securing a child car seat do not require the use of a seatbelt.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶4
text: A booster seat requires a lap and shoulder belt combination.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶5
text: Infants who weigh less than 9 kilograms (20 lbs .) must be buckled into a rear-facing child car seat attached to the vehicle by a seatbelt or the UAS strap.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶5
text: A rear-facing child car seat is always best installed in the back seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶5
text: Never put a rear-facing child car seat in a seating position that has an active airbag.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶5
text: If the airbag inflates, it could seriously injure the child.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶6
text: Toddlers 9 to 18 kilograms (20 to 40 lbs .) must be buckled into a child car seat attached to the vehicle by a seatbelt or a UAS strap; the seat’s tether strap must also be attached to the vehicle’s tether anchor.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶6
text: Children weighing more than 9 kilograms (20 lbs .) may remain in a rear-facing child car seat if it is designed to accommodate the child’s height and weight.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶6
text: Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions when installing a child car seat in your vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶7
text: Booster seats provide 60 per cent more protection than seatbelts alone.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶7
text: These must be used by pre-school and primary-grade-aged children who have outgrown their forward-facing child car seat, are under the age of eight and weigh 18 kilograms (40 lbs .) or more but less than 36 kilograms (80 lbs .), and who are less than 145 centimetres (4 feet, 9 inches) tall.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶7
text: Booster seats raise a child so that the adult seatbelt works more effectively.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶7
text: The child’s head must be supported by the top of the booster, vehicle seat or headrest.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶7
text: You must use a booster seat with a lap/shoulder belt.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶7
text: The lap/shoulder belt should be worn so that the shoulder belt fits closely against the body, over the shoulder and across the centre of the chest and the lap belt sits firmly against the body and across the hips.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶7
text: Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions when installing a booster seat in your vehicle, and secure the booster seat with a seatbelt when a child is not travelling in it, or remove it from the vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶8
text: If your vehicle has lap belts only, secure the child by the lap belt only.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶8
text: Never use a lap belt alone with a booster seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶9
text: Children may begin wearing a seatbelt once they are able to wear it properly (a lap belt flat across the hips, shoulder belt across the centre of the chest and over the shoulder), and if any one of the following criteria is met:

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 1
text: The child turns eight years old.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 2
text: The child weighs 36 kilograms (80 lbs .) or more.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 3
text: The child is 145 centimetres (4 feet 9 inches) tall or taller.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶10
text: Do not place a child in a seating position in front of an air bag that is not turned off.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶10
text: The safest place for a child under age 13 is in the back seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶11
text: Always secure loose objects in the vehicle with cargo nets or straps, or move them to the trunk to prevent them from injuring passengers in a collision or sudden stop.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶12
text: Correct installation of a child car seat is important for ensuring a child’s safety.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶12
text: Your local public health unit is a good resource for finding out how to properly install a child car seat, or visit a local car seat clinic where certified technicians will help you install the seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶13
text: For more information on child car seats visit the Ministry of Transportation website.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶14
text: Note: Be careful if buying a used child car seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶14
text: Considerations should include ensuring the child car seat comes with complete manufacturer’s instructions and all necessary equipment; does not show signs of deterioration or damage; has never been in a collision; is not under recall; and has not exceeded its useful life expectancy as determined by the manufacturer.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶15
text: Seatbelts and child car seats save lives

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · ¶16
text: Seatbelts and child car seats reduce the risk of injury or death in collisions.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 4
text: Seatbelts help keep you inside and in control of the vehicle during a collision.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 4
text: People who are thrown from a vehicle have a much lower chance of surviving a collision.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 5
text: Seatbelts keep your head and body from hitting the inside of the vehicle or another person in the vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 5
text: When a vehicle hits a solid object, the people inside keep moving until something stops them.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 5
text: If you are not wearing your seatbelt, the steering wheel, windshield, dashboard or another person might be what stops you.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 5
text: This “human collision” often causes serious injury.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 6
text: Fire or sinking in water is rare in collisions.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 6
text: If it does happen, seatbelts help keep you conscious, giving you a chance to get out of the vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 7
text: In a sudden stop or swerve, no one can hold onto a child who is not in a seatbelt or child car seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 7
text: Infants or children who are not properly restrained can be thrown against the vehicle’s interior, collide with other people or be ejected.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 8
text: When using a child car seat, make sure that the seat is tightly secured by the vehicle seatbelt or by the universal anchorage system (UAS) strap, and for a forward-facing car seat, ensure the tether strap is also used.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 8
text: When installing the child car seat, press one knee into the seat and use your body weight to push it into the vehicle seat, then tighten the seatbelt or the car-seat UAS strap as much as possible.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 8
text: The installed child car seat should move no more than 2.5 centimetres (1 inch) where the seatbelt or UAS strap is routed through the child car seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 9
text: Use a locking clip where needed to ensure the seatbelt stays locked into position and will not loosen during a collision.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 9
text: Refer to your vehicle owner’s manual to see if you will need to use a locking clip.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 10
text: If a rear-facing child car seat does not rest at the proper 45-degree angle, you can prop up the base of the seat with a towel or a Styrofoam bar (“pool noodle”).

locator: Getting ready to drive › Child safety · item 10
text: Eighty per cent of the base of a forward-facing car seat should be firmly supported by the vehicle seat.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶1
text: Diagram 2-6 - High beams

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶2
text: Headlights enable you to see the roadway in front of your vehicle when visibility is poor, as well as making your vehicle visible to others.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶2
text: Your vehicle’s headlights must shine a white light that can be seen at least 150 metres in front and is strong enough to light up objects 110 metres away.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶2
text: You must also have red rear lights that can be seen 150 metres away and a white light lighting the rear licence plate when headlights are on.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶2
text: Headlights are equipped with the option to use a high beam to enhance vision further down the roadway and the use of a low beam when you are near other vehicles to minimize the glare of your headlights onto others.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶2
text: When you use high-beam headlights, remember to switch to low beams within 150 metres of an oncoming vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶2
text: Use your low beams when you are less than 60 metres behind another vehicle unless you are passing it.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶2
text: These rules apply to all roads, including divided ones.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶3
text: Turning your headlights on activates other required light systems, such as your parking lights, tail lights and rear-licence plate light.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶3
text: Daytime running lights, which are often another mode of your headlights or can be a separate lighting system, are specifically designed to make your vehicle more visible during times of good light conditions, and are automatically activated when your vehicle is in operation and your headlight switch is turned to off.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶4
text: When driving your vehicle, headlights are required to be turned on between one-half hour before sunset and one-half hour after sunrise, and any other time of poor light conditions, such as fog, snow or rain, which keeps you from clearly seeing people or vehicles less than 150 metres away.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶4
text: Please see the section on driving at night and in bad weather .

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶4
text: Don't drive with only one headlight or with lights that are not aimed properly.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶4
text: Have your full lighting system checked regularly, keep them clean, and replace burned-out bulbs as soon as possible.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶5
text: Parking lights are only for parking.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶5
text: In low light, use your headlights, not parking lights.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶6
text: Diagram 2-7 - Low beams

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶7
text: Your daytime running lights are not to be used as headlights during poor lighting conditions.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶7
text: They provide an inappropriate form of light that may cast glare onto others or deactivate other required light systems, such as tail lights.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶7
text: Daytime running lights are only to be used during good light conditions to enhance the visibility of your vehicle.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶7
text: If your vehicle is not equipped with daytime running lights, you should turn your headlights on to provide similar visual enhancement.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶8
text: Driving with your vehicle’s full lighting system set to automatic is recommended, if your vehicle is equipped with this option.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶8
text: This will better ensure that the appropriate lighting system is being used.

locator: Getting ready to drive › Turn on headlights at night and in poor conditions · ¶8
text: You should also monitor the activation and operation of your vehicle’s full lighting system at all times to ensure that appropriate lighting is being provided.

text: By the end of this section, you should know:

text: Factors that may affect your physical and mental readiness to drive

text: How to familiarize yourself with your vehicle’s controls and how to set your seating position

locator: Getting ready to drive › Summary · item 4
text: The legal requirements surrounding seatbelts, booster seats, and child car seats

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Intro · ¶1
text: Notes: A "Z" air brake endorsement is required on a driver’s licence to operate any air brake equipped motor vehicle.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Intro · ¶1
text: An RV endorsement (“T” endorsement) allows drivers with class E, F and G licences to operate a recreational vehicle weighing up to 14,000 kilograms.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Intro · ¶2
text: This chapter tells you what licence you need to drive in Ontario and how to get it, whether you are a new driver, a visitor or a new resident in Ontario.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Intro · ¶3
text: If you are applying for your first licence, this chapter explains the graduated licensing system, how to apply for a licence, the tests you will have to pass and the driving privileges you will have at each licence level.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · ¶1
text: Ontario residents:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 1
text: must be at least 16 years old

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 2
text: must have a valid Ontario driver’s licence

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · ¶2
text: If you have just become an Ontario resident, you have 60 days to continue to use your existing driver’s licence and apply for an Ontario driver’s licence.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · ¶3
text: If you have an Ontario Photo Card and apply for a driver’s licence, you must give up your Ontario Photo Card as part of the process.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · ¶3
text: You cannot hold both an Ontario Driver’s licence and Ontario Photo Card.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · ¶4
text: Visitors to Ontario:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 3
text: must be at least 16 years old

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 4
text: must have a valid driver’s licence from your home province, state or country

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 5
text: must have an international driver’s permit from your own country if visiting Ontario for more than 3 months

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 6
text: are not eligible for an Ontario driver’s licence

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · ¶5
text: As of May 11, 2026, when you apply for your class G or class M licence, you will need to declare that:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 7
text: Ontario is your primary place of residence

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Requirements for driving in Ontario · item 8
text: your presence in Canada is legal

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class A · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive any tractor–trailer combination May also drive in class D and G

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class B · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive any school purposes bus May also drive in class C, D, E, F and G

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class C · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive any regular bus May also drive vehicles in class D, F and G.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class D · ¶1
text: A motor vehicle exceeding 11,000 kilograms gross weight or registered gross weight or any truck or combination provided the towed vehicle is not over 4,600 kilograms May also drive in class G

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class D with RV restriction (“Q”) · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive a recreational vehicle of any weight, but not allowed to drive other vehicles in Class D.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class D with RV restriction (“Q”) · ¶2
text: May also drive in class G

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class E · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive any school purposes bus - maximum of 24-passenger capacity May also drive in class F and G

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class F · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive any regular bus - maximum of 24-passenger capacity - and ambulances May also drive in class G

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class G · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive any car, van or small truck or combination of vehicle and towed vehicle up to 11,000 kilograms provided the vehicle towed is not over 4,600 kilograms.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class G · ¶1
text: A pickup truck towing a house trailer exceeds 4,600 kilograms, but the total combined weight of the truck and trailer does not exceed 11,000 kilograms is deemed a Class G vehicle.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class G1 · ¶1
text: Level One of graduated licensing.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class G1 · ¶1
text: Holders may drive Class G vehicles with an accompanying fully licensed driver with at least four years driving experience.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class G1 · ¶1
text: Subject to certain conditions.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class G2 · ¶1
text: Level Two of graduated licensing.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class G2 · ¶1
text: Holders may drive Class G vehicles without accompanying driver but are subject to certain conditions.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M · ¶1
text: Allowed to drive any motorcycles, including motor tricycles, limited-speed motorcycles (motor scooters) and motor-assisted bicycles (mopeds).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M · ¶1
text: Holders may also drive a Class G vehicle under the conditions that apply to a Class G1 licence holder.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M1 · ¶1
text: Level One of graduated licensing for motorcycles, including motor tricycles, limited-speed motorcycles (motor scooters) and motor-assisted bicycles (mopeds).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M1 · ¶1
text: Holders may drive a motorcycle under certain conditions.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M2 · ¶1
text: Level Two of graduated licensing for motorcycles, including motor tricycles, limited-speed motorcycles (motor scooters) and motor-assisted bicycles (mopeds).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M2 · ¶1
text: Holders may drive a motorcycle but only with a zero blood alcohol level.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M2 · ¶1
text: Holders may also drive a Class G vehicle under the conditions that apply to a Class G1 licence holder.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M with L condition · ¶1
text: Holders may operate a limited-speed motorcycle or moped only.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M with M condition · ¶1
text: Holders may operate a motor tricycle only.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M2 with M condition · ¶1
text: Holders may operate a motor tricycle only.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M2 with M condition · ¶2
text: Notes:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M2 with M condition · ¶3
text: A "Z" air brake endorsement is required on a driver’s licence to operate any air brake equipped motor vehicle.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Driver’s Licence Classification Chart › Class M2 with M condition · ¶4
text: An RV endorsement (“T” endorsement) allows drivers with class E, F and G licences to operate a recreational vehicle weighing up to 14,000 kilograms.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: In Ontario, there are 12 different classes of licences.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: Each one qualifies you to drive a different type of vehicle.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: The class of licence you have must match the type of vehicle you are driving.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: You need a Class G licence to drive a car, van or small truck.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: You must have a Class G licence before you can be licensed to drive any other type of vehicle.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: The only exception is motorcycles.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: You may get a motorcycle licence (Class M) without first getting a Class G licence.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶1
text: The Driver’s Licence Classification Chart shows you what class of licence you need to drive different vehicles.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶2
text: For information on the skills and knowledge you'll need to get a Class M motorcycle licence, study the Official MTO Motorcycle Handbook .

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶2
text: You can get information on other kinds of licences - classes A, B, C, D, E and F - in the Official MTO Truck Handbook and the Official MTO Bus Handbook .

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶2
text: If you want to drive a vehicle equipped with air brakes, the Official MTO Air Brake Handbook tells you how to qualify.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶3
text: Some recreational vehicles have special licence requirements.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶3
text: If you plan to drive an off-road vehicle or snowmobile, read the Off-Road Vehicles section in this handbook.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶3
text: Recreational vehicles exceeding 11,000 kilograms but below 14,000 kilograms can be driven with a Class G, E or F licence with RV endorsement.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶3
text: Recreational vehicles of any weight, including those exceeding 14,000 kilograms, can be driven with a Class A, B, C or D licence, or a Class D licence with RV restriction.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶4
text: You do not need a licence to ride a bicycle in Ontario; however bicycles are defined as vehicles in the Highway Traffic Act and bicyclists have rights and responsibilities similar to other vehicle operators under the Act.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › What kind of licence? · ¶4
text: Information on safe cycling can be found in the Ministry of Transportation publications Cycling Skills and the Young Cyclist Guide.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing · ¶1
text: New drivers applying for their first car or motorcycle licence enter Ontario’s graduated licensing system.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing · ¶1
text: Graduated licensing lets new drivers get driving experience and skills gradually.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing · ¶1
text: The two-step licensing process takes at least 20 months to complete.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing · ¶2
text: To apply for a licence, you must be at least 16 years old, pass a vision test and pass a test of your knowledge of the rules of the road and traffic signs.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing · ¶2
text: After you pass these tests, you will enter Level One and get a Class G1 licence.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing · ¶3
text: You must pass two road tests to become fully licensed.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing · ¶3
text: Passing the first road test lets you move to Level Two (Class G2), and the second one gives you full Class G driving privileges.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶1
text: To apply for a licence, you must show proof of your legal name and date of birth (showing day, month and year of birth).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶1
text: Documents must be original and valid.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶1
text: Photocopies and expired documents are not acceptable.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶2
text: Bring the documents to a DriveTest Centre or Travel Point (a temporary DriveTest Centre where there is no regional centre).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶2
text: Phone ahead to find out where the nearest Travel Point is and when it is open.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶2
text: You can also find it on the Internet at DriveTest Centre .

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶3
text: You must pay a fee when you apply.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶3
text: This fee includes the cost of the knowledge test, your first road test and a five-year licensing fee.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶3
text: There are more charges for your second road test and for any retests you may need to take.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶3
text: To schedule a road-test appointment, you must prepay the fee.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶4
text: When you apply for your licence, you will be asked questions about your health.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶4
text: People with certain physical or medical conditions are not allowed to drive for safety reasons.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶4
text: If your physical or medical condition means you cannot be licensed, you will be told when you apply.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶5
text: Once you have a licence, you should report any change in your medical condition that may affect your ability to drive safely.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶5
text: By law, doctors and optometrists must report the name and address of anyone over 16 who has a condition that may make it unsafe for him or her to drive.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence · ¶6
text: For further details on applying for a licence, visit the Ministry of Transportation website .

text: Any one of the following documents may be used to satisfy the requirement to provide proof of legal name and complete date of birth:

text: Passport (Canadian or foreign)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 2
text: Canadian Citizenship Card with photo

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 3
text: Permanent immigration documents

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 4
text: Permanent Resident Card (PRC)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 5
text: Record of Landing (Form 1000)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 6
text: Confirmation of Permanent Residence (Form IMM 5292)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 7
text: Temporary immigration documents

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 8
text: Student Authorization (IMM 1442)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 9
text: Employment Authorization(IMM 1442)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 10
text: Visitor Record (IMM 1442)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 11
text: Temporary Resident’s Permit (IMM 1442)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Applying for a licence › Proof of identification · item 12
text: Report Pursuant to the Immigration Act (IMM 1442 with photo)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · ¶1
text: The photo on your driver’s licence must meet certain standards.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · ¶1
text: Your face must:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · item 1
text: be completely visible

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · item 2
text: be free of any obstructions

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · item 3
text: have a neutral and relaxed expression (do not smile)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · item 4
text: be facing straight at the camera (not tilted)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · ¶2
text: You can wear headwear for religious or medical reasons but it must not cover any part of your face.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · ¶2
text: You may be asked to remove any other headwear or face wear, for example, hats, eyeglasses or headphones, when taking a photo for government-issued identification.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · ¶3
text: Your hair cannot cover your eyes.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Photos · ¶4
text: If the photo does not meet the required standards, you may be asked to return to have your photo retaken.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Additional documents · ¶1
text: Additional documents are required if the document presented from the previous list does not indicate the legal name or complete date of birth (day, month, year).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Additional documents · ¶1
text: The additional documents must provide proof of the missing or incomplete information.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Additional documents · ¶2
text: The following documents are acceptable as proof of date of birth and legal name:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Additional documents · item 1
text: Canadian or U.S. Birth Certificate

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · ¶1
text: If additional documents presented to prove date of birth do not indicate the applicant’s legal name (for example, the name has been changed or is different on the two documents presented), the applicant will be required to provide additional documents as proof of legal name.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · ¶1
text: The following additional documents are acceptable as proof of legal name:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · item 1
text: Marriage certificate (Canadian or foreign, government-issued)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · item 2
text: Change-of-name certificate

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · item 3
text: Court order for adoption, change of name or divorce (must bear legal name, date of birth and court seal)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · ¶2
text: To confirm complete date of birth where no or only partial date of birth is available:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · item 4
text: Sworn affidavit stating reason why partial or no date is available, with supporting documents.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · item 4
text: Please contact ServiceOntario at 416-235-2999 or toll free at 1-800-387-3445 (Canada-wide) for further information.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Proof of legal name · ¶3
text: Note: Direct identification by a parent or guardian is not acceptable.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements · ¶1
text: Here are the rules you must follow at each level:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements · item 1
text: Level One (Class G1)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements · item 2
text: G1 knowledge test – checklist

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements · item 3
text: G1 exit test – checklist

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements · item 4
text: Level Two (Class G2)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements · item 5
text: Road tests

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements · item 6
text: G2 exit test – checklist

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · ¶1
text: Level One lasts 12 months.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · ¶1
text: The Ministry of Transportation encourages all new drivers to take an approved driver-education course to help learn the proper driving skills and knowledge.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · ¶1
text: You should begin your training as soon as you become a Level One driver so you can get as much driving experience as possible.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · ¶1
text: If you pass an approved course, you can complete Level One in eight months.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · ¶1
text: While at Level One, the following rules apply:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 1
text: You must not drive if you have been drinking alcohol.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 1
text: Your blood-alcohol level must be zero.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 2
text: You must not drive alone; an accompanying driver must sit in the front passenger seat.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 2
text: This is the only person who can be in the front seat with you while you drive.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 2
text: The accompanying driver must have a valid Class G (or higher) licence, at least four years of driving experience and a blood-alcohol level of less than .05% when accompanying you.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 2
text: Time spent at the Class G2 level, as long as the G2 licence was valid (not suspended), does count toward the accompanying driver’s four years of experience.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 2
text: The accompanying driver’s licence may have demerit points, but it cannot be suspended.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 3
text: Each person in the vehicle must have a working seatbelt.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 4
text: You must not drive on 400-series highways with a posted speed limit over 80 km/h .

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 4
text: Also, you must not drive on certain high-speed roads including the Queen Elizabeth Way, Don Valley Parkway and the Gardiner Expressway in the Greater Toronto Area, the E.C.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 4
text: Row Expressway in Windsor and the Conestoga Parkway in Kitchener-Waterloo.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 4
text: However, if your accompanying driver is a driving instructor, you may drive on any road.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · item 5
text: You must not drive between midnight and 5 a.m.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · ¶2
text: You must pass a road test of your driving skills to move to Level Two.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level One (Class G1) · ¶2
text: At this time, you will be given a Class G2 licence.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 knowledge test – checklist · ¶1
text: Before taking the G1 knowledge test, make sure you have studied the Official MTO Driver’s Handbook.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 knowledge test – checklist · ¶2
text: Bring the following items to the test:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 knowledge test – checklist · item 1
text: Two pieces of identification

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 knowledge test – checklist · item 2
text: Money for test fees – cash, debit or credit card

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 knowledge test – checklist · item 3
text: Glasses or contact lenses (if you need to wear them to drive)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 exit test – checklist · ¶1
text: Before taking the G1 exit test, make sure you have studied the Official MTO Driver’s Handbook.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 exit test – checklist · ¶2
text: Bring the following items to the test:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 exit test – checklist · item 1
text: Vehicle in good working order

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 exit test – checklist · item 2
text: Money for test fees (if applicable)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 exit test – checklist · item 3
text: Glasses or contact lenses (if you need to wear them to drive)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G1 exit test – checklist · item 4
text: Arrive at least 30 minutes before Road Test appointment

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶1
text: Level Two lasts at least 12 months.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶1
text: At this level, you have more privileges because of your driving experience.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶2
text: At Level Two:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · item 1
text: You must not drive if you have been drinking alcohol.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · item 1
text: Your blood-alcohol level must be zero.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · item 2
text: Each person in the vehicle must have a working seatbelt.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶3
text: In addition, the following restrictions apply between the hours of midnight and 5 a.m. to G2 drivers aged 19 years and under.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · item 3
text: In the first six months after receiving your G2 licence, you are allowed to carry only one passenger aged 19 or under.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · item 4
text: After six months with your G2 licence and until you obtain your full G licence or turn 20, you are allowed to carry up to three passengers aged 19 or under.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶4
text: Exemptions: The passenger restrictions for G2 drivers aged 19 and under do not apply if you are accompanied by a fully–licensed driver in the front passenger seat, or if the passengers are members of your immediate family (a guardian or those related to you by blood, marriage, common–law relationship or adoption).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶5
text: After 12 months at Level Two, you may take a road test to qualify for full licence privileges.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶5
text: You must pass this test to get a Class G licence.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶6
text: Note: It is now law that all young drivers 21 and under, regardless of licence class, must have a blood-alcohol level of zero.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶7
text: Note: A restricted Class M licence for limited-speed motorcycle and moped drivers allows licence holders to drive only a limited-speed motorcycle and moped.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶7
text: You are not permitted to drive a limited-speed motorcycle or moped on any driver’s licence other than a class M licence (including M1, M2(L),M2, M(L) or M).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Level Two (Class G2): · ¶7
text: For more information on how to obtain a restricted Class M licence to drive a moped, and graduated licensing requirements, please read the Official MTO Motorcycle Handbook .

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶1
text: Road tests check your driving skills in the vehicle and in traffic.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶1
text: You will be tested on your ability to follow the rules of the road and safe driving practices.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶2
text: When you feel qualified to drive safely and confident enough to take your road test, schedule an appointment by internet, phone or in-person at any DriveTest Centre.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶2
text: You can contact the DriveTest Centre at 647-776-0331 or 1-888-570-6110 , or go online to DriveTest Centre .

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶3
text: You must bring the appropriate vehicle to your road test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶3
text: The vehicle must be fit, in proper working condition, plated and insured.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶4
text: If you are a Level One driver, an accompanying driver must come with you to the test centre.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶4
text: If you are a Level Two driver, be prepared to take alternate transportation home in case you fail your road test and are unqualified to drive.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶5
text: No pets or passengers other than the driver examiner are allowed in the vehicle during a road test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶5
text: Driving instructors, friends, relatives and translators may not accompany you during the test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶6
text: All road tests have a set time frame.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶6
text: Before you begin your test, the examiner will inform you of the time you have to complete the test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶6
text: You will not be asked to do anything illegal during the road test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶6
text: The examiner will explain the test, and you should follow his or her instructions.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶6
text: The examiner is not allowed to coach you during the test, so if you have any questions, ask them before you begin.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶7
text: Electronic driving aids such as automatic parallel-parking systems, lane monitoring, cruise control, and back cameras may not be used during the road test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶7
text: On a road test, you are required to demonstrate the proper skills in operating a motor vehicle without the reliance of driving aids (for example, shoulder checks, mirror checks and so on).

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶8
text: At the end of each test, the examiner will give you a complete report of your skills, and explain any mistakes you have made.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶8
text: If you fail the test, the report will show you where you need to improve.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶8
text: When you have had more practice, you can make an appointment to take the test again.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › Road tests · ¶8
text: You must wait at least 10 days between tests.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G2 exit test – checklist · ¶1
text: You must have highway driving experience (experience driving on highways with speed limits of at least 80 km /h) before taking the G2 exit test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G2 exit test – checklist · ¶1
text: You must complete a Declaration of Highway Driving Experience form, describing the highway driving experience you have, before taking the road test.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G2 exit test – checklist · ¶1
text: Bring the following items to the test:

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G2 exit test – checklist · item 1
text: Vehicle in good working order

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G2 exit test – checklist · item 2
text: Money for test fees (if applicable)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G2 exit test – checklist · item 3
text: Glasses or contact lenses (if you need to wear them to drive)

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requirements › G2 exit test – checklist · item 4
text: Arrive at least 30 minutes before Road Test appointment

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Failure to attend road test, or short notice cancellation · ¶1
text: If you cancel or reschedule your road test appointment with less than 48 hours notice, or if you fail to attend your appointment, your prepaid road-test fee will not be refunded.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Failure to attend road test, or short notice cancellation · ¶1
text: Under certain extenuating circumstances only (such as a death in your immediate family), the road-test fee will remain as a credit on your driving record.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Out-of-order road test · ¶1
text: If your vehicle does not meet ministry standards for the purpose of a road test, or if there is a non-vehicle-related reason for which the examiner determines that the road test cannot be completed, the examiner declares the road test out-of-order.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Out-of-order road test · ¶1
text: If your road test is declared out-of-order, you lose 50% of your road test fee.

locator: Getting Your Driver’s Licence › Out-of-order road test · ¶1
text: The other 50% of the fee remains as a credit on your driving record, and may be applied when booking a new road test.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶1
text: Ontario is a road safety leader in Canada and North America.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶1
text: The Ministry of Transportation has introduced a range of measures to maintain this record and to improve the behaviour of all drivers.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶2
text: Most collisions are caused by driver error or behaviours such as following too closely, speeding, failure to yield the right of way, improper turns, running red lights and frequently changing lanes.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶2
text: There are also drivers who intentionally put others at risk through such reckless behaviour.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶2
text: Statistics show that new drivers of all ages are far more likely than experienced drivers to be involved in serious or fatal collisions.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶3
text: Provincial campaigns promoting the correct use of seatbelts and child car seats, and informing people about drinking and driving and aggressive driving, are making a difference.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶3
text: Ontario’s Graduated Licensing System (GLS), which lets new drivers gain skills and experience in low-risk environments, is also helping to develop better, safer drivers.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶4
text: This handbook gives new drivers the basic information they need about learning to drive in Ontario: the rules of the road, safe driving practices and how to get a licence to drive a car, van or small truck.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶4
text: The ministry recommends that all drivers would benefit from taking an advanced course in driver training.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶5
text: As you read, remember that this handbook is only a guide.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶5
text: For official descriptions of the laws, look in the Highway Traffic Act of Ontario and its Regulations .

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶5
text: Information on how to get licences to drive other types of vehicles is available in Part Two of this handbook, the Official MTO Motorcycle Handbook , the Official MTO Truck Handbook , the Official MTO Bus Handbook and the Official MTO Air Brake Handbook.

locator: The Official Ministry of Transportation (MTO) Driver’s Handbook › Introduction · ¶6

text: If you are 80 years of age or older, you are required to renew your driver’s licence every two years.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶1
text: This renewal process helps keep seniors mobile and independent longer, while helping to ensure that unsafe drivers are identified and appropriate actions are taken.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶2
text: Before your licence expires, you will receive a driver’s licence renewal application form and a letter in the mail explaining the steps you need to complete.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶3
text: First, you should:

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶4

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 4

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 5

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 6

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶5

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶6

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶7
text: However, you may also need to pass a road test, follow up with your doctor and submit medical information or provide additional vision information from a doctor or optometrist before being able to renew your licence.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶7

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶8

text: Your health is a key factor in your ability to drive.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · ¶1

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 1

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requalification · ¶1
text: Under graduated licensing, novice drivers (Class G1, G2, M1 and M2) progress through a two-step licensing process by completing the mandatory time periods for each level and passing the required road tests.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requalification · ¶1
text: Except for Class M1, novice drivers have five years to complete the graduated-licensing process.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requalification · ¶1
text: However, if your Class G1, G2 or M2 licence is about to expire and you have not completed the process, you can regain or retain the same class of licence by passing a test and paying the five-year licensing fee.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requalification · ¶1
text: This is called “requalification.”

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requalification · ¶1
text: A notice is sent to Class G1, G2 and M2 drivers before their licence expiry date to inform them of their options.

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requalification · ¶1

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system · ¶1

locator: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system · ¶1
