locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶1
text: Pavement markings combine with road signs and traffic lights to give you important information about the direction of traffic and where you may and may not travel.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶1
text: Pavement markings divide traffic lanes, show turning lanes, mark pedestrian crossings, indicate obstacles and tell you when it is not safe to pass.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶2
text: Yellow lines separate traffic travelling in opposite directions.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶2
text: White lines separate traffic travelling in the same direction.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶3
text: A solid line at the left of your lane means it is unsafe to pass.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶3
text: ('A' should not pass.)

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶4
text: A broken line at the left of your lane means you may pass if the way is clear.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶4
text: ('A' may pass if there are enough broken lines ahead to complete the pass safely.)

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶5
text: Broken lines that are wider and closer together than regular broken lines are called continuity lines.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶5
text: When you see continuity lines on your left side, it generally means the lane you are in is ending or exiting and that you must change lanes if you want to continue in your current direction.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶5
text: Continuity lines on your right mean your lane will continue unaffected.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶6
text: A stop line is a single white line painted across the road at an intersection.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶6
text: It shows where you must stop.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶6
text: If there is no stop line marked on the road, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶6
text: If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶6
text: If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶7
text: A crosswalk is marked by two parallel white lines painted across the road.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶7
text: However, crosswalks at intersections are not always marked.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶7
text: If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶7
text: If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶7
text: If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶8
text: A white arrow painted on a lane means you may move only in the direction of the arrow.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶9
text: Pedestrian crossovers are identified by specific signs, overhead yellow lights, and pavement markings.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶9
text: Pedestrian crossovers are marked by two white double parallel lines across the road with an X in each lane approaching it.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶10
text: Drivers and cyclists must stop before the line and yield to pedestrians until pedestrians have completely crossed the road and cleared the roadway.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶11
text: Two solid lines painted on the pavement guide traffic away from fixed objects such as bridge piers or concrete islands.

locator: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶11
text: Yellow and black markings are also painted on the objects themselves as warnings.

locator: Pavement markings › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Pavement markings › Summary · item 1
text: How pavement markings are used to control traffic

locator: Pavement markings › Summary · item 2
text: What the different colours and types of markings are used to indicate

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶1
text: Pedestrian signals help pedestrians cross at intersections with traffic lights.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶1
text: The signal for pedestrians to walk is a white walking symbol.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶1
text: A flashing or steady orange hand symbol means pedestrians must not begin to cross.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶2
text: A pedestrian facing a walk signal may cross the road in the direction of the signal.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶2
text: While crossing, pedestrians have the right-of-way over all vehicles.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶3
text: A pedestrian facing a flashing or steady hand symbol should not begin to cross the road.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶3
text: Pedestrians who have already begun to cross when the hand signal appears, should go as quickly as possible to a safe area.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶3
text: While they are crossing, pedestrians still have the right-of-way over vehicles.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶4
text: At intersections with traffic lights where there are no pedestrian signals, pedestrians facing a green light may cross.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶4
text: Pedestrians may not cross on a flashing green light or a left-turn green arrow.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶1
text: Where there are pedestrian push-buttons, a pedestrian must use the button to bring on the walk signal.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶1
text: Pedestrian signals give people more time to cross than regular traffic lights.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶1
text: On a busy main road, an intersection pedestrian signal helps people to cross the road safely by signalling traffic to stop.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶1
text: The intersection pedestrian signal has one or more crosswalks; pedestrian walk and don't walk signals; push buttons for pedestrians; and, traffic signal lights on the main road only.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶1
text: Stop signs control traffic on the smaller, less busy crossroad.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶2
text: You must observe, obey the traffic rules and use safe driving skills to drive through these intersections.

locator: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶2
text: See also the section on driving through intersections .

locator: Pedestrian signals › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Pedestrian signals › Summary · item 1
text: What the symbols on pedestrian signals indicate

locator: Pedestrian signals › Summary · item 2
text: What an intersection pedestrian signal is and what to do if you encounter one

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶1
text: Being a safe and responsible driver takes a combination of knowledge, skill and attitude.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶2
text: To begin, you must know the traffic laws and driving practices that help traffic move safely.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶2
text: Breaking these “rules of the road” is the major cause of collisions.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶3
text: Traffic laws are made by federal, provincial and municipal governments, and police from each level can enforce them.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶3
text: If you break a traffic law, you may be fined, sent to jail or lose your driver’s licence.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶3
text: If you get caught driving while your licence is suspended, your vehicle may be impounded.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶4
text: But you need to do more than just obey the rules.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶4
text: You must care about the safety of others on the road.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶4
text: Everyone is responsible for avoiding collisions.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶4
text: Even if someone else does something wrong, you may be found responsible for a collision if you could have done something to avoid it.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶5
text: Because drivers have to co-operate to keep traffic moving safely, you must also be predictable, doing what other people using the road expect you to do.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶5
text: And you must be courteous.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶5
text: Courteous driving means giving other drivers space to change lanes, not cutting them off and signalling your turns and lane changes properly.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶6
text: You must be able to see dangerous situations before they happen and to respond quickly and effectively to prevent them.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶6
text: This is called defensive or strategic driving.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶6
text: There are collision avoidance courses available where you can practice these techniques.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶7
text: Defensive driving is based on three ideas: visibility, space and communication.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶8
text: Visibility is about seeing and being seen.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶8
text: You should always be aware of traffic in front, behind and beside you.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶8
text: Keep your eyes constantly moving, scanning the road ahead and to the side and checking your mirrors every five seconds or so.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶8
text: The farther ahead you look, the less likely you will be surprised, and you will have time to avoid any hazards.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶8
text: Make sure other drivers can see you by using your signal lights as required.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶9
text: Managing the space around your vehicle lets you see and be seen and gives you time and space to avoid a collision.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶9
text: Leave a cushion of space ahead, behind and to both sides.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶9
text: Because the greatest risk of a collision is in front of you, stay well back.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶10
text: Communicate with other road users to make sure they see you and know what you are doing.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶10
text: Make eye contact with pedestrians, cyclists and drivers at intersections and signal whenever you want to slow down, stop, turn or change lanes.

locator: Safe and Responsible Driving › Intro · ¶10
text: If you need to get another person’s attention, use your horn.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Intro · ¶1
text: Ontario’s roads accommodate many road users, including pedestrians, motorcycles, bicycles, large trucks, buses and farm machinery.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Intro · ¶1
text: Be aware of other road users, the speed at which they travel and the space they occupy on the road.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶1
text: Road safety is a responsibility that is shared between pedestrians and drivers.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶1
text: Pedestrians must ensure that drivers have seen them and that drivers are stopped, or are about to stop, before entering the roadway.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶1
text: Drivers need to exercise due diligence in the care and operation of their vehicles, to properly respond to the presence of pedestrians.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶1
text: In most cases, that means yielding to the pedestrian.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶2
text: Reminder: Eye contact between the pedestrian and driver is one of the keys to pedestrian safety.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶3
text: Watch for children – Drive slowly and cautiously through school zones, residential areas and any other location where children may be walking or playing.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶3
text: A driver should not rely on a child's knowledge of traffic laws, so expect the unexpected.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶3
text: A child might dart out from between parked cars or try to cross a street without checking for traffic.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶3
text: Be extra cautious at twilight when children may still be playing outside, but are difficult to see.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶4
text: Watch for all crosswalks – A crosswalk can be the portion of a roadway that:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · item 1
text: connects sidewalks on opposite sides of the roadway into a continuous path

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · item 2
text: has signs, lines or other markings on the roadway for pedestrian crossing Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · item 2
text: A stopped vehicle may be a clue that a pedestrian is crossing.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶5
text: Reminder: Not all crosswalks are marked, but nearly all intersections have crosswalks.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶6
text: Watch for school crossings and guards – Drivers, including cyclists, must stop and yield the whole roadway at pedestrian crossovers, school crossings and other locations where there is a crossing guard.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶7
text: Only when pedestrians and school crossing guards have crossed and are safely on the sidewalk can drivers and cyclists proceed.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶8
text: Watch for community safety zones – Signs indicate areas where the community has identified that there is a special risk to pedestrians.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶9
text: Watch for slow pedestrians – Many modern urban roads often do not allow sufficient time to cross for slow pedestrians during the normal traffic cycle.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶9
text: So be patient and allow all pedestrians time to cross.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶10
text: Seniors or pedestrians with disabilities need extra caution and courtesy from drivers, as they may be slow in crossing the road.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶11
text: Pedestrians who are blind or with a visual disability may use a white cane or guide dog to help them travel safely along sidewalks and across intersections.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶12
text: Watch when driving quiet vehicles – Drivers of hybrid or electric vehicles should be aware that vision-impaired people often rely on the sound of an engine before entering an intersection.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶12
text: When you are slowing or stopping, your vehicle makes little or no discernible noise, so extra caution is required.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶13
text: Watch for wheelchairs and medical scooters – People operating motorized wheelchair and medical scooters are pedestrians too.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶14
text: Watch for streetcars – Some streetcar stops have a special safety island or zone for passengers getting on and off.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶14
text: Pass these safety islands and zones at a reasonable speed.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶14
text: Always be ready, in case pedestrians make sudden or unexpected moves.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶15
text: Watch for texters – A no-texting rule isn’t only for drivers.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶15
text: Pedestrians are often distracted while using devices, including cell phones, ear buds, hand-held device, GPS, and music players.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶15
text: People using ear buds/headphones often can't hear car horn or other traffic noise.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶16
text: Watch for dark clothing – Pedestrians in dark clothing, especially at night, are difficult to see.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶16
text: Extra care is needed when driving in low-light conditions.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶16
text: Twilight and dark clothing often initiate a collision.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶17
text: Watch for new transport – With the introduction of new technology, more vehicles such as e-bikes and e-scooters are appearing on roadways.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶17
text: These vehicles may require increased awareness for all road users.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶18
text: Watch during turns – Safer, signaled crosswalks aren’t immune to vehicle-pedestrian collisions.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with pedestrians · ¶18
text: Many more people get hit by cars turning left than by cars turning right, because both parties are looking elsewhere: The drivers are busy negotiating the intersection while street-crossers are looking straight ahead.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶1
text: Bicycles and mopeds travelling at a lower speed than other traffic are expected to ride about one metre from the curb or parked cars, or as close as practical to the right-hand edge of the road when there is no curb.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶1
text: However, they can use any part of the lane if necessary for safety, such as to:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 1
text: Avoid obstacles such as puddles, ice, sand, debris, rutted or grooved pavement, potholes and sewer grates

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 2
text: Cross railway or streetcar tracks at a 90° angle

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 3
text: Discourage passing where the lane is too narrow to be shared safely

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 4
text: A bike lane may exist adjacent to parking bays (See Diagram 2-10)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶2
text: Cyclists are not required to ride close to the right edge of the road when they are travelling at or faster than the normal speed of traffic at that time and place, or when they are turning left, or getting in position to turn left.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶2
text: (Cyclists are permitted to make a left turn from a left-turn lane, where one is available.)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶3
text: When passing a cyclist, drivers of motor vehicles must maintain a minimum distance of one metre, where practical between their vehicle and the cyclist.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶3
text: (See Diagram 2-11.)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶3
text: Failure to do so may result in a fine and an additional two demerit points on the driver’s record.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶3
text: Whenever possible, you should change lanes to pass.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶4
text: Do not follow too closely behind cyclists.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶4
text: They do not have brake lights to warn you when they are slowing or stopping.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶5
text: Intersections – To avoid collisions with bicyclists at intersections, remember the following:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 5
text: When turning right, signal and check your mirrors and the blind spot to your right to make sure you do not cut off a cyclist.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 6
text: When turning left, you must stop and wait for oncoming bicycles to pass before turning.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · item 7
text: When driving through an intersection, be careful to scan for cyclists waiting to turn left.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶6
text: Do not sound your horn unnecessarily when you are overtaking a cyclist.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶6
text: It may frighten them and cause them to lose control.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶6
text: If you feel that you must use your horn, tap it quickly and lightly while you are still some distance away from the cyclist.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶7
text: Bike lanes are reserved for cyclists.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶7
text: They are typically marked by a solid white line.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶7
text: Sometimes you will need to enter or cross a bike lane to turn right at a corner or driveway.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶7
text: (See Diagram 2-12) Take extra care when you do this.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶7
text: Enter the bike lane only after ensuring that you can do so safely, and then make the turn.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶8
text: Watch for cyclists' hand signals.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶8
text: A cyclist may indicate a right-hand turn by extending their right arm.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶9
text: Try to make eye contact when possible with cyclists.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶10
text: Bike boxes help prevent collisions between motorists and bicycles at intersections.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶10
text: It is typically a painted box on the road with a white bicycle symbol inside.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶10
text: Bicycle lanes approaching and leaving the box may also be painted.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶10
text: As a driver, you must stop for a traffic signal behind the bike box.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶10
text: Do not stop in the box.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶10
text: See (Diagram 2-13)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶11
text: Sharrows A bicycle sharrow, two chevrons painted above a bicycle symbol on the road, indicates the lane is shared.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶11
text: Vehicle or bicycle traffic may be in the lane.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶11
text: Although you should always keep on the lookout for bicyclists, this serves as an additional warning to watch for them in the lane.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶11
text: See (Diagram 2-14)

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶12
text: Children riding bicycles on the street may lack the necessary training and skills for safe cycling.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶12
text: They may not be aware of all the dangers or the rules of the road.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶12
text: Watch for children on oversized bicycles, as they may not have the ability to control it.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with cyclists · ¶12
text: When parked on the side of the roadway, look behind you and check your mirrors and blind spots for a passing cyclist before opening a door.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶1
text: Motorcycles, limited-speed motor­cycles, mopeds and bicycles are harder to see because of their size.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶1
text: Drivers of these vehicles may make sudden moves because of uneven road surfaces or poor weather conditions.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶1
text: Because they are less protected, they are more likely to be injured in a collision.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶2
text: Motorcycles use a full lane; treat them like other vehicles when driving.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶2
text: Since many motorcycle turn signals do not automatically shut off, be careful when turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle with its turn signal on.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with motorcycles and limited-speed motorcycles · ¶2
text: Make sure the motorcyclist is actually turning; he or she may have just forgotten to switch off the turn signal.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶1
text: It is extremely important to know how to drive safely when sharing the road with large commercial vehicles such as tractor-trailers and buses.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶1
text: Recent data show that the majority of fatalities resulting from collisions involving large commercial trucks are not the result of the truck driver’s actions, but of the other driver’s actions.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶1
text: Therefore, sharing the road with large commercial vehicles means you must always be aware of a large vehicle’s capabilities and limitations, such as of the following:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶2
Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶2
text: Blind Spots - Large commercial vehicles have big blind spots on both sides.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶2
text: Avoid tailgating a large vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶2
text: The driver cannot see you if you are directly behind.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶2
text: If the vehicle stops suddenly, you have no place to go.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶2
text: Remember that if you can't see the driver’s face in the large vehicle’s side-view mirror, the driver cannot see you.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶3
Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶3
text: Stopping Distance - Large commercial vehicles require a much longer distance to stop than smaller vehicles.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶3
text: When passing a large vehicle, do not cut in front closely.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶3
text: Not only is this discourteous, it is dangerous; it reduces the space cushion large vehicles require in order to stop safely.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶3
text: Allow more room when passing a large vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶4
Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶4
text: Wide Turns - When making a right turn, a large vehicle may need to first swing wide to the left and around, in order to avoid hitting the right curb.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶4
text: If a large vehicle in front of you is making a right turn, do not move up into the space that opens up in the right lane; you are putting yourself into a very dangerous position.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶4
text: Once the front of the vehicle has cleared the corner, the rest will move partially back into the right lane.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶4
text: If you are in that lane, your vehicle will be squeezed between the trailer and the curb.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶4
text: Stay well back until the truck has completely cleared the lane.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶5
text: This situation can occur on expressway off-ramps that have two left turning lanes.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶5
text: Do not drive up into the left lane when a large vehicle is making a left turn in front of you.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶5
text: Stay well back until the truck has cleared the left turn, or else you may get squeezed between the truck and the curb.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶6
Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶6
text: Rolling Back - Leave plenty of room if you are stopped behind a large vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶6
text: When the driver of a large vehicle releases the brakes after being stopped, the vehicle may roll back.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶7
Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶7
text: Spray - In bad weather, large vehicles are capable of spraying up large amounts of mud, snow and debris, which could land on your windshield and temporarily block your vision.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶8
Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶8
text: Turbulence - Due to various factors such as air pressure and airflow, a large vehicle can create heavy air turbulence.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with large commercial vehicles · ¶8
text: This may affect your ability to control your vehicle when passing a large one.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · ¶1
text: Many municipal roadways have special indented stopping areas for municipal buses, called bus bays, where passengers can get on and off.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · ¶1
text: There are three types of bus bays:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 1
text: Mid-block indented bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 2
text: Indentations immediately before and after intersections

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 3
text: Bus-stop areas between two designated parking areas

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · ¶2
text: When a bus in a bus bay begins flashing its left-turn signals, indicating that it is ready to leave the bus bay, and you are approaching in the lane adjacent to the bus bay, you must allow the bus to re-enter traffic.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 4
text: A: Mid-block indented bays

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 5
text: B: An indentation before an intersection

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 6
text: C: An indentation after an intersection

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with municipal buses · item 7
text: D: Bus stops between legally parked cars

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶1
text: Farm machinery moves quite slowly compared to other road users.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶1
text: Most tractors and combines have a maximum speed of 40 km/h , but travel at less than 40 km/h when towing implements or wagons.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶1
text: Farm machinery is often oversized, wide or long or both, making it difficult for the driver to see vehicles coming up from behind.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶1
text: Farmers often turn directly into fields rather than roads or lanes, or move from lane to lane.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶1
text: Remember that it is common for farmers to be on the roads after dark during peak planting and harvesting seasons.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶2
text: Farm machinery on the road must display an orange and red slow-moving sign on the rear of the vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶2
text: The sign warns other drivers that the vehicle is travelling at 40 km/h or less.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶2
text: If you see one of these signs, slow down and be cautious.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with farm machinery · ¶2
text: Stay well back and do not pass until it is safe to do so.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶1
text: Horse-drawn vehicles are one of the slowest moving of all road users.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶1
text: These vehicles range from two-person carts to open or closed buggies carrying up to eight people, and large, wide farm wagons used to carry crops, equipment and other goods.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶1
text: These vehicles will travel primarily on the shoulder of roadways, but may straddle or enter the paved lane where shoulders are narrow or no shoulder exists – such as bridge crossings.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶1
text: Remember that it is common to see horse-drawn vehicles throughout southwestern Ontario and increasingly in eastern and northern Ontario.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: Horse-drawn vehicles on the road must display an orange and red slow-moving sign on the rear of the buggy.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: In addition, many buggies have highly reflective tape affixed to the side and rear of the vehicle.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: The sign warns other drivers that this vehicle is travelling at 40 km/h or less, and the reflective tape illuminates as headlights hit the buggy.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: If you see a horse-drawn vehicle, slow down and be very cautious.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: Maintain a safe following distance and only pass when it is safe to do so.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: When approaching a horse-drawn vehicle travelling in the opposite direction, move to the far right of your lane.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: When passing, give as much distance between you and them as possible.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with horse-drawn vehicles · ¶2
text: Passing too closely could scare or startle the horse, causing it to change direction suddenly on the roadway.

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶1
text: When you see a school bus with its overhead amber lights flashing:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 1
text: These signals indicate that the bus is coming to a stop to pick up or drop off passengers

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 2
text: Slow down and prepare to stop whether you are behind or approaching the bus

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 3
text: If you are on a road with a median strip, only vehicles approach from the rear of the bus should prepare to stop

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶2
text: Diagram 2-18

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶3
text: When you see a school bus with its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 4
text: You must stop whether you are behind or approaching the bus

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 5
text: If you are on a roadway with a median strip, only vehicles approaching from the rear of the bus must stop

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 6
text: If you are approaching from the rear of the vehicle, stop at least 20 meters away

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 7
text: Do not proceed on your route until the bus moves, the overhead red lights have stopped flashing and its stop arm is no longer activated

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · item 8
text: It is dangerous and illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its overhead red lights flashing or its stop arm activated

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Sharing the road with school buses · ¶4
text: Diagram 2-19

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Summary · ¶1
text: By the end of this section, you should know:

locator: Sharing the road with other road users › Summary · item 1
text: The importance of sharing the road with other road users, especially large vehicles, school buses, cyclists, and pedestrians

text: How to share the road with other road users safely and appropriately

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶1
text: Traffic signs give you important information about the law, warn you about dangerous conditions and help you find your way.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶1
text: Signs use different symbols, colours and shapes for easy identification.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶2
text: Here are some of the many signs you will see on Ontario roads:

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: A stop sign is eight-sided and has a red background with white letters.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: It means you must come to a complete stop.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: Stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶3
text: Wait until the way is clear before entering the intersection.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶4
text: A school zone sign is five-sided and has a fluorescent yellow/green background with black symbols.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶4
text: It warns that you are coming to a school zone.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶4
text: Slow down, drive with extra caution and watch for children.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶5
text: A yield sign is a triangle with a white background and a red border.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶5
text: It means you must let traffic in the intersection or close to it go first.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶5
text: Stop if necessary and go only when the way is clear.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶6
text: A railway crossing sign is X-shaped with a white background and red outline.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶6
text: It warns that railway tracks cross the road.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶6
text: Watch for this sign.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶6
text: Slow down and look both ways for trains.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶6
text: Be prepared to stop.

locator: Signs › Intro · ¶7
text: There are four other kinds of signs: regulatory, warning, temporary conditions and information and direction.

locator: Signs › Regulatory signs · ¶1
text: These signs give a direction that must be obeyed.

locator: Signs › Regulatory signs · ¶1
text: They are usually rectangular or square with a white or black background and black, white or coloured letters.

locator: Signs › Regulatory signs · ¶1
text: A sign with a green circle means you may or must do the activity shown inside the ring.

locator: Signs › Regulatory signs · ¶1
text: A red circle with a line through it means the activity shown is not allowed.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶1
text: Knowing how to stop safely and properly is an important driving skill.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶1
text: Safe and responsible drivers see stops ahead, check their mirrors, begin braking early and stop smoothly.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶1
text: Braking is easier when you sit properly.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶1
text: Use your right foot for both brake and gas pedals so you won't step on both pedals at the same time or activate your brake lights unnecessarily.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶1
text: Press the brake pedal firmly and evenly.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶2
text: In a vehicle with manual transmission, try shifting into a lower gear going down long, steep hills.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶2
text: This will help control your speed and you won't have to brake as sharply.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶2
text: Downshift before starting downhill since it may not be possible once you are going downhill.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶2
text: As a guide, you should be in the same gear going downhill as uphill.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶3
text: You must come to a complete stop for all stop signs and red traffic lights.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶3
text: Stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement (Diagram 2-23).

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶4
text: If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶4
text: If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶4
text: If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection (Diagram 2-24).

locator: Stopping › Intro · ¶4
text: Wait until the way is clear before entering the intersection.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: All railway crossings on public roads in Ontario are marked with large red and white “X” signs.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: Watch for these signs and be prepared to stop.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: You may also see yellow advance warning signs and large “X” pavement markings ahead of railway crossings.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: Some railway crossings have flashing signal lights and some use gates or barriers to keep drivers from crossing the tracks when a train is coming.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: Some less-travelled crossings have stop signs posted.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: Remember it can take up to two kilometres for a train to stop under full emergency braking.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶1
text: On private roads, railway crossings may not be marked, so watch carefully.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · ¶2
text: When you come to a railway crossing, remember:

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 1
text: Slow down, listen and look both ways to make sure the way is clear before crossing the tracks.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 2
text: If a train is coming, stop at least five metres from the nearest rail or gate.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 2
text: Do not cross the track until you are sure the train or trains have passed.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 3
text: Never race a train to a crossing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 4
text: If there are signal lights, wait until they stop flashing and, if the crossing has a gate or barrier, wait until it rises before you cross the tracks.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 5
text: Never drive around, under or through a railway gate or barrier while it is down, being lowered or being raised.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 5
text: It is illegal and dangerous.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 6
text: Avoid stopping in the middle of railway tracks; for example, in heavy traffic, make sure you have enough room to cross the tracks completely before you begin.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 7
text: Avoid shifting gears while crossing tracks.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 8
text: If you get trapped on a crossing, immediately get everyone out and away from the vehicle.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 8
text: Move to a safe place and then contact authorities.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 9
text: Most buses and other public vehicles are required to stop at railway crossings that are not protected by gates, signal lights or a stop sign.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 9
text: School buses must stop at railway crossings whether or not they are protected by gates or signal lights.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 9
text: Watch for these buses and be prepared to stop behind them.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at railway crossings · item 10
text: If you are approaching a railway crossing with a stop sign , you must stop unless otherwise directed by a flagman.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at school crossings · ¶1
text: Where a school-crossing guard displays a red and white stop sign, you must stop before reaching the crossing and remain stopped until all people, including the school crossing guard, have cleared the entire roadway and it is safe to proceed.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at school crossings · ¶1
text: If you have any doubts about when it is safe to drive forward, wait until all the children and the guard have cleared the crossing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping at school crossings · ¶1
text: Drivers who don't follow the stopping requirements may receive a substantial fine and get three demerit points.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶1
text: School buses in Ontario come in a range of sizes.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶1
text: All are chrome yellow and display the words “School Bus.”

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶2
text: You must stop whenever you approach a stopped school bus with its upper alternating red lights flashing, regardless of whether you are behind the bus or approaching it from the front.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶2
text: When approaching the bus from the front, stop at a safe distance for children to get off the bus and cross the road in front of you.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶2
text: If you are coming from behind the bus, stop at least 20 metres away.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶2
text: Do not go until the bus moves or the lights have stopped flashing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶3
text: If you are on a road with a median strip, only vehicles coming from behind the bus must stop.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶3
text: (A median is a physical barrier such as a raised, lowered, earth or paved strip constructed to separate traffic travelling in different directions.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶3
text: Vehicles cannot cross over a median strip.)

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶4
text: You must obey the school bus law on any road, no matter how many lanes or what the speed limit.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶4
text: Be prepared to stop for a school bus at any time, not just within school hours.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶5
text: As well as the upper alternating red flashing lights, school buses use a stop sign arm on the driver’s side of the bus.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶5
text: This arm, a standard stop sign with alternating flashing red lights at top and bottom, swings out after the upper alternating red lights begin to flash.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶5
text: Remain stopped until the arm folds away and all lights stop flashing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶6
text: Note: It is illegal to fail to stop for a stopped school bus that has its red lights flashing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶6
text: If you don't stop, you can be fined heavily and get six demerit points for a first offence.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶6
text: In Ontario, school bus drivers and other witnesses can report vehicles that have illegally passed a school bus.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶6
text: If you are the vehicle’s registered owner, these fines, but not demerit points or jail time, may be applied to you.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶7
text: Watch for school buses near railway crossings.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶7
text: All school buses must stop at all railway crossings.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for school buses · ¶7
text: The upper alternating red lights are not used for these stops, so be alert.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶1
text: Pedestrian crossovers (Diagram 2-29) are designated areas that allow pedestrians to safely cross roads where there are no traffic lights.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶1
text: Always watch for pedestrians and people using wheelchairs at these crossings.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶2
text: Pedestrians may push a button to make the overhead yellow lights flash to warn drivers that they will be crossing.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶2
text: Pedestrians should point or make an indication to drivers that they want to cross before entering the roadway (try making eye contact when possible).

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶2
text: Drivers including cyclists must yield the right-of-way to pedestrians in the crossover.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶2
text: Only when pedestrians and school crossing guards have crossed and are safely on the sidewalk can drivers and cyclists proceed.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶2
text: You must not pass any vehicle within 30 metres of a pedestrian crossover.

locator: Stopping › Stopping for pedestrian crossovers · ¶3
text: For more information on pedestrian crossovers visit Driving near pedestrian crossovers and school crossings .

text: To a person learning to drive.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 8

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 10

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 11

Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶5
text: Never change lanes in traffic without:

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 13

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 14
text: Giving proper signal and looking to make sure the move can be made safely.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 15
text: Blowing your horn and looking to the rear.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 16
text: Decreasing speed and giving correct signal.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶6
Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶6
text: When the driver of another vehicle is about to overtake and pass your vehicle, you must:

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 17
text: Speed up so that passing is not necessary.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 18
text: Move to the left to prevent passing.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 19
text: Signal to the other driver not to pass.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 20
text: Move to the right and allow such vehicle to pass.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶7
Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶7
text: When you are deciding whether or not to make a U-turn, your first consideration should be to check:

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 21

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 22
text: Presence of trees, fire hydrants or poles near the curb.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 23
text: Turning radius of your car.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 24
text: Height of curb.

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶8
Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶8
text: It is more dangerous to drive at the maximum speed limit at night than during daytime as:

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 25

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 26

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 27

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 28
text: The roadways are more apt to be slippery at night.

Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · ¶9
text: You should under all conditions drive at a speed which will allow you to:

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 30

locator: Test yourself - Sample knowledge test questions › Intro · item 31
text: Stop within 60 metres (200 feet).

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶1
text: This chapter tells you what you need to know to tow a trailer behind a car, van or small truck in Ontario.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶1
text: This includes licence and registration requirements, trailer size and characteristics, as well as safety tips to follow when towing a trailer.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶2
text: Before you attempt to tow a trailer, consider the size, power and condition of your vehicle.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶2
text: Make sure it is capable of towing both the trailer and the load you intend to carry, and that your trailer and hitch meet all the requirements described in this chapter.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶3
text: Towing a trailer brings unique challenges to drivers.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶3
text: Almost half of the reported collisions while towing a recreational vehicle are single-vehicle collisions.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶3
text: Another 20 per cent involve rear-end collisions.

locator: Towing › Intro · ¶3
text: In collisions where the driver was determined to be at fault, about 30 per cent of the drivers had “lost control” of their vehicle.

locator: Towing › Licence and permit · ¶1
text: You must have a valid driver's licence (Class G1, G2 or G) or higher class of licence to tow a trailer with a gross vehicle weight of up to 4,600 kilograms.

locator: Towing › Licence and permit · ¶1
text: If your trailer and load exceeds the size and weight specified in the Highway Traffic Act , you may need a higher class of licence or an oversize vehicle permit to tow it.

locator: Towing › Licence and permit · ¶1
text: For questions about the Oversize/Overweight Program, please contact the Ministry of Transportation’s permit office: by telephone 416-246-7166 or Toll-free: 1-800-387-7736 or visit the Oversize/Overweight Permit Office website .

locator: Towing › Licence and permit · ¶2
text: It is against the law to tow more than one trailer behind non-commercial vehicles.

locator: Towing › Registering your trailer · ¶1
text: A trailer is considered a separate vehicle.

locator: Towing › Registering your trailer · ¶1
text: Before you can tow one on any public road, you must register it and pay a one-time registration fee at a ServiceOntario centre.

locator: Towing › Registering your trailer · ¶1
text: When you register your trailer you will receive a licence plate and vehicle permit.

locator: Towing › Registering your trailer · ¶1
text: Attach the licence plate to the back of your trailer where it is clearly visible.

locator: Towing › Registering your trailer · ¶1
text: Always carry your permit, or a copy of it, to show to a police officer when asked.

locator: Towing › Make sure your trailer is in good condition · ¶1
text: Your trailer must be in safe operating condition.

locator: Towing › Make sure your trailer is in good condition · ¶1
text: If it is not, a police officer may remove your trailer from the road until it is made safe to operate.

locator: Towing › Brakes · ¶1
text: If your trailer has a gross trailer weight, vehicle and load of 1,360 kilograms or more, it must have brakes strong enough to stop and hold the trailer.

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶1
text: Your trailer must have:

locator: Towing › Lights · item 1
text: a white licence plate light

locator: Towing › Lights · item 2
text: a red tail light

locator: Towing › Lights · item 3
text: two red reflectors at the rear of the trailer, as far apart as possible

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶2
text: If your trailer is wider than 2.05 metres, it must also have:

locator: Towing › Lights · item 4
text: two yellow clearance lights, one on each side at the front of the trailer, as far apart as possible, to let drivers coming toward you know the width of your trailer

locator: Towing › Lights · item 5
text: two red clearance lights, or reflectors, one on each side at the rear of the trailer, as far apart as possible, to let drivers behind you know the width of your trailer

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶3
text: Your trailer must have mud guards, fenders and flaps or be designed in such a way that it does not spray or splash traffic travelling behind you.

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶4
text: If the load in your trailer blocks your vision to the rear, you must have additional mirrors that provide a clear view of the road to the rear.

locator: Towing › Lights · ¶4
text: Load your trailer carefully so that nothing comes loose or falls off while you are moving.

locator: Towing › Attaching your trailer · ¶1
text: Your trailer must have two separate ways of attaching to your vehicle so that if one fails or comes loose, the trailer will stay attached.

locator: Towing › Attaching your trailer · ¶2
text: If safety chains are used, they must be crossed under the tongue to prevent the tongue from drop­ping to the road if the primary hitch accidentally disconnects.

locator: Towing › Attaching your trailer · ¶2
text: The chain hooks must have latches or devices that will not accidentally become detached.

locator: Towing › No passengers · ¶1
text: You may not carry any person in any trailer, including a house or boat trailer, when it is being towed.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶1
text: Use a good-quality trailer hitch.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶1
text: The class of trailer hitch you use depends upon the gross weight of your trailer - the gross weight being the total weight of the trailer and its load.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶1
text: Make sure you use the right trailer hitch for the weight of your trailer.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶1
text: It should be securely attached to your vehicle following the manufacturer's recommendations.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶2
text: The hitch-ball should be installed so that when the trailer is attached and tightened, it is level with no tilting.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶2
text: If the hitch pulls down the rear of your vehicle, you may need to use a load-equalizing trailer hitch.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶2
text: You may also be able to shift some of the load in the trailer to the rear to reduce the load on the rear of your vehicle.

locator: Towing › Trailer hitch · ¶3
text: In addition to a ball and hitch, be sure to use safety chains or cables strong enough to hold the trailer and load, in case the ball and hitch accidentally come apart.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶1
text: When loading your trailer, strap everything down inside, as well as outside.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶1
text: It is an offence to have a load that may become dislodged or fall off.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶1
text: Do not overload your trailer.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶1
text: Too much weight in the trailer can put a strain on your vehicle and damage your tires, wheel bearings and axle.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶1
text: When carrying a boat on a trailer, do not carry cargo in the boat unless your trailer is designed and equipped for the extra weight.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶2
text: The distribution of the weight in your trailer is also very important.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶2
text: Generally, more of the trailer load should be in front of the trailer axle than behind it for proper hitch weight.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶2
text: About five to 10 per cent of the trailer's total weight should be supported on the hitch, within the weight limit marked on the hitch.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶2
text: Poor load balance can cause your trailer to sway or fishtail.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶2
text: The ball and hitch may also become separated, especially if there is too much weight in the rear of the trailer.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶3
text: Heavy and improperly placed loads can pull down the rear of your vehicle, lifting the front end and affecting your steering, especially in wet and slippery conditions.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶3
text: It may also affect the aim of your headlights so that your low beams blind approaching drivers.

locator: Towing › Loading your trailer · ¶3
text: The alignment of your mirrors may also be affected.

locator: Towing › Starting out · ¶1
text: Before each trip, check the trailer hitch, wheels, tires, lights, load distribution and load security to make sure they are safe.

locator: Towing › Starting out · ¶1
text: Check your tire pressure with the trailer loaded while the tires are still cold.

locator: Towing › Starting out · ¶1
text: When you start to drive, accelerate carefully.

locator: Towing › Starting out · ¶1
text: Drive slowly and carefully.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶1
text: Stay close to the middle of your lane when taking a curve.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶1
text: When making a right turn, check traffic.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶1
text: Look in your right mirror.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶1
text: Signal and slow down.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶1
text: If the turn is sharp, move ahead until your vehicle's front wheels are well ahead of the curb before turning to the right.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶2
text: When making a left turn, check traffic.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶2
text: Signal.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶2
text: Proceed slowly.

locator: Towing › Curves and turns · ¶2
text: When you make your turn, swing wide by driving well into the intersection before turning.

locator: Towing › Slowing down and stopping · ¶1
text: A sudden stop can cause your trailer to jackknife or slide sideways or the load to shift.

locator: Towing › Slowing down and stopping · ¶1
text: To avoid sudden stops, increase the following distance between you and the vehicle ahead.

locator: Towing › Slowing down and stopping · ¶1
text: Keep out of the fast lanes and maintain a speed that will allow you to slow down and stop smoothly in any situation.

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: You cannot accelerate as quickly when you are towing a trailer.

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: You also need more space because the length of your vehicle is much longer with a trailer attached.

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: Before you pass, make sure you have enough time and room to complete the pass.

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: Once you have passed, allow more room before you move back to your lane.

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: Do not cut back into the lane too soon.

locator: Towing › Passing · ¶1
text: This can cause your trailer to sway and make it difficult to control.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: If you are holding up a line of traffic, signal, pull over and let the other vehicles pass.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: Fast-moving trucks and buses create a strong air disturbance behind them.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: If a large bus or truck passes you, the wall of wind behind it may whip your trailer to the side, pushing it out of control.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: When you experience this, do not brake.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: Carefully steer your vehicle and trailer back into position.

locator: Towing › Being passed · ¶1
text: A slight increase in speed may help.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶1
text: Back up very slowly and have someone outside the vehicle direct you.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶1
text: Use a series of small turns to steer.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶1
text: It is a good idea to practise this skill off the road in an empty parking lot until you are comfortable with your ability.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶2
text: To back up to the right, steer to the left.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶2
text: The front end of the trailer will go left, but the rear end will go right.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶2
text: To back up to the left, steer to the right.

locator: Towing › Backing up · ¶2
text: The front end of the trailer will go right, but the rear end will go left.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶1
text: If your vehicle breaks down, you should get help from a tow truck designed to tow vehicles.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶1
text: If you must use another vehicle to tow, use warning signals or emergency flashers and make sure you attach the vehicles securely.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶1
text: Someone must sit in the disabled vehicle and use the brakes to keep the tow cable tight.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶1
text: If the engine cannot run, don't tow vehicles that have power braking and steering.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶1
text: Without the engine, braking and steering is difficult and towing may lead to a collision.

locator: Towing › Towing disabled vehicles · ¶2
text: Trying to start a disabled vehicle by towing is dangerous and could damage both vehicles.

locator: Traffic lights › Intro · ¶1
text: Traffic lights tell drivers and pedestrians what they must do at intersections and along roads.

locator: Traffic lights › Intro · ¶1
text: They tell road users when to stop and go, when and how to turn and when to drive with extra caution.

locator: Traffic lights › Green light · ¶1
text: A green light means you may turn left, go straight or turn right after yielding to vehicles and pedestrians already in the intersection.

locator: Traffic lights › Green light · ¶1
text: When turning left or right you must yield the right-of-way to pedestrians crossing the intersection.

locator: Traffic lights › Yellow light · ¶1
text: A yellow - or amber - light means the red light is about to appear.

locator: Traffic lights › Yellow light · ¶1
text: You must stop if you can do so safely; otherwise, go with caution.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶1
text: A red light means you must stop.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶1
text: Bring your vehicle to a complete stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶1
text: If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶1
text: If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶1
text: If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶2
text: Wait until the light changes to green and the intersection is clear before moving through it.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶3
text: Unless a sign tells you not to, you may turn right on a red light only after coming to a complete stop and waiting until the way is clear.

locator: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶3
text: You may also turn left on a red light if you are moving from a one-way road onto a one-way road, but you must come to a complete stop first and wait until the way is clear.

locator: Traffic lights › Lights and arrows to help turning vehicles · ¶1
text: Flashing green lights and green arrows direct drivers who are turning.

locator: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · ¶1
text: When you face a flashing green light or a left-pointing green arrow and a green light, you may turn left, go straight ahead or turn right from the proper lane.

locator: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · ¶1
text: This is called an advanced green light because oncoming traffic still faces a red light.

locator: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · ¶2
text: Pedestrians must not cross on a flashing green light unless a pedestrian signal tells them to.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶1
text: When a left-turn green arrow is shown with a red light, you may turn left from the left-turn lane.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶1
text: Vehicles turning left from the opposite direction may also be making left turns because they too face a left-turn green arrow.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶2
text: After the left-turn green arrow, a yellow arrow may appear.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶2
text: This means the green light is about to appear for traffic in one or both directions.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶2
text: Do not start your left turn.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶2
text: Stop if you can do so safely; otherwise, complete your turn with caution.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶3
text: You can still turn left when the light is green, but only when the way is clear of traffic and pedestrians.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶3
text: If the light turns red when you are in the intersection, complete your turn when it is safe.

locator: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶4
text: Pedestrians must not cross on a left-turn green arrow unless a pedestrian signal tells them to.

locator: Traffic lights › Transit priority signals · ¶1
text: Traffic and pedestrians must yield to public transit vehicles at a transit priority signal.

locator: Traffic lights › Transit priority signals · ¶1
text: The round signal is on top of a regular traffic signal and shows a white vertical bar on a dark background.

locator: Traffic lights › Transit priority signals · ¶1
text: This allows transit vehicles to go through, turn right or left, while all conflicting traffic faces a red light.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶1
text: Some intersections have separate traffic lights for left-turning traffic and for traffic going through the intersection or turning right.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶2
text: When a left-turn green arrow appears for traffic in the left-turn lane, traffic going straight ahead or turning right will usually see a red light.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶2
text: You may turn left from the left-turn lane when you face a green arrow.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶2
text: Vehicles from the opposite direction may also be turning left.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶3
text: After the left-turn green arrow, a yellow light appears for left-turning vehicles only.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶4
text: After the yellow light, a red light appears for left-turning vehicles only.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶4
text: Traffic going straight ahead or turning right will face a green light or green arrows pointing straight ahead and to the right.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶5
text: In these intersections, you may not begin turning left after the green light appears for traffic going straight ahead or turning right.

locator: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶5
text: If the light turns yellow while you are in the intersection, complete your turn with caution.

locator: Traffic lights › Flashing red light · ¶1
text: You must come to a complete stop at a flashing red light.

locator: Traffic lights › Flashing red light · ¶1
text: Move through the intersection only when it is safe.

locator: Traffic lights › Flashing yellow light · ¶1
text: A flashing yellow light means you should drive with caution when approaching and moving through the intersection.

locator: Traffic lights › Blank traffic lights · ¶1
text: During an electrical power loss, traffic lights at intersections will not work.

locator: Traffic lights › Blank traffic lights · ¶1
text: Yield the right-of-way to vehicles in the intersection and to vehicles entering the intersection from your right.

locator: Traffic lights › Blank traffic lights · ¶1
text: Go cautiously and use the intersection the same way you would use an intersection with all-way stop signs.

locator: Traffic lights › Traffic beacons · ¶1
text: A traffic beacon is a single flashing light hung over an intersection or placed over signs or on obstacles in the road.

locator: Traffic lights › Traffic beacons › Flashing red beacon · ¶1
text: A flashing red beacon above an intersection or stop sign means you must come to a complete stop.

locator: Traffic lights › Traffic beacons › Flashing red beacon · ¶1
text: Move through the intersection only when it is safe to do so.

locator: Traffic lights › Traffic beacons › Flashing yellow beacon · ¶1
text: A flashing yellow beacon above an intersection, above a warning sign or on an obstruction in the road, warns you to drive with caution.

text: Traffic laws include the traffic signs and lights, pedestrian signals and pavement markings that tell drivers and other road users what they must do in certain situations.

locator: Traffic Signs and Lights › Intro · ¶1
text: This chapter shows you what many of those signs, lights and markings look like and explains what they mean to drivers.

text: Signs
