locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Fees and Driver Licenses for Veterans · ¶1
text: Veterans who are honorably discharged and receive compensation for a service-related disability of at least 60 percent are exempt from paying driver license and ID card fees. Individuals applying for a CDL or who are required to register as a sex offender are not eligible for this fee exemption. The veteran must meet all other licensing requirements.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Fees and Driver Licenses for Veterans › Designation on Driver License · ¶1
text: DPS offers Veteran and Disabled Veteran designators with branch of service indicators on the face of the driver license and identification card (ID) for qualifying veterans. For more information on the veteran designations, visit our website at www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/vetServices.htm .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Identification (ID) Cards · ¶1
text: In addition to driver licenses, DPS issues ID cards with a photograph of the applicant. ID cards have a distinguishing number similar to a driver license and are maintained in the driver record file. ID cards are displayed in a vertical format for individuals who are younger than 21 years of age and are horizontal for individuals who are 21 years of age and older. Applicants must provide documents in accordance with DPS ID card policy requirements. For a list of acceptable documents to obtain an ID card, visit our website, http://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/applyforID.htm

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Identification (ID) Cards · row 1
text: ID cards can be issued to any person of any age. Anyone under the age of 21 will have “Under 21” printed on the card. | $15 card + $1 fee = $16 (59 or younger) | Six years

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Identification (ID) Cards · row 2
text: | $5 card + $1 fee = $6 (60 or older) |

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Identification (ID) Cards · row 3
text: * A $1 administrative fee is included in most transactions. However, if you are completing multiple transactions at the same time in-person, telephone and online then you will only be charged the $1 administrative fee once. A $1 administrative fee is not charged for transactions made through the mail.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Medical and Emergency Information · ¶1
text: On the reverse side of the card, state law requires DPS to print the statement “Directive to physician has been filed at telephone #” and “Emergency contact number.” Space is provided on the surface for the license holder to write a telephone number.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Medical and Emergency Information · ¶2
text: Space is also provided on the card to allow individuals to voluntarily indicate if a health condition exists that may impede communication with a peace officer.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Medical and Emergency Information · ¶3
text: Additionally, an application for an original, renewal or replacement driver license or ID includes the option to provide the name, address and telephone number of two individuals who may be contacted in the event of injury or death of the applicant. Driver license and ID card holders may also add or update emergency contacting information online by visiting our website, https://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/emerContactInfo.htm .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Medical and Emergency Information › Allergic Reaction to Drugs · ¶1
text: DPS does not print medical information on driver licenses or ID cards. To add medical information to the back of your driver license or ID card, use a permanent ink pen and write the name of medication that may cause an allergic reaction.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Organ Donation · ¶1
text: DPS offers “Donate Life Texas” pamphlets to any person who visits a driver license office. The pamphlets provide general information on the Donate Life Texas program. If you choose to be an organ donor, a small heart with the word “donor” will be printed on the front of the card. Cards that indicate a person’s wish to be a donor shall be conclusive evidence of a decedent’s status as a donor and serve as consent for organ, tissue, and eye donation. You can get more information and register to be an organ, tissue, and eye donor online at www.DonateLifeTexas.org .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Voluntary Contributions · ¶1
text: If you are applying for an original or renewal driver license or ID card, you can voluntarily make a monetary contribution to the following programs:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Voluntary Contributions · item 1
text: The Blindness Education, Screening, and Treatment Program administered by the Texas Commission for the Blind, which provides screening and treatment for those individuals who are without adequate medical coverage.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Voluntary Contributions · item 2
text: The Glenda Dawson Donate Life Texas Program, which manages the donor registry and statewide donor education projects.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Voluntary Contributions · item 3
text: The Veteran’s Assistance Fund, which provides grants to local government and nonprofit organizations to enhance or improve veteran assistance programs that address the needs of veterans and their families.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Voluntary Contributions · item 4
text: The Sexual Assault Evidence Testing Program, which helps fund the testing of sexual assault evidence (rape) collection kits.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Voluntary Contributions · item 5
text: The Identification Fee Exemption Account, which assists foster and homeless children and youths with payment of fees for driver licenses and IDs.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License · ¶1
text: If you are applying for a Texas driver license, you must comply with the following procedures.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License · ¶1
text: An application for a driver license must be made in person. You may obtain an application at any driver license office or download an application from our website at www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/ApplyforLicense.htm .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License · ¶2
text: All in-office applicants who are at least 17 years and 10 months old are provided the opportunity to complete a voter registration application.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License · ¶3
text: All men 18-25 years of age who are U.S. citizens or immigrants are automatically registered for selective service upon issuance of an ID card or driver license.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · ¶1
text: To apply for a Texas driver license, you must provide the following documents and information.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 1
text: Your full name, proof of residential address, mailing address, current county of residence, place of birth, and date of birth

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 2
text: Identification documents

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 3
text: Social security number verified electronically through the Social Security Administration

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 4
text: Thumb or index fingerprints

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 5
text: Physical description

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 6
text: Answer the medical status and history questions listed on the application. Individuals with certain medical limitations may have their cases reviewed by the Medical Advisory Board (MAB) before the license is issued

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 7
text: Surrender any valid out-of-state driver license

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · item 8
text: U.S. citizenship status or lawful presence

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Required Documents and Application Information · ¶2
text: For additional information and lists of acceptable documents, visit our website, www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/ApplyforLicense.htm .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Driver Record · ¶1
text: A complete record of all your examinations will be recorded on your application and scanned into the Driver License System where it becomes a part of your permanent driving record. Any convictions for moving traffic violations or crashes, including out of state records of convictions, will be recorded as part of your permanent driving record. To find out more information on driver records and how to obtain a copy of your record, visit http://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/driverrecords.htm .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Evidence of Financial Responsibility (Vehicle Insurance) · ¶1
text: When applying for an original driver license, you must provide evidence of financial responsibility or a statement that you do not own a motor vehicle that requires the maintenance of financial responsibility.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Evidence of Financial Responsibility (Vehicle Insurance) · ¶2
text: Evidence of financial responsibility must meet at least the minimum amount required by Texas and cover each motor vehicle the applicant owns that requires maintenance of financial responsibility.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Vehicle Registration · ¶1
text: When surrendering an out-of-state driver license, a new Texas resident must submit, with a driver license application, evidence that each motor vehicle owned by the person is currently registered in Texas, or indicate they do not own a motor vehicle required to be registered. A registration receipt issued by the county tax assessor-collector of the county in which the new resident resides is satisfactory evidence that your motor vehicle has been registered in Texas.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Fees · ¶1
text: The required fee(s) must be submitted before any exams will be given for an original Texas driver license. An additional $1 administrative fee is included in most transactions. However, if you are completing multiple transactions at the same time, in-person, by telephone or online, you will only be charged the $1 administrative fee once. A $1 administrative fee is not charged for transactions made through the mail.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › How to Obtain a Texas Driver License › Applying for a Texas Driver License › Fees · ¶2
text: For more information on all fees, refer to Appendix D of this handbook or visit our website, https://www.dps.texas.gov/section/driver-license/driver-license-fees .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education · ¶1
text: Individuals younger than 25 years of age are required to successfully complete an approved driver education course. For more information on licensing requirements for applicants younger than 25 years of age, visit our website at www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/ApplyforLicense.htm .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education · image
heading: Alt text: “Illustration in the handbook section “Driver Education” (no caption in the PDF)”
text: Illustration in the handbook section “Driver Education” (no caption in the PDF)

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Impact Texas Drivers (ITD) · ¶1
text: All driver license applicants must complete the Impact Texas Drivers (ITD) course appropriate for their age group prior to taking the driving exam. For more information, visit the ITD website, https://impacttexasdrivers.dps.texas.gov .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Minors · ¶1
text: If you are younger than 18 years of age, your application must be signed, under oath, by the parent or guardian with custody. If there is not a guardian, your employer or county judge may sign the application. The person who signs may ask DPS to cancel your license any time before your 18th birthday. This request must be in writing and sworn to before an officer authorized to administer oaths. In addition, the minor applicant and cosigner must acknowledge receipt of information that provides information about distracted driving and explains the zero tolerance law. See Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drugs Impact on the Driving Ability for more information.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations · ¶1
text: Before any exams are given, you must pay the required fee. Your picture will be taken and you will be given a payment receipt. If you do not pass the knowledge and driving exams on your first attempt, your application will be held for 90 days. After 90 days or three failed exams, a new application and fee will be required.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations · ¶2
text: The knowledge and driving exams are not required for applicants 18 years of age and older who surrender a valid out-of-state license. After you have passed all applicable exams, you will be issued a temporary license, which you may use for 45 days or until you receive your permanent license in the mail. If you do not receive your license in 45 days, email our customer service center at https://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/customer_service/Other.aspx .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 1: The Knowledge exam · ¶1
text: As part of the Less Tears More Years Act , all applicants younger than 25 years of age are required to take a driver education course to apply for a driver license. Upon successful completion of certain courses, the person is not required to take the Class C knowledge exam, also known as the written exam, at the driver license office.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 1: The Knowledge exam · ¶2
text: There are three types of knowledge exams.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 1: The Knowledge exam · item 1
text: Class C – Knowledge exam for all original applicants

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 1: The Knowledge exam · item 2
text: Class M – Motorcycle knowledge exam. This exam is waived for applicants who successfully complete a state approved motorcycle operator training course and present proof of completion.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 1: The Knowledge exam · item 3
text: Class A or Class B – Rules exam for operators of Class A and Class B vehicles

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 1: The Knowledge exam · ¶3
text: You must score a grade of 70 percent or better to pass any knowledge exam.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 2: The Vision Examination · ¶1
text: Your vision will be examined when you are at the driver license office. Depending on the results, you may be required to wear corrective lenses while driving if the lenses improve your vision and help increase the safety of your driving. If the results are inconclusive, you may be referred to your doctor.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 3: The Driving Exam · ¶1
text: The driving exam is given only after all other exams are passed and evidence of financial responsibility is presented or the vehicle is exempt under the Texas Motor Vehicle Safety Responsibility Act. The type of vehicle used for the driving exam must match the class of license on the application. No one younger than 18 years of age is exempt from taking the driving exam.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 3: The Driving Exam · image
heading: Examples of Vehicles for Driving Exam · Class A Test in · Class B Test in · Class C Test in | Alt text: “Examples of Vehicles for Driving Exam · Class A Test in · Class B Test in · Class C Test in”
text: Examples of Vehicles for Driving Exam · Class A Test in · Class B Test in · Class C Test in

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 3: The Driving Exam · ¶2
text: Individuals may take a driving exam at a driver license office or through a third party skills testing (TPST) school. The TPST program permits certain schools to administer the non-commercial driving exam.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 3: The Driving Exam · ¶3
text: Individuals who complete the state approved motorcycle operator training course are not required to take a driving exam for a Class M license if the person already has a valid, unrestricted Texas license. Individuals younger than 18 years of age must pass the motorcycle driving exam.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 3: The Driving Exam · ¶4
text: Additionally, the driving exam is not required for anyone applying for a learner license.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Part 3: The Driving Exam · ¶5
text: A $10 exam fee is required when changing from a lower to a higher class license or when removing restrictions from a license. The cost of adding a Class M to an existing license is $15.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · ¶1
text: During the driving exam, you will not be asked to do anything illegal. You must follow all of the instructions given by the LPS. Do not carry on a conversation during the driving exam.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · ¶2
text: If you are not eligible to drive in Texas, a licensed driver must drive the car to the driver license office and exam area. If you are not issued a driver license then the licensed driver must also drive you away from the driver license office.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · ¶3
text: Upon completion of the driving exam, the LPS will explain all driving errors and let you know how to correct those errors.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · ¶4
text: Your application for a license will not be approved if you:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 1
text: Violate the law

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 2
text: Refuse to follow instructions

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 3
text: Drive dangerously or have a crash

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 4
text: Have more than 30 points deducted on the driving exam

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · ¶5
text: All drivers are graded on four basic skills, regardless of the type of driving exam.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 5
text: Control – Your ability to make your car do what you want it to do

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 6
text: Observation – Your ability to see what other traffic is doing and other things that may create problems in traffic

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 7
text: Positioning – Your ability to drive in your lane

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 8
text: Signaling – Your ability to use turn signals as required

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · ¶6
text: You may be graded on your performance on the following skills so it is good to practice before taking the driving exam.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 9
text: Parallel parking (you may use the back-up camera on your vehicle for parallel parking; however, the use of an automated vehicle parking function will not be allowed)

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 10
text: Quick stop – You may be asked to stop your car as quickly as possible at about 20 mph without skidding your tires

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 11
text: Backing – Your ability to back the car for a distance of about 60 feet at a slow rate of speed and as straight and smooth as possible. Turn and look back at all times while backing or you may use the back-up camera and mirrors on your vehicle while backing; however, the use of an automated vehicle parking function will not be allowed

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 12
text: Stop signs

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 13
text: Traffic signals

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 14
text: Use of clutch – On standard transmissions, hold the clutch all the way down when starting the motor, shifting gears, when stopping, and once your speed drops below 10 mph. Do not drive with your foot resting on the clutch

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 15
text: Intersection observance – Use the proper lane; slow down and look both ways before entering the intersection

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 16
text: Turns

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 17
text: Right-of-way

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 18
text: Following, passing, and proper lane observance

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Examinations › Description of the Driving Exam · item 19
text: Posture – Keep hands on steering wheel; don’t rest your elbow on the window

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Pass or Fail Driving Exam · ¶1
text: If you do not pass the driving exam, you will need to schedule time for another driving exam. If you pass the driving exam, always carry your license with you when driving and upon request, show it to:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Pass or Fail Driving Exam · item 1
text: Any peace officer, sheriff, constable, judge, justice of the peace, or state trooper

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Driver Education › Pass or Fail Driving Exam · item 2
text: Anyone with whom you are involved in a crash

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Penalties for Driving Without a License · ¶1
text: During a stop, a law enforcement officer will determine if you have a valid driver license as required.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Penalties for Driving Without a License · row 1
text: 1st conviction | A fine of up to $200.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Penalties for Driving Without a License · row 2
text: 2nd conviction in one year | A fine of $25 to $200.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Penalties for Driving Without a License · row 3
text: Driving without a license, operating a vehicle without insurance at the time of the offense, and driver causes a crash resulting in serious bodily injury or death | Class A misdemeanor punishable by a fine up to $4,000 and/or confinement in jail for not more than 365 days.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Penalties for Driving Without a License · row 4
text: *Additional suspensions may apply.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Restrictions Placed on a License · ¶1
text: A restriction may be placed on your license. This is not meant to interfere with your driving but to make you a safer driver. A complete list of restrictions can be found in Appendix ‘XYZ’ at the end of this handbook. This information is also available on our website at https://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/endrsRestrictions.htm .

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Restrictions Placed on a License › Removing or Adding Restrictions · ¶1
text: Visit your local driver license office for more information concerning the removal or addition of any restrictions from your driver license or learner license.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Replacement (Duplicate) or Change of Information on a Driver License or ID Card · ¶1
text: You may be able to obtain a replacement (duplicate) card or change your address online at https://txapps.texas.gov/tolapp/txdl/ . A change of address must be reported to DPS within 30 days. For more information and requirements, visit the website at https://www.dps.texas.gov/section/driver-license . The fee to replace or change information for online and in-person transactions is: $11 = $10 for license + $1 transaction fee.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Replacement (Duplicate) or Change of Information on a Driver License or ID Card · ¶2
text: If you are not able to use the online feature to change your address, you may mail an Application for Change of Address or Replacement (DL-64) to the address below. If you do not have the required DL-64, you can download the form from our website at https://www.dps.texas.gov/InternetForms/ . Upon receipt of the $10 fee and completed form, a new license or ID card with the correct address information will be mailed to you.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Replacement (Duplicate) or Change of Information on a Driver License or ID Card · ¶3
text: Mailing Address: Texas Department of Public Safety Issuance Services PO Box 149008 Austin, TX 78714-9008

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Replacement (Duplicate) or Change of Information on a Driver License or ID Card · ¶4
text: To change any other information on your driver license or ID card, you will need to visit a driver license office.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Replacement (Duplicate) or Change of Information on a Driver License or ID Card › Out-of-State Licensees · ¶1
text: If you are out-of-state but maintaining a Texas driver license, you may apply for a duplicate license by mail. Visit the website, https://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/nonmilitaryrenewal.htm to to download the appropriate forms and application. Complete and submit the required application with a $10 fee to:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Replacement (Duplicate) or Change of Information on a Driver License or ID Card › Out-of-State Licensees · ¶2
text: Mailing Address: Texas Department of Public Safety Issuance Services PO Box 149008 Austin, TX 78714-9008

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Replacement (Duplicate) or Change of Information on a Driver License or ID Card › Out-of-State Licensees · ¶3
text: NOTE: Some driver licenses are not eligible for online, phone or mail-in transactions. These include limited term, sex offender and licenses issued to persons 79 years of age and older.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License · ¶1
text: A renewal notice invitation may be mailed to the last address you provided to DPS before your license expires. If you do not receive this courtesy notice, it remains your responsibility to renew your license.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · ¶1
text: A Texas driver license must be renewed every eight years. A renewal application must be made in person at any driver license office unless you are eligible to renew online at https://txapps.texas.gov/tolapp/txdl/ , by mail, or by phone at 1-866-DL-RENEW. To check your eligibility to renew, visit us online or call the number provided.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · ¶2
text: A person must appear in a driver license office at least once every sixteen (16) years for a vision exam and to update the photo, signature and fingerprints. Please check the website at www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/ to schedule an appointment at a location near you.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · ¶3
text: Alternate methods to renew will not be extended to:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 1
text: Any person whose license is suspended, cancelled, revoked, or denied

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 2
text: Commercial driver license (CDL) holders

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 3
text: Holders of an occupational license, provisional license, or learner license

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 4
text: Licensees restricted because of driving ability or a medical condition that requires periodic reviews, including any medical or physical condition which may result in progressive changes to a licensee’s ability to safely drive a motor vehicle

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 5
text: Driver license or ID card holders who are subject to sex offender registration requirements

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 6
text: Driver license holders who are 79 years of age or older

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 7
text: Driver license or ID card holders who do not have a social security number or photo on file

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · item 8
text: Non-U.S. citizens, due to a verification process

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Application for Renewal · ¶4
text: When you are at the driver license office you will be asked questions concerning your medical history. If you have certain medical limitations, your case may be referred to the Medical Advisory Board (MAB) for their opinion about how your condition may affect your driving. For more information on MAB, visit our website at http://www.dps.texas.gov/driverlicense/MedicalRevocation.htm

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Individuals Returning to Texas from Military Service · ¶1
text: Within 90 days of being honorably discharged, military personnel, spouses and dependents returning from active duty must present a Texas driver license and separation papers to obtain a renewal license without taking the knowledge and driving exams when the license has been expired for over two years.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · ¶1
text: Eligible individuals who do not currently reside in Texas but whose true, permanent home is in Texas may mail in their application for renewal. Visit the website, https://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/nonmilitaryrenewal.htm to download the appropriate forms and application. The following individuals who are out-of-state are not eligible to renew by mail and must renew in-person.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · item 1
text: A person subject to sex offender registration requirements

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · item 2
text: A person 79 years of age or older

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · item 3
text: A person holding a commercial driver license (CDL)

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · item 4
text: A person who is not a U.S. citizen, unless active duty military

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · ¶2
text: The proper fee and the results of your vision exam, performed by an eye specialist or an authorized driver license employee, must be included with your application. The license will be renewed and will be valid to expiration date shown or until 90 days after your return to Texas, whichever comes first.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · ¶3
text: Make check or money order payable to: TX DPS. Do not send cash. Mail to:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Renewing a License › Out-of-State Texas Licensees · ¶4
text: Mailing Address: PO Box 149008 Austin, TX 78714-9008

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations · ¶1
text: Operating a motor vehicle is a privilege. If this privilege is abused, it may result in a driver license suspension or revocation.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations · ¶2
text: Mandatory suspensions, revocations, and convictions for certain offenses involving fraudulent government records may require $100 reinstatement fee. There is also a $100 reinstatement fee for Drug Education Course. Administrative License Revocations (ALR) require a $125 reinstatement fee. Some mandatory suspensions also require filing a Financial Responsibility Insurance Certificate (SR-22).

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · ¶1
text: Convictions for the following offenses will result in the automatic suspension of your license and driving privilege. For minors, see the Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) section in this chapter.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 1
text: Driving while intoxicated (DWI) by use of alcohol or drugs

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 2
text: Drug offense

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 3
text: Intoxication manslaughter or intoxication assault

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 4
text: Failure to stop and render aid

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 5
text: Causing the death or serious injury of anyone while operating a motor vehicle; involuntary manslaughter

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 6
text: Any offense punishable as a felony under the motor vehicle laws of Texas

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 7
text: Overtaking and passing a school bus (subsequent conviction)

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 8
text: Boating while intoxicated

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 9
text: Evading arrest

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 10
text: Driving while license invalid

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 11
text: Altered/unlawful use of a driver license

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 12
text: Displaying or possessing a fictitious or altered driver license or ID card

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 13
text: Lending a driver license or ID card to someone

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 14
text: Possessing more than one valid driver license or ID card

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 15
text: Providing false information or documents when applying for a driver license

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 16
text: Making, selling, or possessing a document deceptively similar to a driver license or ID card issued by DPS

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 17
text: Graffiti

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 18
text: Fictitious license plate, registration certificate, or safety inspection sticker

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 19
text: Fraudulent government records

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · item 20
text: Racing a motor vehicle on a public highway or street

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · ¶1
text: DPS has the authority to suspend or revoke a driver license or privilege of any driver, after an opportunity for a proper hearing, for any of the reasons listed below. A reinstatement fee is required for all discretionary suspensions and revocations.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 1
text: Driving while license invalid

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 2
text: Causing a serious crash while driving a motor vehicle

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 3
text: Repeated violations of traffic laws, including:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 4
text: Four or more traffic convictions occurring separately within any 12-month period or

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 5
text: Seven or more traffic convictions within any 24-month period

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 6
text: Failure to provide medical information or undergo examinations required by the medical advisory board (MAB).

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 7
text: Failure to take or pass a test when requested

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 8
text: Person has committed an offense in another state, which if committed in this state would be grounds for suspension or revocation

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Administrative Suspensions and Revocations · item 9
text: Violates a probation order set by a previous hearing

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) · ¶1
text: Convictions or failure to comply with the following offenses will result in automatic suspension of the driving privilege of individuals who are less than 21 years of age (See Administrative License Revocation (ALR) section for more suspension information regarding minors.)

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Alcoholic Beverage Code Offenses · item 1
text: Minor in possession

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Alcoholic Beverage Code Offenses · item 2
text: Attempt to purchase alcohol by a minor

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Alcoholic Beverage Code Offenses · item 3
text: Purchase of alcohol by a minor

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Alcoholic Beverage Code Offenses · item 4
text: Consumption of alcohol by a minor

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Alcoholic Beverage Code Offenses · item 5
text: Misrepresentation of age by a minor

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Alcoholic Beverage Code Offenses · item 6
text: Driving or operating a watercraft under the influence of alcohol by a minor

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Alcoholic Beverage Code Offenses · item 7
text: Failure to complete an alcohol awareness class

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Health and Safety Code Violations · item 1
text: Failure to complete a tobacco awareness class when required

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Health and Safety Code Violations · item 2
text: Drug offense

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) › Health and Safety Code Violations · item 3
text: An offense under the Controlled Substance Act

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Occupational License (Essential Need License) · ¶1
text: An occupational license, also called an essential need license, is a special type of restricted license issued to individuals:

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Occupational License (Essential Need License) · item 1
text: Whose driver license has been canceled, suspended, revoked, or denied for certain offenses (other than medical or delinquent child support); and

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Occupational License (Essential Need License) · item 2
text: Who can prove to a court there is an essential need to drive.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Occupational License (Essential Need License) · ¶2
text: Application for an occupational license is made to the district, county, or justice of the peace court in the precinct or county of the licensee’s residence or to the court of original jurisdiction, whichever is applicable. If the court determines an individual is eligible for an occupational license, then a court order will be issued. The court order authorizes DPS to issue the occupational license. The applicant must submit the court order and all required items to DPS before an occupational license can be issued. The fee for this type of license is $10 for one year or $20 if authorized for two years. The court order may be used for 45 days for driving purposes while the occupational license is being processed. After 45 days, you must have both the court order and the occupational license in your possession.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Occupational License (Essential Need License) · ¶3
text: A person issued an occupational license must also carry a certified copy of the court order when operating a vehicle and must allow a law enforcement officer to examine the order at the officer’s lawful request. An occupational license may not be issued to drive a commercial motor vehicle.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Occupational License (Essential Need License) · ¶4
text: For more information on occupational licenses, visit our website at https://www.dps.texas.gov/section/driver-license/occupational-driver-license .

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · ¶1
text: Any drug may affect a person’s ability to drive. Millions of people take over the counter and prescription medications, illegal drugs, or drink alcohol and do not realize they may affect the mental and physical (psychomotor) skills necessary to operate a vehicle and react to external events while driving a vehicle.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · ¶2
text: Each individual is different. The driving skills of persons taking the same drug may be affected differently. A driver’s body weight, emotional state, amount of drug taken, and when the drug was taken will influence the driver’s ability to assess an emergency situation or judge speed and distance. Safe driving always requires an observant eye, a steady hand, and a clear head.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · ¶3
text: When a person drinks alcohol or uses drugs, one of the first effects is they lose their judgement and their sight is impaired, causing slower reactions to sounds and the inability to judge another vehicle’s speed. A person’s ability to reason can all but disappear. Good judgment may be as simple as saying no to a friend who wants to race their car. However, if a person has been drinking alcohol or they are under the influence of drugs, their judgment may turn into, “Sure, take my car.”

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · ¶4
text: Taking more than one drug at the same time is even more dangerous since drugs may have a different overall cumulative effect, especially when alcohol is involved. Besides escalating the overall effects of the other drugs, alcohol can also mask the effects of those drugs, increasing a person’s risk of poor decision making and/or slowing responsive reactions to situations. You should always check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking more than one type of drug or mixing drugs, especially tranquilizers or sedatives.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · row 1
text: Marijuana | Research shows even typical social doses of marijuana can affect concentration, judgment, and sensory and perceptual skills needed for careful driving. People who are under marijuana influence have impaired sensory and perceptual abilities.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · row 2
text: Stimulants | Heavy amphetamine use may keep drivers awake and active for long periods of time. It also makes them less coordinated, edgy, and more likely to be involved in a car crash. Research shows typical social amounts of cocaine can produce lapses in attention and concentration. While caffeine can help drowsy drivers stay alert, it can’t make a drunk driver sober. Studies show ordinary amounts of caffeine don’t improve a drunk driver’s ability to operate a vehicle.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · row 3
text: Tranquilizers / Sedative-Hypnotics | Tranquilizers/Sedative-hypnotic drugs, including barbiturates, are powerful depressants, which calm people down or help them sleep. Tired or over-sedated drivers are not good drivers.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · row 4
text: Over-the-counter drugs | Many over-the-counter drugs cause drowsiness in some people, which can affect their driving. Read the labels and be careful with antihistamines, other cold preparations, or any medicine that relaxes or promotes sleep.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · row 5
text: Any drug | Any drug might affect your ability as a driver. If you take more than one drug or if you mix drugs, especially tranquilizers or other sedative-hypnotics with alcohol, you could be asking for trouble on the road and off. If you have doubts about a drug or drug mix, check with a doctor or pharmacist.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Intro · row 6
text: Alcohol | Each year alcohol, a depressant drug affecting coordination, judgment, perception, and emotional state, is responsible for a significant number of highway deaths. Alcohol increases the depressant effects of tranquilizers and barbiturates. Mixing these drugs, on or off the road, can be hazardous.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › The Number One Killer is Alcohol · ¶1
text: Driving While Intoxicated (DWI) is a problem affecting all Texans. According to the Calendar Year 2018 Texas Motor Vehicle Traffic Crash Facts (TxDOT), 940 persons were killed in a motor vehicle traffic crash with a driver under the influence of alcohol. Alcohol related crashes represent 26% of the total number of persons killed in motor vehicle traffic crashes.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › The Number One Killer is Alcohol · ¶2
text: The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) states that the leading cause of death for U.S. teens is accidental and most of those are motor vehicle crashes. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), 3,255 teen (age 15 to 19) drivers were involved in fatal crashes in 2017 and nearly 25% of those had been drinking.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › The Number One Killer is Alcohol · ¶3
text: In 2018, TxDOT reports that nearly 7% of all fatal crashes involved a driver under the age of 21 who was under the influence of alcohol. Texas law does not allow any amount of blood alcohol concentration (BAC) for minors.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › The Number One Killer is Alcohol · ¶4
text: To make Texas safer, the Texas legislature enacted laws to deter people from drinking and driving by penalizing those who choose to drink and drive. In Texas, a person, age 21 and over, is considered legally intoxicated if the person has a BAC of 0.08 or more. Driving While Intoxicated (DWI) and Driving Under the Influence (DUI) arrests can be a humiliating experience and are costly. Some fines range as high as $10,000 not including the cost of a bail bondsman, attorney, or other court-required expenses. Is it worth the risk?

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › The Number One Killer is Alcohol › Open Container · ¶1
text: It is illegal to possess an open container of alcohol in a motor vehicle passenger area located on a public highway, regardless of whether the vehicle is being operated, stopped, or parked. Conviction of this offense is punishable by a fine not to exceed $500.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › The Number One Killer is Alcohol › Myths about Drinking Alcohol · ¶1
text: Taking cold showers, drinking black coffee, or exercising will not make a person sober. Only time, based on body weight, number of drinks, and food intake can minimize the effects of alcohol. It takes about one hour for the body to rid itself of each drink consumed. If a person has been drinking, someone who has not been drinking should drive.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Tough Alcohol-Related Laws for Minors › Zero Tolerance for Minors · ¶1
text: According to the Texas Alcohol Beverage Code, a minor is any individual who is under 21 years of age. A minor may not purchase, attempt to purchase, consume, or possess an alcoholic beverage. Since a minor should not possess alcohol, Texas passed zero tolerance legislation for minors who commit an offense under the non-driving alcohol-related laws and for minors who drive under the influence.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Tough Alcohol-Related Laws for Minors › Zero Tolerance for Minors · ¶2
text: Zero tolerance means just that. Even if a minor is not intoxicated as defined under the DWI statute, but has any detectable amount of alcohol in his/her system while operating a motor vehicle in a public place or while operating a water- craft, the minor committed the criminal offense of Driving Under the Influence of Alcohol by a Minor (see Table 31).

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Tough Alcohol-Related Laws for Minors › Penalties for Non-Driving Alcohol-Related Offenses by Minors · ¶1
text: The Texas Zero Tolerance law established penalties for minors who commit offenses under the non-driving alcohol-related offenses. A minor may not purchase, attempt to purchase, falsely state he/she is 21 years of age or older, or present any document indicating he/she is 21 years of age or older to a person engaged in the selling or serving of alcoholic beverages. A minor may not consume, or possess an alcoholic beverage. Persons who purchase, furnish, or sell alcohol to a minor can be fined up to $4,000 and/or confined in jail for up to one year.

text: 1st offense | Class C misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, 8 to 12 hours of community service, mandatory attendance of an alcohol awareness course, and license will be suspended (or privilege denied if not licensed) for 30 days. If the minor is under 18, the parent may be required to also attend the alcohol awareness course.

text: 2nd offense | Class C misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, 20 to 40 hours of community service, may be required to attend an alcohol awareness course, and license will be suspended (or privilege denied if not licensed) for 60 days.

text: 3rd offense (Under 17 years of age) | Class C misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, 20 to 40 hours of community service, may be required to attend an alcohol awareness course, and license will be suspended (or privilege denied if not licensed) for 60 days or case can be transferred to Juvenile Court.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Tough Alcohol-Related Laws for Minors › Penalties for Non-Driving Alcohol-Related Offenses by Minors · row 4

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Tough Alcohol-Related Laws for Minors › Penalties for Non-Driving Alcohol-Related Offenses by Minors · ¶2
text: In addition to the above penalties, if a minor is convicted of any moving vehicle violation while suspended due to a non-driving alcohol-related offense (listed above) they are subject to the penalties of Driving While License Invalid (DWLI).

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Tough Alcohol-Related Laws for Minors › Implied Consent Laws for Minors · ¶1
text: A minor implies their consent to take one or more breath or blood specimen for analysis if they are arrested for operating a motor vehicle or watercraft in a public place while intoxicated, or if there is any detectable or noticeable amount of alcohol in their system while operating a motor vehicle in a public place as deemed by an officer. The breath or blood specimen will determine if alcohol is present in their body. It will also identify the amount of alcohol in their system. Additionally, the breath or blood specimen can identify the presence of any other controlled substances or drugs.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Tough Alcohol-Related Laws for Minors › Implied Consent Laws for Minors · ¶2
text: Refusal to provide a breath or blood specimen will result in the suspension of the minor’s license or driving privileges if not licensed.

text: Intoxication manslaughter | Second degree felony punishable by a fine not to exceed $10,000, imprisonment in the Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) for 2 to 20 years, and a suspension of the driver license (or privilege denied if not licensed) for 180 days to 2 years.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Alcohol-Related Laws for Adults › Implied Consent Laws for Adults · ¶1
text: The implied consent for adults is similar to that of minors.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Alcohol-Related Laws for Adults › Implied Consent Laws for Adults · ¶2
text: Like the minor, an adult implies their consent to take one or more breath or blood specimen for analysis if they are arrested for operating a motor vehicle or watercraft in a public place while intoxicated, or if they are an adult up to 21 years of age and there is any detectable or noticeable amount of alcohol in their system while operating a motor vehicle in a public place as deemed by an officer. The breath or blood specimen determines if alcohol is present in their body and will identify the amount of alcohol in their system, as well as the presence of any other controlled substances or drugs.

locator: Chapter 10: Alcohol and Drug Impact on the Driving Ability › Texas Alcohol-Related Laws for Adults › Implied Consent Laws for Adults · ¶3
text: A person who refuses to give a blood or breath specimen for analysis will have their driver license suspended for 180 days or up to 730 days for subsequent offenses. If a person submits to a blood or breath specimen and the results show a BAC of 0.08 or greater, their driver license may be suspended for 90 days or up to 365 days for subsequent offenses. Anyone with a BAC of 0.08 or more is considered intoxicated.
