locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · ¶1
text: When approaching a railroad grade crossing, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail if:

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · item 1
text: A clearly visible railroad signal warns of an approaching train

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · item 2
text: A crossing gate is lowered or a flag person warns of an approaching train

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · item 3
text: A driver is required to stop by an official traffic-control device or a traffic-control signal

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · item 4
text: An approaching train is within about 1,500 feet of the crossing. The train will produce an audible signal to identify the immediate hazard.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · item 5
text: An approaching train is visible and in close proximity to the crossing

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · ¶2
text: You are required to stop at a railroad grade crossing and remain stopped until allowed to proceed or it is safe to proceed.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · ¶3
text: A person who fails to obey the law regarding railroad grade crossings is subject to a fine of $50 to $200.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Railroad Grade Crossings · image
heading: Alt text: “Illustration in the handbook section “Railroad Grade Crossings” (no caption in the PDF)”
text: Illustration in the handbook section “Railroad Grade Crossings” (no caption in the PDF)

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · item 1
text: If a railroad crossing is marked only with a cross-buck sign or reduce speed sign, then look both ways, and listen for a whistle. If a train is approaching, stop. If a train is not approaching, proceed with caution.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · item 2
text: If red lights are flashing at a railroad crossing, stop. If a train is approaching, remain stopped until the train passes and the lights stop flashing.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · item 3
text: If the railroad crossing gates have been lowered, stop. Remain stopped and wait until the train passes and the gates are raised before crossing.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · item 4
text: Be sure the tracks are clear before you proceed to cross. There may be two or more sets of tracks. One train could be blocking the view of another.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · item 5
text: Never stop on the tracks. If your car stalls on the tracks and you cannot restart it, get out and try to push the car off the tracks. If you cannot push the car off the tracks, get help. If a train is approaching and your vehicle is stalled, get out quickly and move away from the tracks. Run toward the approaching train to the side of the tracks and avoid flying debris.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · item 6
text: Remember, trains do not and cannot stop at crossings. Trains always have the right-of-way.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · item 7
text: Audible signs or whistles may be difficult to hear when approaching railroad crossings. Roll your windows down, turn your radio down, and listen carefully.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Right-of-Way at Intersections › Additional Safe Driving Procedures at Railroad Crossings · ¶1
text: If you encounter a railroad grade crossing signal problem, call the Texas Department of Public Safety Communications Center at (800) 772-7677 or call your local police department or county sheriff’s office. Each railroad crossing signal has an identifying number. Please note the number and be ready to provide it when reporting a problem.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Highway-Rail Grade Crossings Emergency Notification System (ENS) · ¶1
text: The mission of the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) is to enable the safe, reliable and efficient movement of people and goods for a strong America, now and in the future.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Highway-Rail Grade Crossings Emergency Notification System (ENS) · image

text: 1 · 2 · 1 Each railroad’s emergency contact number, 2 · The U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) National Crossing Inventory Number, which identifies the exact location of the crossing to the railroads.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Highway-Rail Grade Crossings Emergency Notification System (ENS) · ¶2
text: In Case of Emergency

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Highway-Rail Grade Crossings Emergency Notification System (ENS) · item 1
text: Locate the blue and white Emergency Notification System (ENS) sign at the grade crossing.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Highway-Rail Grade Crossings Emergency Notification System (ENS) · item 2
text: Call for help! Call the railroad’s emergency contact number listed on the blue sign.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Highway-Rail Grade Crossings Emergency Notification System (ENS) · item 3
text: Communicate your location, by providing the identification number (see below) and state the nature of the emergency to the dispatcher.

text: The ENS sign includes: Emergencies and safety concerns at the grade crossing should be reported by using the information on the ENS sign.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · ¶1
text: You must yield the right-of-way to police cars, fire trucks, ambulances, and other emergency vehicles sounding a siren, bell, or flashing red light. If traffic allows, pull to the right edge of the road and stop. If you are unable to pull over to the right, slow down and leave a clear path for the emergency vehicle.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · image
heading: Alt text: “Illustration in the handbook section “Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles” (no caption in the PDF)”
text: Illustration in the handbook section “Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles” (no caption in the PDF)

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · item 1
text: You are not allowed to follow within 500 feet of a fire truck answering an alarm or an ambulance when the flashing red lights are on.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · item 2
text: Do not drive or park on the street where the fire truck has answered an alarm.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · item 3
text: Do not park in a location that interferes with the arrival or departure of an ambulance to or from the scene of an emergency.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · ¶2
text: Unless otherwise directed by a law enforcement officer, drivers who approach a stopped emergency vehicle with its lights activated must:

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · item 4
text: Vacate the lane closest to the emergency vehicle if the highway has two or more lanes traveling in the direction of the emergency vehicle;

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · item 5
text: Slow to a speed not more than 20 mph less than the posted speed limit when the posted speed limit is 25 mph or more; or

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · item 6
text: Slow to a speed less than 5 mph when the posted speed limit is less than 25 mph.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · image
heading: Stop · SCHOOL BUS | Alt text: “Stop · SCHOOL BUS”
text: Stop · SCHOOL BUS

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · ¶1
text: You must yield the right-of-way to school buses. Always drive with care when you are near a school bus. If you approach a school bus from either direction and the bus is displaying alternately flashing red lights, you must stop. Do not pass the school bus until:

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · item 1
text: The school bus has resumed motion;

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · item 2
text: You are signaled by the driver to proceed; or

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · item 3
text: The red lights are no longer flashing.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · ¶2
text: It is not necessary to stop when passing a school bus on a different road or when on a controlled-access highway where the bus is stopped in a loading zone and pedestrians aren’t permitted to cross. A person who fails to obey the law regarding yielding the right-of-way to school buses displaying alternating, flashing lights is subject to the penalties listed in Table 17.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · row 1
text: 1st conviction | A fine of $500 - $1,250.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · row 2
text: 2nd conviction and every conviction after (within 5 years) | A fine not less than $1000 or more than $2000, possible suspension of driver license for up to six months.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · row 3
text: Person causes serious bodily injury to another when passing a stopped school bus | Class A misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $4,000 and/or up to one year in jail.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · row 4
text: Person causes serious bodily injury to another and has previously been convicted of passing a school bus and causing serious bodily injury | State jail felony punishable by 180 days to 2 years confinement and a possible fine of up to $10,000.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield the Right-of-Way to Pedestrians (Persons on Foot) › Avoid Turning a Car into a Deadly Weapon · ¶1
text: You should always be on the lookout for individuals who are on foot (pedestrians) whether they have the right-of-way or not. Drivers must give the right-of-way to pedestrians:

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield the Right-of-Way to Pedestrians (Persons on Foot) › Avoid Turning a Car into a Deadly Weapon · item 1
text: At an uncontrolled intersection (there are not any traffic signs or signals for the pedestrian to enter the crosswalk)

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield the Right-of-Way to Pedestrians (Persons on Foot) › Avoid Turning a Car into a Deadly Weapon · item 2
text: If the pedestrian has a WALK signal or

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield the Right-of-Way to Pedestrians (Persons on Foot) › Avoid Turning a Car into a Deadly Weapon · item 3
text: If there is not a pedestrian control signal, give the pedestrian the right-of-way on a green light.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield the Right-of-Way to Pedestrians (Persons on Foot) › Avoid Turning a Car into a Deadly Weapon · item 4
text: If the light changes after the pedestrian has entered the crosswalk, still give the pedestrian the right-of-way.

text: The “Yield Here to Pedestrians” sign is used when yield lines are used in advance of a marked crosswalk that crosses an uncontrolled multi-lane roadway.

text: A pedestrian hybrid beacon is a special type of pedestrian activated warning device used with signs and pavement markings to warn and control traffic at locations where pedestrians enter or cross a street or highway. Pedestrian hybrid beacons are only installed at a marked crosswalk.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield the Right-of-Way to Pedestrians (Persons on Foot) › In-Roadway Lights · ¶1
text: In-roadway lights are special types of lights installed in the roadway surface to warn roadway users they are approaching a condition on or near the road they may not see, which might require them to slow down or come to a complete stop. In-roadway lights are used as an alternative to traffic lights where pedestrian safety is a concern, and are typically placed at midblock crossings, school crosswalks, marked crosswalks on uncontrolled approaches, or in advance of roundabouts.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Traffic Signals · ¶1
text: Traffic signals help provide for the orderly movement of traffic. Drivers must obey these signals, except when a law enforcement officer is directing traffic. You must obey a law enforcement officer at all times when they are directing traffic even if he/she is telling you to do something which is ordinarily considered against the law.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Traffic Signals › Steady Red Light (Stop) · ¶1
text: Stop before entering the crosswalk or intersection. You may turn right unless prohibited by law. You may also turn left if both streets are one way, unless prohibited by law. You must yield to all pedestrians and other traffic lawfully using the intersection.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Traffic Signals › Steady Red Light (Stop) · image

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Traffic Signals › Steady Red Light (Stop) › A Flashing Red Light · ¶1
text: Stop completely before entering the crosswalk or intersection, then proceed when you can do so safely. Vehicles on the intersecting road may not have to stop.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Traffic Signals › Steady Yellow Light (Caution) · ¶1
text: A steady yellow light warns drivers to use caution and to alert them the light is about to change to red. You must STOP before entering the nearest crosswalk at the intersection if you can do so safely. If a stop cannot be made safely, then you may proceed cautiously through the intersection before the light changes to red.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Traffic Signals › Steady Green Light (Go) · ¶1
text: A steady green light means the driver can proceed on a green light if it is safe to do so. You may drive straight ahead or turn unless prohibited by another sign or signal. Watch for cars and pedestrians in the intersection. Be aware of reckless drivers who may race across the intersection to beat a red light.

heading: Lane-use control signals are overhead signals indicating if motorists should drive in a specific lane. If a red X appears above a lane, a driver should not drive in that lane. A steady yellow X means a driver should prepare to safely vacate the lane over which the signal is located because a lane control change is being made. A steady downward green arrow means a driver is permitted to drive in the lane over which the arrow signal is located. Lane-use control signals can be used on streets or highways.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Railroad Warning Signs › Railroad Crossing · ¶1
text: This sign means you are within a few hundred feet of a railroad crossing. Slow down and be prepared to stop. If you see a train coming, STOP. Never try to beat a train.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Railroad Warning Signs › Railroad Crossbuck · ¶1
text: Railroad crossbuck signs are posted at every railroad, highway, road, or street grade crossing and show the location of the train tracks. If more than one track is to be crossed, the sign will show the number of tracks. Always slow down, look, listen, and be prepared to yield the right-of-way to an approaching train.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Railroad Warning Signs › Emergency Notification System · ¶1
text: Emergency Notification System signs are posted so the public may report unsafe situations and for railroads to respond to malfunctioning warning signals, vehicles stalled on the tracks or other emergency situations. Posted on each sign are an emergency contact number and U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) National Crossing Inventory Number. The inventory number identifies the exact location of the crossing.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Pavement Markings · ¶1
text: Pavement markings help you just like signs and signals. They are used to warn and direct drivers and to regulate traffic.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Pavement Markings › Two-Lane Rural Road with Two-Way Traffic · ¶1
text: Keep to the right of the yellow center line. You may cross a broken line when passing another vehicle or when the right half of the road is closed. Do not cross the line if it is not safe or it is a solid yellow line.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Pavement Markings › Three Lane One-Way Roads · ¶1
text: When each lane on a one way road is marked with a broken white line, you may drive in any lane. When turning from a one-way road, make sure you move into the lane closest to the turn you are going to make well in advance of your turn.

text: White crosswalk lines are painted across a road to indicate pedestrian crossing areas. Pedestrians should use these areas when crossing the road. The solid yellow line on the left edge of the road is a guide for drivers to indicate driving to the left of the yellow line is prohibited. This type of yellow line can be found on interstate highways.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices · ¶1
text: Various traffic control devices are used in construction and maintenance work zones to direct drivers, bicyclists, or pedestrians safely through the work zone and to provide for the safety of the workers.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices · ¶2
text: Special Note: Traffic fines double for violations that occur in construction zones where workers are present.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices · ¶3
text: The most commonly used traffic control devices are signs, barricades, vertical panels, drums, cones, tubes, flashing arrow panels, and flag individuals. Orange is the basic color for these devices.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices · ¶4
text: When you are in a construction and maintenance work zone, be prepared:

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices · item 1
text: To slow down or stop as you approach workers and equipment

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices · item 2
text: To change lanes

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices · item 3
text: For unexpected movements of workers and equipment

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Construction and Maintenance Signs · ¶1
text: Construction and maintenance signs are used to alert drivers of unusual or potentially dangerous conditions in or near work zones. Most signs in work zones are diamond shaped, but a few are rectangular.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices · ¶1
text: Barricades, vertical panels, drums, cones, and tubes are the most commonly used devices to alert drivers of unusual or potentially dangerous conditions in highway and street work zones, and to guide drivers safely through the work zone. At night channelizing devices are often equipped with flashing or steady burn lights.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices · ¶2
text: When you encounter any type of channelizing device:

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices · item 1
text: Slow down and prepare to change lanes when it is safe to do so.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices · item 2
text: Be prepared for drivers who wait until the last second to move to the open lane.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices · item 3
text: Maintain reduced speed until you clear the construction zone. There should be a sign indicating you are leaving the construction zone.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices · item 4
text: Return to the normal driving lane only after checking traffic behind you.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices › Passing Traffic · ¶1
text: The diagonal stripes on the barricade or vertical panel guide the driver towards the direction to where the traffic is to pass.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Channelizing Devices › Pass to the Right · ¶1
text: Stripes sloping downward to the right means the driver should bear to the right.

text: Large flashing or sequencing arrow panels may be used in work zones day and night to guide drivers into certain traffic lanes and to inform them part of the road ahead is closed.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Flag Person · ¶1
text: A flag person is often provided in roadway work zones to stop, slow, or guide traffic safely through the area. A flag person wears an orange vest, shirt, or jacket and uses stop/slow paddles or red flags to direct traffic through work zones.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Flag Person · item 1
text: A flag person is used in cases of extreme hazard.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Flag Person · item 2
text: A flag person’s instructions must be obeyed.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Flag Person · item 3
text: When instructed to stop, do so in your lane and do not veer right or left.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Flag Person · item 4
text: Do not attempt to go forward until the flag person instructs you to do so.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Flag Person · item 5
text: Proceed with caution, expect the unexpected.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Flag Person · item 6
text: Always be on the lookout for oncoming vehicles in your lane of traffic.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Construction and Maintenance Devices › Automated Flagger Assistance Device (AFAD) · ¶1
text: An automated flagger assistance device (AFAD) is used to control road users through temporary traffic zones. An AFAD is designed to be remotely operated, allowing a flag person to be positioned out of the lane of traffic. Temporary traffic control in roadway work zones can also include pilot/escort vehicles, advanced warning signs, or temporary traffic signals.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Obey Warning Signs and Barricades · ¶1
text: It is a violation to disobey the instructions, signals, warnings, or markings of a warning sign, or to drive around a barricade.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Obey Warning Signs and Barricades · ¶2
text: The offense is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $1 to $200. Fines double in a construction or maintenance work zone when workers are present anywhere in the construction zone.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Obey Warning Signs and Barricades · ¶3
text: The offense is a Class B misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $2,000 and/or up to 180 days in jail when a warning sign or barricade has been placed at a location where water is over any portion of a road, street, or highway.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Slow-Moving Vehicle Emblem · ¶1
text: This emblem is required for all slow-moving vehicles. Slow-moving vehicles are those designed to operate at a maximum speed of 25 mph or less, and the term includes all vehicles, farm and other machinery, and any other road machinery drawn by either animals or slow moving motor vehicles.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Slow-Moving Vehicle Emblem · item 1
text: The use of this emblem is prohibited on anything other than a slow-moving vehicle. It must not be used on other vehicles or on stationary objects.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Slow-Moving Vehicle Emblem · item 2
text: Exceptions. The following do not need the special emblem:

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Slow-Moving Vehicle Emblem · ¶2
text: 1) A vehicle being used in actual construction work while traveling within the limits of a construction zone marked as required by the Texas Transportation Commission;

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Slow-Moving Vehicle Emblem · ¶3
text: 2) An implement or machinery being towed by a slow-moving vehicle bearing an emblem, if this emblem remains visible.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · ¶1
text: A good driver always lets others know if he/she is going to turn or stop. Signaling communicates your intention when driving and helps other drivers around you to plan ahead. A surprise move often results in a crash. Always be alert, watch for others, and give signals for your movements.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · ¶2
text: Always signal when you are going to:

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · item 1
text: Change lanes

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · item 2
text: Make a turn

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · item 3
text: Pull away from a parking space parallel to the curb

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · item 4
text: Slow down or stop

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · item 5
text: Enter or leave a highway

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling · item 6
text: Pull over to the side of the road

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling › How to Signal · ¶1
text: You may either use turn signal lights or hand and arm signals. If using hand signals, extend your hand and arm well out of the car window as shown below. Always make sure your signals can be easily seen by others, and signal in plenty of time.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling › How to Signal · ¶2
text: Hand and arm signals are usually difficult to see during non-daylight hours, so it is important to make sure your signal lights are working properly. When signaling a stop, pump your brakes a few times to attract attention.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Signaling › How to Signal · ¶3
text: Signal continuously for at least 100 feet before turning or stopping, and be sure to turn off your signal lights once your turn is complete. Your unintended signal still means “turn” to other drivers.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · ¶1
text: Never drive on the left side of the road when:

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · image
heading: Alt text: “Sign: LEFT LANE FOR PASSING ONLY”
text: Sign: LEFT LANE FOR PASSING ONLY

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 1
text: Pavement markings or signs prohibit driving on the left (a “No Passing Zone” or solid lane lines)

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 2
text: There are two or more traffic lanes in each direction

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 3
text: Within 100 feet of or crossing an intersection or railroad crossing

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 4
text: On a hill, curve, or any other place where vision is limited

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 5
text: Within 100 feet of a bridge, viaduct, or tunnel

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · ¶2
text: Always keep to the right side of the road except when:

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 6
text: Passing another vehicle on a two- or three-lane street

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 7
text: Driving on a one-way street

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Keep to the Right · item 8
text: The right side of the road is blocked

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · ¶1
text: It is not always safe to pass. Be patient and wait until the time is right. Crashes resulting from improper passing often result in head on crashes and can be deadly.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 1
text: Make certain the way is clear.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 2
text: Give the proper signal before changing lanes.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 3
text: Tap your horn when necessary to avoid surprising the driver ahead.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 4
text: Avoid cutting in too quickly if you must return to your original lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 1
text: Keep enough distance between you and the car in front of you so you can see ahead clearly. Check the rearview mirror, your side mirrors, and look over your shoulder in your blind spot to make sure the roadway is clear and no other vehicles are passing you. Turn on your left turn signal to alert any drivers behind you.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 2
text: Check well ahead for signs and pavement markings for no passing zones, and always check for oncoming traffic in the left lane. Be sure you have enough time and space to overtake the car ahead and return to the right lane before an approaching car comes within 200 feet of you.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 3
text: Tap your horn when necessary to alert the driver ahead.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 4
text: Pass on the left and do not return to the right lane until you have safely cleared the overtaken vehicle. Wait until you can see the car you have just passed in your rearview mirror before returning to the right lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 5
text: Turn on your right turn signal and return to the right lane. Be sure to turn your signal off after you have completed the lane change.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · image

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · ¶1
text: In Texas, you can pass on the right only when conditions permit you to do so safely.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · item 1
text: The road is clear of parked vehicles or other lane obstructions and is wide enough for two or more lanes in each direction.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · item 2
text: You are on a one-way road.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · item 3
text: You may pass on a paved shoulder when the vehicle you are passing is slowing or stopped on the main traveled portion of the highway, disabled, or preparing to make a left turn.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · ¶2
text: Do not pass on the right by driving off the paved portion of the highway.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 1
text: Do not increase your speed.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 2
text: Stay in your lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 3
text: Safely move as far to the right as you can when being passed on the left and the lanes are not marked.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 4
text: Make it as safe and easy as possible for the other driver to pass you.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Blind Spot Driving · ¶1
text: When you are passing, do not drive or linger in the other driver’s blind spot. Either pass the other driver or slow down so you are not in another driver’s blind spot. It is likely the other driver cannot see you if you are in or near their blind spot.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Blind Spot Driving · image

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · ¶1
text: Turning a corner appears to be a simple operation. However, many crashes and confusion in traffic are caused by drivers who do not turn properly.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · ¶2
text: Refer to the diagrams showing the correct method of making right and left turns. There are seven steps in making a safe turn.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · item 1
text: Decide before you get to the turning point. Never make a last minute turn; it is dangerous.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · item 2
text: Look behind and to both sides to see where other vehicles are before you change lanes.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · item 3
text: Move into the proper lane as soon as possible. The faster the traffic is moving, the sooner you should move into the proper lane. If you cannot get into the proper lane within one-half block before turning, do not turn, and continue straight ahead.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · item 4
text: Give the proper turn signal at least 100 feet before you turn. If using a hand signal, hold the signal until you are close enough to the intersection for others to know your intention. Do not hold the signal while making the turn; you need both hands on the wheel.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · item 5
text: Slow down to a reasonable turning speed prior to making the turn. Don’t use the brake or clutch while turning.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · item 6
text: To properly execute the turn, stay in the proper turn lane at all times. Make the turn correctly. This will be easy if you are in the proper lane and proceeding slowly enough at the time you begin to turn.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning · item 7
text: Finish the turn in the proper lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Right Turn · item 1
text: Signal for a lane change well ahead of the turning point. When it is safe, move your vehicle to the far right lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Right Turn · item 2
text: Use your right turn signal and slow down at least 100 feet from the corner.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Right Turn · item 3
text: Look both ways before starting to turn.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Right Turn · item 4
text: Keep as close as possible to the right edge of the road.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Right Turn · item 5
text: Turn using both hands on the wheel.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Right Turn · image
heading: Incorrect right turn | Alt text: “Incorrect right turn”
text: Incorrect right turn

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Left Turn · item 1
text: Well ahead of the turning point, signal for a lane change. When it is safe, move into the center lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Left Turn · item 2
text: Use the left turn signal and slow down at least 100 feet from the corner.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Left Turn · item 3
text: Look in all directions before starting to turn. Stay to the right of the center line as you enter the intersection. Yield the right-of-way to any vehicle approaching from the opposite direction.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Left Turn · item 4
text: To complete a left turn you should turn to the right of the center line of the road into which you are turning by entering the lane in which you will interfere the least with other traffic.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › How to Make a Left Turn · item 5
text: Once you have completed your left turn, you may signal and change lanes if necessary.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › Making a Left Turn From a One-Way Onto a Two-Way Street · ¶1
text: If you are turning left from a one-way street you should turn from the left lane into the right lane, moving in the same direction.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › Making a Left Turn From a One-Way Onto a Two-Way Street · image

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › Making a Left Turn From a Two-Way Onto a One-Way Street · ¶1
text: If you are turning left onto a one-way street, enter the street in the lane in which you will interfere the least with other traffic.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › Other Turning Procedures · ¶1
text: Watch for pavement markings and signs that:

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › Other Turning Procedures · item 1
text: Permit turning right or left from or into two or more traffic lanes

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Turning › Other Turning Procedures · item 2

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Intro · ¶1
text: Not all crashes happen while a vehicle is moving. An improperly parked vehicle may also cause a crash. When you leave your vehicle, turn the motor off, set the parking brake and remove the key. Be sure to look behind you for any oncoming traffic before opening your car door.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · ¶1
text: In the following situations, you should not park, stop, or allow a vehicle to stand idling:

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 1
text: On the road side of any vehicle stopped or parked at the edge or curb of a street

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 2
text: On a sidewalk or crosswalk

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 3
text: Within an intersection

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 4
text: Between a safety zone and adjacent curb or within 30 feet of a place on the curb immediately opposite the end of a safety zone

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 5
text: Alongside or opposite of any street excavation or obstruction when stopping, standing, or parking would obstruct traffic

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 6
text: On a bridge or other elevated structure on a highway or within a highway tunnel

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 7
text: On any railroad track

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · item 8
text: At any place where an official sign prohibits stopping

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park, Stop, or Stand a Vehicle · ¶2
text: Special Note: Temporarily stopping to obey signs, signals, etc. is not considered parking or standing.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park or Stand a Vehicle · ¶1
text: Whether occupied or not, do not park or allow a vehicle to stand idling:

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park or Stand a Vehicle · item 1
text: In front of a public or private driveway

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park or Stand a Vehicle · item 2
text: Within 15 feet of a fire hydrant

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park or Stand a Vehicle · item 3
text: Within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park or Stand a Vehicle · item 4
text: Within 30 feet upon the approach to any flashing signal, stop sign, yield sign, or other traffic control signal located at the side of a road

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park or Stand a Vehicle · item 5
text: Within 20 feet of the driveway entrance to any fire station and on the side of a street opposite the entrance to any fire station within 75 feet of entrance

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park or Stand a Vehicle · item 6
text: At any place where an official sign prohibits parking or standing

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle · item 1
text: Do not park a vehicle, occupied or not, within 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle · item 2
text: Do not park a vehicle at any place where an official sign prohibits parking.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parking, Stopping, or Standing on a Highway Outside an Urban Area · ¶1
text: Never park or leave a vehicle to stand idling on the paved part of any highway outside of a business or residential district when you can park off the road. If you cannot park off the road:

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parking, Stopping, or Standing on a Highway Outside an Urban Area · item 1
text: Leave plenty of room for others to pass

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parking, Stopping, or Standing on a Highway Outside an Urban Area · item 2
text: Be sure your vehicle can be seen for at least 200 feet from each direction

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parking, Stopping, or Standing on a Highway Outside an Urban Area · item 3
text: If at night, use your parking lights or leave your headlights on dim

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parking, Stopping, or Standing on a Highway Outside an Urban Area · item 4
text: A person may stop, stand, or park a bicycle on a sidewalk if the bicycle does not impede the normal and reasonable movement of pedestrian or other traffic on the sidewalk.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · ¶1
text: It is a violation for a person to park, stand, or stop a vehicle in a parking space designated as disabled parking. Illegally parking in a space reserved for individuals with disabilities is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $500 to $750 for the first offense. This fine increases with additional offenses up to $1,250 for five or more offenses. Additional offenses also include community service.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · ¶2
text: Texas law specifically states:

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · item 1
text: You may not park in a disabled parking space unless the vehicle has a disabled license plate or state issued removable windshield identification card.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · item 2
text: You may not use a disabled parking windshield identification card unless transporting the disabled person to whom it was issued.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · item 3
text: You may not lend your windshield identification card to someone else.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · item 4
text: You may not block an access or curb ramp.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · item 5
text: You may not make, sell, possess, or display a counterfeit disabled parking windshield identification card, or alter a disabled parking windshield identification card.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · ¶3
text: Certain municipalities also prohibit stopping or standing in a disabled parking space unless a disabled parking windshield identification card is visible or the vehicle has a disabled license plate.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · image
heading: Alt text: “Illustration in the handbook section “Disabled Parking” (no caption in the PDF)”
text: Illustration in the handbook section “Disabled Parking” (no caption in the PDF)

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Disabled Parking · ¶4
text: Do not park in striped areas adjacent to disabled parking spaces or in a striped area in front of an entrance to a business adjacent to a disabled parking space. Striped areas are for wheelchair lifts.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Unattended Motor Vehicle · ¶1
text: It is illegal for any driver to permit their car to stand idling unattended without turning off the engine, locking the ignition, removing the key from the ignition, and setting the brake; and when standing on any grade, without turning the front wheels to the curb or side of the road.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Unattended Motor Vehicle · ¶2
text: The requirements regarding turning off the engine, locking the ignition, and removing the key do not apply to a driver who starts the engine by using a remote starter or other similar device that remotely starts the engine without the key in the ignition. Before the vehicle can be operated, the key must be placed in the ignition or must be physically present in the vehicle.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · item 1
text: Choose a space large enough for your car to fit. Signal then stop even with the front of the car about two feet out from the space. To alert drivers who may be behind you be sure to signal before you pass the spot you want to parallel park in.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · item 2
text: Make sure you will not interfere with oncoming traffic then turn your front wheels all the way to the right and back slowly toward the curb.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · ¶1
text: Special Note:

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · ¶2
text: Special Note: On a roadway that allows two-way traffic, the driver must park with the vehicle‛s right-hand wheels within 18 inches of the right-hand curb or edge of the roadway.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · item 3
text: When your front seat is opposite the rear bumper of the car ahead, turn your steering wheel all the way to the left. Back slowly toward the car behind you without touching it. You should be about six inches from the curb. Do not park more than 18 inches from the curb or edge of the road.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · image

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · item 4
text: Straighten your front wheels and pull into the final parking position. Center your car in the space.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Leaving a Parking Space · ¶1
text: Use caution when leaving any parking space and check all of your mirrors to make sure nothing is obstructing your vehicle’s path, especially pedestrians or children. Children often play between parked cars. Look back before and while you’re backing up. Be sure to use your signal to notify other drivers you are leaving your current parking spot.

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Coasting · ¶1
text: It is illegal to coast on a downgrade with the gears or transmission in neutral.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · ¶1
text: Generally, you should drive at the same speed as the main stream of traffic and always be aware of how fast you are traveling. You must always obey the speed limit and you should consider these best practices below:

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · ¶2
text: Special Note: When the vehicle ahead of you passes a fixed object and you reach the same fixed object in less than two seconds, you are following too closely.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · item 1
text: You should keep a safe distance between your car and the one in front of you. The faster you drive, the greater the distance you should keep from the car ahead of you. For speeds 30 mph or less, the minimum time between your car and the one in front of you is 2 seconds with good road conditions. For speeds above 30 mph, maintain a 4 second gap between cars during good road conditions. During periods of poor road conditions, allow more time. Using a four-second following interval is the best practice for a beginning or less experienced driver.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · item 2
text: You should adjust your speed and following distance according to your physical condition and the conditions of the vehicle and road. If you are tired or not feeling well, do not drive. Never force yourself to drive.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · item 3
text: You should know when to slow down and increase the following distance.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · item 4
text: Slow down and increase the following distance when the road is wet. Many drivers find out too late what a small amount of rain can do. Roads become slippery when wet, making your car harder to control. Slow down and make sure you have complete control of the situation at all times.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · item 5
text: Slow down and increase the following distance when the road is crowded.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · item 6
text: Slow down and increase the following distance when your vision is limited. You should always be able to stop within the distance you can see ahead of your car. In the dark or in bad weather, do not over-drive your range of vision.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed Limits · ¶1
text: Drivers are required to obey posted minimum and maximum speed limits. These limits are designed to provide for the orderly flow of traffic under normal driving conditions. During periods of heavy traffic, bad weather, low visibility, or other poor driving conditions, you must adjust your speed and following distance to help avoid crashes.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed Limits · ¶2
text: The Speed Limits table shows the maximum speed limits for all vehicles under different conditions. Drivers must also be aware cities and counties have the authority to change these limits. Entities that establish or alter a speed limit must establish the same speed limit for daytime and nighttime.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed Limits · ¶3
text: The Texas Transportation Commission, regional mobility authorities and local governments have authority to raise or lower speed limits based on traffic studies and other statutory requirements. Many limited access highways have speed limits of 75 up to 85 mph. Always be aware of and observe the posted speed limit for the roadway on which you are driving.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · ¶1
text: If an emergency medical vehicle, law enforcement vehicle, fire truck, tow truck, utility service vehicle, Texas Department of Transportation vehicle (TxDOT, or other highway construction or maintenance vehicle) is stopped on the road with its lights activated (the lights are on or flashing), then the driver is required:

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · item 1
text: To reduce his/her speed to 20 mph below the speed limit; or

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · item 2
text: Move out of the lane closest to the emergency medical vehicle, law enforcement vehicle, fire truck, tow truck or a TxDOT vehicle if the road has multiple lanes traveling in the same direction.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · ¶2
text: There are other instances where it is important to be observant of vehicles stopped on the road. Mail, delivery, and trash-collection vehicles often make frequent stops in the roadway. Drivers must proceed with caution, and, if possible, change lanes before safely passing one of these vehicles on the road.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · ¶1
text: Street racing, also known as drag racing, is illegal and can result in serious injuries or fatalities. Illegal street racers put other drivers at risk because races are typically held on public roads. Due to the high speeds, drivers are unable to react to common road hazards or other driving situations, which often results in crashes.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · ¶2
text: Illegal street racing also causes unnecessary property damage, including extensive wear on roads (due to the high-powered engines damaging asphalt), which requires costly repairs at the expense to the tax-payer.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · ¶3
text: Please visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) https://www.nhtsa.gov/risky-driving/speeding for speed related fatalities.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · ¶4
text: A person may not participate in:

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · item 1
text: A race;

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · item 2
text: A vehicle speed competition or contest;

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · item 3
text: A drag race or acceleration contest;

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · item 4
text: A test of physical endurance of the operator of a vehicle; or

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · item 5
text: In connection with a drag race, an exhibition of vehicle speed or acceleration, or to make a speed record.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · ¶5
text: The criminal penalty for a conviction of Speed Racing ranges from a Class B misdemeanor to a second-degree felony.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Intro · ¶1
text: Driving at night is much more dangerous than driving during the day. Many people do not see as well at night. When taking a trip, it is safer to drive during daylight hours. Also, never drive when you are tired.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · ¶1
text: Slow down when driving at night and be sure you can stop within the distance lit by your headlights.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · ¶2
text: You must use your headlights beginning 30 minutes after sunset and ending 30 minutes before sunrise, or anytime when individuals or vehicles cannot be seen clearly for at least 1,000 feet.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · ¶3
text: Avoid looking directly into the headlights of approaching vehicles; shift your eyes down to the lower right side of your traffic lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · ¶4
text: Use your low beam headlights when:

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · item 1
text: Within 500 feet of an approaching vehicle

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · item 2
text: Following closely (within 300 feet) behind another vehicle

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · item 3
text: Driving on lighted roads

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · item 4
text: Driving in fog, heavy rain, sleet, snow, or dust

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Headlights · ¶5
text: If you must park on an unlighted highway at night, leave your parking lights or low beam headlights on.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving · ¶1
text: Freeways, toll-roads, throughways, turnpikes, and expressways are designed for maximum safety, but you must know how to use them properly. In Texas, a highway is defined as the width between the boundary lines of a publicly maintained way, any part of which is open to the public for vehicular travel.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Before Using a Highway · ¶1
text: Plan your trip in advance so you know your entrance, direction, and exit. Make sure you and your car are in good condition. If you cannot or do not want to drive at or above the minimum speed limit, do not use the highway.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Entering the Highway · item 1
text: You must yield the right-of-way to vehicles already on the highway.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Entering the Highway · item 2
text: Enter the speed change lane, stay to the right, signal left, and when it is clear, increase your speed to merge with the flow of traffic.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Entering the Highway · image
heading: Speed up when entering the freeway | Alt text: “Speed up when entering the freeway”
text: Speed up when entering the freeway

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Choose the Proper Lane · item 1
text: Use the right lane to drive at the minimum posted speed limit or below the normal flow of traffic.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Choose the Proper Lane · item 2
text: Use the middle or left lane if you are traveling faster than other traffic or passing other vehicles.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Choose the Proper Lane · item 3
text: If you plan to leave the freeway soon, change to the exit lane as soon as possible.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Observe Specific Instructions · ¶1
text: Observe specific instructions indicating the lane you should drive in.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Observe Specific Instructions · image

text: Metropolis · 56 · Newport · 24 EXIT 1 MILE · US · Utopia

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Once You are in the Proper Lane · item 1
text: Stay in the middle of your lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Once You are in the Proper Lane · item 2
text: Do not weave in and out of traffic.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Once You are in the Proper Lane · item 3
text: Maintain a constant speed. Keep pace with the traffic. Don’t speed up and slow down unnecessarily.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Once You are in the Proper Lane · item 4
text: Stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead of you. In bad weather, increase the time to at least four seconds. Watch the cars ahead of you. Be prepared if one of the cars ahead of you stops suddenly.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Once You are in the Proper Lane · item 5
text: Adjust your speed to allow others to enter the highway safely.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Once You are in the Proper Lane · item 6
text: Vehicles in any lane, except the right lane used for slower traffic, should be prepared to move to another lane to allow faster traffic to pass.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Leaving the Highway · item 1
text: Move into the proper lane well in advance of the exit. The greater the amount of traffic, the earlier you should move into the proper lane. Exit signs are usually placed at least 1,000 yards ahead of the exit.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Leaving the Highway · item 2
text: Slow down on the exit ramp so by the time you are off the highway, you are within the new, slower speed limit.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Fight Highway Hypnosis · ¶1
text: A condition of drowsiness or unawareness can be brought on by reduced activity and steady sounds of wind, engine, and tire hum. This is known as highway hypnosis. All drivers should be aware of its danger and of the methods for fighting it.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Fight Highway Hypnosis · item 1
text: Stop often. Even if you are feeling well, you should stop at least every two hours or every 100 miles. Get out of your car and walk around. Allow your muscles to relax.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Fight Highway Hypnosis · item 2
text: Do not drive more than eight hours per day.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Fight Highway Hypnosis · item 3
text: Keep shifting your eyes. Look at different objects; near and far, left and right. Read the road signs as you approach them. Check your rearview mirror.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Highway Safety Tips · item 1
text: Keep a window open so there is always fresh air in the car to help keep you alert and awake.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Highway Safety Tips · item 2
text: On bright days, wear good sunglasses. Never wear sunglasses at night.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Highway Safety Tips · item 3
text: Stay out of another driver’s blind spot. Traveling where the driver ahead of you cannot see your vehicle can be dangerous. Stay behind or go around the other vehicle. Do not follow to the side.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Highway Safety Tips · item 4
text: Avoid using a cell phone while driving; use may cause distraction and driver inattention. If you must use a cell phone, safely pull off the road or use a hands-free headset. If you are under 18 years of age, it is illegal to use a cell phone while driving even if it is a hands-free device except in the case of emergency.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Vehicle Breakdown · item 1
text: If you can’t get the car off the road, get everyone out of the car and off the road. Portable warning devices should be used to warn oncoming traffic.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Vehicle Breakdown · item 2
text: Move your car off the pavement to the side of the road. A car with a flat tire or blowout can be driven slowly off the road.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Vehicle Breakdown · item 3
text: Turn on your emergency warning lights. If you do not have warning lights, use your taillights. At night, in addition to your taillights and warning lights, turn the lights on inside of the car.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Vehicle Breakdown · item 4
text: Tie a white cloth to your radio antenna, door handle, or some other place where it may be easily seen. If you do not have a white cloth, raise your hood.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations · ¶1
text: There is one basic rule which applies in all driving situations, think before you act .

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Steering Out of a Skid · ¶1
text: An automobile skids when its tires lose their grip on the road surface. If the car starts to skid, follow these safety tips.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Steering Out of a Skid · item 1
text: Do not hit the brakes suddenly and hard. Take your foot off the gas pedal (accelerator).

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Steering Out of a Skid · item 2
text: Turn your steering wheel in the direction of the skid. As you recover control, gently straighten the wheels.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Steering Out of a Skid · item 3
text: Avoid a situation that could cause a skid by slowing down when the road and weather conditions are poor. Also, check your car’s tires. Old or worn tires that have minimal or damaged tread are dangerous. (In the illustration below, the direction of the skid is to the right.)

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Steering Out of a Skid · image
heading: Steering out of a skid · Turn steering wheel in direction of skid | Alt text: “Steering out of a skid · Turn steering wheel in direction of skid”
text: Steering out of a skid · Turn steering wheel in direction of skid

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Brake Failure · ¶1
text: If your car brakes fail, do not panic. Remember you can use your parking brake and shift to a lower gear. Apply your parking brake cautiously to keep from locking the brakes and throwing your car into a skid.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Running Off the Pavement · ¶1
text: If something causes you to swerve and run off the pavement:

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Running Off the Pavement · item 1
text: Do not hit the brakes suddenly and hard. Grip the steering wheel tightly and take your foot off the gas pedal.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Running Off the Pavement · item 2
text: Use your brakes carefully and do not swing back onto the pavement. Wait until your speed is reduced, check the traffic behind you, and then carefully drive back onto the pavement.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Flat Tire or Blowout · ¶1
text: If you have a flat tire or a blowout:

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Flat Tire or Blowout · item 1
text: Do not hit the brakes suddenly and hard

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Flat Tire or Blowout · item 2
text: Take your foot off the gas pedal and gently apply the brakes

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Flat Tire or Blowout · item 3
text: Steer straight ahead to a stop

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Controlling a Car in Special Situations › Driving Down a Steep Hill · ¶1
text: When driving down a steep hill, you can shift your car into a low gear to help slow your vehicle. Never coast in neutral or for cars with a standard transmission, never coast with your foot on the clutch.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Winter Driving · ¶1
text: Most drivers realize winter creates additional hazards, but many drivers don’t know what to do about it. Here are a few precautions you should follow during winter.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Winter Driving · row 1
text: Maintain a safe interval | Increase the distance from the vehicle ahead of you according to the conditions of the pavement. Many rear-end collisions occur on icy streets because drivers don’t leave space to stop. Snow tires will slide on ice or packed snow. To keep safe, you must keep your distance.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Winter Driving · row 2
text: Reduce speed to correspond with conditions | There is no such thing as a “safe” speed range at which you may drive on snow or ice. You must be extremely cautious until you are able to determine how much traction you can expect from your tires. Avoid locking of brakes on ice as it will cause a loss of steering and control. Every city block and every mile of highway may be different, depending upon sun or shade and the surface of the road.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Winter Driving · row 3
text: Keep windows clear | Remove snow and ice before you drive, even if you’re just driving a few miles. Make certain the windshield wipers and defroster are working properly.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Winter Driving · row 4
text: Watch for danger spots ahead | There may be ice on bridges when the rest of the pavement is clear. Snow melts more slowly in shady areas. Take precautions when approaching turns.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Winter Driving · row 5
text: Get a feel for the road | Start out very slowly. It is useless to burn the rubber off your tires by spinning the wheels. Test your brakes gently after the car is in motion to determine how much traction you have. Start slowing down before you come to a turn.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Winter Driving · row 6
text: Equip your vehicle with chains or snow tires | Chains are the most effective and should be used where ice and snow remain on the road. One word of caution, neither chains nor snow tires will permit you to drive on slick pavement at normal speeds so don’t get a false feeling of security.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Modern Roundabout · ¶1
text: A modern roundabout is a one-way, circular intersection where traffic flows counter clockwise around a center island. Modern roundabouts use yield signs rather than traffic lights to control vehicles entering the intersection. This intersection design only has eight potential conflict points, opposed to a traditional “four-way” signalized intersection which has 32 potential conflict points.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · ¶1
text: Road signs, pavement markings and its design help guide drivers through a modern roundabout.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · image
heading: Modern roundabouts reduce severe crashes at intersections by an average of 80%. | Alt text: “Modern roundabouts reduce severe crashes at intersections by an average of 80%.”
text: Modern roundabouts reduce severe crashes at intersections by an average of 80%.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · ¶2
text: To drive in a modern roundabout, follow these simple steps: slow down as you approach the intersection, yield to traffic already in the circle, enter the circle and follow the loop in a counter clockwise direction, and then make a right turn to exit the roundabout.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · ¶3
text: There are two types of modern roundabouts: single-lane roundabouts and multi-lane roundabouts.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · ¶4
text: Single-lane roundabout: Slow down as you approach the roundabout intersection and observe any posted advisory speed signs. Yield to traffic driving in the circle. When there is an acceptable gap, enter the circle and travel counterclockwise around the circle. Make a right turn by using your turn signal when exiting the circle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · ¶5
text: Observe traffic signs and pavement markings when navigating a roundabout. Also, look for bicyclists and pedestrians using the crosswalks on the roundabout approaches and exits.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · ¶6
text: Multi-lane roundabouts: Go through the same steps as a single-lane roundabout and follow these additional steps. When approaching a multi-lane roundabout, observe the advance lane movement sign for choosing the correct entry lane. Also, do not change lanes while driving in the circle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Roundabouts › Driving in a Modern Roundabout · ¶7
text: When navigating all roundabouts, give space for large vehicles, such as semitrailers, buses, and fire trucks that need more than one lane when driving around the circle. Also, pull over for emergency vehicles on the roundabout approaches and exits. However, do not stop for emergency vehicles in the roundabout circle. Clear the circle first and then pull over for the emergency vehicle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · ¶1
text: Floods are one of the most common hazards in the U.S. Nearly half of all flash flood fatalities are vehicle-related.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · ¶2
text: These are the facts:

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · item 1
text: Six inches of water will reach the bottom of most passenger cars, causing loss of control and possible stalling.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · item 2
text: Twelve inches of water will float many cars.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · item 3
text: Two feet of rushing water will carry away pick-up trucks, SUVs, and most other vehicles.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · item 4
text: Water across a road may hide a missing segment of roadbed or a missing bridge. Roads weaken under floodwater and drivers should proceed cautiously after waters have receded since the road may collapse under the vehicle’s weight.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · ¶3
text: National Weather Service and Texas Division of Emergency Management officials say if your vehicle stalls in floodwater, get out quickly and move to higher ground. Better yet, when there’s water on the road, Turn Around Don’t Drown®. Saving your life is as simple as choosing an alternate route.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Floods · ¶4
text: Turn Around Don’t Drown® (Note: Per National Weather Service any use of Turn Around Don’t Drown must include the registration symbol.)
