locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) · ¶1
text: Whether you are sharing the road with a passenger car, motorcycle, truck, bus, or other vehicle, it is important to obey traffic laws, abide by the rules of the road, and drive defensively. Trucks are designed to carry products to and from towns and cities; they are designed to be as maneuverable as cars. Trucks have longer stopping and accelerating distances, a wider turning radius, and weigh more.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 1
text: When passing a truck, first check to your front and rear, check mirrors and blind spots, then move into the passing lane only if it is clear and you are in a legal passing zone. Let the truck driver know you are passing by flashing your headlights, especially at night. The truck driver should make it easier for you to pass by staying to the far side of the lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 2
text: On a level highway, it takes three to five seconds longer to pass a truck than a car. On an upgrade, a truck often loses speed so it’s easier to pass than a car. On a downgrade, the truck’s momentum causes the truck to go faster so you may need to increase your speed. Complete your pass as quickly as possible and don’t stay alongside the other vehicle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 3
text: If the driver flashes the truck’s lights after you pass, it’s a signal that it is clear for you to pull back in front of the truck. Be sure to move back only when you can see the entire front of the truck in your rearview mirror. After you pass a truck, maintain your speed.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 4
text: When a truck passes you, help the truck driver by keeping to the far side of your lane. You’ll make it easier for the truck driver if you slightly reduce your speed. Don’t speed up while the truck is passing. After passing, the truck driver should signal to let you know he is returning to your lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 5
text: When you meet a truck coming from the opposite direction, keep as far to the side as possible to avoid a sideswipe crash and to reduce the wind turbulence between the two vehicles. Remember, turbulence pushes vehicles apart; it does not pull them together.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Following a Truck · item 1
text: Tractor-trailers take longer to stop than a car traveling at the same speed. The average passenger car traveling at 55 mph can stop in approximately 240 feet, which is about three-fourths the length of a football field. A fully loaded tractor-trailer may take more than 400 feet to completely stop, well over the length of a football field.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Following a Truck · item 2
text: If you’re following a truck, stay out of its blind spot at the rear. The blind spot is the area behind the truck that the driver cannot see in his rearview mirrors. Avoid following too closely, and position your vehicle so the truck driver can see your vehicle in the truck’s side view mirror. An excellent rule of thumb for motorists sharing the road with a tractor-trailer is, “If you can’t see the truck driver in his side mirror, he can’t see you.” By avoiding the truck driver’s blind spot, you will have a good view of the road ahead, and the truck driver can give you plenty of warning for a stop or a turn. This will allow you more time to react and make a safe stop.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Following a Truck · item 3
text: When you follow a truck at night always dim your headlights. Bright lights from a vehicle behind will blind the truck driver when the lights reflect off the truck’s large side mirrors.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Following a Truck · item 4
text: If you are stopped behind a truck on an upgrade, leave space in case the truck drifts back when it starts to move. Also, keep to the left in your lane so the driver can see you’re stopped behind the truck.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Right Turns · ¶1
text: Pay attention to turn signals. Trucks make wide, right turns and sometimes leave an open space to the right just before the turn. To avoid a crash, don’t pass a truck on the right if there is a possibility the truck might make a right turn.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Backing Crashes · ¶1
text: Never cross behind a truck preparing to back up. When a truck driver is preparing to back the truck from a road into a loading area, the road is temporarily blocked. Wait for the truck to complete its maneuver before trying to pass. If you pass too closely behind the truck, a crash may occur because you are in the truck’s blind spot.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Maneuverability · ¶1
text: On multi-lane highways, tractor-trailers stay in the center lane to help the flow of local traffic on and off the highway. Staying in the center lane also increases the truck driver’s options if he/she has to switch lanes to avoid a crash. Be aware of common mistakes drivers should avoid when driving around trucks and buses.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Cutting Off a Vehicle to Reach Your Exit or Turn · ¶1
text: Never cut in front of a truck. Cutting into the open space in front of a truck or bus removes the driver’s cushion of safety. Trying to beat a truck to a single-lane construction zone represents a particularly dangerous situation. Either slow down and exit or stay behind the truck.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Never Underestimate the Size and Speed of an Approaching Tractor-trailer · ¶1
text: Because of its large size, a tractor-trailer often appears to be traveling at a slower speed than it is. A substantial number of car and truck collisions take place at intersections because the driver of the car does not realize how close the truck is or how quickly it is approaching.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles · ¶1
text: Individuals who operate a motorcycle have the same rights and privileges as any other vehicle on the road.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles · ¶2
text: For various reasons, drivers may not see the motorcyclist, and approximately one-half of all motorcycle crashes involve another vehicle. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, motorcyclists are about 35 times more likely to die in a traffic crash than passenger car occupants. A few of the most common reasons are provided below.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles · item 1
text: Many drivers tend to look for other cars, not for motorcyclists.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles · item 2
text: The profile of a motorcycle is much smaller than the profile of a car, making an approaching motorcyclist harder to see.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles · item 3
text: Estimating the distance and speed of a motorcycle is more difficult than it is for a car.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles · item 4
text: Motorcycle riding requires frequent lane movements to adjust to changing road conditions.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles · item 5
text: Distracted driving, such as texting or talking on a cell phone.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Situations When Crashes Are Most Likely to Occur · ¶1
text: Motorcycle crashes are most likely to occur in the high-risk situations described below.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Situations When Crashes Are Most Likely to Occur › Left Turns · ¶1
text: The most common crash between cars and motorcycles is at an intersection when the driver of a car is making a left turn in front of a motorcycle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Situations When Crashes Are Most Likely to Occur › A Car’s Blind Spot · ¶1
text: Motorcyclists are often hidden in a vehicle’s blind spot or missed in a quick look due to their smaller size. Always make a visual check for motorcycles by checking mirrors and blind spots before entering or leaving a lane of traffic and at intersections.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Situations When Crashes Are Most Likely to Occur › A Car’s Blind Spot · image
heading: Alt text: “Illustration in the handbook section “A Car’s Blind Spot” (no caption in the PDF)”

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Situations When Crashes Are Most Likely to Occur › Hazardous Road Conditions · ¶1
text: Road conditions that are a minor annoyance to you may pose a major hazard to motorcyclists. Motorcyclists may suddenly change speed or adjust their position within a lane in reaction to changes in the weather, road, or traffic conditions. This may include potholes, gravel, railroad crossings, and wet or slippery surfaces which impair the motorcyclists’ braking and handling abilities. Expect and allow room for such actions by the motorcyclist.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Situations When Crashes Are Most Likely to Occur › Strong Winds · ¶1
text: A strong gust of wind can move a motorcycle across an entire lane if the rider isn’t prepared for it. Wind gusts from large trucks in the other lane can also be a hazard.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Situations When Crashes Are Most Likely to Occur › Large Vehicles · ¶1
text: A large vehicle such as a van, bus, or truck can block a motorcycle from a driver’s view and the motorcyclist may seem to suddenly appear from nowhere.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Motorcycle Driving Awareness › Look Out for Motorcyclists · ¶1
text: Although you may not see any cars, be aware there may be a motorcycle. Be careful at intersections, and always take a second look for a motorcycle before turning at an intersection, particularly when making left turns.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Motorcycle Driving Awareness › Signal Your Intentions · ¶1
text: Always signal before changing lanes or merging with traffic. This allows the motorcyclist to anticipate traffic flow and find a safe lane position. Signal even if you don’t see cars or motorcycles. Be careful when making left turns across lanes of approaching traffic. Look carefully in all directions for approaching motorcyclists. Don’t be fooled by a flashing turn signal. Motorcycle signals usually are not self-canceling and riders sometimes forget to turn them off. Wait to be sure the motorcycle is going to turn before you proceed.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Motorcycle Driving Awareness › Respect a Motorcycle · ¶1
text: Allow the motorcyclist a full lane width. Although it may seem as though there is enough room in the traffic lane for an automobile and a motorcycle, the motorcycle is entitled to a full lane and may need the room to maneuver safely. Do not attempt to share the lane with a motorcycle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Motorcycle Driving Awareness › Allow Plenty of Space When Following a Motorcycle · ¶1
text: The slightest contact can mean a spill or injury for the rider. Allow more following distance, at least four to six seconds, when following a motorcycle so the motorcyclist has enough time to maneuver or stop in an emergency. Stop a safe distance behind the motorcyclist at intersections, signals, or crossings. A full vehicle length is recommended to help prevent impact with the motorcycle should your vehicle suffer a rear end collision. In dry conditions, motorcycles can stop more quickly than a car, so being aware and alert at all times can help prevent a collision.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Motorcycle Driving Awareness › Allow Plenty of Space When Following a Motorcycle · ¶2
text: Special Note: If you drive aware of motorcyclists in these situations, you can help make the streets and roads safer for everyone.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Motorcycle Driving Awareness › Texas Motorcycle Operator Training Program · ¶1
text: The Texas Legislature created the Motorcycle Operator Training and Safety program in 1983 and moved its administration from DPS to TDLR in 2020. The Program’s aim is to improve rider skills and reduce the number and severity of motorcycle crashes in Texas. A portion of each motorcycle license fee is used to support this program. The program develops curriculum and monitors motorcycle training classes throughout the state and promotes motorcycle safety and awareness through campaigns, exhibits, and materials.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Motorcycles › Motorcycle Driving Awareness › Texas Motorcycle Operator Training Program · ¶2
text: Contact TDLR at https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/ for more information about motorcycle safety and training courses.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Light Rail · ¶1
text: In recent years, light rail has been established in many major cities in Texas. As you travel these areas, you may notice these trains move along the streets just like other vehicles. Light rail is very quiet; and, in fact, quieter than most buses and cars. So whether you are riding a light rail or just walking or driving near the train or tracks, it’s important to stay alert and observe the safety rules.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Light Rail · row 1
text: Stop | - Don’t walk in front of, between, or behind a train. - Trains can’t start or stop quickly regardless of traffic flow. - Do not drive, stop, or park your vehicle on the tracks. It’s dangerous and illegal.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Light Rail · row 2
text: Look | - Cross the tracks only at designated crossings and only when it is safe. - Look both ways before crossing the tracks. Trains travel in both directions. - Obey all warning signs, flashing lights, signals, and crossing gates. A law enforcement officer will issue tickets to violators.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Light Rail · row 3
text: Listen | - Stay alert. Light rail is quieter than a bus or most cars. You may not hear a light rail coming. - Listen for train horns and signal bells. - Always follow instructions from a law enforcement officer.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Light Rail · row 4
text: Don’t | - Never race a train, run in front of a train, or put anything on or near the tracks. - Never try to beat the train to a crossing. Even in a tie, you lose. - Never drive around crossing gate arms.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles · ¶1
text: A bicycle is a vehicle. Any person riding a bicycle has all of the rights and responsibilities as a driver of a vehicle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 1
text: Bicyclists are not restricted to the right lane of traffic. One-way, multi-lane streets are one example of this. Another instance is when the bicyclist is changing lanes to make a left turn. The bicyclists should follow the same path any other vehicle would take traveling in the same direction.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 2
text: A motorist should merge with bicycle traffic when preparing for a right turn. Avoid turning directly across the path of bicycle traffic.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 3
text: Bicyclists are required to ride as far to the right in the lane as possible only when the lane can be shared safely by a car and a bicycle, side-by-side. Even then, there are certain conditions that allow a bicyclist to take the full lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 4
text: The bicyclist is overtaking and passing another, vehicle proceeding in the same direction.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 5
text: The bicyclist is preparing for a left turn at an intersection or onto a private road or driveway.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 6
text: There are unsafe conditions in the road, such as fixed or moving objects, parked or moving vehicles, pedestrians, animals, potholes, or debris.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 7
text: The lane is of substandard width, making it unsafe for a car and a bicycle to safely share the lane side-by-side. When this is the case, it is best for the cyclist to take the full lane, whether riding single file or two abreast.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Car-Bicycle Crashes · ¶1
text: Be on the lookout for cyclists on the road, especially at intersections. The most common car-bicycle crashes caused by a motorist are:

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Car-Bicycle Crashes · item 1
text: A motorist turns left in front of oncoming bicycle traffic. Oncoming bicycle traffic is often overlooked or its speed misjudged.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Car-Bicycle Crashes · item 2
text: A motorist turns right across the path of the bicycle. The motorist should slow down and merge with the bicycle traffic for a safe right turn.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Car-Bicycle Crashes · item 3
text: A motorist pulls away from a stop sign and fails to yield the right-of-way to bicycle cross traffic. At intersections, the right-of-way rules apply equally to motor vehicles and bicycles.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · ¶1
text: Whenever you are driving a vehicle and your attention is not on the road, you’re putting yourself, your passengers, other vehicles, and pedestrians in danger. Distracted driving can result when you perform any activity that may shift your full attention from the driving task. Taking your eyes off the road or hands off the steering wheel presents obvious driving risks. Mental activities that take your mind away from driving are just as dangerous. Your eyes can gaze at objects in the driving scene but fail to see them because your attention is distracted elsewhere.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · ¶2
text: Activities that can distract your attention include texting, talking to passengers, adjusting the radio, CD player or climate controls; eating, drinking or smoking; reading maps or other literature; picking up something that fell; reading billboards and other road advertisements; watching other people and vehicles including aggressive drivers; talking and/or texting on a cell phone or CB radio; using telematics devices (such as navigation systems, pagers, etc.); daydreaming or being occupied with other mental distractions.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · ¶3
text: If drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions, crashes double. Some tips to follow so you won’t become distracted:

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 1
text: Review and be totally familiar with all safety and usage features on any in-vehicle electronics, including your wireless device or cell phone, before you drive.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 2
text: Pre-program radio stations.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 3
text: Pre-load your favorite CDs or cassette tapes.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 4
text: Clear the vehicle of any unnecessary objects.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 5
text: Review maps and plan your route before you begin driving.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 6
text: Adjust all mirrors for the best all-round visibility before you start your trip.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 7
text: Do not attempt to read, text, or write while you drive.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 8
text: Avoid smoking, eating and drinking while you drive.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 9
text: Don’t engage in complex or emotionally intense conversations with other occupants.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · ¶4
text: You need to be able to recognize other drivers who are engaged in any form of driving distraction. Not recognizing other distracted drivers can prevent you from perceiving or reacting correctly in time to prevent a crash. Watch for:

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 10
text: Vehicles that may drift over the lane divider lines or within their own lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 11
text: Vehicles traveling at inconsistent speeds.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 12
text: Drivers who are preoccupied with maps, food, cigarettes, cell phones, or other objects.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · item 13
text: Drivers who appear to be involved in conversations with their passengers.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · ¶5
text: Give a distracted driver plenty of room and maintain your safe following distance.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · ¶6
text: Be very careful when passing a driver who seems to be distracted. The other driver may not be aware of your presence, and they may drift in front of you.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Texting While Driving · ¶1
text: It is against the law to read, write, or send messages on a cell phone or other portable wireless device. If your cell phone rings, do not answer the call or respond to the text message. Convictions for violations of this law are subject to fines.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Texting While Driving · ¶2
text: You may use a cell phone to contact law enforcement or during an emergency. If you must make a call, pull safely off the road and make the call. Try to keep the conversation short, or have a passenger make the call for you, if possible.

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › Introduction · ¶1
text: The Texas Department of Public Safety, Driver License Division, is committed to creating a faster, easier, and friendlier driver license experience and a safer Texas. One step toward achieving these important goals is to continuously improve the Texas Driver Handbook by providing you with accurate information on traffic laws, clear images of road signs, examples of common driving situations, and general safety tips. We have also included special tips to emphasize important information you need to know.

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › Introduction · ¶2
text: Although the Texas Driver Handbook has been revised, its primary purpose remains the same: 1) to help you qualify for a Texas driver license, and 2) to help you become a safer driver.

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › Introduction · ¶3
text: The information contained in this handbook is not an official legal reference to Texas traffic laws. The information provided is only intended to explain applicable federal and state laws you need to understand in order to successfully operate a motor vehicle in Texas. If you would like to know the actual language of any traffic or criminal laws referenced in this handbook, please refer to the Texas Transportation Code and Texas Penal Code.

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › Introduction · ¶4
text: Once you receive your Texas driver license, keep this handbook as a reference on traffic safety and update it as needed. The Texas Legislature meets every two years and regularly makes changes to traffic laws. For the most current information on driver licensing, visit our website at http://www.dps.texas.gov/DriverLicense/ .

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › Contact Us · ¶1
text: Please contact us if you have any questions regarding this handbook or if you need additional information.

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › ADA Accommodations · ¶6
text: Dear Texas Resident:

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › ADA Accommodations · ¶7
text: Operating a motor vehicle is an important privilege and responsibility for drivers, especially in a state as large as Texas with more than 314,000 miles of public roadways. Tragically, every year in Texas, approximately 3,500 people are killed in traffic crashes and more than 15,000 are seriously injured. Today, more than ever, drivers must avoid distractions in their own vehicle while also staying alert for impaired or unsafe drivers sharing the roadway – failing to do so could have tragic consequences.

locator: Texas Driver Handbook › ADA Accommodations · ¶8
text: The goal of the Texas Department of Public Safety is to provide you with critical safety information about driving in Texas in an effort to keep you, your passengers and other travelers safe on our roadways. Please carefully review and learn the information in this handbook, and always be mindful of the great responsibility that goes with obtaining a driver license and operating a motor vehicle in Texas.

locator: Chapter 1: Your License to Drive › Suspensions and Revocations › Mandatory Suspension · ¶1
text: Convictions for the following offenses will result in the automatic suspension of your license and driving privilege. For minors, see the Suspensions and Revocations (Under 21) section in this chapter.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · ¶1
text: You must yield the right-of-way to school buses. Always drive with care when you are near a school bus. If you approach a school bus from either direction and the bus is displaying alternately flashing red lights, you must stop. Do not pass the school bus until:

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · ¶1
text: If an emergency medical vehicle, law enforcement vehicle, fire truck, tow truck, utility service vehicle, Texas Department of Transportation vehicle (TxDOT, or other highway construction or maintenance vehicle) is stopped on the road with its lights activated (the lights are on or flashing), then the driver is required:

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · item 1
text: To reduce his/her speed to 20 mph below the speed limit; or

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · item 2
text: Move out of the lane closest to the emergency medical vehicle, law enforcement vehicle, fire truck, tow truck or a TxDOT vehicle if the road has multiple lanes traveling in the same direction.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Slow Down or Move Over · ¶2
text: There are other instances where it is important to be observant of vehicles stopped on the road. Mail, delivery, and trash-collection vehicles often make frequent stops in the roadway. Drivers must proceed with caution, and, if possible, change lanes before safely passing one of these vehicles on the road.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · ¶4
text: A person may not participate in:

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · item 1
text: A race;

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Street Racing · ¶5
text: The criminal penalty for a conviction of Speed Racing ranges from a Class B misdemeanor to a second-degree felony.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Choose the Proper Lane · item 1
text: Use the right lane to drive at the minimum posted speed limit or below the normal flow of traffic.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Choose the Proper Lane · item 2
text: Use the middle or left lane if you are traveling faster than other traffic or passing other vehicles.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Driving on the Highway › Once You are in the Proper Lane · item 6
text: Vehicles in any lane, except the right lane used for slower traffic, should be prepared to move to another lane to allow faster traffic to pass.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · item 1
text: The school bus has resumed motion;

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Highway Driving › Highway Safety Tips · item 3
text: Stay out of another driver’s blind spot. Traveling where the driver ahead of you cannot see your vehicle can be dangerous. Stay behind or go around the other vehicle. Do not follow to the side.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 1
text: When passing a truck, first check to your front and rear, check mirrors and blind spots, then move into the passing lane only if it is clear and you are in a legal passing zone. Let the truck driver know you are passing by flashing your headlights, especially at night. The truck driver should make it easier for you to pass by staying to the far side of the lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 2
text: On a level highway, it takes three to five seconds longer to pass a truck than a car. On an upgrade, a truck often loses speed so it’s easier to pass than a car. On a downgrade, the truck’s momentum causes the truck to go faster so you may need to increase your speed. Complete your pass as quickly as possible and don’t stay alongside the other vehicle.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 3
text: If the driver flashes the truck’s lights after you pass, it’s a signal that it is clear for you to pull back in front of the truck. Be sure to move back only when you can see the entire front of the truck in your rearview mirror. After you pass a truck, maintain your speed.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 4
text: When a truck passes you, help the truck driver by keeping to the far side of your lane. You’ll make it easier for the truck driver if you slightly reduce your speed. Don’t speed up while the truck is passing. After passing, the truck driver should signal to let you know he is returning to your lane.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Passing · item 5
text: When you meet a truck coming from the opposite direction, keep as far to the side as possible to avoid a sideswipe crash and to reduce the wind turbulence between the two vehicles. Remember, turbulence pushes vehicles apart; it does not pull them together.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Right Turns · ¶1
text: Pay attention to turn signals. Trucks make wide, right turns and sometimes leave an open space to the right just before the turn. To avoid a crash, don’t pass a truck on the right if there is a possibility the truck might make a right turn.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Backing Crashes · ¶1
text: Never cross behind a truck preparing to back up. When a truck driver is preparing to back the truck from a road into a loading area, the road is temporarily blocked. Wait for the truck to complete its maneuver before trying to pass. If you pass too closely behind the truck, a crash may occur because you are in the truck’s blind spot.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Trucks (Large trucks and truck-tractor combinations) › Cutting Off a Vehicle to Reach Your Exit or Turn · ¶1
text: Never cut in front of a truck. Cutting into the open space in front of a truck or bus removes the driver’s cushion of safety. Trying to beat a truck to a single-lane construction zone represents a particularly dangerous situation. Either slow down and exit or stay behind the truck.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 3
text: Bicyclists are required to ride as far to the right in the lane as possible only when the lane can be shared safely by a car and a bicycle, side-by-side. Even then, there are certain conditions that allow a bicyclist to take the full lane.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to School Buses · item 2
text: You are signaled by the driver to proceed; or

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 4
text: The bicyclist is overtaking and passing another, vehicle proceeding in the same direction.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 5
text: The bicyclist is preparing for a left turn at an intersection or onto a private road or driveway.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 6
text: There are unsafe conditions in the road, such as fixed or moving objects, parked or moving vehicles, pedestrians, animals, potholes, or debris.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Share the Road with Bicycles › Rules for Motorists and Bicyclists · item 7
text: The lane is of substandard width, making it unsafe for a car and a bicycle to safely share the lane side-by-side. When this is the case, it is best for the cyclist to take the full lane, whether riding single file or two abreast.

locator: Chapter 9: Some Special Driving Situations › Distracted driving · ¶6
text: Be very careful when passing a driver who seems to be distracted. The other driver may not be aware of your presence, and they may drift in front of you.

locator: Chapter 13: Bicycle Laws and Safety › Bicycle Traffic Laws › Do’s · item 11
text: A person operating a bicycle who is moving slower than the other traffic on the road shall ride as near as possible to the right curb or edge of the road unless:

locator: Chapter 13: Bicycle Laws and Safety › Bicycle Traffic Laws › Do’s · item 12
text: The person is overtaking and passing another vehicle proceeding in the same direction

locator: Chapter 13: Bicycle Laws and Safety › Bicycle Traffic Laws › Do’s · item 13
text: The person is preparing for a left turn at an intersection or onto a private road or driveway

locator: Chapter 13: Bicycle Laws and Safety › Bicycle Traffic Laws › Do’s · item 14
text: There are unsafe conditions in the road such as fixed or moving objects, parked or moving vehicles, pedestrians, animals, potholes, or debris, or

locator: Chapter 13: Bicycle Laws and Safety › Bicycle Traffic Laws › Do’s · item 15
text: The person is operating a bicycle in an outside lane that is: Less than 14 feet in width and doesn’t have a designated bicycle lane adjacent to that lane; or The lane is too narrow for a bicycle and a motor vehicle to safely travel side by side.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Pavement Markings › Solid Lines · ¶1
text: Solid white lines are used for pavement edge lines, shoulder markings, channelizing, transitions, and lane use control. Crossing a solid white line should be avoided if possible. The solid yellow line on the left edge of the road is a guide for drivers to indicate driving to the left of the yellow line is prohibited. This type of yellow line can be found on interstate highways.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Pavement Markings › Solid Lines · ¶2
text: Crossing is prohibited where there is a pavement marking of double solid white lines.

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Obey Warning Signs and Barricades · ¶1

locator: Chapter 5: Signals, Signs, and Markers › Obey Warning Signs and Barricades · ¶2
text: The offense is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $1 to $200. Fines double in a construction or maintenance work zone when workers are present anywhere in the construction zone.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · ¶1
text: It is not always safe to pass. Be patient and wait until the time is right. Crashes resulting from improper passing often result in head on crashes and can be deadly.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 1
text: Make certain the way is clear.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 2
text: Give the proper signal before changing lanes.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 3
text: Tap your horn when necessary to avoid surprising the driver ahead.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Basic Safety Rules When You Are Passing · item 4
text: Avoid cutting in too quickly if you must return to your original lane.

locator: Chapter 4: Right-of-Way › Yield Right-of-Way to Emergency Vehicles · item 6
text: Slow to a speed less than 5 mph when the posted speed limit is less than 25 mph.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 1
text: Keep enough distance between you and the car in front of you so you can see ahead clearly. Check the rearview mirror, your side mirrors, and look over your shoulder in your blind spot to make sure the roadway is clear and no other vehicles are passing you. Turn on your left turn signal to alert any drivers behind you.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 2
text: Check well ahead for signs and pavement markings for no passing zones, and always check for oncoming traffic in the left lane. Be sure you have enough time and space to overtake the car ahead and return to the right lane before an approaching car comes within 200 feet of you.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 3
text: Tap your horn when necessary to alert the driver ahead.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 4
text: Pass on the left and do not return to the right lane until you have safely cleared the overtaken vehicle. Wait until you can see the car you have just passed in your rearview mirror before returning to the right lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · item 5
text: Turn on your right turn signal and return to the right lane. Be sure to turn your signal off after you have completed the lane change.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › How to Pass on a Two-Lane Road · image
text: Diagram: a car passes another car on a two-lane road, moving into the left lane and back to the right lane

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · ¶1
text: In Texas, you can pass on the right only when conditions permit you to do so safely.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · item 1
text: The road is clear of parked vehicles or other lane obstructions and is wide enough for two or more lanes in each direction.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · item 2
text: You are on a one-way road.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · item 3
text: You may pass on a paved shoulder when the vehicle you are passing is slowing or stopped on the main traveled portion of the highway, disabled, or preparing to make a left turn.

text: Stop · SCHOOL BUS

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Passing on the Right · ¶2
text: Do not pass on the right by driving off the paved portion of the highway.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 1
text: Do not increase your speed.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 2
text: Stay in your lane.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 3
text: Safely move as far to the right as you can when being passed on the left and the lanes are not marked.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › When Another Vehicle is Passing · item 4
text: Make it as safe and easy as possible for the other driver to pass you.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Blind Spot Driving · ¶1
text: When you are passing, do not drive or linger in the other driver’s blind spot. Either pass the other driver or slow down so you are not in another driver’s blind spot. It is likely the other driver cannot see you if you are in or near their blind spot.

locator: Chapter 6: Signaling, Passing, and Turning › Passing › Blind Spot Driving · image
text: Blind Spot

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parking, Stopping, or Standing on a Highway Outside an Urban Area · item 1
text: Leave plenty of room for others to pass

locator: Chapter 7: Parking, Stopping, or Standing › Do Not Park a Vehicle › Parallel Parking · item 1
text: Choose a space large enough for your car to fit. Signal then stop even with the front of the car about two feet out from the space. To alert drivers who may be behind you be sure to signal before you pass the spot you want to parallel park in.

locator: Chapter 8: Speed and Speed Limits › Speed · ¶2
text: Special Note: When the vehicle ahead of you passes a fixed object and you reach the same fixed object in less than two seconds, you are following too closely.
